A UI library, its runtime, and the framework built on top of it

React, from the JavaScript up

Starting where most people actually start — knowing some JavaScript and wondering what React is for — and ending with an app deployed on Next.js. The bridge from the language to the library — closures, immutability, async, and the JavaScript toolkit React code leans on: promises built from scratch, error handling, debounce, throttle and rate limiting. Every fundamental, with the semantics that bite rather than the tour. What React genuinely does underneath: elements, reconciliation, fiber, render and commit, hooks as a linked list, concurrent scheduling. Everything new in React 19 and what it replaced. Then Next.js in full: the App Router, the server/client boundary, the caching model that confuses everybody, and the rendering strategies. Plus interview chapters and a bank of 563 questions with written answers.

00

What React actually is

Before anything else: React is a library for describing what the UI should look like for a given state, and a runtime that works out how to make the real DOM match that description. Everything else — hooks, fiber, server components, Next.js — is machinery in service of that one sentence.

01 · You write
A descriptioncomponents returning elements
02 · React calls
Renderrun the functions, build a tree
03 · React diffs
Reconcileold tree vs new tree
04 · React applies
Committhe minimum DOM changes
05 · Browser
Paintthe user sees it

The one idea

UI = f(state) You do not write "when the count changes, find the span and update its text". You write "the span contains the count" — and when the count changes, React works out that the span's text must change. imperative declarative ───────────────────────────── ──────────────────────────── const el = document.querySelector function Counter({ count }) { ('#count'); return <span>{count}</span>; el.textContent = count; } if (count > 9) el.classList .add('warn'); React figures out the rest. else el.classList.remove('warn'); The imperative version is not wrong. It is that you have to write the transition for every pair of states — and the number of pairs grows as the square of the number of states. That is the bug factory React was built to close.

What React is not

NotBecause
A frameworkNo router, no data layer, no build system, no opinion about folder structure. That gap is exactly what Next.js fills
Fast because of the virtual DOMDiffing two trees is work. React is fast because it batches and minimises DOM writes, and because you rarely hand-optimise it wrong. A careful imperative implementation beats it
A template languageJSX compiles to ordinary function calls. There is no template runtime, and everything is JavaScript
Only for single-page appsServer Components and streaming SSR mean a React page can ship almost no JavaScript at all
SimpleThe mental model is small. The runtime — fiber, lanes, hydration, the server boundary — is not, and Part III is about that

How to read this book

  1. Part I is the bridge. If you know JavaScript but React feels arbitrary, start here — it explains what each React idea replaces.
  2. Part II is the fundamentals, with the semantics people get wrong: state as a snapshot, why keys matter, what an effect is actually for.
  3. Part III is the runtime. Reading it is what turns “React re-rendered” from a mystery into a mechanism, and it is what senior interviews are about.
  4. Part IV is React 19 — Actions, use(), Server Components — and what each one replaced.
  5. Part V is Next.js, including the honest version of “React vs Next.js”.
  6. Part VI is TypeScript from the basics to end-to-end type safety — why it, JS vs TS, generics, narrowing, the utility types, and a TypeScript interview chapter.
  7. Part VII builds twelve things end to end — the three utility hooks, infinite scroll and virtualization, a sortable table, a checkout wizard, a Kanban board, a file tree, a dialog, an OTP field, tabs and a carousel.
  8. Part VIII is interviews: the understanding-level questions, with the answers written out.
A note on versions

This book is written against React 19.x and the Next.js App Router (15.x and later). React moves slowly and carefully — most of Parts I–III has been true since 2019 and will still be true in five years. Parts IV and V move faster: Server Components, the caching defaults and the compiler have all changed meaningfully within the last two years, so where something is new or in flux the text says so, and you should check the release notes rather than trusting a book's date stamp.

Interview follow-up

“What problem does React solve?” Not “it makes UIs fast” — that is both wrong and the answer everyone gives. It removes the need to write state transitions. In imperative UI code you describe how to get from every state to every other state, and the number of those transitions grows quadratically, which is where the bugs live. React lets you describe only the end state for any given data, and takes responsibility for the transition. Everything else about the library — the diffing, the batching, the hooks — exists to make that trade affordable.

J01

The problem React solves

Nobody adopts a library because it is elegant. React won because a specific kind of code — UI that changes over time — was genuinely miserable to write by hand, in a way that got worse as the app grew. This chapter shows that misery concretely, because every React concept is an answer to some part of it.

Build it by hand first

javascript · a filterable todo list, imperatively
// A todo list with a filter and a count. About as small as a real
// feature gets, and already unpleasant.
let todos = [];
let filter = 'all';

const list   = document.querySelector('#list');
const count  = document.querySelector('#count');
const input  = document.querySelector('#new');
const empty  = document.querySelector('#empty');

function addTodo(text) {
  todos.push({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), text, done: false });
  // Now every part of the UI that depends on `todos` must be updated,
  // BY HAND, and you have to remember all of them.
  renderList();
  renderCount();
  renderEmptyState();
  input.value = '';
}

function toggleTodo(id) {
  const t = todos.find(t => t.id === id);
  t.done = !t.done;
  // Which parts change now? The item's class, the count, and — if the
  // filter is 'active' — whether the item is visible at all.
  document.querySelector(`[data-id="${id}"]`).classList.toggle('done', t.done);
  renderCount();
  if (filter !== 'all') renderList();      // easy to forget
  renderEmptyState();                      // easier to forget
}

function setFilter(next) {
  filter = next;
  document.querySelectorAll('.filter').forEach(b =>
    b.classList.toggle('active', b.dataset.filter === next));
  renderList();
  renderEmptyState();
  // renderCount()? Depends whether the count means "all" or "visible".
  // The answer is not in the code, it is in someone's head.
}

function renderList() {
  const visible = todos.filter(t =>
    filter === 'all' ? true : filter === 'done' ? t.done : !t.done);

  // The blunt approach: throw it all away and rebuild.
  list.innerHTML = '';
  for (const t of visible) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.dataset.id = t.id;
    li.className = t.done ? 'done' : '';
    li.textContent = t.text;
    li.addEventListener('click', () => toggleTodo(t.id));
    list.append(li);
  }
  // …which destroys focus, scroll position, text selection, any CSS
  // transition in flight, and the state of any input inside an item.
}
The thing that actually gets you is not any single line

It is that every action must know about every piece of UI that depends on the data it touched. Add a “5 items remaining” label and you must find every mutation site and add a call. Add a filter and every mutation site needs to reconsider visibility. The relationships are not written down anywhere — they live in the developer's memory, and they decay. The alternative, rebuilding everything on every change, is correct and destroys focus, scroll and selection.

Why it gets worse, precisely

N pieces of state × M pieces of UI = N×M relationships you maintain state: todos · filter · editingId · isSaving · error UI: list · count · empty state · filter buttons · save button · error banner · document title 5 × 7 = 35 possible dependencies, and you must know which of them are real. Miss one and you get the classic bug report: "the count is wrong after I delete the last item". And the transitions, not just the states. Imperative code describes how to get from one state to another, so what you actually maintain is the set of state PAIRS: empty → has items has items → empty has items → filtered filtered → empty results editing → saved editing → cancelled saving → error error → retrying With k distinguishable states there are up to k² transitions. Every one is a code path. Most are never tested. React's trade: describe only what the UI looks like for each state, and give up control of the transition. You write k descriptions instead of k² transitions, and the library computes the difference.

The same feature, declaratively

jsx · the entire component
function TodoList() {
  const [todos, setTodos]   = useState([]);
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('all');

  // Derived, not stored. There is no "visible todos" state to keep in
  // sync, because it is recomputed from the two things that ARE state.
  const visible = todos.filter(t =>
    filter === 'all' ? true : filter === 'done' ? t.done : !t.done);
  const remaining = todos.filter(t => !t.done).length;

  function add(text) {
    // A NEW array, not a mutation. Why that matters is J03.
    setTodos([...todos, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), text, done: false }]);
  }

  function toggle(id) {
    setTodos(todos.map(t => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)));
  }

  // One description. Not one per transition.
  return (
    <div>
      <NewTodo onAdd={add} />

      {visible.length === 0
        ? <p className="empty">Nothing here</p>
        : <ul>
            {visible.map(t => (
              <li key={t.id}
                  className={t.done ? 'done' : ''}
                  onClick={() => toggle(t.id)}>
                {t.text}
              </li>
            ))}
          </ul>}

      <p>{remaining} remaining</p>

      {['all', 'active', 'done'].map(f => (
        <button key={f}
                className={filter === f ? 'active' : ''}
                onClick={() => setFilter(f)}>
          {f}
        </button>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

// Add a "5 items remaining" label? One line, in one place. Add a filter?
// The list expression already reads from `filter`. Nothing has to be
// notified, because nothing is subscribing — the whole description is
// recomputed and React works out the difference.

What you gave up

Given upGained
Direct control of when the DOM changesYou stop maintaining transitions; the library derives them
Mutating data in placeChange detection becomes a reference comparison, which is why immutability is not a style preference (J03)
Some raw performanceA careful hand-written implementation is faster. React trades a little speed for a large reduction in a specific class of bug
A build stepJSX, module bundling, and a toolchain you now have to keep working
Being able to read the code top to bottomRendering is now a scheduled, interruptible process — which is what Part III is for
React is not fast because of the virtual DOM

This is the most repeated wrong answer in React interviews. Diffing two trees is extra work that hand-written DOM code does not do. React is fast enough because it batches updates, writes to the DOM once per commit rather than once per change, and reads layout properties rarely — and because the code you would have written by hand would eventually contain a innerHTML = '' rebuild that is far worse. The virtual DOM is a programming-model feature that makes declarative UI affordable, not a performance feature.

Why not jQuery, or plain DOM, or web components

ApproachWhat it fixesWhat it does not
jQueryBrowser inconsistencies, terse selection and traversalNothing about state synchronisation — it is a nicer imperative API for the same problem
Template strings + innerHTMLDescribing markup is pleasant againRebuilds everything: focus, scroll, selection and event listeners are lost on every update
Web ComponentsEncapsulation, reuse, a real browser primitiveGives you a component boundary and leaves the update logic entirely to you
Two-way binding (Angular 1, Knockout)Removes the manual update callsData flows in both directions, so “what changed this?” becomes unanswerable in a large app — the reason one-way flow won
React, Vue, Svelte, SolidThe state→UI relationship is declared onceThey differ in how — diffing, fine-grained signals, compilation — not in the idea
The competition agrees on the idea and disagrees on the mechanism

Svelte compiles your component into imperative DOM updates at build time. Solid and the newer Vue use fine-grained reactivity, where a signal knows exactly which DOM node depends on it. Both avoid diffing entirely and are measurably faster at the update step. React's bet is different: keep the runtime dumb and general, re-run the component function, and diff the result — which costs performance and buys a model where a component is just a function with no reactive graph to reason about. Knowing that this is a trade, and being able to name what each side gets, is a much better interview answer than “virtual DOM is fast”.

When React is the wrong choice

Do not use React for: · a mostly-static site with a contact form → an HTML file, or Astro, or a static generator · a page with three interactive widgets on an existing server-rendered app → a few lines of vanilla JS, or Alpine, or htmx · a data-visualisation canvas where you control every pixel → React fights you; use the canvas API directly · a team that does not have a build pipeline and does not want one Use React when: · the UI has meaningful state that changes over time · that state is read by many parts of the screen · you will maintain it for more than a few months · more than one person will work on it The honest summary: React's value is proportional to how much state your UI has. For a page with none, it is pure cost.
Interview follow-up

“Why would you use React rather than plain JavaScript?” Answer with the quadratic, not with performance. Imperative UI code makes you maintain the transitions between states, and the number of those grows as the square of the number of states — which is where the “count is wrong after deleting the last item” class of bug comes from. React lets you describe only the end state for any given data and takes responsibility for the transition. Then be honest about the cost: a build step, a runtime, and worse peak performance than carefully hand-written DOM code. An interviewer is listening for whether you understand it as a trade rather than as an upgrade.

J02

The JavaScript that React actually depends on

Most “React is confusing” is JavaScript being confusing in a place where React makes it visible. Six language features carry almost all of React's weight, and closures carry the most by a wide margin — nearly every genuinely puzzling React bug is a closure behaving exactly as specified.

Closures, which are the whole game

javascript · a function remembers where it was created
function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;                       // lives in makeCounter's scope
  return function increment() {
    count += 1;                        // …and this function can still see it
    return count;
  };
}

const next = makeCounter();
next(); // 1
next(); // 2   ← the variable outlived the call that created it

// The rule, stated precisely: a function captures the VARIABLE, not its
// value at creation time. Two functions over the same variable see each
// other's writes.
function pair() {
  let n = 0;
  return [() => n++, () => n];
}
const [inc, read] = pair();
inc(); inc();
read(); // 2

// Now the version that catches everyone, in plain JS:
function delayed() {
  let message = 'first';
  setTimeout(() => console.log(message), 1000);
  message = 'second';
}
delayed(); // logs "second" — the closure reads the variable LATER
This is the single most important paragraph in Part I

A React component function runs on every render, and every render creates a fresh set of variables and a fresh set of functions closing over them. So an event handler, an effect callback or a timer created during render number 3 sees render 3's values forever — even if renders 4 and 5 have happened since. It is not React being weird; it is closures working correctly. Chapter R04 calls this “state as a snapshot”, and it explains roughly a third of all React bugs.

javascript · the same closure, now in React
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handleClick() {
    // Three separate reads of the SAME captured value. `count` is a
    // const in this render's scope — it cannot change mid-function.
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
    // count is 0 here, so this is setCount(1) three times → 1, not 3.
  }

  function handleClickFixed() {
    // The updater form receives the latest value rather than closing
    // over one. React applies these in order during the update.
    setCount(c => c + 1);
    setCount(c => c + 1);
    setCount(c => c + 1);   // → 3
  }

  function handleAsync() {
    setCount(count + 1);
    setTimeout(() => {
      // Still THIS render's count, three seconds later. Not a bug in
      // React; the closure captured the variable and nothing reassigns
      // it, because a new render creates a NEW variable.
      console.log(count);
    }, 3000);
  }

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>;
}

Destructuring

javascript · objects, arrays, parameters, defaults
// Objects — by NAME, order is irrelevant.
const user = { id: 1, name: 'Ada', email: 'a@b.c' };
const { name, email } = user;
const { name: displayName } = user;          // rename
const { role = 'member' } = user;            // default when undefined
const { id, ...rest } = user;                // rest: { name, email }

// Arrays — by POSITION, which is why useState returns one.
const [first, second] = [10, 20];
const [, onlySecond] = [10, 20];             // skip
const [head, ...tail] = [1, 2, 3];           // tail: [2, 3]

// This is the whole reason useState's API looks the way it does:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
// It returns an ARRAY so you can name both halves whatever you like.
// An object would have forced everyone to write
//   const { value: count, setValue: setCount } = useState(0)

// In parameters, which is how props are almost always read:
function Avatar({ src, alt = '', size = 40 }) { /* … */ }
// equivalent to: function Avatar(props) { const { src } = props; … }

// Nested, with a default at each level. Useful and easy to overdo —
// past two levels it stops being readable.
function Card({ user: { name, avatar = '/default.png' } = {} }) { /* … */ }
A default only fires for undefined

{ count = 0 } uses 0 when the property is missing or explicitly undefined, and does not when it is null, 0, '' or false. So a component with function Toggle({ on = true }) rendered as <Toggle on={null} /> receives null, not true. This is the same distinction as ?? versus ||, and it is a recurring source of “why is my default not applied”.

Spread and rest

javascript · copying, merging, forwarding
// Arrays: a NEW array containing the same elements.
const next = [...todos, newTodo];
const without = todos.filter(t => t.id !== id);
const inserted = [...todos.slice(0, i), item, ...todos.slice(i)];

// Objects: a new object, later keys winning.
const updated = { ...todo, done: true };
const merged  = { ...defaults, ...overrides };

// Rest in parameters, which is how a component forwards unknown props
// to the DOM element underneath it — a very common pattern.
function Button({ variant = 'primary', children, ...props }) {
  return (
    <button className={`btn btn-${variant}`} {...props}>
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}
// <Button onClick={f} disabled aria-label="Save" /> works, because
// onClick, disabled and aria-label all land in ...props.

// CRITICAL: spread is SHALLOW. One level deep, and no further.
const a = { user: { name: 'Ada' }, tags: ['x'] };
const b = { ...a };
b.user.name = 'Grace';   // mutates a.user too — SAME object
b.tags.push('y');        // mutates a.tags too — SAME array

// So updating nested state means spreading at every level you change:
setState({
  ...state,
  user: { ...state.user, name: 'Grace' },
});
// Past two levels this becomes unreadable, which is the signal to
// flatten the state or reach for Immer (R12).

Arrow functions, and this

javascript · why hooks made this irrelevant
// Arrows have no `this` of their own — they inherit it from where they
// were DEFINED. In class components that mattered enormously:
class Old extends React.Component {
  handleClick() {
    this.setState(…);       // `this` is undefined when passed as a callback
  }
  handleOk = () => {
    this.setState(…);       // arrow: `this` is the instance, always
  };
  render() {
    return <button onClick={this.handleClick.bind(this)}>…</button>;
  }
}

// With function components there is no `this` at all. This is not a
// small quality-of-life improvement — it removed an entire category of
// bug, and it is a large part of why hooks won.

// The concise-body trap, which does still bite:
const good = (x) => ({ id: x });     // returns an object
const bad  = (x) => { id: x };       // returns undefined — that is a BLOCK
// In JSX: () => ({ ...state, done: true })  ← the parentheses matter

// And the one that catches everyone in JSX:
<button onClick={handleClick()}>      // WRONG: calls it during render
<button onClick={handleClick}>        // right: passes the function
<button onClick={() => handleClick(id)}>  // right: passes a new function

Modules

javascript · named, default, and why it matters for bundling
// Named exports — preferred, because the name is fixed at both ends so
// imports are greppable and renames are mechanical.
export function Button() {}
export const SIZES = ['sm', 'lg'];
import { Button, SIZES } from './Button';
import { Button as UIButton } from './Button';

// Default export — one per module, and the importer chooses the name,
// which means the same component can be imported under three different
// names in three files. Some frameworks REQUIRE it: a Next.js page must
// default-export its component (X02).
export default function Page() {}
import AnythingAtAll from './page';

// Dynamic import: returns a promise, and is the split point a bundler
// uses. React.lazy is built directly on it (R15).
const Chart = lazy(() => import('./Chart'));

// Modules are SINGLETONS: evaluated once, and every importer gets the
// same instance. Top-level code runs on first import.
export const cache = new Map();   // one Map for the whole app
console.log('runs once');         // …and once per server process on SSR
Module-level state is shared, which matters more on the server

In the browser a module-level Map is per-tab and usually harmless. On a server rendering React — Next.js, or any SSR setup — that same module is evaluated once per process and shared by every user's request. Putting a cache, a current-user variable or a request-scoped value at module scope is therefore a cross-request data leak, and it is one of the most damaging mistakes in server-rendered React. Chapter X03 returns to this; the rule is that module scope holds constants and connections, never per-request state.

The rest of the shortlist

javascript · things you will read in every React file
// Optional chaining and nullish coalescing — for data that may not have
// arrived yet, which in React is most data.
user?.profile?.avatar            // undefined instead of throwing
onChange?.(value)                // call only if provided
const name = user.name ?? 'Anonymous';   // only null/undefined
const name = user.name || 'Anonymous';   // ALSO replaces '' and 0 — a bug
                                          // for counts and empty strings

// Template literals — class names, URLs, labels.
const cls = `btn ${active ? 'active' : ''} ${size}`;

// Computed keys — for dynamic form state, everywhere.
setForm({ ...form, [event.target.name]: event.target.value });

// Short-circuit rendering, and its one famous trap:
{items.length > 0 && <List items={items} />}
{items.length && <List items={items} />}   // renders "0" when empty!
// Because 0 is falsy AND a valid React child. Always compare explicitly.

// Labelled object shorthand
const props = { id, name, onClick };   // { id: id, name: name, … }

// Array methods that build new arrays — the core of React data work.
todos.map(t => ({ ...t, done: true }))   // transform → new array
todos.filter(t => !t.done)               // subset    → new array
todos.find(t => t.id === id)             // one item  → NOT a new array
todos.some(t => !t.done)                 // boolean
todos.reduce((sum, t) => sum + t.points, 0);
The && trap is worth memorising now

{count && <Badge />} renders the number 0 on screen when count is zero, because 0 && x evaluates to 0, and React renders 0 as text while ignoring false, null and undefined. The same applies to an empty string. Write {count > 0 && …} or use a ternary. It is the single most common “why is there a stray 0 in my UI” question, and it appears in interviews for exactly that reason.

What you can safely not know yet

Skip for nowBecause
class, this, bind, prototypesFunction components removed the need. You will meet them only in old code
Generators, iterators, symbolsAlmost never appear in application React
Proxies and ReflectLibrary internals — Immer and MobX use them so you do not have to
var and hoisting rulesconst and let only. Hoisting matters for reading legacy code, not for writing new
Deep prototype-chain inheritanceReact composes with functions and props; it has no inheritance model
Interview follow-up

“Why does this setTimeout log the old state?” Because the callback closed over the variable from the render in which it was created, and a new render creates entirely new variables rather than reassigning the old ones — so the old closure keeps seeing the old value indefinitely. Say that it is not a React quirk but closures behaving exactly as specified, and name the two fixes: the updater form setState(prev => …) when you need the latest value during an update, and a ref when you need the latest value inside a long-lived callback. That distinction is the follow-up question, so get there first.

J03

Immutability, and why React insists on it

“Don't mutate state” sounds like a style rule. It is not — it is load-bearing. React decides whether anything changed by comparing references, so a mutated object is indistinguishable from an unchanged one, and your update silently does nothing.

The mechanism

React's change detection is Object.is(previous, next). That is it. const next = todos; Object.is → true "nothing changed" next.push(item); still true. Same reference. setTodos(next); → React bails out. No re-render. const next = [...todos, item]; Object.is → false "changed" setTodos(next); → re-render Why a reference check rather than a deep comparison? Because deep-comparing every piece of state on every update would be O(size of your data) per render, on every keystroke. A reference check is one CPU instruction. React pushes that cost onto you — you create new objects — and gets O(1) change detection in return. This is the same bargain the whole ecosystem made. memo, useMemo, useCallback, useEffect's dependency array, Redux, Zustand and every selector library all compare by reference. Mutate once and all of them are wrong at the same time.

Which array methods mutate

Mutates — avoid on stateReturns new — use these
push, unshift[...arr, x], [x, ...arr], concat
pop, shift, spliceslice, filter, toSpliced
sorttoSorted, or [...arr].sort()
reversetoReversed
arr[i] = xwith(i, x), or map
fill, copyWithinmap
—map, flatMap, concat, slice, filter already return new arrays
The toSorted family is the modern answer

toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with are ES2023 and are in every current browser and Node 20+. They do exactly what the mutating method does and return a copy, which removes the [...arr].sort() dance and the bug where someone forgets the spread. If you support older runtimes, the spread form is identical in behaviour — just noisier.

Nested updates, and where they stop being readable

javascript · spreading at every level you touch
// Spread is SHALLOW, so every level you modify needs its own copy.
// Levels you do NOT modify can be shared — that is the point, and it is
// what makes this cheap rather than a deep clone.

// one level
setUser({ ...user, name: 'Grace' });

// two levels
setUser({ ...user, address: { ...user.address, city: 'Berlin' } });

// three levels, and already unpleasant
setState({
  ...state,
  users: {
    ...state.users,
    [id]: {
      ...state.users[id],
      settings: { ...state.users[id].settings, theme: 'dark' },
    },
  },
});

// An item inside an array inside an object — the shape that produces
// the worst code in most React apps:
setBoard({
  ...board,
  columns: board.columns.map(col =>
    col.id !== colId ? col : {
      ...col,
      cards: col.cards.map(card =>
        card.id !== cardId ? card : { ...card, title }
      ),
    }
  ),
});
Deep spreading is a smell, not a skill to perfect

When an update needs three levels of spread, the problem is usually the state shape rather than the syntax. Two fixes, in order of preference: normalise — store entities in a flat { [id]: entity } map and keep arrays of ids, so an update touches one level; or reach for Immer, which lets you write the mutation and produces the immutable copy for you. Reaching for Immer first, before trying to flatten, tends to hide a state shape that is also hard to query and hard to reason about.

javascript · the two escapes
// 1 · Normalise. The same update, with a flat shape:
const [cards, setCards] = useState({
  'c1': { id: 'c1', title: 'Draft', columnId: 'col1' },
  'c2': { id: 'c2', title: 'Review', columnId: 'col1' },
});
setCards({ ...cards, [cardId]: { ...cards[cardId], title } });
// One level. Also: finding a card is O(1) instead of a nested scan.

// 2 · Immer. You write a mutation; it produces a new object, sharing
//     every untouched branch.
import { produce } from 'immer';

setBoard(produce(draft => {
  const card = draft.columns
    .find(c => c.id === colId).cards
    .find(c => c.id === cardId);
  card.title = title;
}));

// useImmer wraps useState with the same idea:
const [board, updateBoard] = useImmer(initialBoard);
updateBoard(draft => { draft.columns[0].cards[0].title = title; });

Structural sharing

An immutable update does not copy the whole tree. It copies only the path from the root to the thing that changed, and shares the rest. before after setUser({...u, city:'Berlin'}) user ● user ● user' ● ├── name "Ada" ◀──────────────────┼────────────────┘ shared ├── tags [...] ◀──────────────────┘ shared └── address ● address ● address' ● ├── city "Wien" │ city "Berlin" └── zip "1010" ◀───────────────┴──────────────── shared Two new objects, not a deep clone. A 10,000-item list where one item changes allocates one new array of 10,000 pointers plus one new item object — the other 9,999 items are the same objects as before. This is also why memo works: every child whose props are shared objects sees Object.is === true and skips re-rendering (R14).

Where mutation is fine

Mutation is fine when…Example
The object was created in this function and has not been handed to React yetconst next = [...todos]; next.sort(); setTodos(next);
It is a local variable during render, not stateBuilding an array before returning it from map
It is a ref — refs are explicitly not stateref.current.count += 1 (R10)
Immer is producing the copy for youproduce(draft => { draft.x = 1 })
The bug that survives because it usually works

Mutating state and calling a setter with a new reference — todo.done = true; setTodos([...todos]) — appears to work. React re-renders because the array is new, and the mutated item shows its new value. It breaks in three places: a memo'd child comparing that item's props sees the same object and skips; useEffect with that item as a dependency never fires; and anything holding the previous state for comparison or undo now sees the mutated past. These fail intermittently, long after the mutation, which is why they are hard to trace back.

Interview follow-up

“Why does React require immutable updates?” Because change detection is Object.is on the reference, so a mutated object is indistinguishable from an unchanged one and the update is silently dropped. Then add the two things that make this a good answer rather than a recited one: it is a deliberate trade — O(1) change detection in exchange for you allocating new objects, versus O(n) deep comparison on every render — and it is not just setState. Dependency arrays, memo, useMemo and every external store library compare the same way, so a single mutation breaks all of them at once.

J04

Async JavaScript, and how it lands in React

Every interesting UI waits for something. Promises and async/await are the language half; the React half is that a component function must be synchronous, so every asynchronous result has to arrive as a state update — and that mismatch produces a specific set of bugs worth knowing before you meet them.

The language part, briefly

javascript · promises, await, and the patterns you will use
// A promise is a value that will exist later, or an error that will.
const res = await fetch('/api/users');
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);  // fetch does NOT
const users = await res.json();                      // throw on 4xx/5xx

// Parallel vs serial — the difference is one keyword and often seconds.
const a = await getUser();      // waits
const b = await getPosts();     // then waits again        → 2 round trips

const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([getUser(), getPosts()]);
                                                             // → 1 wait

// allSettled when partial failure is acceptable
const results = await Promise.allSettled([getUser(), getPosts()]);
results[0].status;   // 'fulfilled' | 'rejected'

// An async function ALWAYS returns a promise, even when it returns a
// plain value or throws. This matters below.
async function f() { return 1; }
f();            // Promise<1>, not 1

// AbortController — the mechanism for cancelling a request. React's
// cleanup functions are built around it.
const ac = new AbortController();
fetch(url, { signal: ac.signal });
ac.abort();     // the fetch rejects with an AbortError

The mismatch

A component function must be synchronous. React calls it and needs the element tree back immediately — it cannot wait. async function Profile() { … } ← returns a Promise, not elements. React (on the client) cannot render it. So anything asynchronous has to follow this shape: 1 render synchronously, with whatever you have now 2 start the async work as a SIDE EFFECT 3 when it resolves, call a setter 4 React renders again, now with the data Which is why loading states are not a React inconvenience — they are the direct consequence of "render must return now". Two exceptions worth knowing early: · Server Components may be async, because they render on the server where waiting is fine (N04) · use() lets a client component read a promise and suspend while it settles, which moves the loading state to a boundary rather than into the component (N03)

The four bugs, in order of how often they happen

javascript · 1 — setting state after unmount
// The request resolves after the user has navigated away. In React 18+
// this no longer warns, and it is no longer a "memory leak" — but the
// work is wasted and, worse, it can overwrite newer data.
useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;                    // the simplest guard

  fetchUser(id).then(user => {
    if (!cancelled) setUser(user);
  });

  return () => { cancelled = true; };       // cleanup runs on unmount
}, [id]);
javascript · 2 — the race condition, which is the real one
// The user types "a", then "ab", then "abc". Three requests are in
// flight. They can resolve in ANY order — and if "a" resolves last, the
// user sees results for a query they finished typing two seconds ago.
//
// This is not rare. It is the default behaviour of the obvious code.

// ── the guard, which handles it correctly ────────────────────────────
useEffect(() => {
  let current = true;

  search(query).then(results => {
    if (current) setResults(results);   // stale responses are DISCARDED
  });

  // Cleanup runs before the NEXT effect, not only on unmount — so each
  // superseded request marks itself irrelevant.
  return () => { current = false; };
}, [query]);

// ── or cancel the request outright ──────────────────────────────────
useEffect(() => {
  const ac = new AbortController();

  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal: ac.signal })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(setResults)
    .catch(err => {
      if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setError(err);   // aborts are normal
    });

  return () => ac.abort();
}, [query]);
The cleanup function is what makes async effects correct

It runs before every re-run of the effect and on unmount — not just on unmount, which is what most people assume. That is precisely the hook you need for cancellation: each time the dependency changes, the previous request is either aborted or marked irrelevant before the new one starts. An async effect without a cleanup is a race condition waiting for a slow network, and it will pass every test you run on localhost.

javascript · 3 — async functions passed to useEffect
// WRONG: useEffect expects the return value to be a CLEANUP FUNCTION or
// undefined. An async function returns a Promise, which React will try
// to call as a cleanup — and React warns about exactly this.
useEffect(async () => {
  const data = await fetchData();
  setData(data);
}, []);

// RIGHT: define an async function inside and call it.
useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;

  (async () => {
    try {
      const data = await fetchData();
      if (!cancelled) setData(data);
    } catch (err) {
      if (!cancelled) setError(err);
    } finally {
      if (!cancelled) setLoading(false);
    }
  })();

  return () => { cancelled = true; };
}, []);

// Event handlers, by contrast, MAY be async — nothing consumes their
// return value.
async function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  await save(form);
}
javascript · 4 — the stale closure over state
// This handler captured `count` from the render in which it was
// created. Five seconds later, that render is ancient history — but the
// closure still sees its value (J02).
function Delayed() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handleClick() {
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log(count);       // the value at CLICK time, not now
      setCount(count + 1);      // overwrites anything that happened since
    }, 5000);
  }
}

// Fix A — the updater form, when you need the latest value to compute
// the next one:
setCount(c => c + 1);

// Fix B — a ref, when you need to READ the latest value inside a
// long-lived callback (R10):
const countRef = useRef(count);
countRef.current = count;                 // updated on every render
setTimeout(() => console.log(countRef.current), 5000);   // current value

The three states every async read has

javascript · and why a boolean pair is the wrong shape
// The naive shape allows states that cannot happen, and you will
// eventually render one of them:
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
const [error, setError]     = useState(null);
const [data, setData]       = useState(null);
// loading && error? loading && data? error && data? All representable.

// A single status makes the impossible states unrepresentable:
const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle' });
// { status: 'idle' }
// { status: 'loading' }
// { status: 'success', data }
// { status: 'error', error }

if (state.status === 'loading') return <Spinner />;
if (state.status === 'error')   return <Error err={state.error} />;
if (state.status === 'success') return <List items={state.data} />;
return null;

// In practice you write this three times and then reach for a library,
// because it also wants caching, deduplication, retries, refetch on
// focus and pagination — see the note below.
Do not hand-roll data fetching past the first screen

useEffect plus fetch is the right way to learn what is happening, and the wrong way to ship a real app. You will need request deduplication, caching, stale-while-revalidate, retries, refetch on window focus, pagination and cache invalidation after a mutation — and each is a subtle piece of work. TanStack Query and SWR do all of it; in a Next.js app the server does most of it before the component ever runs (X04). Reach for one as soon as you have more than a couple of endpoints.

Where async goes in modern React

ApproachWhere the wait happensChapter
useEffect + fetchAfter the first render, on the clientR08
A query librarySame, with caching and deduplication handledR08
Server Component with awaitOn the server, before any HTML is sentN04
use(promise) + <Suspense>The component suspends; the boundary shows a fallbackN03
Actions / useActionStateMutations, with pending state managed by ReactN01
Interview follow-up

“Your search-as-you-type sometimes shows results for an earlier query. Why?” Because responses are not guaranteed to arrive in the order the requests were sent, so a slow response for “a” can land after a fast one for “abc” and overwrite it. The fix is to make each superseded request irrelevant: either a boolean captured in the effect's closure and flipped in the cleanup, or an AbortController aborted in the cleanup. The detail that shows you have debugged this is that the cleanup runs before the next effect, not only on unmount — which is exactly the hook needed, and is why the naive version passes every local test and fails on a real network.

J05

JSX is function calls

JSX looks like HTML inside JavaScript, which is why people assume it is a template language with its own runtime. It is not. It is syntax sugar that a compiler rewrites into ordinary function calls, and every rule that seems arbitrary follows from that.

The transform

Every JSX rule falls out of that rewrite: · className, not class — the props become an object literal, and class was a reserved word when JSX was designed. Same for htmlFor instead of for. · {} holds an expression, not a statement — because its contents become a value in an argument list. {if (x) …} cannot work; {x ? a : b} can. · camelCase event props — they are object keys, and onclick would collide with nothing but reads as the DOM attribute it is not. · One root element — a function returns one value. Two siblings would be two return values, hence Fragments. · Attributes are props, and take any JavaScript value: <Chart data={rows} onSelect={fn} /> passes an array and a function, which no HTML attribute could. · A capitalised name is a variable; lowercase is a string. <button> → _jsx('button', …) <Button> → _jsx(Button, …) That is the entire reason components must be capitalised.
The capitalisation rule is not a convention

The compiler decides between a string and an identifier by looking at the first character. <myButton /> compiles to _jsx('myButton', …) — React then tries to create a DOM element called myButton, produces nothing visible, and warns in the console. This is why a component defined as function userCard() silently renders nothing, and why the fix is a rename rather than anything to do with React.

What an element actually is

javascript · a plain object, and nothing more
const el = <button className="btn">Save</button>;

console.log(el);
// {
//   $$typeof: Symbol(react.element),   ← guards against JSON injection
//   type: 'button',                    ← string = DOM, function = component
//   key: null,
//   props: { className: 'btn', children: 'Save' },
//   ref: null,
// }

// It is INERT. Creating it does not touch the DOM, does not call the
// component, and costs one object allocation. It is a DESCRIPTION.
const many = Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, i) => <Row key={i} />);
// 10,000 objects. Zero DOM nodes. Zero component functions called.

// Which is also why this is a common misunderstanding:
function Parent() {
  const child = <ExpensiveChild />;   // does NOT call ExpensiveChild
  return condition ? child : null;    // it is called only if RENDERED
}

// And why elements are immutable — React reuses them for diffing:
el.props.className = 'other';   // frozen in development; do not
const modified = cloneElement(el, { className: 'other' });  // if you must

Children

javascript · children is just a prop
// These two are identical:
<Card>Hello</Card>
<Card children="Hello" />

// Which means children can be anything JavaScript can hold — including
// a function, which is the whole "render prop" pattern (R03):
<DataLoader>
  {(data) => <List items={data} />}
</DataLoader>

// What React renders, and what it ignores:
<div>
  {'a string'}        {/* rendered */}
  {42}                {/* rendered as "42" */}
  {null}              {/* ignored */}
  {undefined}         {/* ignored */}
  {false}             {/* ignored — this is why && works */}
  {true}              {/* ignored */}
  {[<A key="a" />, <B key="b" />]}   {/* arrays are flattened */}
  {new Date()}        {/* THROWS: objects are not valid children */}
</div>

// The gap: 0 and '' are NOT ignored — they are rendered.
{count && <Badge />}        {/* renders "0" when count is 0 */}
{count > 0 && <Badge />}    {/* correct */}

Fragments, and why they exist

javascript
// A function returns one value, so JSX needs one root. When a wrapper
// div would break the layout — inside a flex row, a table, or a grid —
// a Fragment groups without producing a DOM node.
function Row() {
  return (
    <>
      <td>Name</td>
      <td>Email</td>
    </>
  );
}

// The shorthand cannot take a key, so in a list you need the long form:
{items.map(item => (
  <React.Fragment key={item.id}>
    <dt>{item.term}</dt>
    <dd>{item.def}</dd>
  </React.Fragment>
))}

// Returning an array is also legal, and reads worse:
return [<td key="a">Name</td>, <td key="b">Email</td>];

Props on the wire

JSXBecomesNote
disableddisabled: trueBare attribute is shorthand for {true}
value="5"value: '5'Quotes make a string
value={5}value: 5Braces make it a number
style={{color:'red'}}style: {color:'red'}Double braces = an object inside an expression
{...props}spread into the objectLater keys win; order matters
data-id="1"passed throughdata-* and aria-* keep their dashes
key={id}not a propExtracted by React; unreadable inside the component (R06)
ref={r}a prop in React 19Was special-cased before 19 (N06)
Spread order decides who wins

<Input {...props} value={v} /> lets the explicit value override anything the caller passed; <Input value={v} {...props} /> lets the caller override value. Both are legitimate and they mean opposite things — put your own props after the spread for values the component must control, and before it for defaults the caller may replace. Getting this backwards on className or onClick produces components that silently ignore either your styling or the caller's handler.

The runtime, and why you no longer import React

javascript · the classic and automatic transforms
// CLASSIC (React ≤ 16, and still configurable):
//   <div />  →  React.createElement('div', null)
// which is why every file needed `import React from 'react'` even when
// the name was never used — the compiler emitted it.

// AUTOMATIC (React 17+, the default everywhere now):
//   <div />  →  _jsx('div', {})
// with the import injected by the compiler:
import { jsx as _jsx, jsxs as _jsxs } from 'react/jsx-runtime';

// So the React import is only needed for what you actually use:
import { useState } from 'react';     // yes
import React from 'react';            // no longer required for JSX

// In development the compiler emits jsxDEV instead, which carries the
// source file and line — that is where component stack traces come from,
// and why production stacks are less helpful.

JSX is not React's

Any function can be the target

JSX is a syntax extension with a configurable output, not a React feature. Setting jsxImportSource points it at Preact, Solid, Hono's HTML renderer, or your own function — which is how those libraries use identical-looking code with completely different runtimes. It is worth knowing because it clarifies the boundary: JSX contributes syntax and nothing else. Reconciliation, hooks and the component lifecycle are React, and none of them is implied by the angle brackets.

Interview follow-up

“Is JSX HTML?” No — it is syntax sugar that compiles to function calls returning plain objects, and saying that immediately lets you explain every rule that otherwise looks arbitrary: one root element because a function returns one value, className because props are an object literal and class was reserved, expressions rather than statements in braces because the contents become an argument, and capitalised component names because the compiler distinguishes a string tag from an identifier by the first character. The good follow-up to volunteer is that the resulting element is inert — creating it calls nothing and touches no DOM — which is why const x = <Expensive /> costs one object.

J06

Components: functions that return UI

A component is a JavaScript function that takes an object and returns elements. That is the entire definition — and holding onto it, rather than thinking of components as objects with lifecycles, is what makes the rest of React make sense.

The whole thing

javascript · three equivalent definitions
// A function, taking one argument, returning elements.
function Greeting(props) {
  return <h1>Hello, {props.name}</h1>;
}

// Destructured at the parameter, which is how almost everyone writes it.
function Greeting({ name, greeting = 'Hello' }) {
  return <h1>{greeting}, {name}</h1>;
}

// An arrow, which is identical except that it is not hoisted.
const Greeting = ({ name }) => <h1>Hello, {name}</h1>;

// Used, it is an element whose type is the function itself:
<Greeting name="Ada" />
// → _jsx(Greeting, { name: 'Ada' })
// React calls Greeting({ name: 'Ada' }) when it renders that element.
What React does with your function 1 finds an element whose type is your function 2 calls it with the props object 3 takes the returned elements 4 repeats for any component elements inside them 5 produces a complete tree of DOM descriptions 6 compares it with the previous tree and updates the real DOM Consequences worth internalising now: · your function runs many times — once per render, not once per component "instance" · local variables inside it are recreated every time; that is why state must live somewhere React controls · it must return the same output for the same props and state, with no side effects during the call — React may call it twice (StrictMode), abandon a call part-way, or call it on the server

The rules

javascript · pure, capitalised, top-level
// 1 · PURE during render. Same inputs → same output, no side effects.
function Bad({ items }) {
  items.sort();                      // mutates a prop
  document.title = 'Items';          // side effect during render
  analytics.track('viewed');         // fires twice in StrictMode
  return <List items={items} />;
}

function Good({ items }) {
  const sorted = [...items].sort();  // local copy
  useEffect(() => {                  // side effects belong here (R08)
    document.title = 'Items';
  }, []);
  return <List items={sorted} />;
}

// 2 · CAPITALISED, or the compiler emits a string tag (J05).

// 3 · DEFINED AT THE TOP LEVEL. Never inside another component:
function Parent() {
  // WRONG. A NEW function identity on every render, so React sees a
  // different component type, unmounts the old subtree and mounts a new
  // one — destroying its state, its DOM nodes and its focus, every time
  // the parent renders.
  function Child() { return <input />; }
  return <Child />;
}

// Right: define it outside, and pass data as props.
function Child() { return <input />; }
function Parent() { return <Child />; }
Defining a component inside another is the most destructive common mistake

React identifies a component by its function reference. Redefining it on every parent render produces a new reference each time, so reconciliation concludes that the old component was removed and a different one added — it unmounts the subtree, discards its state, tears down its DOM nodes, remounts, and runs every effect again. The symptoms are an input that loses focus while typing, state that resets for no reason, and animations that restart. It is worth a lint rule, and react/no-unstable-nested-components is that rule.

Composition, not configuration

javascript · passing elements as props is the core technique
// A layout that knows nothing about what goes in it:
function SplitPane({ left, right }) {
  return (
    <div className="split">
      <div className="pane">{left}</div>
      <div className="pane">{right}</div>
    </div>
  );
}

<SplitPane left={<FileTree />} right={<Editor />} />

// This also solves prop drilling without Context. A parent that holds
// the data renders the consumer and passes it DOWN as an element, so
// the intermediate layers never see it:
function Page() {
  const user = useUser();
  return <Layout sidebar={<Profile user={user} />} />;
  //     ^ Layout never receives `user` at all
}

// The compound-component pattern, which is what Card.Header is:
function Card({ children }) { return <div className="card">{children}</div>; }
Card.Header = function CardHeader({ children }) { … };
Card.Body   = function CardBody({ children }) { … };
// Just properties on a function. No React machinery involved.

How big should a component be?

Split when…Do not split when…
A piece is genuinely reused elsewhereYou are extracting it purely because the file is long
It has its own state that nothing else needsThe child would need five props to do its job
It renders a different kind of thing (a row, a dialog)The split produces two files you always open together
You need to memo part of the tree (R14)You are only naming a JSX block; a variable does that
The nesting has passed about three levelsIt is one if and a heading
A local variable is often the right “extraction”

Before creating a component, try assigning the JSX to a const inside the same function. It names the piece, shortens the return, and costs nothing — no new props interface, no new file, no indirection when reading. Extract a real component when it needs its own state, is used in more than one place, or needs a memo boundary. A codebase full of single-use components that each take eight props is harder to follow than a few longer functions.

Class components, for reading old code

javascript · the mapping
class Old extends React.Component {
  state = { count: 0 };                          // useState
  componentDidMount()    { subscribe(); }        // useEffect(fn, [])
  componentDidUpdate(prev) { … }                 // useEffect(fn, [deps])
  componentWillUnmount() { unsubscribe(); }      // the cleanup return
  shouldComponentUpdate()  { … }                 // memo
  render() { return <div>{this.state.count}</div>; }
}

// Classes are NOT deprecated and still work. Two things only they can
// still do:
//   · componentDidCatch — error boundaries have no hook equivalent (R15)
//   · getSnapshotBeforeUpdate — rarely needed
// Everything else has a hook, and hooks compose where lifecycle methods
// did not: two independent concerns in one componentDidMount cannot be
// separated, while two useEffect calls already are.
Interview follow-up

“What happens if you define a component inside another component?” It is redefined on every render of the parent, so its function reference changes, and React's reconciliation compares element types by reference — a different type means unmount the old subtree and mount a new one. The visible result is state resetting, inputs losing focus mid-keystroke, and effects re-running, all seemingly at random. Mentioning that the cause is reference identity rather than “React re-renders it” is the part that shows you understand reconciliation rather than having memorised the rule.

J07

Props and state: the two inputs

A component's output is a function of exactly two things. Props come from the parent and the component may not change them; state belongs to the component and changing it is what causes a re-render. Almost every architectural question in React reduces to deciding which of the two a given value should be — and where it should live.

The distinction

PropsState
Comes fromThe parentThe component itself
Who may change itThe parent, by re-renderingThis component, via a setter
Mutable here?No. Read-only, alwaysOnly through the setter
Survives re-render?Replaced each timePreserved by React
Causes a re-render?A new value from the parent doesCalling the setter does
AnalogyFunction argumentsA variable that outlives the call
javascript · both, in one component
function Counter({ label, step = 1, onReachLimit }) {
  //              ─────────────────────────────────  props: from the parent
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  //     ─────  ────────                              state: ours

  function increment() {
    const next = count + step;
    setCount(next);                       // our state — we may change it
    if (next >= 10) onReachLimit?.(next);  // tell the parent; do not reach up
  }

  // step = 5;              ← never. Props are read-only.
  // count = count + 1;     ← never. The setter is how state changes.

  return <button onClick={increment}>{label}: {count}</button>;
}
Props are read-only, and this is not enforced by the language

Nothing stops props.items.push(x) from running — and it will appear to work, because you have mutated an object the parent also holds. React will not re-render (the reference is unchanged, J03), the parent's own state is now silently wrong, and any memo on a sibling comparing that array sees no change. React documents components as pure functions of their props precisely so that this does not have to be checked at runtime; violating it produces bugs that surface far from the mutation.

Data flows down; events flow up

┌──────────────┐ │ App │ holds: todos │ const [todos, setTodos] │ └───┬──────────────────────▲──────┘ props │ │ callback todos ────────┤ ├──── onToggle(id) ▼ │ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ TodoList │───────────┘ └───┬──────────────────────▲──────┘ props │ │ todo ─────────┤ ├──── onToggle(todo.id) ▼ │ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ TodoItem │───────────┘ └──────────────┘ A child never reaches upward. It calls a function the parent gave it, and the parent decides what that means. That one-way constraint is why "what changed this value?" is always answerable: only the owner of the state can change it, and you find the owner by going up. The cost: a value needed three levels down must be threaded through two components that do not care about it — "prop drilling". The fixes, in order of preference: pass ELEMENTS as props instead of data (J06), then Context (R11), then a store.

Lifting state up

javascript · when two components need the same value
// The problem: two sibling inputs must stay in sync. Neither can see
// the other's state, because state is private to the component.

// The fix: move it to their closest common parent, and pass the value
// down with a callback to change it.
function TemperatureConverter() {
  const [celsius, setCelsius] = useState(20);

  return (
    <>
      <Input
        label="°C"
        value={celsius}
        onChange={setCelsius}
      />
      <Input
        label="°F"
        value={celsius * 9 / 5 + 32}
        onChange={f => setCelsius((f - 32) * 5 / 9)}
      />
    </>
  );
}

// Input is now a CONTROLLED component: it owns no state, it displays
// what it is given, and it reports changes. This is the single most
// important structural pattern in React.
function Input({ label, value, onChange }) {
  return (
    <label>
      {label}
      <input value={value} onChange={e => onChange(Number(e.target.value))} />
    </label>
  );
}

Where should this value live?

Ask four questions, in order. The first "no" is your answer. 1 Can it be computed from props or existing state? → then it is not state. Compute it during render. const total = items.reduce(…) not useState + useEffect const visible = items.filter(…) This is the most common mistake in React, and R09 is about it. 2 Does it change over time? → no: a constant, or a prop. Not state. 3 Does the component still need it after a re-render? → no: a plain local variable inside the function. → yes but it must NOT cause a re-render: a ref (R10). 4 Do other components need it? → no: keep it here. Local state is the default, always. → yes: lift it to the closest common parent. → yes, and that parent is five levels up: Context (R11). → yes, and it is genuinely global and often written: a store. The bias that keeps codebases healthy: push state down, as far as it will go. A modal's open/closed flag in a global store is a smell; in the component that renders the modal it is invisible.
Derived values are not state

const [total, setTotal] = useState(0) kept in sync with items by an effect is the single most common piece of unnecessary React code. It adds a render, it can be out of sync for one frame, and it will eventually drift when someone adds a code path that updates items without updating total. const total = items.reduce(…) cannot be wrong, costs a few microseconds, and disappears entirely once the React Compiler is in play. Chapter R09 works through the variations.

Props from state: the anti-pattern that looks reasonable

key is the idiomatic way to reset state

It is not only for lists. Giving a component a key that changes when the underlying entity changes tells React that this is a different instance, so it unmounts the old one and mounts a new one with fresh state — which is exactly the semantics you want for an edit form when the selected record changes. The alternative, an effect that resets the state when the prop changes, renders once with the wrong value first and is harder to read. R06 explains why key has this power.

Interview follow-up

“How do you decide whether something should be state?” Work down a short list and stop at the first no. Can it be computed from what you already have? Then it is derived, not state — and copying it into state with an effect is the most common unnecessary code in React. Does it change over time? Does the component need it to survive a re-render, and does changing it need to cause one — if not, it is a ref. Only then: who else needs it, and what is the closest common parent. The bias worth stating out loud is toward pushing state down; most “we need global state” conversations are really about two components that should have shared a parent.

J08

Promises, built from scratch

You can use promises for years without knowing how they work, right up until something behaves oddly — a .then that fires in the wrong order, a rejection nobody catches, a chain that swallows an error. Building one removes all of that, and it is the most common deep-JavaScript interview exercise there is.

What a promise actually is

A promise is a state machine with a callback queue. Nothing more. ┌─────────────┐ │ PENDING │ ── resolve(v) ──▶ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ │ FULFILLED │ value = v │ │ ── reject(e) ──▶ ├──────────────┤ └─────────────┘ │ REJECTED │ reason = e └──────────────┘ Three rules that define the whole thing: 1 · settling is one-way and final once fulfilled or rejected, the state and value never change. Calling resolve twice is a no-op the second time. 2 · callbacks are queued, not lost .then on a pending promise stores the callback; .then on an already-settled promise still runs asynchronously, never synchronously. 3 · .then returns a NEW promise that is what makes chaining work, and what makes a thrown error inside a handler become a rejection of the next link. Everything else — catch, finally, all, race — is built from those.

The implementation

javascript · my-promise.js — the core
const PENDING = 'pending', FULFILLED = 'fulfilled', REJECTED = 'rejected';

class MyPromise {
  #state = PENDING;
  #value = undefined;
  #handlers = [];          // queued { onFulfilled, onRejected } pairs

  constructor(executor) {
    if (typeof executor !== 'function') {
      throw new TypeError('Executor must be a function');
    }
    const resolve = (value) => this.#settle(FULFILLED, value);
    const reject  = (reason) => this.#settle(REJECTED, reason);
    try {
      // The executor runs SYNCHRONOUSLY, immediately. This is why
      // `new Promise(() => { console.log('a') })` logs before the
      // line after it.
      executor(resolve, reject);
    } catch (err) {
      reject(err);         // a throw in the executor rejects
    }
  }

  #settle(state, value) {
    if (this.#state !== PENDING) return;      // rule 1: one-way, final

    // THENABLE ASSIMILATION: resolving with a promise (or anything
    // with a .then) adopts its state instead of wrapping it. This is
    // why `Promise.resolve(p)` is p's result, not a promise of a
    // promise — and it is the part most hand-written versions miss.
    if (state === FULFILLED && value && typeof value.then === 'function') {
      value.then(
        (v) => this.#settle(FULFILLED, v),
        (e) => this.#settle(REJECTED, e),
      );
      return;
    }

    this.#state = state;
    this.#value = value;
    this.#flush();
  }

  #flush() {
    if (this.#state === PENDING) return;
    // rule 2: ALWAYS async. queueMicrotask schedules on the microtask
    // queue — after the current synchronous code, before any timer.
    queueMicrotask(() => {
      for (const h of this.#handlers) {
        this.#state === FULFILLED ? h.onFulfilled(this.#value)
                                  : h.onRejected(this.#value);
      }
      this.#handlers = [];
    });
  }

  then(onFulfilled, onRejected) {
    // rule 3: a NEW promise
    return new MyPromise((resolve, reject) => {
      const handle = (cb, fallback) => (value) => {
        if (typeof cb !== 'function') {
          // Pass-through: .then(null, fn) forwards the value, and a
          // missing onRejected forwards the rejection down the chain.
          fallback(value);
          return;
        }
        try {
          resolve(cb(value));   // a returned promise is assimilated above
        } catch (err) {
          reject(err);          // a THROW inside a handler rejects the
        }                       // next promise — this is the mechanism
      };                        // that makes .catch work at any depth

      this.#handlers.push({
        onFulfilled: handle(onFulfilled, resolve),
        onRejected:  handle(onRejected, reject),
      });
      this.#flush();            // already settled? queue it now
    });
  }

  catch(onRejected) {
    return this.then(undefined, onRejected);   // that is all catch is
  }

  finally(onFinally) {
    return this.then(
      // Note: finally does NOT receive or change the value. It passes
      // it through — unless onFinally throws or returns a rejected
      // promise, in which case that wins.
      (value)  => MyPromise.resolve(onFinally()).then(() => value),
      (reason) => MyPromise.resolve(onFinally()).then(() => { throw reason; }),
    );
  }
}
The two details that separate a real implementation from a toy

Thenable assimilation — resolving with something that has a .then adopts its eventual value instead of wrapping it. Without it, fetch().then(r => r.json()).then(…) would hand you a promise rather than the parsed body, and every chain would need manual unwrapping. Microtask scheduling — .then on an already-settled promise must still fire asynchronously. If it ran synchronously, whether your callback runs before or after the next line would depend on timing, and the same code would behave differently on a cache hit versus a miss. That guarantee is why promise code is reasonable at all.

The static methods

javascript · resolve, reject, all, allSettled, race, any
MyPromise.resolve = (value) =>
  value instanceof MyPromise ? value : new MyPromise((res) => res(value));

MyPromise.reject = (reason) => new MyPromise((_, rej) => rej(reason));

// ALL — fails fast. One rejection rejects the whole thing, and the
// other promises keep running; they are not cancelled, because
// promises have no cancellation.
MyPromise.all = (iterable) => new MyPromise((resolve, reject) => {
  const items = [...iterable];
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let remaining = items.length;
  if (remaining === 0) return resolve([]);        // empty resolves now

  items.forEach((item, i) => {
    MyPromise.resolve(item).then((value) => {
      results[i] = value;                          // ORDER is by index,
      if (--remaining === 0) resolve(results);     // not by completion
    }, reject);
  });
});

// ALL SETTLED — never rejects. Every entry reports its outcome.
MyPromise.allSettled = (iterable) => {
  const items = [...iterable].map((item) =>
    MyPromise.resolve(item).then(
      (value)  => ({ status: 'fulfilled', value }),
      (reason) => ({ status: 'rejected', reason }),
    ));
  return MyPromise.all(items);
};

// RACE — first to SETTLE wins, fulfilled or rejected.
MyPromise.race = (iterable) => new MyPromise((resolve, reject) => {
  for (const item of iterable) MyPromise.resolve(item).then(resolve, reject);
  // An empty iterable stays pending forever. That is per spec, and it
  // is a real deadlock source.
});

// ANY — first to FULFIL wins; rejects only if all reject.
MyPromise.any = (iterable) => new MyPromise((resolve, reject) => {
  const items = [...iterable];
  const errors = new Array(items.length);
  let remaining = items.length;
  if (remaining === 0) {
    return reject(new AggregateError([], 'All promises were rejected'));
  }
  items.forEach((item, i) => {
    MyPromise.resolve(item).then(resolve, (err) => {
      errors[i] = err;
      if (--remaining === 0) {
        reject(new AggregateError(errors, 'All promises were rejected'));
      }
    });
  });
});

// withResolvers (ES2024) — the deferred pattern, now built in.
MyPromise.withResolvers = () => {
  let resolve, reject;
  const promise = new MyPromise((res, rej) => { resolve = res; reject = rej; });
  return { promise, resolve, reject };
};

Choosing between the combinators

MethodResolves whenRejects whenUse for
allAll fulfilAny rejects (immediately)Parallel data a page cannot render without
allSettledAll settleNeverIndependent work where partial success is fine — sending N emails, warming N caches
raceFirst settles (either way)First settles with a rejectionTimeouts, first-response-wins
anyFirst fulfilsAll reject (AggregateError)Redundant mirrors where one success is enough
Promise.all does not cancel the losers

When one promise rejects, all rejects immediately — but the other requests are still in flight and will still complete, still consume quota, and still write to whatever they were going to write. Promises are not cancellable by design: a promise is a value that will exist, and a consumer cannot revoke it because other consumers may be waiting on the same one. If you need real cancellation, the work must accept an AbortSignal; Promise.all only stops you waiting.

The patterns worth having

javascript · timeout, retry, concurrency limit, promisify
// TIMEOUT — race against a timer, and clear the timer either way so
// you do not keep the event loop alive for nothing.
function withTimeout(promise, ms, message = 'Timed out') {
  let timer;
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(message)), ms);
  });
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}
// Better, when the work supports it — actually abort it:
function fetchWithTimeout(url, ms) {
  return fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) });
}

// RETRY with exponential backoff and jitter. The jitter matters: a
// thousand clients retrying at exactly 1s, 2s, 4s produce synchronised
// thundering herds that keep the service down.
async function retry(fn, { attempts = 3, base = 200, factor = 2, signal } = {}) {
  let lastError;
  for (let i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn(i);
    } catch (err) {
      if (signal?.aborted || err.name === 'AbortError') throw err;
      if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;       // do not retry a 400
      lastError = err;
      if (i === attempts - 1) break;
      const delay = base * factor ** i * (0.5 + Math.random());
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
    }
  }
  throw lastError;
}

// CONCURRENCY LIMIT — 500 items, at most 5 in flight. Mapping with
// Promise.all over 500 URLs opens 500 connections and gets you
// rate-limited or blocked.
async function pool(items, limit, worker) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  const runners = Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) },
    async () => {
      while (next < items.length) {
        const i = next++;
        results[i] = await worker(items[i], i);
      }
    });
  await Promise.all(runners);
  return results;
}

// PROMISIFY — wrapping a callback API.
const promisify = (fn) => (...args) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    fn(...args, (err, value) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve(value))));

Microtasks, and why ordering surprises people

javascript · predict the output before reading on
console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('4'));
console.log('5');

// 1, 5, 3, 4, 2
//
// Synchronous code first: 1, 5.
// Then the MICROTASK queue drains completely: 3, 4.
// Only then does the event loop take one MACROTASK: 2.
//
// The consequence that matters: microtasks can starve the event loop.
// A .then that schedules another .then forever will never let a
// setTimeout, a click handler or a paint through — the page freezes
// with no error and no busy loop to find in a profiler.

// And this is why React's batching works the way it does: state
// updates are processed in a microtask, so everything in one
// synchronous block is batched into a single render.

async/await is this, with syntax

An async function always returns a promise

Even one with no await and a plain return 1 — the value is wrapped. And await on a non-promise still yields to the microtask queue, so await 1 is not free. The practical consequence is the one from R08: two awaits in a row are two round trips, and if the second does not depend on the first, they should be Promise.all. Start both, then await both — const a = f(); const b = g(); await Promise.all([a, b]) works too, because the calls start the work and the await only decides when you block.

Interview follow-up

“Implement Promise.all.” The four things being checked: a counter rather than a length check, since results arrive out of order; writing into results[i] so output order matches input order rather than completion order; wrapping each item in Promise.resolve so non-promise values work; and handling the empty iterable, which must resolve immediately rather than hang. If you finish early, add the thing most candidates miss — that a rejection does not cancel the others, so a failed all still leaves work running.

J09

Errors: try, catch, finally and the failure model

Most codebases handle errors by accident. A try/catch gets added where one crashed, a console.error where someone was debugging, and the result is an application that fails in ways nobody designed. This chapter is the mechanics — what catch can and cannot reach — and then the design decision that matters: which failures are values and which are exceptions.

The mechanics

javascript · the parts people get wrong
try {
  risky();
} catch (err) {            // the binding is optional since ES2019:
  handle(err);             // `catch { }` is legal when you do not
} finally {                // need the error
  cleanup();               // runs on success, on throw, AND on an
}                          // early return from inside try

// FINALLY BEATS RETURN — and this is a real bug source:
function f() {
  try { return 'a'; }
  finally { return 'b'; }   // returns 'b'. The 'a' is discarded.
}
// A `return` or `throw` inside finally overrides whatever the try or
// catch was going to do, including swallowing an in-flight exception.
// Never return or throw from finally; use it only for cleanup.

// THROW ANYTHING — JavaScript does not require an Error.
throw 'something broke';           // legal, and awful
throw { code: 500 };               // legal, and awful
// Both lose the stack trace. Always throw an Error:
throw new Error('Upload failed');

// So `err` in a catch is genuinely unknown. In TypeScript it is typed
// `unknown` for exactly this reason, and normalising is worth doing:
function toError(value) {
  if (value instanceof Error) return value;
  return new Error(typeof value === 'string' ? value : JSON.stringify(value));
}

What catch cannot reach

A try/catch guards the synchronous call stack it wraps. Nothing else. ✗ a callback that runs later try { setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('boom'); }, 0); } catch (e) { /* NEVER RUNS */ } By the time the callback executes, the try block has long since returned and its stack frame is gone. The error becomes an uncaught exception at the top level. ✗ a promise you did not await try { doAsyncThing(); // no await } catch (e) { /* NEVER RUNS */ } The function returns a promise immediately; the rejection happens later. This is the single most common version of the mistake, and it produces an unhandled rejection with a stack trace pointing somewhere unhelpful. ✗ an event handler button.addEventListener('click', () => { throw x; }); Same reason: a different turn of the event loop. ✓ what it DOES reach synchronous throws, and awaited rejections — because await re-enters the function's own stack frame, which is precisely what makes async/await worth using.

Async error handling

javascript
// await turns a rejection into a throw, so try/catch works normally:
async function save(data) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/save', { method: 'POST', body: data });

    // fetch does NOT reject on 4xx or 5xx. It only rejects on network
    // failure, CORS, or abort. This check is not optional.
    if (!res.ok) {
      throw new HttpError(res.status, await res.text());
    }
    return await res.json();      // note the await: without it, a JSON
                                  // parse failure escapes this try
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;      // expected, not an error
    throw err;                                   // let the caller decide
  }
}

// PARALLEL failures: Promise.all rejects with the FIRST rejection and
// discards the rest. If you need all of them, use allSettled:
const results = await Promise.allSettled([a(), b(), c()]);
const failures = results.filter(r => r.status === 'rejected');

// THE FLOATING PROMISE — the bug a linter should catch for you:
