saveDraft();          // fire-and-forget: a rejection here is unhandled
void saveDraft().catch(reportError);   // explicit, and honest

// Top-level nets. These are for REPORTING, not recovery:
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', (e) => {
  report(e.reason);
  e.preventDefault();      // stops the console noise; does not fix it
});
window.addEventListener('error', (e) => report(e.error));

Typed errors

javascript · lib/errors.ts
export class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, { code, status = 500, cause, expected = false } = {}) {
    super(message, { cause });        // `cause` preserves the original
    this.name = new.target.name;      // so the subclass name shows up
    this.code = code;
    this.status = status;
    this.expected = expected;         // is this a normal outcome?
    Error.captureStackTrace?.(this, new.target);   // V8: trim the frame
  }
}

export class ValidationError extends AppError {
  constructor(fields) {
    super('Validation failed', { code: 'VALIDATION', status: 422, expected: true });
    this.fields = fields;
  }
}
export class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(what) {
    super(`${what} not found`, { code: 'NOT_FOUND', status: 404, expected: true });
  }
}
export class HttpError extends AppError {
  constructor(status, body) {
    super(`HTTP ${status}`, { code: 'HTTP', status });
    this.body = body;
  }
}

// `cause` (ES2022) is how you keep the original without losing context:
try {
  await db.insert(row);
} catch (err) {
  throw new AppError('Could not save the notebook', { cause: err });
}
// The logger prints both; the user sees only the outer message.

// instanceof works across your own code, but NOT across a serialisation
// boundary — an error sent from a Server Function to the client arrives
// as a plain object. Check a `code` field there, not the class.
Expected failures are values; unexpected failures are exceptions

This is the design decision the whole chapter is for. A validation failure, a 404, a declined card, a duplicate email — these are normal outcomes of a correct program, and modelling them as thrown exceptions means every call site needs a try/catch to handle a case the type system never mentioned. Return them: { ok: false, error }, or an action's state object. A failed database connection, a bug, a null dereference — these are not normal, nobody can meaningfully handle them locally, and they should propagate to a boundary that logs and shows a generic message. Get this split right and most of your try/catch blocks disappear.

Result-style errors in practice

How this maps onto React

Where it failsCaught byWhat you do
During renderAn error boundaryNothing — it is a bug; log it and show a fallback
In an event handlerNothingtry/catch in the handler, then set error state
In an effect's async callbackNothingCatch inside; ignore AbortError; set error state
In a data fetch under SuspenseThe nearest error boundaryProvide a retry via reset
In a Server FunctionThe boundary, if thrownReturn expected failures as state instead
In a Server Componenterror.tsx for that segmentLog with the digest; show a reference code
In the root layoutglobal-error.tsxKeep it dependency-free — everything else has failed
javascript · the two React-specific traps
// 1 · An error boundary does NOT catch this, because the throw happens
//     in a different turn of the event loop:
<button onClick={async () => {
  await deleteItem(id);        // if this rejects, the boundary never
}}>Delete</button>             // sees it — and neither does the user

//     Do this instead:
const [error, setError] = useState(null);
async function onDelete() {
  setError(null);
  try {
    await deleteItem(id);
  } catch (err) {
    setError(err instanceof AppError ? err.message : 'Could not delete.');
  }
}

// 2 · redirect() and notFound() in Next.js WORK BY THROWING. A
//     try/catch around them swallows the control-flow error, so the
//     redirect silently never happens and your catch reports a failure
//     for an operation that succeeded.
try {
  await createPost(data);
  redirect('/posts');          // ✗ swallowed
} catch (err) { … }

let post;
try { post = await createPost(data); }
catch (err) { return { error: 'Could not save.' }; }
redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`);  // ✓ outside the try

What to show the user, and what to log

LOG everything: the error, its cause chain, the stack, a request id, the route, the user id where lawful. Structured JSON, one line, to stdout. SHOW for an expected failure: exactly what went wrong and what to do — "That email is already registered. Sign in instead?" for an unexpected failure: a generic message plus a reference the user can quote. Never the raw message — it leaks table names, file paths and query fragments. NEVER swallow silently. `catch (e) {}` is a decision to make a future incident undiagnosable. If a failure genuinely does not matter, say so in a comment and log at debug level — do not write an empty block. RETRY only what can plausibly succeed on a second attempt: a network blip, a 429, a 503. Never a 400, a 401, or a validation failure — retrying those is just load.
The empty catch block is the most expensive line in most codebases

It converts a loud failure into a silent wrong answer. The page renders, the data is stale or missing, nothing is logged, and six weeks later someone is reading the code trying to work out why a field is occasionally blank. If you cannot handle an error, let it propagate to something that can; if you are deliberately ignoring one — an aborted fetch, an analytics call that failed — write the comment saying so, and narrow the catch to that specific case rather than swallowing everything.

Interview follow-up

“Why does this try/catch not catch the error?” — shown with a throw inside a setTimeout or an un-awaited promise. The answer is that try/catch guards a synchronous call stack, and by the time the callback runs that stack frame no longer exists; await is the exception because it resumes the original frame. The follow-up that separates candidates is the design question: which failures should throw at all. Expected outcomes — validation, not-found, conflict — are better returned as values, because throwing hides them from the signature and forces every caller to guess; exceptions are for the genuinely unexpected, handled once at a boundary.

J10

Debounce, throttle and rate limiting — implemented

Three techniques for doing less work, constantly confused with each other because all three involve a timer. They answer different questions: debounce asks has it stopped?, throttle asks has enough time passed?, and rate limiting asks have we used our budget? Each is a short function, and writing them is a standard interview exercise.

The difference, on a timeline

Events: ●●●●● ● ●●●●●●●●●●●●●● ─────────────────────────────────────────▶ time DEBOUNCE (trailing, 300ms) — fire once, after it goes quiet ▲ ▲ ▲ Waits for a gap. Bursts collapse to one call. If events never stop, it never fires — which is why a debounce with no maxWait can starve. → search-as-you-type, autosave, resize-complete THROTTLE (300ms) — fire at most once per interval ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ Steady rate regardless of burst shape. Fires during a continuous stream, which debounce does not. → scroll position, mousemove, progress updates RATE LIMIT (5 per minute) — a budget, then refusal ▲▲▲▲▲ ✗✗✗✗✗ ✗✗✗ ─── refill ─── ▲▲▲ Not about smoothing; about a quota you must not exceed. Excess is rejected or queued, not merged. → API quotas, login attempts, expensive endpoints The one-line test: if merging the extra calls is correct, you want debounce or throttle. If the extra calls must be refused, you want a rate limiter.

Debounce, built up

javascript · the naive version, then the real one
// The eight-line version everyone writes first. Fine for a search box.
function debounce(fn, wait = 300) {
  let timer;
  return function (...args) {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), wait);
    //                                  ^ apply, not fn(...args), so
    //                                    `this` survives when it is a
    //                                    method
  };
}

// The production version. Four additions, each earning its place:
//   leading  — fire immediately on the first call of a burst
//   maxWait  — guarantee it fires even if events never stop
//   cancel   — drop a pending call (for cleanup)
//   flush    — run a pending call now (for "save before you navigate")
function debounce(fn, wait = 300, { leading = false, trailing = true,
                                    maxWait = null } = {}) {
  let timer = null, maxTimer = null;
  let lastArgs = null, lastThis = null, result;

  function invoke() {
    clearTimeout(maxTimer); maxTimer = null;
    const args = lastArgs, ctx = lastThis;
    lastArgs = lastThis = null;
    result = fn.apply(ctx, args);
    return result;
  }

  function debounced(...args) {
    lastArgs = args; lastThis = this;
    const isFirst = timer === null;

    if (isFirst && leading) invoke();

    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => {
      timer = null;
      // Do not fire again for a burst of exactly one when leading
      // already handled it.
      if (trailing && lastArgs) invoke();
    }, wait);

    // maxWait: the escape hatch for a stream that never pauses.
    if (maxWait != null && maxTimer === null) {
      maxTimer = setTimeout(() => {
        clearTimeout(timer); timer = null;
        if (lastArgs) invoke();
      }, maxWait);
    }
    return result;
  }

  debounced.cancel = () => {
    clearTimeout(timer); clearTimeout(maxTimer);
    timer = maxTimer = lastArgs = lastThis = null;
  };
  debounced.flush = () => (lastArgs ? invoke() : result);
  debounced.pending = () => timer !== null;

  return debounced;
}

Throttle

javascript · timestamp-based, plus the rAF version
function throttle(fn, interval = 200, { leading = true, trailing = true } = {}) {
  let last = 0, timer = null, lastArgs = null, lastThis = null;

  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now();
    lastArgs = args; lastThis = this;

    // Skipping the leading call means the first event in a burst is
    // delayed by a full interval — usually wrong for scroll.
    if (!last && !leading) last = now;

    const remaining = interval - (now - last);

    if (remaining <= 0) {
      clearTimeout(timer); timer = null;
      last = now;
      fn.apply(lastThis, lastArgs);
      lastArgs = null;
    } else if (trailing && !timer) {
      // Guarantee the FINAL event is not dropped — without this, the
      // last scroll position before stopping is never recorded.
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        last = leading ? Date.now() : 0;
        timer = null;
        if (lastArgs) { fn.apply(lastThis, lastArgs); lastArgs = null; }
      }, remaining);
    }
  };
}

// For anything that touches layout or paint — scroll, resize,
// mousemove-driven positioning — rAF is better than a timer: it runs
// once per frame, aligned with the browser's paint, so you never do
// two updates the user cannot see.
function rafThrottle(fn) {
  let queued = false, lastArgs;
  return function (...args) {
    lastArgs = args;
    if (queued) return;
    queued = true;
    requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      queued = false;
      fn.apply(this, lastArgs);
    });
  };
}
// Also: prefer IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver and CSS
// scroll-driven animations to a throttled scroll listener where they
// apply. They do the work off the main thread entirely.

Rate limiting

javascript · token bucket and sliding window
// TOKEN BUCKET — allows a burst up to `capacity`, then a steady rate.
// This is what most APIs actually implement, and what you want for a
// client that should be allowed to be briefly busy.
class TokenBucket {
  constructor({ capacity = 10, refillPerSecond = 2 }) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
    this.tokens = capacity;
    this.rate = refillPerSecond;
    this.last = Date.now();
  }
  #refill() {
    const now = Date.now();
    this.tokens = Math.min(
      this.capacity,
      this.tokens + ((now - this.last) / 1000) * this.rate,
    );
    this.last = now;
  }
  tryTake(n = 1) {
    this.#refill();
    if (this.tokens >= n) { this.tokens -= n; return { ok: true }; }
    const deficit = n - this.tokens;
    return { ok: false, retryAfter: Math.ceil(deficit / this.rate) };
  }
  // Queue instead of refusing, when the caller can wait:
  async take(n = 1) {
    for (;;) {
      const r = this.tryTake(n);
      if (r.ok) return;
      await new Promise((res) => setTimeout(res, r.retryAfter * 1000));
    }
  }
}

// SLIDING WINDOW — simpler to reason about for "N per minute" rules
// such as login attempts, where a burst is exactly what you want to
// prevent.
class SlidingWindow {
  #hits = new Map();                       // key -> timestamps[]
  constructor({ limit = 5, windowMs = 60_000 }) {
    this.limit = limit; this.windowMs = windowMs;
  }
  check(key) {
    const now = Date.now();
    const cutoff = now - this.windowMs;
    const hits = (this.#hits.get(key) ?? []).filter((t) => t > cutoff);
    if (hits.length >= this.limit) {
      return { ok: false, retryAfter: Math.ceil((hits[0] - cutoff) / 1000) };
    }
    hits.push(now);
    this.#hits.set(key, hits);
    return { ok: true, remaining: this.limit - hits.length };
  }
}
In-memory rate limiting does not work on more than one server

Every instance keeps its own counter, so a limit of 5 becomes 5 × N across N instances — and on serverless it is worse, because each cold start begins with an empty map and an attacker gets a fresh budget by arriving at a new instance. Real rate limiting needs a shared store: Redis with an atomic increment-and-expire, or a managed limiter. Key it by user id and by IP, because keying only by user lets an attacker create accounts and keying only by IP punishes everyone behind one NAT. And rate limiting on the client is a courtesy, never a control — anyone can call your endpoint directly.

Using them in React

javascript · the idiomatic React version — no debounce function at all
// Debouncing a VALUE rather than a callback fits React's model better:
// the cleanup function IS the debounce, and there is nothing to cancel
// on unmount because React does it for you.
function useDebounced(value, delay = 300) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);      // every change cancels the last
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}

function Search() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const debounced = useDebounced(query, 300);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!debounced) return;
    const c = new AbortController();
    search(debounced, { signal: c.signal }).then(setResults).catch(ignoreAbort);
    return () => c.abort();            // and the RACE is handled too
  }, [debounced]);

  return <input value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} />;
}

// And for the specific case of "the input must stay fast while an
// expensive render lags", React has a built-in that needs no timer at
// all — it yields to input instead of waiting a fixed delay (R14, W06):
const deferred = useDeferredValue(query);
const results = useMemo(() => filter(items, deferred), [items, deferred]);

Which one, when

SituationUseWhy
Search-as-you-type against a serverDebounce ~300ms + abortOnly the final query matters; cancel the rest
Filtering a list already in memoryuseDeferredValueNo network, so no delay is needed — just lower priority
Autosave a draftDebounce 1–2s with maxWaitSave when they pause, but never go minutes without saving
Scroll position, sticky headersrafThrottleOnce per frame is the most that can ever be visible
Window resize layoutResizeObserver, else throttle + trailingThe final size must be applied, so trailing is mandatory
Analytics on mousemoveThrottle 100–200msContinuous stream; debounce would fire only when they stop
A button that hits an expensive endpointDisable while pendingClearer than any timer, and it tells the user why
Login attempts, OTP sendsServer-side sliding windowMust be refused, and must be enforced where it cannot be bypassed
Calling a third-party API with a quotaToken bucket + concurrency poolSmooth the rate and cap parallelism (J08)
Debouncing is not a substitute for cancelling

A 300 ms debounce reduces ten requests to one, but the one it sends can still be overtaken: type rea, pause, type ct, and if the first response is slow it can land after the second and leave the wrong results on screen. Debounce controls how often you start work; an AbortController controls what happens to work already started. Search boxes need both, and the second is the one that causes the bug report nobody can reproduce.

Interview follow-up

“Implement debounce, then throttle.” Write the eight-line debounce, then say out loud what it is missing — leading edge, maxWait so a continuous stream still fires, and cancel for cleanup — and add whichever they want. For throttle, the detail that gets noticed is the trailing call: without it the last event in a burst is dropped, so a throttled scroll handler never records the final position. Close with the React-specific point that a debounced function created in the component body is recreated every render and therefore never debounces anything, which is the version of this bug that actually ships.

R01

State, and why it behaves like a snapshot

useState is four lines of API and one genuinely surprising idea: within a single render, state is a constant. Setting it does not change the variable you are looking at — it schedules a new render in which a new variable will hold the new value. Nearly every “why is my state one step behind” question comes from missing that.

The API

const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue)
javascript · every form of it
const [count, setCount]   = useState(0);
const [user, setUser]     = useState(null);
const [items, setItems]   = useState([]);          // never useState() for arrays
const [form, setForm]     = useState({ name: '', email: '' });

// LAZY INITIALISER. The argument form runs on EVERY render and throws
// the result away after the first; the function form runs once.
const [data, setData] = useState(expensiveParse(raw));     // runs every render
const [data, setData] = useState(() => expensiveParse(raw)); // runs once

// Which matters more than it looks for anything touching storage:
const [theme, setTheme] = useState(() => localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? 'light');

// DIRECT vs UPDATER
setCount(5);                 // "the next value is 5"
setCount(c => c + 1);        // "the next value is one more than whatever
                             //  it is when this is applied"

// The updater is not optional styling. Use it whenever the next value
// depends on the current one, because `count` in scope is this render's
// value and may already be stale.

State is a snapshot

A render is a photograph. Everything in the component function — variables, props, event handlers, effect callbacks — belongs to that one photograph and never changes afterwards. render #1 count = 0 ├─ handleClick closes over count = 0 ← forever └─ effect closes over count = 0 click → setCount(1) → React schedules render #2 render #2 count = 1 ← a NEW variable ├─ handleClick a NEW function, count = 1 └─ effect a NEW closure, count = 1 Render #1's handleClick still exists, still sees 0, and will keep seeing 0 if anything still holds a reference to it — a timer, a promise, a subscription. So this logs 0, not 1: function handleClick() { setCount(count + 1); console.log(count); 0 — `count` is a const in this scope } React cannot change it. count is a const binding created when the function ran; reassigning it is not something a setter can do from outside. Nothing about this is a React quirk (J02).
javascript · the three consequences you will meet
// 1 · Multiple sets in one handler do not accumulate.
function handleTriple() {
  setCount(count + 1);    // count is 0 → schedules 1
  setCount(count + 1);    // count is STILL 0 → schedules 1
  setCount(count + 1);    // still 0 → schedules 1
}                         // result: 1

function handleTripleFixed() {
  setCount(c => c + 1);   // 0 → 1
  setCount(c => c + 1);   // 1 → 2
  setCount(c => c + 1);   // 2 → 3
}                         // result: 3

// 2 · An async callback sees the value from when it was created.
function handleDelayed() {
  setCount(count + 1);
  setTimeout(() => alert(count), 3000);   // the OLD value, 3s later
}

// 3 · Reading state right after setting it never works.
function handleSave() {
  setSaving(true);
  save(form);
  console.log(saving);    // false — this render's value
}

Batching

React does not re-render per setter call. It collects every update triggered by the same "unit of work" and renders once at the end. onClick ├─ setA(1) ┐ ├─ setB(2) ├─ batched └─ setC(3) ┘ → one render, with all three applied React 18 made this universal. Before it, batching happened only inside React event handlers; updates in a promise, a timeout or a native event listener each triggered their own render. // React 17: two renders. React 18+: one. fetch(url).then(() => { setLoading(false); setData(d); }); Opting out, for the rare case where you need the DOM updated before the next statement: import { flushSync } from 'react-dom'; flushSync(() => setItems(next)); // DOM is updated synchronously listRef.current.scrollTop = listRef.current.scrollHeight; flushSync forfeits the batching and any concurrent scheduling for that update. It is an escape hatch for measuring or scrolling right after a change, not a fix for "my state is stale".

How the updates are applied

javascript · the queue, and what it means for mixing forms
// React keeps a QUEUE of pending updates per state, and applies them in
// order when it computes the next render's value.
//
//   setCount(5)        → queue: [replace with 5]
//   setCount(c => c+1) → queue: [replace with 5, then apply c => c+1]
//   → next value: 6

function handleMixed() {
  setCount(count + 5);    // replace: 0 + 5 = 5
  setCount(c => c + 1);   // update:  5 + 1 = 6
  setCount(42);           // replace: 42   ← discards everything before it
}                         // result: 42

// A direct value DISCARDS earlier queued updates, because "the next
// value is 42" says nothing about what came before. That is why mixing
// the two forms in one handler is a reliable source of confusion, and
// why the updater form should be the default.
The updater function must be pure

React may call it more than once — in StrictMode during development it deliberately does, to surface impurity. So it must compute a value from its argument and do nothing else: no fetch, no logging you care about, no mutation of anything outside. The most common violation is mutating the previous state and returning it: setItems(prev => { prev.push(x); return prev; }) returns the same reference, so React bails out and nothing renders (J03).

Bail-out

javascript · setting the same value is (mostly) free
// If the new value is Object.is-equal to the current one, React skips
// the re-render entirely.
setCount(count);                 // no render
setUser(user);                   // no render — same reference
setItems([...items]);            // RENDERS — new array, different reference

// One detail that surprises people: React may still render ONCE more
// before bailing out, because the check happens after it has begun
// processing the update. It will not render the children, and it will
// not commit — but the component function may run. This is why a
// console.log in the body can appear when "nothing changed".

// The practical form of this: a state update that produces an equal
// object still re-renders, so normalising before setting is worthwhile
// on hot paths.
setFilters(prev =>
  prev.query === query ? prev : { ...prev, query }   // keep the reference
);

Structuring state

RuleWhy
Group values that change together{ x, y } for a position beats two states you must always set together and can forget to
Split values that change independentlyOne giant object means every update spreads the whole thing and re-renders everything reading it
Avoid contradictory stateisLoading + isError allows true/true. One status string cannot (J04)
Avoid redundant stateA fullName alongside first and last will drift. Compute it (R09)
Avoid duplicated stateStore a selectedId, not a copy of the selected object — the copy goes stale when the list updates
Avoid deeply nested stateThree levels of spread is the signal to normalise (J03)

When state resets

State lives at a position in the tree, not in the component

React keeps state keyed by where a component sits in the render tree — its type and its position among siblings. Render the same component in the same place and state survives; render a different component type there, or move it to a different position, and the old state is discarded. This is why {cond ? <Input /> : <Input />} preserves state (same type, same slot) while {cond ? <Input /> : <div><Input /></div>} does not. It is also the mechanism behind resetting with key (R03), and it is a favourite interview question because the answer is “position”, not “props”.

Interview follow-up

“Why does calling setCount(count + 1) three times only increment once?” Because count is a const belonging to the current render — all three calls read the same value, so all three schedule “set it to 1”. React batches them and renders once. The updater form setCount(c => c + 1) queues functions that each receive the result of the previous one, giving 3. The follow-up worth pre-empting is why React works this way at all: a render must be a consistent snapshot, so props and state cannot change midway through a component function — otherwise the top and bottom of the same render could disagree.

R02

Rendering and re-rendering

“Re-render” is the most overloaded word in React, and most confusion about performance comes from conflating three separate things: React calling your function, React comparing the result to the previous one, and the browser actually changing the DOM. They are not the same, and only the last one is usually expensive.

Three separate things

1 RENDER React calls your component function. It returns elements. Nothing has touched the DOM. Cost: running your JavaScript. Usually microseconds. 2 RECONCILE React compares the new element tree with the old one and works out the minimal set of changes. Cost: proportional to the tree size. Cheap per node. 3 COMMIT React applies those changes to the real DOM, then the browser recalculates style, layout and paint. Cost: by far the largest, and the only one users see. A render that produces an identical tree commits nothing. The function ran, the comparison ran, and the DOM was untouched — which is why "my component re-rendered 40 times" is often not a problem at all, and why measuring before memoising matters (R14).

What triggers a render

TriggerWhat re-renders
A state setter with a different valueThat component, and all of its descendants
A parent re-renderingEvery child, regardless of whether its props changed
A consumed context value changingEvery consumer of that context, wherever it sits
A subscribed external store changingComponents using useSyncExternalStore for it
The key changingUnmount and remount — a new component, with fresh state
Props changingNothing, by itself. Props change because the parent rendered — the parent render is the cause
React does not re-render a child because its props changed

It re-renders a child because the parent rendered, and it does so whether or not any prop is different. This is the fact that makes React's model simple and that surprises people who expect prop-level dependency tracking. It is also why memo exists: it inserts an explicit props comparison that React otherwise does not perform. Signals-based libraries such as Solid do the opposite — they track dependencies precisely and re-run only what reads the changed value — which is the core design difference between the two approaches.

javascript · the cascade, and the composition that stops it
function App() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>
      <ExpensiveTree />     {/* re-renders on every click.
                                 It takes no props at all. */}
    </div>
  );
}

// Fix 1 — move the state DOWN, so the expensive tree is not a sibling
// of the thing that changes. This is almost always the right answer and
// it needs no memoisation.
function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Counter />          {/* owns its own state */}
      <ExpensiveTree />    {/* never re-renders */}
    </div>
  );
}

// Fix 2 — pass it as CHILDREN. The element is created in a component
// that is not re-rendering, so React sees the same element object and
// skips the subtree entirely. No memo required.
function Wrapper({ children }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

<Wrapper><ExpensiveTree /></Wrapper>   {/* created by the PARENT */}

// Fix 3 — memo. Real, and the last resort, because it adds a comparison
// on every render and is defeated by a single unstable prop (R14).
const ExpensiveTree = memo(function ExpensiveTree() { … });
The children trick is worth understanding properly

When <ExpensiveTree /> is written inside Wrapper, a new element object is created every time Wrapper renders, so reconciliation has new work to do. When it is passed as children, the element was created by the parent, which did not re-render — so children is the same object reference, React's reconciler sees an identical element, and the whole subtree is skipped. It is memoisation without memo, it survives refactoring better, and it is the technique that most often makes a “we need to memo everything” conversation unnecessary.

Reading the render, in practice

React DevTools Profiler
Commit at 1,204ms — 18.2ms

  App                          0.4ms   rendered
  ├─ Header                    0.1ms   rendered (parent rendered)
  ├─ Sidebar                   ——      did not render (memo, props equal)
  └─ Dashboard                 17.4ms  rendered
     ├─ ChartPanel            16.9ms  ← the whole commit is this
     │  └─ recharts internals
     └─ StatsRow               0.3ms

# "Why did this render?" — enable it in the Profiler settings. It tells
# you which of the four causes applied:
#
#   · Props changed (name, name, name)
#   · Hooks changed
#   · Parent rendered
#   · Context changed
#
# "Parent rendered" with no prop changes is the signature of a cascade,
# and the fix is usually composition rather than memo.

StrictMode's double render

javascript · why your logs appear twice in development
<StrictMode>
  <App />
</StrictMode>

// In DEVELOPMENT ONLY, React calls each component function twice and
// runs each effect twice (mount → unmount → mount). It is deliberate,
// and it surfaces two classes of bug that would otherwise appear later:
//
//   1 · impure renders — a component that mutates something outside
//       itself produces different results on the second call
//   2 · missing effect cleanup — an effect that subscribes without
//       unsubscribing leaks visibly when run twice

function Bad({ items }) {
  items.push('x');          // visible immediately: the array grows by 2
  return <List items={items} />;
}

useEffect(() => {
  const sub = source.subscribe(handler);
  // Without the cleanup, StrictMode leaves TWO subscriptions — which is
  // exactly what happens in production on any re-run of the effect.
  return () => sub.unsubscribe();
}, []);

// It does NOT happen in production. Disabling StrictMode to "fix"
// double logs removes the check without removing the bug.

Rendering is not the DOM

A frequent misdiagnosis: "This component renders 60 times a second, we need memo" Check first. If each render produces the same tree, the commit does nothing and the cost is running your function — which for a component returning twenty elements is on the order of tens of microseconds. Sixty of those is one millisecond a second. What actually costs: · rendering a list of 5,000 rows, all at once → virtualise · a component doing real work in its body → useMemo · layout thrash: reading offsetHeight after a write → batch reads · a chart library re-initialising on every render → memo, or a ref · a context value that is a new object each render → memoise it (R11) Order of operations: profile → find the expensive commit → look at what is actually slow in it → fix that one thing. Blanket memoisation before measuring adds comparisons everywhere, makes the code harder to change, and reliably fails to help.
Interview follow-up

“When a component's state changes, what re-renders?” That component and every descendant, regardless of whether their props changed — and the important correction to volunteer is that props changing does not cause a render; the parent rendering does, which is also why the props changed. Then name the three fixes in order: move state down so the expensive subtree is not under the thing that changes; pass the subtree as children so its element is created by a component that did not re-render; and only then memo. Finishing with “and re-rendering is not the same as updating the DOM” is what separates this from a memorised answer.

R03

Lists, keys and identity

A key is not a performance hint. It is how you tell React which element in the new list corresponds to which element in the old one — and getting it wrong does not make rendering slow, it makes state attach itself to the wrong row.

Rendering a list

javascript
function TodoList({ todos }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.map(todo => (
        <TodoItem key={todo.id} todo={todo} />
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// `key` goes on the element returned by map — the outermost one — not
// on something inside it:
{todos.map(t => (
  <li key={t.id}><Row todo={t} /></li>      // correct
))}
{todos.map(t => (
  <li><Row key={t.id} todo={t} /></li>      // wrong: the li has no key
))}

// With a Fragment wrapper you need the long form, because <> takes no
// attributes:
{entries.map(e => (
  <React.Fragment key={e.id}>
    <dt>{e.term}</dt>
    <dd>{e.definition}</dd>
  </React.Fragment>
))}

// key is NOT a prop. It is extracted by React and is not readable
// inside the component:
function TodoItem({ key, todo }) {   // key is always undefined here
  …
}
// If the child needs the id, pass it separately: <Item key={id} id={id} />

What the key is actually for

When React reconciles two lists, it needs to answer one question per item: "is this the same thing as before, or a different thing?" Without keys it compares by POSITION. before: [ A , B , C ] after: [ Z , A , B , C ] ← Z was prepended position 0: A → Z "same slot, different content" → UPDATE A into Z position 1: B → A → UPDATE B into A position 2: C → B → UPDATE C into B position 3: — → C → CREATE C Four DOM operations, and every component's state stayed at its old position while the data moved past it. With keys it compares by IDENTITY. before: [ A:a , B:b , C:c ] after: [ Z:z , A:a , B:b , C:c ] z is new → CREATE a, b, c are unchanged → MOVE, keep their DOM nodes and their state One DOM insertion. And, far more importantly, a's state is still a's state.
The index-as-key bug, in full

key={index} means “the item at position 2 is the same thing as whatever was at position 2 before”, which is exactly the positional comparison keys exist to replace. Delete the first row of a list of inputs and every remaining row shifts up one index — so React thinks each row's content changed while its identity stayed, keeps the DOM nodes in place, and the text you typed into row 2 is now sitting next to row 1's data. Nothing errors. The list looks right until someone notices the values are attached to the wrong records.

Choosing a key

SourceVerdict
A database idBest. Stable, unique, already there
A natural unique field (slug, ISBN, email)Fine, if genuinely unique and it never changes
A client-generated id created when the item is createdCorrect for items with no server id yet — crypto.randomUUID() at creation
crypto.randomUUID() during renderBroken. A new key every render means unmount-and-remount, every time
JSON.stringify(item)Broken. The key changes whenever any field changes, destroying the row
The array indexAcceptable only if the list never reorders, never filters, never has items inserted or removed, and its items hold no state
Keys are scoped to their siblings, not global

Two different lists on the same page may both use key="1" without conflict, because React only compares keys among the children of the same parent. The common mistake in the other direction is combining two arrays into one list and getting duplicate keys — React warns, and then behaves unpredictably about which item is which. Namespace them when merging: key={`user-${u.id}`} and key={`team-${t.id}`}.

key as a reset mechanism

javascript · the other half of what keys do
// Because a changed key means "this is a different component instance",
// it is also the idiomatic way to force a remount and throw away state.

// 1 · Reset a form when the selected record changes (J07)
<EditForm key={selectedId} record={record} />

// 2 · Restart an animation or a video
<Player key={trackId} src={track.url} />

// 3 · Reset an error boundary after the user retries (R15)
<ErrorBoundary key={retryCount}><Widget /></ErrorBoundary>

// 4 · Clear a whole subtree's state on logout
<App key={session?.userId ?? 'anon'} />

// The alternative — an effect that resets state when a prop changes —
// renders once with the WRONG data, then again with the reset value,
// and is harder to read:
useEffect(() => { setName(record.name); }, [record.id]);   // avoid

Long lists

javascript · when the problem is genuinely the number of nodes
// 10,000 rows is 10,000 DOM nodes: slow to create, slow to lay out, and
// heavy on memory. No amount of memoisation helps, because the cost is
// in the commit, not the render (R02).
//
// Virtualisation renders only what is visible plus a small buffer.
import { useVirtualizer } from '@tanstack/react-virtual';

function BigList({ rows }) {
  const parentRef = useRef(null);
  const virtualizer = useVirtualizer({
    count: rows.length,
    getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current,
    estimateSize: () => 48,
    overscan: 8,
  });

  return (
    <div ref={parentRef} style={{ height: 600, overflow: 'auto' }}>
      <div style={{ height: virtualizer.getTotalSize(), position: 'relative' }}>
        {virtualizer.getVirtualItems().map(v => (
          <div
            key={rows[v.index].id}          // still the ITEM's id, not v.index
            style={{
              position: 'absolute', top: 0, left: 0, width: '100%',
              height: v.size, transform: `translateY(${v.start}px)`,
            }}
          >
            <Row row={rows[v.index]} />
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

// Before reaching for this: paginate. A user cannot read 10,000 rows,
// and 50 per page with a search box is usually the better product.
CSS content-visibility is the cheap first try

content-visibility: auto with a contain-intrinsic-size hint tells the browser to skip layout and paint for off-screen elements, which recovers a large part of the benefit of virtualisation for a one-line change and no library. It does not reduce the number of DOM nodes, so it will not save you at 50,000 rows, and it interacts awkwardly with in-page search. But for a list in the low thousands it is worth trying before restructuring the component.

Interview follow-up

“Why can't you use the array index as a key?” Because a key answers “is this the same item as before”, and the index answers “is this the same position” — which is precisely the positional matching that keys exist to replace. Give the concrete failure rather than the rule: delete the first row of a list of inputs and every subsequent row shifts index, so React keeps each DOM node in place and re-labels it, leaving typed text and focus attached to the wrong record. Add that the second job of key is the mirror image — changing it deliberately forces a remount, which is the idiomatic way to reset a form when the selected record changes.

R04

Conditional rendering

Showing different UI for different states is most of what a component does. The mechanics are ordinary JavaScript — but three details decide whether the result is readable and correct: the falsy-value trap, whether a branch preserves or destroys state, and when a chain of conditions is telling you the state shape is wrong.

The forms

javascript · five ways, and when each reads best
// 1 · Early return — best when a branch means "render nothing else".
function Profile({ user }) {
  if (!user) return <Skeleton />;
  return <div>{user.name}</div>;
}

// 2 · Ternary — best for two alternatives in one slot.
<div>{isLoggedIn ? <Dashboard /> : <Login />}</div>

// 3 · && — best for "show this or nothing". Mind the trap below.
{errors.length > 0 && <ErrorList errors={errors} />}

// 4 · A variable — best when the condition is long or nested.
let content;
if (status === 'loading')      content = <Spinner />;
else if (status === 'error')   content = <Error err={error} />;
else if (items.length === 0)   content = <Empty />;
else                           content = <List items={items} />;
return <section>{content}</section>;

// 5 · A lookup object — best for a closed set of variants.
const byStatus = {
  idle:    () => null,
  loading: () => <Spinner />,
  error:   () => <Error err={error} />,
  success: () => <List items={data} />,
};
return byStatus[status]();
// Functions rather than elements, so only the chosen branch is built.
The falsy trap, properly

React renders 0 and '' as text and ignores false, null and undefined. So {count && <Badge />} prints a bare 0 when the count is zero, and {name && <Label />} prints nothing visible but still creates a text node when the name is an empty string. The fix is to make the left side a genuine boolean — {count > 0 && …}, {!!name && …}, or a ternary ending in null. It is the most frequently seen React bug in code review and a standard interview question for exactly that reason.

Conditions change identity

javascript · the same component in a different position is a different component
// State is keyed by TYPE and POSITION in the tree (R01). These two look
// equivalent and behave completely differently.

// A · same type, same slot → state SURVIVES the toggle
{isEditing
  ? <Input value={draft} onChange={setDraft} />
  : <Input value={draft} onChange={setDraft} disabled />}

// B · different position → state is DESTROYED
{isEditing
  ? <Input … />
  : <div><Input … /></div>}     // now nested one level deeper

// C · the classic surprise: two branches, same component, same slot
{showA ? <Counter label="A" /> : <Counter label="B" />}
// Toggling keeps the COUNT, because React sees "a Counter in slot 0"
// both times and only the props changed. Usually not what you meant.

// Force separate identities when the branches are conceptually
// different things:
{showA
  ? <Counter key="a" label="A" />
  : <Counter key="b" label="B" />}
Mounting vs hiding — they are not the same, and the difference is usually the point. {isOpen && <Panel />} · not rendered at all when closed · state is destroyed on close, recreated on open · effects run on every open (subscribe / unsubscribe) · nothing in the DOM, so nothing to style or measure <Panel hidden={!isOpen} /> (CSS display:none) · always in the DOM · state and scroll position PRESERVED · effects run once · costs layout and memory while hidden Choose by what should happen to the state. A modal that should forget its form on close: unmount it. A tab panel the user flips between and expects to find as they left it: hide it. React 19.2 added <Activity mode="hidden">, which is the proper third option — the subtree is unmounted from the DOM but its state is preserved, and its effects are torn down. That is exactly the semantics tab UIs have always hand-rolled (N06).

Guard clauses beat nesting

An early return must come after every hook

Hooks are matched by call order (W05), so a return before a useState or useEffect changes how many hooks run and React throws “Rendered fewer hooks than expected”. Put every hook at the top of the component and every conditional return below them. If a branch genuinely needs different hooks, that is the signal to split it into two components and choose between them in the parent — which is also usually clearer.

When the conditions are telling you something

javascript · four booleans describing one thing
// Four booleans allow sixteen combinations, of which four are valid.
// You will eventually render one of the other twelve.
const [isLoading, setLoading] = useState(false);
const [isError, setError]     = useState(false);
const [isEmpty, setEmpty]     = useState(false);
const [isSuccess, setSuccess] = useState(false);

// One discriminated value makes the impossible states unrepresentable,
// and the rendering becomes a switch rather than a tree of guards:
const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle' });

switch (state.status) {
  case 'idle':    return null;
  case 'loading': return <Spinner />;
  case 'error':   return <Error err={state.error} />;
  case 'success':
    return state.data.length
      ? <List items={state.data} />
      : <Empty />;
}

// In TypeScript this also gives you exhaustiveness: adding a status and
// forgetting a branch becomes a compile error.
function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled status: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

Rendering nothing

javascript
return null;         // valid, renders nothing, component still "mounts"
return undefined;     // also valid since React 18
return false;         // valid
return <></>;         // an empty fragment — same result, more typing

// Returning null still MOUNTS the component: its hooks run, its effects
// run, and its state persists. That is often exactly what you want —
// a component that subscribes to something and renders nothing.
function KeyboardShortcuts() {
  useEffect(() => {
    const onKey = e => { if (e.key === '/') focusSearch(); };
    window.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
  }, []);
  return null;
}

// Contrast with not rendering it at all — {enabled && <KeyboardShortcuts />}
// — where the effect is torn down when `enabled` goes false.
Interview follow-up

“What is wrong with {items.length && <List />}?” It renders a literal 0 when the array is empty, because 0 && x evaluates to 0 and React renders numbers as text while ignoring false, null and undefined. Then take it one step further than asked, because that is what distinguishes the answer: the same pattern with a string renders an empty text node, and the general fix is to force a boolean on the left of && rather than to remember which values are falsy. Mentioning that a ternary ending in null avoids the whole class shows you have thought about the failure mode rather than the instance.

R05

Events

React's event system looks like the DOM's and differs in four ways that matter: handlers are props rather than listeners, the event object is React's own, everything is attached at the root rather than per element, and every handler is recreated on every render — which is where the memoisation conversation starts.

Attaching a handler

javascript · pass the function, do not call it
<button onClick={handleClick}>          // ✓ passes the function
<button onClick={handleClick()}>        // ✗ CALLS it during render and
                                        //   passes the return value
<button onClick={() => handleClick(id)}> // ✓ a new function that calls it

// The middle one is the single most common beginner error, and its
// symptom is memorable: the handler fires immediately on render, often
// setting state, which triggers a render, which fires it again — an
// infinite loop that freezes the tab.

// Passing arguments: an inline arrow is fine and is what everyone does.
{todos.map(todo => (
  <li key={todo.id} onClick={() => toggle(todo.id)}>{todo.text}</li>
))}

// The alternative, for a long list where the arrow allocation matters:
// put the data on the element and read it from the event.
<li data-id={todo.id} onClick={handleToggle}>
function handleToggle(e) { toggle(e.currentTarget.dataset.id); }
// Measure before doing this. An arrow per row is a few nanoseconds; the
// readability cost is permanent.

The synthetic event

React wraps the native event in a SyntheticEvent — a cross-browser object with the same interface plus nativeEvent. e.target the element that was actually clicked e.currentTarget the element the HANDLER is attached to ← usually what you want e.preventDefault() e.stopPropagation() e.nativeEvent the real DOM event, if you need it Delegation. React does not attach a listener per element. It attaches one listener per event type at the root container and dispatches from there, which is why 10,000 rows with onClick cost one real listener rather than 10,000. Two consequences of that: · e.stopPropagation() in a React handler stops propagation through React's tree. A native listener added with addEventListener on an ancestor DOM node still fires, because React's own listener is at the root and the native event has already bubbled past that ancestor. · In React 17 and later the root is your app container, not document. That matters when embedding React inside another app: a document-level listener sees the event first. Pre-React-17 pooling is gone. Events were recycled, so reading e.target asynchronously required e.persist(). Since React 17 the event object is ordinary and keeping it is safe.

The handlers you will actually use

PropFiresNote
onClickClick, and keyboard activation on buttons/linksUse a real <button>; a clickable div is not keyboard-accessible
onChangeEvery keystroke on an inputUnlike the DOM's change, which fires on blur. React normalises it to input
onInputSame as onChange in ReactPrefer onChange; they are aliases in practice
onBlur / onFocusFocus leaves / entersReact's versions bubble (they map to focusin/focusout)
onSubmitForm submissionNeeds e.preventDefault() unless you are using an Action (N01)
onKeyDownKey pressede.key for the character, e.code for the physical key
onPointerDownMouse, touch and pen, unifiedPrefer over separate mouse and touch handlers
onClickCaptureDuring the capture phaseEvery event has a *Capture variant
javascript · forms and keyboards
function SearchForm({ onSearch }) {
  const [q, setQ] = useState('');

  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();      // or the browser navigates and reloads
    onSearch(q.trim());
  }

  function handleKeyDown(e) {
    // e.key is what was typed; e.code is which physical key. For
    // shortcuts, e.key is usually right — and check the modifier
    // explicitly rather than assuming a platform.
    if (e.key === 'Escape') setQ('');
    if (e.key === 'Enter' && (e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey)) handleSubmit(e);
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input
        value={q}
        onChange={e => setQ(e.target.value)}
        onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}
      />
      <button type="submit">Search</button>
      {/* type="button" on anything inside a form that should NOT submit
          — the default is "submit", which catches everyone once */}
      <button type="button" onClick={() => setQ('')}>Clear</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Handler identity

javascript · a new function every render, and when that matters
function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  // A NEW function object on every render. That is normal and almost
  // always free.
  const handleClick = () => console.log('clicked');

  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>

      {/* For a DOM element: irrelevant. React swaps the stored handler
          and does not touch the DOM. */}
      <button onClick={handleClick}>plain</button>

      {/* For a memo'd child: this DEFEATS the memo, because the prop is
          a different reference every time (R14). */}
      <MemoChild onClick={handleClick} />

      {/* For an effect dependency: this re-runs the effect every render. */}
    </>
  );
}

// The fix is useCallback — and only where one of those two cases
// actually applies:
const handleClick = useCallback(() => console.log('clicked'), []);

// The React Compiler memoises these automatically, which is why
// hand-written useCallback is shrinking as a practice (W07).
Wrapping every handler in useCallback is a net loss

useCallback is not free: it allocates, it stores the function and its dependency array, and it runs a comparison on every render. For a handler passed to a plain DOM element it buys nothing at all, because React simply swaps the stored reference. It pays only when the consumer performs a reference comparison — a memo'd child, a dependency array, or an external subscription. Applying it everywhere makes the code noisier, adds work, and hides the two places where it genuinely mattered.

Native listeners, and when you need one

javascript · the cases React's props cannot cover
// 1 · Listening on window or document
useEffect(() => {
  function onKey(e) { if (e.key === 'Escape') close(); }
  window.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);
  return () => window.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
}, [close]);

// 2 · A non-passive listener. React attaches scroll and touch listeners
//     as PASSIVE for performance, so preventDefault() in a React
//     onTouchMove handler does nothing. You must attach it yourself.
useEffect(() => {
  const el = ref.current;
  function onWheel(e) { e.preventDefault(); zoom(e.deltaY); }
  el.addEventListener('wheel', onWheel, { passive: false });
  return () => el.removeEventListener('wheel', onWheel);
}, []);

// 3 · Events React does not synthesise, or custom events from a
//     non-React widget:
el.addEventListener('my-widget:selected', handler);

// 4 · Interop: a React handler's stopPropagation does NOT stop a native
//     listener on an ancestor, because React listens at the root. If
//     you need that, stop the native event:
function handleClick(e) {
  e.nativeEvent.stopImmediatePropagation();
}
Accessibility is decided by the element you pick

An onClick on a div is invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users: it is not focusable, Enter and Space do nothing, and it is announced as a generic group. A <button> gets all of that free, and a <a href> additionally supports open-in-new-tab and is announced as a link. If you genuinely must make a non-interactive element interactive you owe it role, tabIndex={0}, and key handling for both Enter and Space — which is three lines to reimplement badly what the right tag already does.

Interview follow-up

“How does React's event system differ from the DOM's?” Handlers are props rather than registered listeners, the event is React's synthetic wrapper with a normalised cross-browser interface, and — the part worth leading with — React attaches one listener per event type at the root container and delegates, so a thousand rows cost one real listener. Then give the consequence that actually bites: stopPropagation in a React handler stops React's own propagation, but a native addEventListener on an intermediate DOM node has already fired, because the event only reaches React at the root. Adding that event pooling was removed in React 17 shows you know the history rather than a cached blog post.

R06

Forms: controlled and uncontrolled

There are two ways to run a form in React, and the industry has been quietly shifting between them. Controlled inputs put React in charge of every keystroke; uncontrolled inputs let the DOM keep the value and read it at submit. React 19's Actions push the second one back into favour for a large class of forms.

The two models

ControlledUncontrolled
Source of truthReact stateThe DOM node
Renders per keystrokeOneZero
Live validationEasyNeeds a listener, or wait for submit
Formatting as you typeEasyAwkward
Conditional fields depending on valuesEasyNeeds some state anyway
Reading at submitAlready in statenew FormData(form)
ResettingSet state backform.reset(), or a key
Best forSearch-as-you-type, dependent fields, masked inputMost forms: login, settings, anything submitted as a whole
Default to uncontrolled, reach for controlled per field

The received wisdom that “forms should be controlled” comes from an era before Actions and before the modern form libraries, and it costs a render per keystroke across every field in the form. Start with FormData at submit, and promote an individual field to controlled when it genuinely needs live behaviour — a search box that filters as you type, a card number that formats itself, a field that shows or hides another. Mixing the two in one form is normal and is not a smell.

The controlled input, correctly

javascript · one state object for the whole form
function SignupForm() {
  const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: '', email: '', plan: 'free',
                                     terms: false });

  // One handler for every field, keyed by the input's `name`. Note the
  // different property per input type — this is where bugs live.
  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, type, value, checked } = e.target;
    setForm(f => ({ ...f, [name]: type === 'checkbox' ? checked : value }));
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="name"  value={form.name}  onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} type="email" />

      <select name="plan" value={form.plan} onChange={handleChange}>
        {/* React uses `value` on the select — NOT `selected` on options */}
        <option value="free">Free</option>
        <option value="pro">Pro</option>
      </select>

      <input name="terms" type="checkbox"
             checked={form.terms} onChange={handleChange} />
      {/* checkboxes and radios use `checked`, not `value` */}

      <textarea name="bio" value={form.bio ?? ''} onChange={handleChange} />
      {/* React uses `value`, not a child — unlike HTML */}
    </form>
  );
}
The controlled/uncontrolled switch warning

value={user.name} where user.name is undefined on the first render makes the input uncontrolled, and React warns loudly when a later render supplies a string and flips it to controlled. The cause is almost always data that has not loaded yet. Two fixes: default the value (value={user.name ?? ''}), or do not render the form until the data exists. The same applies to checked, and to value on a select.

javascript · the other controlled-input traps
// 1 · value without onChange makes a read-only input, and React says so.
<input value={name} />                    // warns
<input value={name} readOnly />           // intentional, no warning
<input defaultValue={name} />             // uncontrolled, editable

// 2 · Number inputs return STRINGS.
<input type="number" value={qty}
       onChange={e => setQty(e.target.value)} />       // qty is "5"
       onChange={e => setQty(Number(e.target.value))} /> // 5, but "" → 0
       onChange={e => setQty(e.target.value === '' ? '' : Number(…))}
// Keeping the raw string in state and converting at submit is usually
// simpler than fighting the empty-string case.

// 3 · Files are ALWAYS uncontrolled — you cannot set a file input's
//     value for security reasons.
<input type="file" ref={fileRef} onChange={e => setFile(e.target.files[0])} />

// 4 · The cursor jumps when you transform the value. Uppercasing as the
//     user types moves the caret to the end on every keystroke.
onChange={e => setCode(e.target.value.toUpperCase())}   // caret jumps
// Fix: transform on blur, or restore the selection with a ref after the
// update — or use CSS text-transform and uppercase at submit instead.

Uncontrolled, with FormData

javascript · the whole form in three lines
function SettingsForm({ user, onSave }) {
  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(e.currentTarget);

    onSave({
      name:   data.get('name'),
      email:  data.get('email'),
      // Unchecked checkboxes are ABSENT from FormData, not false.
      notify: data.get('notify') === 'on',
      // Multiple values with the same name:
      tags:   data.getAll('tags'),
      // Or the whole thing at once, for flat forms:
      // ...Object.fromEntries(data)
    });
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="name"  defaultValue={user.name} />
      <input name="email" defaultValue={user.email} type="email" required />
      <input name="notify" type="checkbox" defaultChecked={user.notify} />
      <button>Save</button>
      <button type="reset">Reset</button>   {/* free, no code */}
    </form>
  );
}

// Resetting to NEW data when the user prop changes: give the form a key
// (R03). defaultValue is only read on mount, so without this the form
// keeps showing the previous user.
<SettingsForm key={user.id} user={user} onSave={save} />

Validation

Three layers, and you need all three. 1 The browser required · type="email" · min · max · pattern Free, accessible, works before any JS loads. Style with :user-invalid, NOT :invalid — the latter matches empty required fields on load. 2 The client cross-field rules, async checks (is this username taken), friendly messages. A convenience. Never a guarantee. 3 The server the only one that counts. Everything above runs on the attacker's machine. When to show an error — the pattern that feels right to users: on submit always on blur after the field has been touched once while typing ONLY to clear an error already shown (never to show a new one — "invalid email" after two characters is hostile)
javascript · errors that a screen reader announces
<div>
  <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
  <input
    id="email"
    name="email"
    type="email"
    required
    aria-invalid={!!errors.email}
    aria-describedby={errors.email ? 'email-error' : undefined}
  />
  {errors.email && (
    <p id="email-error" role="alert">{errors.email}</p>
  )}
</div>

// The three pieces: a real <label htmlFor> so clicking it focuses the
// field and screen readers announce it; aria-describedby linking the
// error to the input; and role="alert" so the message is announced when
// it appears. A red border alone communicates nothing to a large number
// of users.

When to use a form library

SituationReach for
Login, settings, a contact formNothing. FormData plus an Action (N01)
One field with live behaviouruseState for that field only
Fifteen fields, cross-field rules, a schema you already haveReact Hook Form + Zod — uncontrolled by default, so it does not render per keystroke
A wizard with per-step validation and persistenceA form library, plus a reducer for the step machine (R12)
A dynamic form built from a server-supplied schemaA library — the field-array handling alone justifies it
Interview follow-up

“Controlled or uncontrolled — which do you use?” The honest answer is both, chosen per field, and the reasoning is what matters: controlled costs a render per keystroke and buys live validation, formatting and dependent fields, so it earns its keep on a search box and not on a settings form. Volunteer the modern shift — React 19's Actions take a FormData, so uncontrolled is now the default path for submission and the pending state comes free — and mention the trap that shows real experience: an input whose value is undefined on the first render starts uncontrolled and React warns when it flips, which is nearly always data that has not loaded yet.

R07

useEffect: the escape hatch

An effect synchronises your component with something outside React — a subscription, a browser API, a third-party widget, the document title. It is not a lifecycle callback, and thinking of it as “componentDidMount” is the root of most effect bugs. The right question is never “when should this run” but “what is this keeping in sync”.

The signature

useEffect(setup, dependencies?) setup may return a cleanup function
javascript · the three dependency forms
// No array — after EVERY render. Almost always a mistake.
useEffect(() => { … });

// Empty array — after the first render only, cleanup on unmount.
useEffect(() => { … }, []);

// With dependencies — after the first render, and after any render
// where one of them changed by Object.is.
useEffect(() => { … }, [userId, roomId]);

// The full shape:
useEffect(() => {
  const conn = connect(roomId);         // SETUP
  conn.on('message', handleMessage);

  return () => {                        // CLEANUP
    conn.disconnect();
  };
}, [roomId]);

// Timing: after React has committed to the DOM and the browser has
// painted. So an effect never blocks the user seeing the update — which
// is also why measuring DOM layout in one causes a visible flicker
// (useLayoutEffect is for that, below).
The cleanup runs more often than people expect. mount setup(roomId = 'a') roomId → 'b' cleanup(a) then setup(b) roomId → 'c' cleanup(b) then setup(c) unmount cleanup(c) It is not "on unmount". It is before every re-run, and on unmount. That is exactly what you need: each effect tears down what it set up before the next one sets up something new. An effect without a cleanup that subscribes, opens, or starts something is a leak — and in StrictMode (R02) you see it immediately, which is the point. The mental model that makes this natural: an effect does not "do something at a moment". It describes a synchronised state: "while this component is showing roomId, there should be a connection to roomId". The cleanup says how to stop being in that state.

What effects are legitimately for

Use caseBecause
Subscribing to something outside ReactWebSocket, event emitter, store, matchMedia, IntersectionObserver
Browser APIsdocument.title, localStorage, focus, scroll position
Non-React widgetsA map, a chart, an editor that owns its own DOM
TimerssetInterval, setTimeout — with the cleanup clearing them
Fetching, on the client, without a frameworkLegitimate but rarely the best tool — R08
Analytics for a page viewA genuine external system. Not for a button click — that is a handler
What effects are not for

Transforming data for rendering, resetting state when a prop changes, updating one piece of state in response to another, or reacting to a user event. Every one of those is either a plain calculation during render, a key, or code that belongs in the event handler — and putting it in an effect adds a render, introduces an intermediate frame with stale UI, and creates a dependency chain that eventually loops. Chapter R09 works through each case.

The dependency array

javascript · it is not a "run when" list
// The array is not a trigger list you choose. It must contain EVERY
// reactive value the effect reads — props, state, and anything derived
// from them — because React needs to know when the effect is stale.
useEffect(() => {
  const conn = connect(serverUrl, roomId);
  conn.connect();
  return () => conn.disconnect();
}, [serverUrl, roomId]);     // both are read, both must be listed

// Lying about it does not make the effect run less — it makes the
// effect read STALE values, silently:
useEffect(() => {
  const timer = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(timer);
}, []);          // ← lies. `count` is read but not listed.
// Result: the interval closes over count = 0 forever, so it sets 1 every
// second and the counter sticks at 1 (J02).

// Fix by not reading the value at all:
useEffect(() => {
  const timer = setInterval(() => setCount(c => c + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(timer);
}, []);          // now honest: the effect reads nothing reactive
When the linter fights you, the effect is wrong — not the linter

react-hooks/exhaustive-deps is right far more often than it is wrong, and suppressing it with a comment is how stale-closure bugs get shipped. When adding the missing dependency causes an infinite loop or a re-subscribe on every render, the real problem is one of four things: a value that should not be reactive (use a ref or useEffectEvent), an object or function recreated every render (move it inside the effect, or memoise it), an effect that is really two effects, or an effect that should not exist at all. Fixing the cause is nearly always shorter than the suppression plus the eventual bug.

javascript · the four ways to remove a dependency honestly
// 1 · Move the value INSIDE the effect, so it is no longer read from
//     the outer scope.
useEffect(() => {
  const options = { serverUrl, roomId };   // created here, not a dep
  const conn = connect(options);
  return () => conn.disconnect();
}, [serverUrl, roomId]);                   // primitives, not an object

// 2 · Use the updater form so state is not read.
setCount(c => c + 1);       // instead of setCount(count + 1)

// 3 · A ref for a value the effect must READ but must not RE-RUN for.
const onMessageRef = useRef(onMessage);
useEffect(() => { onMessageRef.current = onMessage; });   // every render
useEffect(() => {
  const conn = connect(roomId);
  conn.on('message', (m) => onMessageRef.current(m));     // always latest
  return () => conn.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);                                            // onMessage is not a dep

// 4 · useEffectEvent (React 19.2+) — the supported version of (3).
//     An "effect event" always sees the latest props and state and is
//     explicitly NOT reactive, so it is excluded from the dep array.
const onMessage = useEffectEvent((message) => {
  showNotification(message, theme);        // reads `theme` — always current
});
useEffect(() => {
  const conn = connect(roomId);
  conn.on('message', onMessage);
  return () => conn.disconnect();
}, [roomId]);                              // theme change does NOT reconnect

The effect loop

javascript · the two shapes, and why they spin
// A · setting state that is in your own dependencies
useEffect(() => {
  setCount(count + 1);
}, [count]);          // render → effect → state → render → effect → …

// B · an object or array dependency, recreated every render
const options = { userId, includeArchived: true };   // NEW object each render
useEffect(() => {
  load(options);
}, [options]);        // Object.is is false every time → runs every render

// Fix B by depending on the primitives instead:
useEffect(() => {
  load({ userId, includeArchived: true });
}, [userId]);

// or by memoising the object, when it must be shared:
const options = useMemo(() => ({ userId, includeArchived: true }), [userId]);

// The same applies to FUNCTIONS as dependencies — a function defined in
// the component body is a new reference every render (R05), so either
// move it inside the effect or wrap it in useCallback.

useLayoutEffect, and when it is required

useEffect commit → browser paints → effect runs Asynchronous. The user may see one frame of the pre-effect state. useLayoutEffect commit → effect runs → browser paints Synchronous, BLOCKING. Nothing is painted until it returns. Use useLayoutEffect only when you must measure the DOM and change it before the user sees anything: · positioning a tooltip relative to its trigger · reading scrollHeight to decide whether to show "expand" · preventing a visible flash when correcting layout Everything else is useEffect. Layout effects block painting, so a slow one is a dropped frame — and they do not run during server-side rendering, which produces a warning if a component uses one unconditionally on the server (X03).
javascript · measuring, without the flicker
function Tooltip({ targetRect, children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  const [height, setHeight] = useState(0);

  // With useEffect, the tooltip paints at the wrong position for one
  // frame, then jumps. With useLayoutEffect, the correction happens
  // before paint and the user never sees it.
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    setHeight(ref.current.getBoundingClientRect().height);
  }, []);

  const top = targetRect.top - height < 0
    ? targetRect.bottom          // no room above; flip below
    : targetRect.top - height;

  return (
    <div ref={ref} style={{ position: 'absolute', top }}>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

The effect checklist

Before writing one, in order: 1 Can this be computed during render? → do that (R09) 2 Does it belong in an event handler? → put it there 3 Is it resetting state when a prop changes? → use a key (R03) 4 Is it fetching data? → R08 5 Is it genuinely syncing with something outside React? → an effect And once you have written it: □ every reactive value it reads is in the dependency array □ it returns a cleanup for anything it subscribes/opens/starts □ it survives running twice in a row (StrictMode proves this) □ objects and functions are not in the dependency array unless memoised □ it does not set state that is in its own dependencies
Interview follow-up

“When does the cleanup function run?” Before every re-run of the effect and on unmount — not only on unmount, which is the assumption that produces leaks and race conditions. Then reframe the whole thing, because that is the answer an interviewer is actually listening for: an effect is not a lifecycle hook, it is a description of synchronisation with an external system, and the cleanup says how to stop being synchronised. Once you say that, “should this be in an effect?” has an obvious test — is there an external system involved — and most of the code people put in effects visibly fails it.

R08

Data fetching in components

Fetching in an effect is the first thing everyone learns and the first thing everyone outgrows. It works, and then you need deduplication, caching, retries, refetch-on-focus and invalidation after a mutation — each of which is a small piece of hard work. This chapter builds the hand-written version properly, then explains exactly what you are buying when you replace it.

The hand-written version, done correctly

javascript · everything the naive version is missing
function useUser(id) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle' });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!id) return;                       // nothing to fetch

    const ac = new AbortController();
    setState({ status: 'loading' });

    (async () => {
      try {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { signal: ac.signal });
        // fetch does NOT throw on 4xx/5xx — you must check.
        if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status, await res.text());
        const data = await res.json();
        setState({ status: 'success', data });
      } catch (err) {
        // An abort is expected, not a failure. Reporting it produces
        // phantom errors every time the user types.
        if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;
        setState({ status: 'error', error: err });
      }
    })();

    // Runs before the next effect AND on unmount, so a superseded
    // request is cancelled rather than racing the new one (J04).
    return () => ac.abort();
  }, [id]);

  return state;
}

// In the component, the three states are exhaustive and cannot
// contradict each other:
function Profile({ id }) {
  const user = useUser(id);
  if (user.status === 'loading') return <Skeleton />;
  if (user.status === 'error')   return <Error err={user.error} />;
  if (user.status !== 'success') return null;
  return <div>{user.data.name}</div>;
}
Four things the tutorial version gets wrong

1 · No abort, so responses race and an old query can overwrite a new one. 2 · No res.ok check, so a 500 returning an HTML error page is parsed as JSON and fails with a confusing syntax error instead of the status. 3 · Aborts reported as errors, so the UI flashes a failure on every keystroke. 4 · Separate loading/error/data booleans, which permit states that cannot happen and eventually render one.

What you still do not have

The hook above is correct for ONE component fetching ONE thing. A real app needs all of this, and none of it is in the ninety lines you would write next: deduplication three components mounting with the same id should issue one request, not three caching navigating away and back should not refetch from scratch and show a spinner again stale-while-revalidate show the cached value immediately, refetch in the background, swap when it arrives invalidation after a mutation, which queries are now wrong? refetch on focus / reconnect the tab was in the background for an hour retries with backoff a 503 should be retried; a 404 should not pagination and infinite scroll keeping previous pages while the next loads request cancellation on unmount ← the only one we have Each is a few days of work and a source of subtle bugs. This is the argument for a library, and it is a strong one.

A query library

javascript · TanStack Query, which is the default choice
import { useQuery, useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Profile({ id }) {
  const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({
    // The key IS the cache identity. Two components with the same key
    // share one request and one cache entry.
    queryKey: ['user', id],
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetchUser(id, signal),   // abort handled
    staleTime: 60_000,        // do not refetch for a minute
    enabled: Boolean(id),     // skip entirely when there is no id
  });

  if (isPending) return <Skeleton />;
  if (error)     return <Error err={error} />;
  return <div>{data.name}</div>;
}

function EditName({ id }) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();

  const mutation = useMutation({
    mutationFn: (name) => updateUser(id, { name }),

    // Optimistic update: show it immediately, roll back on failure.
    onMutate: async (name) => {
      await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['user', id] });
      const previous = qc.getQueryData(['user', id]);
      qc.setQueryData(['user', id], old => ({ ...old, name }));
      return { previous };
    },
    onError: (_err, _name, ctx) => {
      qc.setQueryData(['user', id], ctx.previous);
    },
    // Whatever happened, make the cache agree with the server again.
    onSettled: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['user', id] }),
  });

  return <button onClick={() => mutation.mutate('Grace')}>Rename</button>;
}
Server state is not application state

The insight that makes query libraries click: data owned by a server is not really your state — it is a cached copy of someone else's, and it can be stale, shared, refetched and invalidated. Treating it as ordinary component state (or worse, putting it in Redux) means hand-writing a cache with none of those concepts. Once you separate server state (a query library) from client state (useState, or a small store), most applications discover they barely need a global store at all — it was holding fetched data.

Where the fetch should happen

ApproachRunsWaterfall riskUse when
useEffect + fetchclientHigh — one per component, after renderLearning; a single simple screen
Query libraryclientMedium — prefetching helpsA client-rendered SPA with meaningful caching needs
Server Component awaitserverLow — runs before HTML is sentThe default in a Next.js app (N04, X04)
Route loader (React Router, TanStack Router)bothLow — starts with navigationA client SPA with a router that supports it
use(promise) + SuspenseclientLow, if the promise starts earlyPassing a server-started promise into a client component (N03)
