The request waterfall is the real performance problem

Fetching in an effect means the request cannot start until the component has rendered — and if a child fetches too, its request cannot start until the parent's data has arrived and the child has rendered. Three levels of that is three sequential round trips before anything is on screen, and on a mobile connection that is a second and a half of blank page. It is why loaders, Server Components and prefetching all exist: they let requests start before or in parallel with rendering rather than as a consequence of it. Diagnosing a waterfall in the network panel — a staircase rather than a block — is a standard interview exercise.

Error and loading UI

javascript · three things that make loading states feel fast
// 1 · A skeleton matching the final layout, not a centred spinner. The
//     page does not shift when data arrives, which is both a better
//     experience and a better CLS score.
if (isPending) return <PostSkeleton />;

// 2 · Keep the previous data while refetching, so pagination does not
//     flash empty between pages.
const { data, isPlaceholderData } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['posts', page],
  queryFn: () => getPosts(page),
  placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
});
<div style={{ opacity: isPlaceholderData ? 0.6 : 1 }}>…</div>

// 3 · Do not show a spinner for a request that will take 100ms — the
//     flash is worse than the wait. Delay it.
const showSpinner = useDelayedFlag(isPending, 300);

// And for errors: a retry that actually retries, and a message that
// distinguishes "offline" from "not found" from "our fault".
if (error) return (
  <ErrorState
    title={error.status === 404 ? 'Not found' : 'Something went wrong'}
    onRetry={() => refetch()}
  />
);
Interview follow-up

“What is wrong with fetching in useEffect?” Not that it is broken — it is that it is the latest possible moment to start. The request cannot begin until after render, so nested components produce a waterfall of sequential round trips, and you are left hand-writing deduplication, caching, retries and invalidation that a library or the server already solves. Then give the concrete failure that shows you have shipped it: without an abort or a cancellation flag in the cleanup, responses race and a slow request for an old query overwrites the results for the current one — which passes every test on localhost and appears the first time a real user is on a train.

R09

You probably do not need that effect

The most common structural mistake in React codebases is using useEffect as a general-purpose “when X changes, do Y” mechanism. Six patterns account for nearly all of it, and each has a shorter, more correct alternative. This is the highest-value chapter in Part II.

1 · Transforming data for rendering

If it can be computed from props and state, it is not state

Derived values stored in state introduce a render where the two disagree, and they drift the moment a new code path updates the source without updating the copy. Compute them in the component body. The cost is real but small — filtering a thousand items is well under a millisecond — and if profiling ever shows otherwise, useMemo wraps the calculation without reintroducing a second source of truth.

2 · Resetting state when a prop changes

javascript · when only PART of the state should reset
// Remounting is too blunt when some state should survive. The supported
// alternative is to adjust state DURING render — React documents this,
// and it re-renders immediately without committing the intermediate
// result, so there is no visible flash.
function List({ items }) {
  const [selection, setSelection] = useState(null);

  // A previous-value comparison in the render body. React sees the
  // setState during render, discards the in-progress output, and
  // re-runs the component before touching the DOM.
  const [prevItems, setPrevItems] = useState(items);
  if (items !== prevItems) {
    setPrevItems(items);
    setSelection(null);       // clear the selection when the list changes
  }
  // …
}
// This is a narrow, documented escape hatch — not a general pattern.
// Only the SAME component may do it, and only to adjust its own state.

3 · Handling a user event

The distinction that resolves almost every case: Did this happen because the user did something? → an event handler. Did this happen because the component is on screen? → an effect. "Send an analytics event when the user clicks buy" → handler "Send a page-view event because this page is showing" → effect "POST the form because they submitted it" → handler "Open a WebSocket because this room is displayed" → effect An effect cannot tell you why it ran — only that a dependency changed. That is exactly the information an event handler has and an effect has lost, which is why moving the code up to the handler usually makes it both shorter and correct.

4 · Chains of effects

5 · Initialising the application

javascript · once per app, not once per mount
// WRONG: runs twice in StrictMode, and again if the component ever
// remounts — which a router will do.
function App() {
  useEffect(() => {
    loadDataFromLocalStorage();
    checkAuthToken();
  }, []);
}

// RIGHT: module scope, which runs exactly once per page load.
if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {     // guard for SSR (X03)
  checkAuthToken();
}
function App() { … }

// Or a guard, when it must be inside a component for some reason:
let didInit = false;
function App() {
  useEffect(() => {
    if (didInit) return;
    didInit = true;
    checkAuthToken();
  }, []);
}

6 · Subscribing to an external store

useSyncExternalStore exists because effects can tear

With concurrent rendering, React can start rendering, pause, and resume — and an external value read in an effect can change in between, so two components reading the same store in one commit can display different values. That is “tearing”, and it is why every state library now uses this hook underneath. You will rarely call it directly in application code, but knowing what it is for explains why subscribing in an effect is no longer the recommended pattern.

The cases where an effect is right

LegitimateShape
Connecting to a chat room, socket or streamSetup + cleanup, keyed on the room id
Controlling a non-React widgetCreate in the effect, destroy in the cleanup
Syncing to document.title, localStorage, the URLWrite in the effect; nothing reads it back
A page-view analytics eventBecause the component is on screen, not because of a click
TimerssetInterval + clearInterval in the cleanup
Fetching, on the client, with no frameworkWith abort and a status union (R08)
Interview follow-up

“When should you not use useEffect?” Give the test rather than a list: an effect is for synchronising with something outside React, so if no external system is involved it probably should not be one. Then name the two biggest categories — derived data, which belongs in the render body, and reactions to user events, which belong in the handler — and explain why the second matters beyond tidiness: an effect only knows that a dependency changed, not why, so the cause is lost and the code fires again on remount or in StrictMode. Finishing with “and if I delete this effect, what breaks?” as a review question is a good signal.

R10

Refs and the DOM

A ref is a box whose contents survive re-renders and whose changes do not trigger one. That single difference from state is the whole API, and it gives refs two distinct jobs: reaching a DOM node, and remembering a value that the UI does not display.

State versus ref

useStateuseRef
Survives re-renderYesYes
Changing it re-rendersYesNo
Changed byA setterAssigning .current directly
Readable during renderYesAvoid — it may be stale or mid-mutation
Mutation allowedNo (J03)Yes, that is the point
Use forAnything the UI displaysDOM nodes, timer ids, previous values, "has this happened yet" flags
javascript · the two jobs
// JOB 1 — a handle on a DOM node
function SearchBox() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    inputRef.current.focus();      // populated by the time effects run
  }, []);

  return <input ref={inputRef} />;
}

// JOB 2 — a mutable value that must NOT cause a render
function Stopwatch() {
  const [elapsed, setElapsed] = useState(0);
  const intervalRef = useRef(null);      // storing this in state would
  const startRef = useRef(null);         // re-render for no reason

  function start() {
    startRef.current = Date.now();
    intervalRef.current = setInterval(() => {
      setElapsed(Date.now() - startRef.current);
    }, 50);
  }
  function stop() {
    clearInterval(intervalRef.current);
  }

  useEffect(() => () => clearInterval(intervalRef.current), []);
  return <div>{elapsed}ms</div>;
}
Do not read or write a ref during render

React may call your component twice (StrictMode), abandon a render part-way, or render on the server where there is no DOM — so a ref read during render can be stale, and a ref written during render makes the component impure and the result unpredictable. The rule: refs are touched in event handlers and effects, never in the component body. The one sanctioned exception is lazy initialisation (if (ref.current === null) ref.current = create()), which is idempotent and therefore safe.

When the ref is populated

render ref.current is still null on the first render — you are describing the element, it does not exist yet commit React creates the DOM node and assigns it layout effect ref.current is available, before paint effect ref.current is available, after paint cleanup React sets ref.current back to null BEFORE the cleanup runs for an unmounting node — so a cleanup that needs the node must capture it first: useEffect(() => { const el = ref.current; capture const obs = new ResizeObserver(…); obs.observe(el); return () => obs.unobserve(el); not ref.current }, []); This is a real and common bug: the cleanup reads ref.current, finds null, and silently fails to unobserve.

Callback refs

javascript · when you need to know the node changed
// A function passed as `ref` is called with the node on attach and with
// null on detach. Unlike an object ref, it RUNS — so it is the right
// tool when attaching means doing something.
function AutoFocus() {
  const setRef = useCallback((node) => {
    if (node) node.focus();
  }, []);
  return <input ref={setRef} />;
}

// React 19 lets a callback ref return a CLEANUP function, which removes
// the null-check dance entirely:
<div ref={(node) => {
  const obs = new ResizeObserver(onResize);
  obs.observe(node);
  return () => obs.disconnect();      // called on detach
}} />

// A callback ref defined inline is a NEW function every render, so React
// detaches and reattaches on every render — calling it with null and
// then with the node. Harmless for a focus call, wasteful for an
// observer. useCallback fixes it, or define it outside.

// Measuring a node whose size matters to the render:
function Measured({ children }) {
  const [height, setHeight] = useState(0);
  const measure = useCallback((node) => {
    if (node) setHeight(node.getBoundingClientRect().height);
  }, []);
  return <div ref={measure}>{children}</div>;
}

Refs on components

javascript · React 19 made ref an ordinary prop
// BEFORE React 19: ref was special-cased and never appeared in props,
// so passing one through a component required forwardRef.
const Input = forwardRef(function Input(props, ref) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...props} />;
});

// REACT 19: ref is just a prop. forwardRef is deprecated and the
// codemod is a delete.
function Input({ ref, ...props }) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...props} />;
}

<Input ref={inputRef} />              // works in both, with the right defn

// useImperativeHandle — expose a narrow API instead of the raw node.
// Handing out the DOM element lets a parent do anything to it; this
// exposes exactly what the component chooses to support.
function VideoPlayer({ ref, src }) {
  const videoRef = useRef(null);

  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    play:  () => videoRef.current.play(),
    pause: () => videoRef.current.pause(),
    seek:  (t) => { videoRef.current.currentTime = t; },
  }), []);

  return <video ref={videoRef} src={src} />;
}

// Use it sparingly. An imperative handle is an escape from the
// declarative model, and a prop usually expresses the same thing
// better: <VideoPlayer playing={isPlaying} /> beats calling .play().

The legitimate DOM cases

Do this with a refWhy there is no declarative option
Focus, blur, text selectionFocus is browser state React does not own
Scroll position, scrollIntoViewSame
Measuring (getBoundingClientRect)Only the real layout knows
Playing media, triggering an animationImperative APIs on the element
Integrating a non-React libraryIt wants a container node to own
<dialog>'s showModal()Modal state lives in the element, not an attribute
Observers: resize, intersection, mutationThey take a node
Never use a ref to change something React renders

ref.current.textContent = 'Saved' or ref.current.style.display = 'none' works exactly once — until React re-renders that subtree and overwrites it with what the JSX says, at a moment you cannot predict. Worse, it can leave React's tree and the DOM disagreeing, which produces genuinely baffling bugs. A ref is for reading the DOM and for calling imperative methods the element owns; anything React put there, React must be the one to change.

Integrating a non-React library

javascript · the shape for a chart, map or editor
function Chart({ data, options }) {
  const containerRef = useRef(null);
  const chartRef = useRef(null);

  // Create ONCE. Creating in a data-dependent effect would destroy and
  // rebuild the chart on every data change, losing zoom and animation.
  useEffect(() => {
    chartRef.current = new ChartLib(containerRef.current, options);
    return () => {
      chartRef.current.destroy();     // essential: the library owns DOM
      chartRef.current = null;        // and timers React knows nothing of
    };
  }, []);                             // options intentionally omitted

  // Update imperatively when the data changes.
  useEffect(() => {
    chartRef.current?.setData(data);
  }, [data]);

  // React must NOT manage the children of this div — the library does.
  // An empty div with a ref is the correct boundary.
  return <div ref={containerRef} style={{ height: 320 }} />;
}

Other things refs are good for

javascript · the value patterns
// The previous value of a prop or state
function usePrevious(value) {
  const ref = useRef(undefined);
  useEffect(() => { ref.current = value; });   // after every render
  return ref.current;                          // the value from last time
}

// The latest value, for a long-lived callback that must not re-subscribe
function useLatest(value) {
  const ref = useRef(value);
  ref.current = value;        // during render — the sanctioned exception,
  return ref;                 // because it is idempotent
}

// Lazy, expensive initialisation — useRef takes no initialiser function
function Video() {
  const playerRef = useRef(null);
  if (playerRef.current === null) {
    playerRef.current = new VideoPlayer();     // created once
  }
}

// A flag for "this has already happened", surviving StrictMode
const hasLoggedRef = useRef(false);
useEffect(() => {
  if (hasLoggedRef.current) return;
  hasLoggedRef.current = true;
  trackPageView();
}, []);
Interview follow-up

“When would you use a ref instead of state?” When the value must survive re-renders but changing it should not cause one — a timer id, a DOM node, a previous value, a “has this already run” flag. The sharper framing is that state is for anything the user sees and refs are for everything else, and the test is simple: if changing the value should update the screen, it is state. Then add the two rules that show you have used them: do not read or write a ref during render, because that makes the component impure; and capture ref.current into a local variable at the top of an effect, because React nulls it before the cleanup runs.

R11

Context

Context solves one problem: passing a value to a deep descendant without threading it through every component in between. It is not a state manager, it has a performance characteristic that surprises people, and there is a simpler technique that removes the need for it more often than most codebases realise.

The mechanics

javascript · create, provide, consume
// 1 · Create. The argument is the DEFAULT, used only when a consumer
//     has no provider above it — which is usually a bug, so making it
//     `null` and throwing in the hook is better than a plausible value.
const ThemeContext = createContext(null);

// 2 · Provide. React 19 lets you render the context itself; earlier
//     versions need <ThemeContext.Provider>.
function App() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  return (
    <ThemeContext value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
      <Layout />
    </ThemeContext>
  );
}

// 3 · Consume — and always behind a custom hook, never the raw context.
function useTheme() {
  const ctx = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (ctx === null) {
    // A clear error at the point of use beats `undefined is not an
    // object` three components away.
    throw new Error('useTheme must be used inside <ThemeProvider>');
  }
  return ctx;
}

function Button() {
  const { theme } = useTheme();
  return <button className={theme}>…</button>;
}
How a consumer finds its value React walks up the tree from the consumer until it finds a provider for that context object. Nearest one wins. <ThemeContext value="dark"> <Page> <ThemeContext value="light"> ← nested override <Sidebar> <Button /> ← reads "light" </Sidebar> </ThemeContext> <Footer /> ← reads "dark" </Page> </ThemeContext> Nesting is a feature, not an edge case — a themed section, a form-level locale, a sandboxed preview all use it. The propagation rule that matters: when the provider's value changes, every consumer re-renders, no matter how deep and regardless of memo. Context bypasses memo — that is what makes it work through arbitrary trees, and what makes the value's shape a performance decision.

The two performance traps

javascript · trap 2 — one context holding unrelated things
// A single context with everything in it means a component reading only
// the theme re-renders when the cart changes.
<AppContext value={{ user, theme, cart, notifications }}>

// SPLIT BY CHANGE FREQUENCY. Each context re-renders only its own
// consumers.
<UserContext value={user}>
  <ThemeContext value={theme}>
    <CartContext value={cart}>
      …

// The most valuable split is STATE from DISPATCH, because the setter is
// stable and the value is not. A component that only dispatches then
// never re-renders when the state changes:
const StateContext    = createContext(null);
const DispatchContext = createContext(null);

function Provider({ children }) {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial);
  return (
    <StateContext value={state}>
      {/* dispatch is referentially stable for the component's lifetime,
          so this provider's value never changes */}
      <DispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</DispatchContext>
    </StateContext>
  );
}

// An "add to cart" button reads only dispatch → it never re-renders.
Context has no selector, and that is the whole limitation

A consumer subscribes to the entire context value; there is no way to say “re-render me only when value.user.name changes”. So a frequently-changing value in a context read by a large subtree re-renders that whole subtree on every change — which is exactly the problem external store libraries solve. If you find yourself wanting a selector, you have outgrown context: reach for Zustand, Jotai or Redux Toolkit, all of which provide one and all of which use useSyncExternalStore underneath (R09).

What context is genuinely for

Good fitBecause
Theme, locale, directionRead everywhere, changes almost never
The authenticated userRead widely, changes on login and logout
A router's current locationGenuinely ambient, and every router does this
A form's shared state, scoped to that formDeep, and the provider wraps only the form
Dependency injection for testsSwap a real client for a fake at the boundary
Compound components (Tabs, Accordion)Parent and children coordinate without prop drilling through arbitrary markup
Poor fitUse instead
Server dataA query library, or a Server Component (R08, N04)
High-frequency values (mouse position, scroll)A ref plus a subscription, or a store with selectors
State only two components needLift it to their common parent (J07)
Large application state with many independent slicesA store with selectors
Avoiding passing one prop down one levelPass the prop

The technique that removes the need

javascript · pass elements, not data
// The prop-drilling complaint, in its usual form:
<Page user={user}>
  <Layout user={user}>
    <Sidebar user={user}>
      <Profile user={user} />      // only THIS one needs it
    </Sidebar>
  </Layout>
</Page>

// Reaching for context here is premature. The component that HAS the
// data can render the component that NEEDS it, and pass the result down
// as an element — so the intermediate layers never see `user` at all
// (J06):
function App() {
  const user = useUser();
  return (
    <Page>
      <Layout sidebar={<Sidebar><Profile user={user} /></Sidebar>} />
    </Page>
  );
}
// Page and Layout are now generic, reusable, and testable without a
// provider. No context, no re-render cascade, no indirection.

// Context earns its place when the consumer's POSITION is unknown —
// a theme read by any component anywhere, a toast function callable
// from arbitrary depth. That is a genuinely different problem.

A provider, written well

javascript · the shape worth copying
// ThemeContext.tsx — context object NOT exported, so nobody can consume
// it without the hook and its error message.
const ThemeContext = createContext(null);

export function ThemeProvider({ children, initial = 'system' }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState(initial);

  const toggle = useCallback(() => {
    setTheme(t => (t === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark'));
  }, []);

  const value = useMemo(() => ({ theme, setTheme, toggle }), [theme, toggle]);

  // Sync to the DOM here, once, rather than in every consumer.
  useEffect(() => {
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme;
  }, [theme]);

  return <ThemeContext value={value}>{children}</ThemeContext>;
}

export function useTheme() {
  const ctx = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useTheme must be used inside <ThemeProvider>');
  return ctx;
}

// Consumers import { useTheme }, never the context object. The provider
// can change its internals freely, and a missing provider fails with a
// sentence rather than a null dereference.
Provider nesting gets deep, and that is fine

Six providers wrapping the app looks alarming and costs nothing — they are components that render their children. Flattening them into one mega-context is a regression, because it reunites values with different change frequencies. If the nesting genuinely bothers you, a small compose helper or a single <Providers> component that does the nesting in one place keeps the app root readable without merging the contexts themselves.

Interview follow-up

“Is Context a state management solution?” No — it is a transport mechanism. It moves a value down the tree without prop drilling and has no opinion about how that value is produced or updated; the state still lives in a useState or useReducer somewhere. The limitation worth naming is that it has no selector: a consumer subscribes to the whole value, so every consumer re-renders on any change, and memo does not stop it. That is precisely what libraries like Zustand and Redux add, and being able to say “context plus useReducer is enough until you need selectors” is a much better answer than either “context replaces Redux” or “always use Redux”.

R12

useReducer and state architecture

When several pieces of state change together, or the next state depends on the current one in non-trivial ways, scattered useState calls stop describing the logic. A reducer moves the “what happens when X occurs” rules into one testable function, and turns the component into a description of what it looks like.

The shape

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialArg, init?) reducer(state, action) → next state
javascript · the same feature, both ways
// ── with useState: the rules are spread across the handlers ──────────
const [items, setItems]       = useState([]);
const [editingId, setEditing] = useState(null);
const [filter, setFilter]     = useState('all');
const [selected, setSelected] = useState(new Set());

function remove(id) {
  setItems(items.filter(i => i.id !== id));
  if (editingId === id) setEditing(null);          // easy to forget
  setSelected(s => { const n = new Set(s); n.delete(id); return n; });
}
// Four states, and every handler must know which of them it affects.

// ── with useReducer: the rules are in one place ──────────────────────
function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'added':
      return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] };

    case 'removed': {
      const selected = new Set(state.selected);
      selected.delete(action.id);
      return {
        ...state,
        items: state.items.filter(i => i.id !== action.id),
        editingId: state.editingId === action.id ? null : state.editingId,
        selected,
      };
    }

    case 'filter_changed':
      // Changing the filter clears the selection — a rule that lives
      // HERE, not in whichever component happens to change the filter.
      return { ...state, filter: action.filter, selected: new Set() };

    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown action: ${action.type}`);
  }
}

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, {
  items: [], editingId: null, filter: 'all', selected: new Set(),
});

dispatch({ type: 'removed', id });

When to reach for it

SignalWhy a reducer helps
Several states always change togetherOne transition instead of several setters that can diverge
The next state depends on the current one in several waysThe reducer receives it as an argument, so no stale closures
The same transition happens from several placesOne action name instead of duplicated handler bodies
You want to test the logic without renderingA reducer is a pure function; call it with a state and an action
You want to log or replay what happenedActions are a serialisable history
dispatch is passed deep through contextIt is referentially stable, so it never causes a re-render (R11)
Two or three related useState calls are fine

A reducer is not an upgrade — it is a different trade. It adds indirection: reading a handler now means finding the action name, then finding the case. For a component with a couple of independent values, useState is shorter and clearer, and converting it to a reducer makes it worse. The threshold is roughly “when I change one thing, do I have to remember to change others?” — that is coupling, and coupling is what a reducer is for.

Writing the reducer

javascript · the rules, and why each one
// 1 · PURE. No fetch, no Date.now(), no Math.random(), no mutation.
//     React may call it twice (StrictMode), and impurity makes replay
//     and testing meaningless.
case 'created':
  // WRONG — different result every call
  return { ...state, items: [...state.items, { id: crypto.randomUUID() }] };
  // RIGHT — generate the id in the handler, pass it in the action
  return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] };

// 2 · Name actions for WHAT HAPPENED, not what to set. The reducer
//     decides what that means — which is the entire point.
dispatch({ type: 'setEditingId', id: null });        // a setter in disguise
dispatch({ type: 'edit_cancelled' });                // an EVENT

// 3 · Return a NEW object. Mutating and returning the same reference
//     means React bails out and nothing renders (J03).
case 'toggled':
  state.items[i].done = true;   // WRONG
  return state;
  return { ...state, items: state.items.map(…) };   // right

// 4 · Handle the default honestly. Throwing catches typos immediately;
//     silently returning state hides them until someone notices a
//     button does nothing.
default:
  throw new Error(`Unknown action: ${action.type}`);

// 5 · Lazy initialisation, when the initial state is expensive or
//     derived — the third argument runs once with the second as input.
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, savedId, (id) => ({
  ...emptyState,
  ...JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(`draft:${id}`) ?? '{}'),
}));

Reducers are trivially testable

javascript · no rendering, no mocking, microseconds per case
test('removing an item clears it from the selection and stops editing', () => {
  const before = {
    items: [{ id: 'a' }, { id: 'b' }],
    editingId: 'a',
    selected: new Set(['a', 'b']),
    filter: 'all',
  };

  const after = reducer(before, { type: 'removed', id: 'a' });

  expect(after.items).toEqual([{ id: 'b' }]);
  expect(after.editingId).toBeNull();
  expect([...after.selected]).toEqual(['b']);
  // And the input was not mutated — a property worth asserting once:
  expect(before.items).toHaveLength(2);
});

// This is the strongest argument for a reducer in a complex component.
// The same coverage through the UI needs a render, a click, and an
// assertion on the DOM — slower, more brittle, and it tests the
// rendering as well as the rule.

A state machine, when the states are genuinely exclusive

javascript · actions that only apply in certain states
// A reducer with a flat switch permits every action in every state, so
// "retry" while already loading, or "submit" twice, are representable.
// Switching on the STATE first makes illegal transitions impossible.
function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
      if (action.type === 'submit') return { status: 'saving', data: action.data };
      return state;

    case 'saving':
      // A second submit while saving is IGNORED — not by a guard in the
      // component, but because there is no transition for it.
      if (action.type === 'succeeded') return { status: 'done', result: action.result };
      if (action.type === 'failed')    return { status: 'error', error: action.error };
      return state;

    case 'error':
      if (action.type === 'retry') return { status: 'saving', data: state.data };
      return state;

    case 'done':
      if (action.type === 'reset') return { status: 'idle' };
      return state;
  }
}

// The double-submit bug disappears without a `disabled` flag, and the
// rendering becomes exhaustive:
switch (state.status) {
  case 'idle':   return <Form onSubmit={d => dispatch({type:'submit', data:d})} />;
  case 'saving': return <Spinner />;
  case 'error':  return <Error onRetry={() => dispatch({type:'retry'})} />;
  case 'done':   return <Success />;
}
Side effects do not go in the reducer

A reducer is called during render and must be pure, so the fetch belongs in the handler or an effect, and the reducer only records what happened. The usual shape is: handler dispatches submit, an effect watching status === 'saving' performs the request, and its resolution dispatches succeeded or failed. If that effect chain becomes elaborate, that is the point at which XState earns its complexity — but most components never get there, and a four-state switch is enough.

Reducer plus context

javascript · the standard "no library" architecture
const StateContext    = createContext(null);
const DispatchContext = createContext(null);

export function TasksProvider({ children }) {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);
  return (
    <StateContext value={state}>
      <DispatchContext value={dispatch}>{children}</DispatchContext>
    </StateContext>
  );
}

export const useTasks    = () => useContext(StateContext);
export const useDispatch = () => useContext(DispatchContext);

// The split matters: `dispatch` is stable for the provider's lifetime,
// so a component that only dispatches never re-renders when the state
// changes. An "add task" button is free.

// This covers a large number of applications. You outgrow it when you
// need SELECTORS — "re-render only when state.tasks.length changes" —
// because context has none (R11). That is the moment for Zustand,
// Jotai or Redux Toolkit, and not before.
Interview follow-up

“useState or useReducer?” Not “reducer for complex state” — give the test: do several pieces of state change together, so that updating one means remembering to update others? That coupling is what a reducer removes, by putting every transition in one pure function that receives the current state as an argument. Then add the two benefits people forget: the reducer is testable without rendering anything, and dispatch is referentially stable, so passing it through context costs nothing while passing a set of setters would. Be willing to say that two or three independent useState calls are better as they are.

R13

Custom hooks

A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and which calls other hooks. There is no React machinery behind it — the convention is the whole feature. What it buys is the ability to share stateful logic between components, which is the thing class components could never do without wrapping the tree.

Extracting one

javascript · before and after
// Repeated in four components:
function ChatRoom({ roomId }) {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => {
    const on  = () => setOnline(true);
    const off = () => setOnline(false);
    window.addEventListener('online', on);
    window.addEventListener('offline', off);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('online', on);
      window.removeEventListener('offline', off);
    };
  }, []);
  …
}

// Extracted — a function, nothing more:
function useOnlineStatus() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    (cb) => {
      window.addEventListener('online', cb);
      window.addEventListener('offline', cb);
      return () => {
        window.removeEventListener('online', cb);
        window.removeEventListener('offline', cb);
      };
    },
    () => navigator.onLine,
    () => true,                  // the server has no navigator
  );
}

function ChatRoom({ roomId }) {
  const online = useOnlineStatus();
  …
}
Hooks share logic, not state

Two components calling useCounter() each get their own independent counter — the hook is a function, and calling it runs it again with fresh state. This surprises people who expect a hook to behave like a singleton store. If two components must see the same value, the state has to live above both of them: lift it (J07), put it in context (R11), or use an external store. A custom hook duplicates the behaviour; it does not share the data.

The rules of hooks, and why they exist

1 Only call hooks at the top level. Not in conditions, loops, or after an early return. 2 Only call hooks from components or other hooks. Not from a plain function, a handler, or a class. Why: React does not know your hooks' names. It stores them in a linked list on the fiber, matched by CALL ORDER (W05). render 1 render 2, with a condition ───────────────────── ───────────────────────────── useState('') → slot 0 useState('') → slot 0 useState(0) → slot 1 skipped useEffect(…) → slot 2 useEffect(…) → slot 1 ✗ WRONG SLOT The effect now reads the state that belonged to the other hook, and React throws "Rendered fewer hooks than expected" — or worse, does not, and silently mixes them up. The convention is what makes this enforceable: the use prefix is how the lint rule knows a function contains hooks, so getWindowSize() calling useState is invisible to it. That is the only reason the naming rule exists.
javascript · conditional hooks, and the fix
// WRONG in all four shapes:
if (isLoggedIn)   { const [x] = useState(0); }
for (const id of ids) { useEffect(…); }
if (!user) return null;  const [x] = useState(0);   // hook after return
function handleClick() { const [x] = useState(0); } // in a handler

// RIGHT: the CONDITION moves inside the hook, not around it.
const [x, setX] = useState(0);
useEffect(() => {
  if (!isLoggedIn) return;        // condition inside
  subscribe();
}, [isLoggedIn]);

// And when two branches genuinely need different hooks, that is two
// components — chosen by the parent, which is also clearer:
{isEditor ? <EditorView doc={doc} /> : <ReaderView doc={doc} />}

What a good hook returns

javascript · array for two, object for more
// Two values, where the caller will want to rename: an ARRAY, like
// useState. Positional destructuring lets every caller choose names.
function useToggle(initial = false) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = useCallback(() => setOn(v => !v), []);
  return [on, toggle];
}
const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle();
const [isDark, toggleDark] = useToggle(true);

// Three or more, or optional ones: an OBJECT. Names are self-documenting
// and the caller takes only what it needs.
function useForm(initialValues) {
  …
  return { values, errors, isValid, isDirty, handleChange, reset, submit };
}
const { values, handleChange, reset } = useForm({ name: '' });

// Keep the returned identity STABLE, or every consumer's effects and
// memos see a change on every render:
return useMemo(
  () => ({ values, errors, handleChange, reset }),
  [values, errors, handleChange, reset],
);
// (The React Compiler makes this automatic — W07.)

Hooks worth having

javascript · four that appear in nearly every codebase
// 1 · Debounce a rapidly changing value
function useDebounced(value, delay = 300) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);      // cancels the previous timer
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}
const debouncedQuery = useDebounced(query, 300);
// Note: React's own useDeferredValue often does this better, because it
// is interruptible and adapts to how fast the device actually is (W06).

// 2 · Persist state to localStorage
function useLocalStorage(key, initial) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(() => {
    // Lazy: reads storage once, not on every render (R01). And in a
    // try/catch, because storage throws in private mode and when full.
    try {
      const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : initial;
    } catch { return initial; }
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    try { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value)); } catch {}
  }, [key, value]);

  return [value, setValue];
}
// Caveat: this reads storage during the FIRST render, which differs
// between server and client and causes a hydration mismatch in SSR.
// See X03 for the correct server-safe version.

// 3 · Observe an element's size
function useResizeObserver() {
  const [rect, setRect] = useState(null);
  const ref = useCallback((node) => {
    if (!node) return;
    const ro = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => setRect(entry.contentRect));
    ro.observe(node);
    return () => ro.disconnect();     // React 19 cleanup-from-callback-ref
  }, []);
  return [ref, rect];
}

// 4 · A media query, without tearing
function useMediaQuery(query) {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    (cb) => {
      const mql = window.matchMedia(query);
      mql.addEventListener('change', cb);
      return () => mql.removeEventListener('change', cb);
    },
    () => window.matchMedia(query).matches,
    () => false,                       // the server has no viewport
  );
}

When not to extract

Extract when…Do not when…
The same stateful logic appears in two or more componentsYou are extracting on the first occurrence, speculatively
It has a name that describes a behaviourThe best name you can find is useLogic or useStuff
It hides a non-obvious effect + cleanup pairIt just wraps one useState with no added rule
It gives a subtle thing a testable boundaryThe hook takes eight arguments and returns twelve values
It isolates an external system (storage, sockets, observers)It is an entire component's logic — that is the component
A hook that is only a wrapper makes the code harder to read

function useName() { return useState('') } adds a file, an import and an indirection while explaining nothing. The value of a custom hook comes from the rule it encodes — the cleanup you would forget, the race you would not handle, the storage exception you would not catch. Extracting for the sake of a shorter component moves the same code somewhere less visible and makes the component's behaviour harder to trace. Keep hooks for things with a name you would use in conversation: useOnlineStatus, useDebounced, useIntersection.

The pattern this replaced

Before hooks, sharing stateful logic meant wrapping the tree. Higher-order components export default withRouter(withTheme(connect(mapState)(MyComponent))) · nested wrappers in DevTools, several layers deep · prop collisions, with no way to see where a prop came from · typing them was famously painful · a component could not see which HOC provided what Render props <Mouse>{({x, y}) => <Theme>{theme => <Size>{size => …}</Size>}</Theme>}</Mouse> · no prop collisions, but the "pyramid of doom" · the tree structure now encodes data flow, not layout Hooks const { x, y } = useMouse(); const theme = useTheme(); const size = useSize(); · flat, composable, obvious where each value comes from · no wrapper components in the tree at all Both older patterns still have uses — render props for genuinely polymorphic children, HOCs at framework boundaries — but for sharing stateful logic, hooks replaced them entirely, and that was the point of introducing hooks in the first place.
Interview follow-up

“Why can't hooks be called conditionally?” Because React identifies them by call order, not by name — they live in a linked list on the fiber, and slot 2 on this render must be the same hook as slot 2 on the last one. Skip one and every subsequent hook reads the wrong slot. Then give the consequence people find memorable: this is why the use prefix is a rule rather than a style, because the lint rule that enforces call-order safety can only recognise a function containing hooks by its name. Mentioning that custom hooks share logic but not state is the follow-up most candidates miss.

R14

memo, useMemo and useCallback

Three tools for the same underlying problem — React re-rendering more than it needs to — that are wrong to apply by default. Each one costs a comparison and an allocation on every render, each is defeated by a single unstable reference, and the React Compiler is in the process of making most hand-written uses unnecessary.

What each one does

MemoisesPrevents
memo(Component)The rendered output of a componentRe-rendering when props are shallow-equal
useMemo(fn, deps)The result of a calculationRecomputing, and a new object reference
useCallback(fn, deps)The function itselfA new function reference
javascript · useCallback is useMemo, specialised
useCallback(fn, deps)
// is exactly
useMemo(() => fn, deps)

// Both return the same reference until a dependency changes. The only
// difference is ergonomic: useCallback saves you writing the wrapper.

const handleClick = useCallback(() => save(id), [id]);
const handleClick = useMemo(() => () => save(id), [id]);   // identical

memo

javascript · and the single prop that defeats it
const Row = memo(function Row({ item, onSelect }) {
  return <li onClick={() => onSelect(item.id)}>{item.name}</li>;
});

// memo adds a SHALLOW comparison of props before rendering. If every
// prop is Object.is-equal to last time, React skips the component and
// its whole subtree.

function List({ items }) {
  // A NEW function every render → every memo'd Row re-renders anyway.
  // The memo is now pure overhead: a comparison that always fails.
  return items.map(i => <Row key={i.id} item={i} onSelect={id => …} />);
}

function ListFixed({ items, onSelect }) {
  // Stable, so the comparison can succeed.
  const handleSelect = useCallback((id) => onSelect(id), [onSelect]);
  return items.map(i => <Row key={i.id} item={i} onSelect={handleSelect} />);
}
// And `item` must be stable too — if the parent maps over the array
// creating new objects each render, memo fails on that prop instead.

// A custom comparator, for the rare case where shallow is wrong:
const Row = memo(RowImpl, (prev, next) => prev.item.id === next.item.id);
// Dangerous: you are now responsible for every prop. Forgetting one
// means the component silently stops updating — a much worse bug than
// an unnecessary render.
memo is all-or-nothing on props

One unstable prop defeats the entire memo, and the component re-renders exactly as it would have — except you now also pay for the comparison. This is why sprinkling memo around a codebase reliably fails to help: an inline arrow, a fresh object literal, a style={{…}}, or an array built during the parent's render is enough, and those are everywhere. Memoising one component means auditing every prop it receives, which is why it should be a targeted fix after profiling rather than a habit.

useMemo

javascript · two reasons, and one of them is not performance
// REASON 1 — an expensive calculation.
const sorted = useMemo(
  () => [...rows].sort(byColumn(sortKey)),   // 50k rows: measurable
  [rows, sortKey],
);
// For a 200-item filter this is NOT worth it. The comparison and the
// closure allocation cost more than the filter.

// REASON 2 — REFERENTIAL STABILITY, which is often the real reason.
// The value may be cheap to compute; what matters is that it is the
// SAME object, because something downstream compares by reference.
const options = useMemo(() => ({ page, pageSize: 20 }), [page]);

useEffect(() => { load(options); }, [options]);   // without memo: every render
<MemoChild config={options} />                     // without memo: memo defeated

// A context value is the classic case (R11):
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, login, logout }), [user, login, logout]);

// What NOT to memo — the overhead exceeds the work:
const doubled = useMemo(() => count * 2, [count]);         // pointless
const full    = useMemo(() => `${first} ${last}`, [first, last]);  // pointless
const arr     = useMemo(() => [1, 2, 3], []);              // use a module const
The cost of memoising, which is never zero every render: allocate the deps array compare each dep with Object.is keep the previous value alive (memory) and, for useMemo/useCallback, allocate the closure whether or not the memo hits So the question is never "could this be memoised" but: is the work I am skipping bigger than the work I am adding? For a filter over 100 items: no. For a sort over 50,000: yes. For referential stability feeding a memo'd subtree: yes, because the thing you are skipping is a whole subtree render. And measure the right thing. A component "re-rendering 40 times" is not automatically a problem — if each render produces the same tree, the commit does nothing and the cost is microseconds (R02).

The decision procedure

1 Do not memoise. Write the obvious code. 2 Is something actually slow? Profile it. React DevTools Profiler, with "Record why each component rendered" on. 3 Found a slow commit. Is the cost in rendering or in the DOM? A 5,000-row list is a commit problem — virtualise it, and no amount of memo will help (R03). 4 It is a render cost. Can you fix it structurally instead? · move state down, so the expensive tree is not a sibling · pass the expensive subtree as children · split the context that is over-notifying These are free at runtime and survive refactoring. Memo does not. 5 Only now: memo the component, and stabilise every prop it receives. Verify in the profiler that it actually helped. The two exceptions where memoising up front is reasonable: · a context value (R11) — cheap, and the blast radius is large · a dependency of an effect that subscribes to something expensive

The React Compiler

javascript · what it changes
// The compiler analyses your components at build time and inserts
// memoisation automatically — at a finer granularity than you would
// write by hand, because it can memoise individual expressions rather
// than whole values.

// You write:
function ProductPage({ products, filter }) {
  const visible = products.filter(p => p.category === filter);
  const handleSelect = (id) => select(id);
  return <List items={visible} onSelect={handleSelect} />;
}

// The compiler emits roughly the equivalent of useMemo around `visible`
// and useCallback around `handleSelect`, keyed on what they actually
// read — so `List` receives stable props without you writing either.

// Enabling it (Vite, Next.js, Babel all support it via the plugin):
// babel-plugin-react-compiler, or the framework's own flag.

// What it requires: your components must FOLLOW THE RULES. Mutating
// props, writing to a ref during render, or side effects in the render
// body all make the analysis unsafe — and the compiler's linter tells
// you which components it had to skip.

// What it does not do: it will not virtualise your list, will not fix a
// waterfall, and will not make a genuinely expensive calculation cheap.
// It removes the boilerplate, not the need to think about the commit.
The compiler shifts the advice, it does not delete it

Once it is on, hand-written useMemo and useCallback for referential stability become redundant, and memo on most components becomes unnecessary — which is a large reduction in noise. What does not change is everything structural: waterfalls, oversized lists, contexts that notify too widely, and expensive work that should not be in a render at all. It also has a real prerequisite, which is that impure components are skipped, so a codebase with mutation in render gets partial benefit and a lint report explaining why.

The mistakes

Empty dependency arrays are a stale-closure factory

useCallback(fn, []) freezes the function at its first render, so every prop and state value it closes over is permanently the initial one (J02). The linter catches it, and suppressing the warning is how a handler ends up sending the first-ever form values forever. If you genuinely need a stable identity and current values, the answer is a ref holding the latest function, or useEffectEvent — not a lie in the dependency array.

Interview follow-up

“When would you use useCallback?” Only when something downstream compares the function by reference — a memo'd child, a dependency array, or an external subscription. For a handler passed to a plain DOM element it does nothing except cost an allocation and a comparison. Then give the reason blanket memoisation fails in practice: memo is all-or-nothing, so one inline arrow or object literal among the props defeats it entirely while you keep paying for the check. Finishing with “and the React Compiler now does this automatically, so the remaining work is structural — waterfalls, list size, context scope” shows you are current rather than reciting 2019 advice.

R15

Suspense, lazy and error boundaries

Two mechanisms for the two things that can go wrong below a point in the tree: it is not ready yet, and it broke. Both work by declaring a boundary — a place in the tree that catches the condition and renders something else — which moves loading and error UI out of every component that might need it.

Suspense

javascript · a boundary, and what can trigger it
<Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
  <Profile userId={id} />
</Suspense>

// When anything inside SUSPENDS, React shows the fallback instead of
// that subtree, and swaps it back when the subtree is ready. The
// component itself contains no loading state at all.

// Three things suspend:
//   1 · a lazy component whose chunk has not loaded
//   2 · use(promise) on an unresolved promise            (N03)
//   3 · a Server Component awaiting data, when streaming (N04)
//
// NOT: a plain fetch in useEffect. That is invisible to Suspense —
// which is why "Suspense for data fetching" needed use() and RSC to
// become generally usable.
Where you put the boundary is a design decision. One boundary at the top: <Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}> <Header /><Sidebar /><Feed /><Comments /> </Suspense> → the whole page waits for the SLOWEST thing. One spinner, and a long blank period. A boundary per independent region: <Header /> <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}><Feed /></Suspense> <Suspense fallback={<SideSkeleton />}><Sidebar /></Suspense> → the header is instant, each region fills in as it is ready. This is streaming, and it is why layouts in Next.js are structured around it (X05). Nesting reveals content progressively: <Suspense fallback={<PageShell />}> <Article /> <Suspense fallback={<CommentsSkeleton />}> <Comments /> ← the article appears without waiting </Suspense> </Suspense> Rule of thumb: a boundary belongs wherever the user would accept seeing a placeholder while the rest of the page is usable.

lazy and code splitting

javascript · splitting the bundle at a component
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

// The dynamic import is the split point — the bundler emits a separate
// chunk, fetched the first time this component renders.
const Chart = lazy(() => import('./Chart'));       // needs a DEFAULT export

// A named export needs a shim:
const Chart = lazy(() =>
  import('./Chart').then(m => ({ default: m.Chart })));

function Dashboard() {
  const [showChart, setShowChart] = useState(false);
  return (
    <>
      <button
        onClick={() => setShowChart(true)}
        // Start the download on HOVER, so by the time they click it is
        // usually already there. One line, and it removes most of the
        // perceived cost of code splitting.
        onMouseEnter={() => import('./Chart')}
      >
        Show chart
      </button>

      {showChart && (
        <Suspense fallback={<ChartSkeleton />}>
          <Chart />
        </Suspense>
      )}
    </>
  );
}

// Define lazy components at MODULE level. Inside a component, lazy()
// runs on every render and creates a new component type each time —
// which unmounts and remounts the subtree (J06).
Split at routes and at heavy widgets, not everywhere

Every split is an extra network request, and a chunk of 3 KB costs more in round-trip latency than it saves in parse time. The two splits that reliably pay: routes, because a user visits one page and not the other twelve; and heavy optional widgets — a chart library, a rich-text editor, a map, a date picker with locale data — which are frequently larger than the rest of the application combined. Check with a bundle analyser before splitting anything else, and preload on hover or on intent so the split is invisible.

Error boundaries

javascript · still a class, because there is no hook
class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
  state = { error: null };

  // Called during render: return the new state. Must be pure.
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) {
    return { error };
  }

  // Called after commit: the place for logging. Receives a component
  // stack, which is far more useful than the JS stack.
  componentDidCatch(error, info) {
    reportError(error, { componentStack: info.componentStack });
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.error) {
      return this.props.fallback(this.state.error, () =>
        this.setState({ error: null }));
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

// In practice, use react-error-boundary — it wraps this with a hook API,
// reset keys, and an onReset callback:
import { ErrorBoundary } from 'react-error-boundary';

<ErrorBoundary
  FallbackComponent={ErrorFallback}
  onError={(e, info) => reportError(e, info)}
  resetKeys={[userId]}          // auto-reset when this changes
>
  <Profile userId={userId} />
</ErrorBoundary>
What error boundaries do not catch

They catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of the tree below them. They do not catch: errors in event handlers (use try/catch — the app is not broken, one action failed), asynchronous code including setTimeout and promise rejections, errors in the boundary itself, or errors during server-side rendering. And a boundary does not catch its own children's errors if it is rendered by the same component that threw — the boundary must be above the throwing component in the tree.

javascript · where to put boundaries
// Several levels, each degrading less than the one above.
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<FullPageError />}>          {/* app: last resort */}
  <Layout>
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<RouteError />}>         {/* route */}
      <Page>
        <ErrorBoundary fallback={<WidgetError />}>    {/* widget */}
          <RevenueChart />    {/* if this breaks, the page survives */}
        </ErrorBoundary>
        <Rest />
      </Page>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  </Layout>
</ErrorBoundary>

// Without a boundary anywhere, React 18+ UNMOUNTS THE ENTIRE TREE on an
// uncaught render error — a white screen. That is deliberate: React
// considers a partially-rendered UI after an error more dangerous than
// nothing, because it may show wrong data. So at least one boundary is
// not optional in production.

// The retry fallback, which is what makes a boundary useful rather than
// just tidy:
function ErrorFallback({ error, resetErrorBoundary }) {
  return (
    <div role="alert">
      <p>Something went wrong.</p>
      <pre>{import.meta.env.DEV ? error.message : null}</pre>
      <button onClick={resetErrorBoundary}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  );
}

The two together

javascript · the standard wrapping
// Error boundary OUTSIDE, Suspense INSIDE. If loading the chunk fails —
// a deploy invalidated it, the network dropped — lazy() rejects, and
// that rejection is a render error the boundary must catch.
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<RouteError />}>
  <Suspense fallback={<RouteSkeleton />}>
    <LazyRoute />
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>

// The reverse order means a failed chunk load escapes past the Suspense
// boundary to whatever is above it — usually the app-level fallback,
// so one failed widget blanks the page.

// Chunk-load failures specifically deserve a reload, because the most
// common cause is a deploy that replaced the file:
window.addEventListener('vite:preloadError', () => window.location.reload());

Transitions and stale content

javascript · avoiding the fallback flash on an update
// Problem: a Suspense boundary that already has content will hide it and
// show the fallback again when its data changes — so switching tabs
// flashes a skeleton over content the user was reading.

// startTransition marks an update as non-urgent, and React keeps the
// PREVIOUS content on screen while the new one prepares.
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

function selectTab(next) {
  startTransition(() => setTab(next));   // no fallback flash
}

<button
  onClick={() => selectTab('posts')}
  style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1 }}   // subtle "working" hint
>
  Posts
</button>

// useDeferredValue is the same idea for a value rather than an update —
// keep showing results for the old query while the new one loads:
const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);
const stale = query !== deferredQuery;
<Results query={deferredQuery} className={stale ? 'dim' : ''} />
// More on both in W06.
Interview follow-up

“What do error boundaries not catch?” Event handlers, asynchronous code, server-side rendering, and errors thrown by the boundary itself — and the reason is worth stating: a boundary intercepts errors that propagate through rendering, and a click handler is not part of a render, so a plain try/catch is the right tool there. Then add the fact that makes them non-optional: since React 18, an uncaught render error unmounts the whole tree rather than leaving a partial UI, so an app with no boundary shows a white screen. Finishing with the ordering rule — error boundary outside, Suspense inside, so a failed chunk load is caught rather than escaping to the top — is the detail that shows you have shipped this.

R16

State management: which library, and when

Almost every argument about state management is really an argument about server state — data that lives in a database and is being cached in the browser. Once you separate that out, the amount of genuinely global client state left in a typical application is small enough that the library choice stops being dramatic.

Classify before you choose

1 · SERVER STATE lives in a database; the browser has a copy posts, users, orders, anything fetched needs: caching, deduplication, revalidation, retry, staleness, request cancellation → TanStack Query, SWR, or Server Components ✗ NOT a job for Redux, Zustand or context. Putting it there means reimplementing all of the above, badly. 2 · URL STATE belongs in the address bar filters, sort, pagination, tab, search query, open modal needs: shareable, bookmarkable, survives reload, back button → searchParams / nuqs / router ✗ NOT useState. A link that shows the sender something different from the recipient is a bug users notice. 3 · FORM STATE transient, per-form field values, touched, errors, submitting → React Hook Form, or useActionState for server actions ✗ NOT global. A form's draft is nobody else's business. 4 · CLIENT/UI STATE genuinely shared, genuinely client-side theme, sidebar open, cart before checkout, undo stack, selected rows, a wizard's step → useState → lift → context → a store, in that order The honest observation: after removing 1–3, most applications have a handful of values in category 4. That is why "do I need Redux?" usually answers itself.

The escalation path

1
useState in the component. Stay here as long as possible. Most state is local and should remain local.
2
Lift it up. Two siblings need it — move it to their parent. Still no library, still trivially traceable.
3
useReducer. Several values change together, or the transitions have rules. The reducer is testable in isolation and dispatch is stable.
4
Context. Many components at different depths need it and it changes rarely. Split by update frequency; memoise the value (R11).
5
A store. Context re-renders every consumer on every change and that has become a measurable problem, or you need state outside React, or devtools and middleware would genuinely help.
The ceiling of context is specific, and it is not "too many components"

Context is not slow because many components read it. It is slow because every consumer re-renders when the value changes, regardless of which part they use. A context holding { user, theme, cartItems, cursorPosition } re-renders the theme toggle on every mouse move. The correct first response is to split it into several contexts by change frequency — which fixes most cases for free. Reach for a store when you need consumers to subscribe to slices of one fast-changing value, which context cannot express.

Zustand — the default recommendation

javascript · stores/cart.ts
import { create } from 'zustand';
import { persist } from 'zustand/middleware';

export const useCart = create()(
  persist(
    (set, get) => ({
      items: [],

      // Actions live IN the store, so components dispatch intent
      // rather than computing new state themselves.
      add: (product, qty = 1) => set((s) => {
        const existing = s.items.find((i) => i.id === product.id);
        return existing
          ? { items: s.items.map((i) =>
              i.id === product.id ? { ...i, qty: i.qty + qty } : i) }
          : { items: [...s.items, { ...product, qty }] };
      }),
      remove: (id) => set((s) => ({ items: s.items.filter((i) => i.id !== id) })),
      clear: () => set({ items: [] }),

      // Derived values as getters — not stored, so they cannot go stale.
      total: () => get().items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0),
    }),
    { name: 'cart', partialize: (s) => ({ items: s.items }) },
  ),
);

// IN A COMPONENT — select the narrowest slice. This is the whole
// performance story: this component re-renders when `items.length`
// changes and not when anything else in the store does.
function CartBadge() {
  const count = useCart((s) => s.items.length);
  return <span>{count}</span>;
}

// Actions are stable, so selecting one never causes a re-render:
function AddButton({ product }) {
  const add = useCart((s) => s.add);
  return <button onClick={() => add(product)}>Add to cart</button>;
}

// Selecting an OBJECT returns a new reference every time and defeats
// the whole mechanism. Use useShallow, or select twice.
const { add, remove } = useCart(useShallow((s) => ({ add: s.add, remove: s.remove })));

// Outside React — a store is a plain subscribable object:
useCart.getState().clear();
useCart.subscribe((s) => console.log(s.items.length));
A module-scope store and SSR

create() at module scope makes one store per process. In the browser that is one per tab, which is what you want. On a server rendering many users' requests in one Node process, it is shared between users — one person's cart can appear in another's render. For anything server-rendered and user-specific, create the store per request and pass it through a context provider, or keep the store strictly client-only and hydrate it after mount. This is the same hazard as module-scope mutable state in a Server Component (X03), and it is a data-leak bug, not a performance one.

Jotai — when the unit is a value, not a store

javascript
import { atom, useAtom, useAtomValue, useSetAtom } from 'jotai';

const filterAtom = atom('');
const itemsAtom  = atom([]);

// Derived atoms recompute only when their dependencies change, and
// only components reading THEM re-render. This is the atomic model:
// the dependency graph is the optimisation, with no selectors.
const visibleAtom = atom((get) =>
  get(itemsAtom).filter((i) => i.name.includes(get(filterAtom))));

const countAtom = atom((get) => get(visibleAtom).length);

function Count() {
  const count = useAtomValue(countAtom);   // re-renders only when the
  return <b>{count}</b>;                    // COUNT changes
}
function FilterInput() {
  const setFilter = useSetAtom(filterAtom); // never re-renders
  return <input onChange={(e) => setFilter(e.target.value)} />;
}

// Write-only atoms act like actions:
const addItemAtom = atom(null, (get, set, item) =>
  set(itemsAtom, [...get(itemsAtom), item]));

// Choose Jotai over Zustand when state is naturally many small
// independent values with derivations between them — a canvas editor,
// a spreadsheet, a form builder. Choose Zustand when it is one
// cohesive domain object with actions — a cart, a player, a session.

Redux Toolkit — when it is still the right answer

javascript · features/board/boardSlice.ts
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

const boardSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'board',
  initialState: { columns: {}, cards: {}, selection: [] },
  reducers: {
    // Immer is built in, so this MUTATING code produces an immutable
    // update. Modern Redux is nothing like the 2018 boilerplate.
    cardMoved(state, action) {
      const { id, toColumn, index } = action.payload;
      const card = state.cards[id];
      state.columns[card.columnId].cardIds =
        state.columns[card.columnId].cardIds.filter((c) => c !== id);
      state.columns[toColumn].cardIds.splice(index, 0, id);
      card.columnId = toColumn;
    },
    selectionChanged(state, action) { state.selection = action.payload; },
  },
});

export const { cardMoved, selectionChanged } = boardSlice.actions;
export default boardSlice.reducer;

// Redux Toolkit earns its weight when you have:
//   · a large team that benefits from one enforced pattern
//   · genuinely complex client state with many interacting slices
//   · undo/redo, time-travel, or replayable action logs
//   · middleware needs — analytics on every action, optimistic
//     queues, offline sync
//   · the devtools, which remain the best in the ecosystem for
//     answering "what changed this, and when"
//
// It does NOT earn its weight for a theme toggle and a cart, and RTK
// Query is a real alternative to TanStack Query if you are already
// invested in the Redux ecosystem.

TanStack Query — not a state library

javascript · the category that removes most "global state"
const { data, isPending, error, refetch } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['posts', { tag, page }],   // the key IS the cache identity
  queryFn: ({ signal }) => getPosts({ tag, page, signal }),
  staleTime: 60_000,                    // how long before it refetches
  gcTime: 5 * 60_000,                   // how long unused data is kept
});

const qc = useQueryClient();
const { mutate } = useMutation({
  mutationFn: createPost,
  onMutate: async (draft) => {
    // Optimistic update, with a snapshot to roll back to.
    await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['posts'] });
    const previous = qc.getQueryData(['posts']);
    qc.setQueryData(['posts'], (old) => [draft, ...old]);
    return { previous };
  },
  onError: (_err, _draft, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(['posts'], ctx.previous),
  onSettled: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['posts'] }),
});

// What you get for free, and would otherwise hand-roll into a store:
//   deduplication of identical in-flight requests
//   background refetch on focus, reconnect and interval
//   stale-while-revalidate with per-query staleness
//   retry with backoff, and request cancellation via signal
//   pagination and infinite scroll primitives
//   a devtools panel showing every cache entry's state
//
// Replacing this with `posts: []` in a Zustand store and a useEffect
// is the single most common architectural mistake in React apps.

URL state

javascript · the category everyone forgets
// Next.js server page — read it as a prop, render filtered results on
// the server, no client state at all:
export default async function Page({ searchParams }) {
  const { tag = 'all', page = '1' } = await searchParams;
  const posts = await getPosts({ tag, page: Number(page) });
  return <List posts={posts} />;
}

// Client-side, with a typed helper (nuqs) so you are not parsing
// strings by hand and not losing state on reload:
import { useQueryState, parseAsInteger } from 'nuqs';
const [tag, setTag]   = useQueryState('tag', { defaultValue: 'all' });
const [page, setPage] = useQueryState('page', parseAsInteger.withDefault(1));

// The test for whether something belongs in the URL: if a user copies
// the address bar and sends it to a colleague, should the colleague
// see the same thing? Filters, sort, tab, page, search — yes. A
// half-typed comment — no.

Comparison

ToolBest forCostAvoid when
useState / liftAlmost everythingNoneThe same value is needed in five distant places
useReducerRelated values with transition rulesNoneA single boolean
ContextRarely-changing values read widelyAll consumers re-renderThe value changes often
ZustandOne cohesive client domain; state outside React~1 kB; module-scope SSR hazardIt is really server data
JotaiMany small independent values with derivationsAtom sprawl if undisciplinedOne cohesive object with actions
Redux ToolkitLarge teams, complex interacting state, undo, middlewareMost boilerplate; a real bundle costThe app has five global values
TanStack QueryAll server data in a client-fetching appA concept to learnEverything is a Server Component already
URL / nuqsFilters, tabs, pagination, searchSerialisation onlyTransient or private values

What Server Components change

RSC removes the reason most stores existed

A global store was usually a place to cache fetched data so several components could read it without refetching. In an RSC application that data is fetched on the server, deduplicated within the render, and cached by the framework — so the store has nothing to hold. What survives is the genuinely client-side set: a theme, an open drawer, a cart before checkout, an editor's undo stack, selected rows in a table. That is typically small enough for context plus useState, with a store only where a fast-changing value needs slice subscriptions. If you are adding Redux to a Next.js App Router project, check first whether what you are storing is actually server state.

The anti-patterns

Three more worth naming

One giant store. A single object holding every value in the application means every change is a candidate re-render and nothing can be deleted with confidence — split by domain. Derived state stored alongside its source. A total field kept in sync with items will disagree with it eventually; compute it in a selector or a getter. Reaching for a library at step one. Adding Redux before you have felt the problem it solves gives you the boilerplate without the benefit, and a component whose state lives three files away is harder to read than one whose state lives in it.

Interview follow-up

“How do you decide on state management?” Do not name a library first — that is the trap. Classify the state: server data goes in a cache such as TanStack Query or on the server entirely; URL state goes in the URL; form state goes in the form. Then say that what remains is usually a handful of client values, handled by useState, lifting, and context, with a store like Zustand only when context's all-consumers-re-render behaviour becomes measurable or you need to read state outside React. Finish with when Redux Toolkit is still correct — large teams, complex interacting state, undo, middleware, its devtools — so it is clear you are choosing rather than dismissing.

R17

Redux Toolkit, fully explained

Most of what people dislike about Redux was fixed in 2019 and they have not looked since. Redux Toolkit is the official, batteries-included way to write it: Immer built in, the store configured for you, thunks included, and a data-fetching layer in the box. This chapter is the whole thing, in the order you would actually build it.

The three principles, and what they buy

1 · ONE STORE a single object tree for the application 2 · READ-ONLY STATE the only way to change it is to dispatch an action describing what happened 3 · PURE REDUCERS (state, action) → new state, no side effects Everything Redux is good at follows from those three: time-travel debugging because every state is reachable by replaying actions from the start predictability because the only mutation path is a named action you can log middleware because every change passes through one pipe you can tap testability because reducers are pure functions And the cost is equally clear: indirection. Reading a value means finding the selector; changing it means finding the action, the reducer and the dispatch. That price is worth paying when several parts of an app change the same state in ways that must be auditable — and not worth paying for a theme toggle.

The store

javascript · app/store.ts
import { configureStore } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import boardReducer from '@/features/board/boardSlice';
import filtersReducer from '@/features/filters/filtersSlice';
import { api } from '@/services/api';

export const makeStore = () => configureStore({
  reducer: {
    board: boardReducer,
    filters: filtersReducer,
    [api.reducerPath]: api.reducer,
  },

  // configureStore already sets up: redux-thunk, the DevTools
  // extension, and in development two checks that catch the two
  // classic Redux bugs —
  //   serializableCheck: warns if you put a Date, Map, Promise or
  //     class instance in state or an action (breaks time travel)
  //   immutableCheck: warns if a reducer mutated state outside Immer
  middleware: (getDefault) => getDefault({
    serializableCheck: {
      // RTK Query's internal actions carry non-serializable values.
      ignoredActions: ['persist/PERSIST'],
    },
  }).concat(api.middleware, analyticsMiddleware),

  devTools: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production',
});

// A FACTORY, not a module-scope store. On the server one module-scope
// store would be shared between every user's request — the same
// hazard as any module-scope mutable state (X03, R16).
export type AppStore = ReturnType<typeof makeStore>;
export type RootState = ReturnType<AppStore['getState']>;
export type AppDispatch = AppStore['dispatch'];
javascript · app/hooks.ts — always use these, never the raw hooks
import { useDispatch, useSelector, useStore } from 'react-redux';

// Pre-typed versions, so every call site gets RootState and the thunk-
// aware dispatch without repeating the generics.
export const useAppDispatch = useDispatch.withTypes<AppDispatch>();
export const useAppSelector = useSelector.withTypes<RootState>();
export const useAppStore = useStore.withTypes<AppStore>();

// Without these, `dispatch(fetchBoard())` is a type error because the
// plain Dispatch type does not know about thunks, and `state` in every
// selector is `unknown`.

A slice

javascript · features/board/boardSlice.ts
import { createSlice, createAsyncThunk, PayloadAction } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

const initialState = {
  columns: {},          // normalized: id -> column
  cards: {},            // normalized: id -> card
  columnOrder: [],
  selection: [],
  status: 'idle',       // idle | loading | succeeded | failed
  error: null,
};

const boardSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'board',                 // prefixes every action type: board/…
  initialState,
  reducers: {
    // IMMER IS BUILT IN. This mutating code produces an immutable
    // update — Immer records the mutations on a draft proxy and
    // applies them to a structurally-shared copy. Unchanged branches
    // keep their identity, so memoised selectors still work.
    cardMoved(state, action: PayloadAction<{ id: string; to: string; index: number }>) {
      const { id, to, index } = action.payload;
      const card = state.cards[id];
      const from = state.columns[card.columnId];
      from.cardIds = from.cardIds.filter((c) => c !== id);
      state.columns[to].cardIds.splice(index, 0, id);
      card.columnId = to;
    },

    selectionChanged(state, action: PayloadAction<string[]>) {
      state.selection = action.payload;
    },

    // The `prepare` callback handles anything non-deterministic, so
    // the reducer itself stays pure and replayable.
    cardAdded: {
      reducer(state, action) {
        state.cards[action.payload.id] = action.payload;
        state.columns[action.payload.columnId].cardIds.push(action.payload.id);
      },
      prepare(columnId, title) {
        return { payload: { id: nanoid(), columnId, title, createdAt: Date.now() } };
      },
    },
  },

  // extraReducers responds to actions defined ELSEWHERE — thunk
  // lifecycle actions, or actions owned by another slice. This is how
  // two slices react to one event without importing each other.
  extraReducers: (builder) => {
    builder
      .addCase(fetchBoard.pending, (state) => { state.status = 'loading'; })
      .addCase(fetchBoard.fulfilled, (state, action) => {
        state.status = 'succeeded';
        Object.assign(state, action.payload);
      })
      .addCase(fetchBoard.rejected, (state, action) => {
        state.status = 'failed';
        state.error = action.error.message ?? 'Could not load the board';
      })
      // A matcher handles a whole family at once:
      .addMatcher((a) => a.type.endsWith('/rejected'), (state) => {
        state.pendingWrites = 0;
      });
  },
});

export const { cardMoved, selectionChanged, cardAdded } = boardSlice.actions;
export default boardSlice.reducer;
The one Immer rule: mutate the draft, or return a value — never both

Inside createSlice you may write state.items.push(x), or you may return newState, but doing both in the same reducer throws.
