The common accident is an early return inside a branch that also mutated — and the subtler one is state = something, which merely reassigns the local variable and does nothing at all, silently. Two more: Immer only tracks mutations on the draft you were given, so mutating an object you captured in a closure outside the reducer does nothing; and createSlice's Immer applies only inside createSlice and createReducer — a hand-written reducer still needs spreads.

Naming actions as events, not setters

Selectors

javascript · features/board/selectors.ts
import { createSelector } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

// useSelector re-renders when the result changes by reference
// equality. So a selector that DERIVES a new array or object
// re-renders on every dispatch, anywhere in the app:
const bad = (state) => state.board.columnOrder.map((id) => state.board.columns[id]);
//    ^ new array every call → every action re-renders this component

// createSelector memoises on its inputs, so the output keeps its
// identity until an input actually changes:
export const selectColumns = createSelector(
  [(s) => s.board.columnOrder, (s) => s.board.columns],
  (order, columns) => order.map((id) => columns[id]),
);

// PARAMETERISED selectors need care: a memoised selector has a cache
// of size one by default, so two components calling it with different
// ids thrash the cache and neither is memoised. RTK 2 ships a
// configurable cache — or create the selector per component:
export const makeSelectCardsInColumn = () => createSelector(
  [(s) => s.board.cards, (s, columnId) => s.board.columns[columnId].cardIds],
  (cards, ids) => ids.map((id) => cards[id]),
);

function Column({ id }) {
  // useMemo so each Column instance gets its own memoised selector.
  const selectCards = useMemo(makeSelectCardsInColumn, []);
  const cards = useAppSelector((s) => selectCards(s, id));
}

// SELECT NARROWLY. This is the single biggest Redux performance rule:
const board = useAppSelector((s) => s.board);          // ✗ any change
const title = useAppSelector((s) => s.board.cards[id].title);   // ✓

// For an object of several fields, either select each separately or
// pass a shallow comparison:
import { shallowEqual } from 'react-redux';
const { title, assignee } = useAppSelector(
  (s) => ({ title: s.board.cards[id].title, assignee: s.board.cards[id].assignee }),
  shallowEqual,
);

Async: thunks

javascript · createAsyncThunk
export const fetchBoard = createAsyncThunk(
  'board/fetch',                       // generates board/fetch/pending,
                                       // /fulfilled and /rejected
  async (boardId, { rejectWithValue, signal, getState, dispatch }) => {
    try {
      // The thunk receives an AbortSignal, so dispatching again or
      // calling .abort() cancels the in-flight request.
      const res = await fetch(`/api/boards/${boardId}`, { signal });
      if (!res.ok) {
        // rejectWithValue puts a SERIALIZABLE payload on the rejected
        // action. Throwing puts action.error there instead, which is a
        // stringified error and loses your status code and fields.
        return rejectWithValue({ status: res.status, message: await res.text() });
      }
      return res.json();
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.name === 'AbortError') throw err;
      return rejectWithValue({ message: 'Network error' });
    }
  },
  {
    // Skip the request entirely if it is already loaded or in flight —
    // the deduplication a hand-rolled thunk usually lacks.
    condition: (boardId, { getState }) => {
      const { status } = getState().board;
      return status !== 'loading' && status !== 'succeeded';
    },
  },
);

// An optimistic write, with rollback — the pattern Redux is genuinely
// good at, because the rollback is just another action.
export const moveCard = createAsyncThunk(
  'board/moveCard',
  async ({ id, to, index }, { dispatch, getState, rejectWithValue }) => {
    const snapshot = getState().board;
    dispatch(cardMoved({ id, to, index }));        // optimistic
    try {
      return await api.moveCard({ id, to, index });
    } catch (err) {
      dispatch(boardRestored(snapshot));           // rollback
      return rejectWithValue(err.message);
    }
  },
);

RTK Query, which replaces most thunks

javascript · services/api.ts
import { createApi, fetchBaseQuery } from '@reduxjs/toolkit/query/react';

export const api = createApi({
  reducerPath: 'api',
  baseQuery: fetchBaseQuery({
    baseUrl: '/api',
    prepareHeaders: (headers, { getState }) => {
      const token = getState().auth.token;
      if (token) headers.set('authorization', `Bearer ${token}`);
      return headers;
    },
  }),
  tagTypes: ['Board', 'Card'],

  endpoints: (build) => ({
    getBoard: build.query({
      query: (id) => `/boards/${id}`,
      // Tags are the invalidation graph — the same idea as Next.js
      // cache tags (X04): describe the DATA, and a mutation
      // invalidates it without knowing which components read it.
      providesTags: (result, error, id) => [{ type: 'Board', id }],
    }),

    moveCard: build.mutation({
      query: ({ id, ...patch }) => ({
        url: `/cards/${id}/move`, method: 'PATCH', body: patch,
      }),
      invalidatesTags: (r, e, { boardId }) => [{ type: 'Board', id: boardId }],

      // Optimistic update, with automatic rollback on failure.
      async onQueryStarted({ id, boardId, to, index }, { dispatch, queryFulfilled }) {
        const patch = dispatch(
          api.util.updateQueryData('getBoard', boardId, (draft) => {
            // Immer again — mutate the cached response directly.
            const card = draft.cards[id];
            draft.columns[card.columnId].cardIds =
              draft.columns[card.columnId].cardIds.filter((c) => c !== id);
            draft.columns[to].cardIds.splice(index, 0, id);
            card.columnId = to;
          }),
        );
        try { await queryFulfilled; } catch { patch.undo(); }
      },
    }),
  }),
});

export const { useGetBoardQuery, useMoveCardMutation } = api;

// In a component — and note there is no slice, no thunk, no loading
// state to write:
const { data, isLoading, error, refetch } = useGetBoardQuery(boardId);
const [moveCard, { isLoading: isMoving }] = useMoveCardMutation();
If you are adding Redux for server data, add RTK Query instead

RTK Query gives you caching, request deduplication, tag-based invalidation, polling, refetch on focus and reconnect, optimistic updates with rollback, and generated hooks — the same feature set as TanStack Query, already integrated with the store and the devtools. Writing slices full of status fields and createAsyncThunk lifecycles to hold server data is reimplementing it by hand, which is the most common way a modern Redux codebase becomes tedious. Keep hand-written slices for genuine client state — selection, drafts, undo stacks, UI mode — and let RTK Query own everything that came from a server.

Middleware

javascript · the capability nothing else gives you as cleanly
// Every state change in the app passes through one pipe, so
// cross-cutting concerns are written once.
const analyticsMiddleware = (store) => (next) => (action) => {
  const result = next(action);
  if (TRACKED.has(action.type)) {
    track(action.type, { ...action.payload, boardId: store.getState().board.id });
  }
  return result;
};

// The listener middleware is the modern, cancellable alternative to
// hand-written middleware and to sagas:
import { createListenerMiddleware } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

export const listener = createListenerMiddleware();

listener.startListening({
  actionCreator: cardMoved,
  effect: async (action, api) => {
    // Debounce: cancel any earlier run of this effect still pending.
    api.cancelActiveListeners();
    await api.delay(500);
    await api.dispatch(persistBoard());
  },
});

listener.startListening({
  // React to a computed condition rather than one action type:
  predicate: (action, current, previous) =>
    current.cart.items.length !== previous.cart.items.length,
  effect: (action, api) => localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(api.getState().cart)),
});
// This replaces redux-saga for the great majority of cases, without
// generators and without a second mental model.

Redux with Next.js

javascript · app/StoreProvider.tsx
'use client';
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { Provider } from 'react-redux';
import { makeStore } from './store';

export function StoreProvider({ children }) {
  const storeRef = useRef(null);
  // ONE STORE PER REQUEST on the server, one per tab in the browser.
  // A module-scope `export const store = makeStore()` would be shared
  // across every user the server instance handles — a data leak, not
  // a performance issue.
  if (!storeRef.current) storeRef.current = makeStore();
  return <Provider store={storeRef.current}>{children}</Provider>;
}

// In the root layout, wrapping server-rendered children:
// <StoreProvider>{children}</StoreProvider>
// The provider is a Client Component; its children can still be
// Server Components, because they are passed in already rendered (X03).

// And ask the prior question first: in the App Router, most of what a
// store used to hold is server data that now lives on the server. A
// Redux store in a Next.js app should be holding client state —
// an editor's undo stack, a complex selection, a drag interaction —
// not a cache of rows (R16).

Testing

javascript · the payoff for pure reducers
// A reducer is a pure function, so there is nothing to mount and
// nothing to mock:
test('cardMoved moves a card between columns', () => {
  const next = reducer(state, cardMoved({ id: 'c1', to: 'done', index: 0 }));
  expect(next.columns.done.cardIds).toEqual(['c1', 'c3']);
  expect(next.columns.todo.cardIds).not.toContain('c1');
  expect(next).not.toBe(state);              // immutability held
});

// Selectors are pure too:
test('selectColumns returns columns in order', () => {
  expect(selectColumns(rootState).map((c) => c.id)).toEqual(['todo', 'doing']);
});

// And a component test builds a real store with preloaded state —
// no mocking of useSelector, which would test nothing:
function renderWithStore(ui, { preloadedState } = {}) {
  const store = makeStore(preloadedState);
  return render(<Provider store={store}>{ui}</Provider>);
}

When Redux Toolkit is the right choice

Use it whenDo not when
Complex client state with many interacting slicesThe app has five global values
Undo/redo, or a replayable action logThe state is really server data — use RTK Query or TanStack Query
Cross-cutting middleware: analytics, offline queue, syncA theme toggle and a cart
A large team that benefits from one enforced patternA small team that will resent the indirection
You need the devtools to answer “what changed this?”You are adding it because it is what you know
State that must be read and written from outside ReactZustand does this in a fraction of the code (R18)
The mistakes that survive into modern Redux codebases

Non-serializable values in state — a Date, a Map, a class instance or a function breaks time travel and persistence; store an ISO string or a plain object. Selecting whole slices, so every dispatch anywhere re-renders the component. Deriving new arrays in an inline selector without createSelector, which does the same. Setter-shaped actions, which turn the action log into noise and push logic into components. And putting everything in the store — a form's draft value, a dropdown's open flag and a hover state belong in useState, where they cost nothing and are local to the component that owns them.

Interview follow-up

“Is Redux still relevant?” Yes, in a narrower place than it used to occupy — and the strong answer explains the narrowing. Server state, which was the bulk of what stores held, has moved to query caches and Server Components; what remains is genuine client state, and for a handful of values useState plus context is simpler. Redux Toolkit earns its place when that client state is complex and interacting, when you need undo or a replayable log, when middleware must observe every change, or when the devtools' answer to “what changed this and when” is worth the indirection. Then show you know the modern API: createSlice with Immer so reducers look mutating but are not, createSelector because useSelector compares by reference, the listener middleware instead of sagas, and RTK Query rather than hand-written thunks for anything fetched.

R18

Zustand, implemented

Zustand is about a kilobyte, has no provider, no actions, no reducers and no selectors registry — and it does the thing context cannot: let a component subscribe to a slice of fast-changing state. It is small enough that we can build a working version of it first, which makes everything it does afterwards obvious.

Building it, in thirty lines

javascript · lib/mini-zustand.ts — the whole idea
import { useSyncExternalStore, useRef, useCallback } from 'react';

export function create(createState) {
  let state;
  const listeners = new Set();

  const setState = (partial, replace = false) => {
    const next = typeof partial === 'function' ? partial(state) : partial;
    // Bail out if nothing changed by reference — the same Object.is
    // check React uses, so an action that produces an identical value
    // costs nothing.
    if (Object.is(next, state)) return;
    // MERGE by default, unlike useState's replace. This is why you can
    // call set({ count: 1 }) without spreading the rest of the store.
    state = replace ? next : { ...state, ...next };
    listeners.forEach((l) => l());
  };

  const getState = () => state;
  const subscribe = (listener) => {
    listeners.add(listener);
    return () => listeners.delete(listener);
  };

  // The store is created by calling the user's initialiser with set
  // and get, so actions live inside the store and close over both.
  state = createState(setState, getState, { setState, getState, subscribe });

  // The hook. useSyncExternalStore is doing all the React integration:
  // it subscribes, reads a snapshot, and guarantees no tearing under
  // concurrent rendering (W06).
  const useStore = (selector = getState) =>
    useSyncExternalStore(
      subscribe,
      useCallback(() => selector(getState()), [selector]),
      useCallback(() => selector(getState()), [selector]),   // SSR
    );

  Object.assign(useStore, { getState, setState, subscribe });
  return useStore;
}

// That is genuinely the core. Everything else Zustand ships —
// middleware, persistence, shallow comparison, devtools — is built on
// top of these four functions.
Why this beats context for fast-changing state

Context delivers one value to every consumer, so React re-renders all of them when that value changes, regardless of which field each one reads (R11). A store delivers a subscription: each component runs its own selector and re-renders only when its own result changes. That is the entire performance difference, and it is why splitting contexts by update frequency is the fix for most context problems while a store is the fix for the rest. The trade is that a store lives outside the React tree, so it cannot be scoped per-subtree unless you deliberately put it in a provider — which is exactly what you must do for SSR.

A real store

javascript · stores/editor.ts
import { create } from 'zustand';
import { devtools, persist, subscribeWithSelector } from 'zustand/middleware';
import { immer } from 'zustand/middleware/immer';

export const useEditor = create()(
  devtools(
    persist(
      subscribeWithSelector(
        immer((set, get) => ({
          // ── state ──────────────────────────────────────────────
          blocks: {},
          order: [],
          selection: [],
          history: { past: [], future: [] },

          // ── actions, co-located with the state they change ─────
          // With the immer middleware these can mutate the draft,
          // exactly as in a Redux slice (R17). Without it, spread.
          blockUpdated: (id, patch) => set((s) => {
            Object.assign(s.blocks[id], patch);
          }, false, 'editor/blockUpdated'),
          //  ^ third arg is the devtools action name; without it the
          //    timeline shows a wall of anonymous "setState" entries

          blockAdded: (block, index) => set((s) => {
            s.blocks[block.id] = block;
            s.order.splice(index ?? s.order.length, 0, block.id);
          }, false, 'editor/blockAdded'),

          selectionChanged: (ids) => set({ selection: ids }, false, 'editor/selection'),

          // Actions can read current state with get(), and can be async.
          save: async () => {
            const { blocks, order } = get();
            set({ saving: true }, false, 'editor/saveStart');
            try {
              await api.saveDocument({ blocks, order });
              set({ saving: false, dirty: false }, false, 'editor/saveDone');
            } catch (err) {
              set({ saving: false, error: err.message }, false, 'editor/saveFailed');
            }
          },

          // ── derived values as functions, never stored ──────────
          // Storing a derived value means keeping two things in sync
          // and eventually having them disagree (R16).
          selectedBlocks: () => get().selection.map((id) => get().blocks[id]),
        })),
      ),
      {
        name: 'editor-draft',
        // Persist only what should survive a reload. Without
        // partialize the whole store is written, including transient
        // flags like `saving` — which then restore as `true`.
        partialize: (s) => ({ blocks: s.blocks, order: s.order }),
        version: 2,
        migrate: (persisted, version) =>
          version < 2 ? { ...persisted, order: persisted.ids ?? [] } : persisted,
      },
    ),
    { name: 'editor' },
  ),
);

Selecting, and the one mistake everyone makes

javascript
// ✓ NARROW: re-renders only when this block's title changes.
const title = useEditor((s) => s.blocks[id].title);

// ✓ ACTIONS are stable references, so selecting one never re-renders.
const blockUpdated = useEditor((s) => s.blockUpdated);

// ✗ THE MISTAKE: an object literal is a new reference every call, so
// the snapshot never compares equal and the component re-renders on
// EVERY store change — and in Zustand v5 this throws a warning about
// an unstable snapshot, because it is also an infinite-loop risk.
const { blockUpdated, blockAdded } = useEditor((s) =>
  ({ blockUpdated: s.blockUpdated, blockAdded: s.blockAdded }));

// ✓ FIX ONE — useShallow, comparing one level deep:
import { useShallow } from 'zustand/react/shallow';
const { blockUpdated, blockAdded } = useEditor(
  useShallow((s) => ({ blockUpdated: s.blockUpdated, blockAdded: s.blockAdded })),
);

// ✓ FIX TWO — select twice. Two subscriptions, both primitives or
// stable references, and no comparison function needed.
const blockUpdated = useEditor((s) => s.blockUpdated);
const blockAdded   = useEditor((s) => s.blockAdded);

// ✓ A common convention: keep actions in a nested object created once,
// so the whole group can be selected with a stable reference.
//   actions: { blockUpdated, blockAdded, … }
const actions = useEditor((s) => s.actions);        // never re-renders

// ✗ Selecting everything defeats the entire point:
const store = useEditor();                          // every change

Outside React

javascript · the capability that decides the choice
// A store is a plain object with getState, setState and subscribe. No
// hook, no component, no provider required — so non-React code can
// read and write it directly.

// In an event handler, a web worker, a websocket callback, a service:
useEditor.getState().blockUpdated(id, { title });
const isDirty = useEditor.getState().dirty;

// Subscribe to a slice, with subscribeWithSelector:
const unsubscribe = useEditor.subscribe(
  (s) => s.dirty,
  (dirty) => { document.title = dirty ? '• Untitled' : 'Untitled'; },
  { fireImmediately: true },
);

// Sync to a websocket without any component involved:
socket.on('remote-edit', (patch) => useEditor.getState().applyRemote(patch));
useEditor.subscribe((s) => s.blocks, (blocks) => socket.emit('edit', blocks));

// And read the LATEST state inside a callback without re-subscribing —
// the stale-closure problem (R01), solved by construction:
const onSave = useCallback(() => {
  const { blocks } = useEditor.getState();   // always current
  post(blocks);
}, []);                                       // no dependencies needed

SSR: the store must be per request

javascript · stores/editor-provider.tsx
'use client';
import { createStore, useStore } from 'zustand';
import { createContext, useContext, useRef } from 'react';

// A module-scope store is ONE PER PROCESS. In the browser that is one
// per tab, which is correct. On a server rendering many users'
// requests in one Node process it is SHARED BETWEEN USERS — one
// person's draft can appear in another's render. This is a data leak,
// not a performance issue (R16, X03).

export const createEditorStore = (initial) =>
  createStore()(immer((set, get) => ({ ...defaults, ...initial, /* actions */ })));

const EditorStoreContext = createContext(null);

export function EditorStoreProvider({ children, initial }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  if (!ref.current) ref.current = createEditorStore(initial);
  return (
    <EditorStoreContext.Provider value={ref.current}>
      {children}
    </EditorStoreContext.Provider>
  );
}

// Context now carries the STORE, which never changes identity — so
// consumers do not re-render when state changes. The subscription,
// not the context, delivers updates. This is the pattern that gets
// you per-request isolation AND slice subscriptions at once.
export function useEditorStore(selector) {
  const store = useContext(EditorStoreContext);
  if (!store) throw new Error('useEditorStore must be used inside EditorStoreProvider');
  return useStore(store, selector);
}

// It also lets you scope a store per SUBTREE — one store per open
// document tab, per modal, per board — which a module-scope singleton
// cannot express.

// PERSISTENCE + SSR: the persist middleware reads storage on the
// client only, so the first render differs from the server's.
// Zustand exposes a hydration hook for exactly this (B01):
const hydrated = useEditor.persist.hasHydrated();
if (!hydrated) return <Skeleton />;
The module-scope store is the one genuinely dangerous Zustand mistake

Everything else on this page is a performance or ergonomics issue. This one is a correctness and privacy bug, and it is invisible in development because you are the only user and the dev server often rebuilds between requests. If a store holds anything user-specific and the app is server-rendered, create it per request behind a provider. The module-scope form is fine for a purely client-side SPA, and fine on the server for genuinely user-independent data — a feature-flag snapshot, a static config — and nothing else.

Slices, for a store that has grown

javascript · splitting one store into composable pieces
// One giant store means every change is a candidate re-render and
// nothing can be deleted with confidence. Two options:

// 1 · SEPARATE STORES — the default. Independent domains should be
//     independent stores; there is no cost to having five.
export const useCart = create(…);
export const useAuth = create(…);
export const useUI = create(…);

// 2 · SLICES IN ONE STORE — when the pieces genuinely need to read
//     each other, since a store cannot see another store's state
//     without importing it.
const createCartSlice = (set, get) => ({
  items: [],
  add: (p) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, p] })),
  // This slice can read the auth slice through get(), because they
  // share one state object:
  checkout: () => api.checkout(get().items, get().user.id),
});
const createAuthSlice = (set) => ({
  user: null,
  signIn: async (c) => set({ user: await api.signIn(c) }),
});

export const useApp = create()((...a) => ({
  ...createCartSlice(...a),
  ...createAuthSlice(...a),
}));
// Watch for name collisions: the spread means a later slice silently
// overwrites an earlier one's key of the same name.

Zustand against the alternatives

ZustandRedux ToolkitContext
Bundle~1 kB~12 kB + React-Redux0
Provider requiredNo (but yes for SSR)YesYes
Slice subscriptionsYes, via selectorsYes, via useSelectorNo — all consumers re-render
Usable outside ReactYes, directlyYes, via store.dispatchNo
Devtools timelineVia middleware, if you name actionsBest in classNone
Enforced patternNone — a benefit and a riskStrongNone
Server-data cachingNo — use a query cacheRTK Query, includedNo
BoilerplateMinimalModerateMinimal until it is not
Zustand's freedom is the thing to manage

There are no enforced conventions, so a codebase can end up with actions in components, state mutated through setState from four unrelated files, derived values stored next to their sources, and a devtools timeline of anonymous setState entries. Impose the conventions yourself: actions live in the store, never in components; always pass the third set argument so the devtools timeline is readable; derive with functions or selectors, never store computed values; and keep server data out — it belongs in a query cache. Redux imposes these; with Zustand they are a code-review responsibility.

Interview follow-up

“Why Zustand over Context?” Because context delivers one value to every consumer, so all of them re-render when it changes regardless of which field they read; a store delivers a subscription, so each component runs its own selector and re-renders only when its own result changes. Then show you know the mechanics: it is built on useSyncExternalStore, which is what guarantees no tearing under concurrent rendering; selecting an object literal creates a new reference every call and defeats the comparison, so you need useShallow or separate selections; and because the store is a plain object with getState and subscribe, non-React code can drive it — which also makes stale closures a non-issue. Finish with the trap: a module-scope store is shared across users on a server, so anything user-specific needs a per-request store behind a provider.

W01

Elements, the tree, and the “virtual DOM”

The phrase “virtual DOM” has done more to obscure React than to explain it. What actually exists is a tree of plain objects describing what the UI should be, and a second structure — fiber — tracking what it currently is. Understanding the distinction is the foundation for everything else in Part III.

Three trees, not one

1 The element tree what you return from components plain objects, immutable, created fresh on every render, thrown away immediately after 2 The fiber tree React's internal bookkeeping mutable, persistent across renders, holds state, hooks, effects and the DOM pointer 3 The DOM what the browser actually has "Virtual DOM" usually means (1), sometimes means (2), and is therefore not a useful term. React's own documentation has largely stopped using it. ┌─ element tree (this render) ──┐ ┌─ fiber tree (persistent) ──────┐ │ {type: App, props: {…}} │ │ FiberNode(App) │ │ {type: 'div', props: {…}} │──▶│ ├─ memoizedState: hooks │ │ {type: Button, props:{…}} │ │ ├─ stateNode: DOMElement │ │ │ │ ├─ child / sibling / return │ │ discarded after reconciling │ │ └─ alternate: previous fiber │ └───────────────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────────┘

An element, concretely

javascript · the whole object
const el = <Button variant="primary">Save</Button>;

{
  $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element'),
  //         ^ a SYMBOL, so it cannot come from JSON. If an element
  //           could be created from parsed JSON, a server returning
  //           user-controlled data could inject arbitrary components —
  //           and symbols do not survive JSON.parse. That is the entire
  //           reason this field exists.

  type: Button,        // a function → component; a string → DOM element
  key: null,           // identity among siblings (R03)
  ref: null,           // in React 19 this is also in props
  props: { variant: 'primary', children: 'Save' },
}

// Frozen in development. Elements are reused during reconciliation, so
// mutating one would corrupt the comparison.
Object.isFrozen(el);   // true in dev

// Creating one is CHEAP and does nothing:
console.time('100k');
const els = Array.from({ length: 100_000 }, (_, i) => <Row key={i} />);
console.timeEnd('100k');   // a few milliseconds. Zero DOM. Zero renders.
Creating an element does not call the component

const x = <Expensive /> allocates one object whose type is the Expensive function. React calls that function only when it renders the element, which happens during reconciliation. This is why passing an element as a prop is free, why {cond ? a : b} where both are elements costs two allocations and one render, and why the children optimisation in R02 works — the element already exists, unchanged, so React skips the subtree entirely.

Why a description tree at all

The DOM is a bad target to compute against: · reading it is expensive — offsetHeight forces layout · it is enormous per node (hundreds of properties) · you cannot build one "off to the side" cheaply and compare · it is not serialisable, so it cannot cross to a server A tree of plain objects is: · cheap to build and discard · cheap to compare (reference checks, then shallow props) · serialisable — which is what makes Server Components possible at all (N04): the server produces an element tree and streams it · target-independent — the same tree drives react-dom, react-native, react-three-fiber, Ink (terminal UIs) and test renderers, because the tree says what and the renderer decides how That last point is the real reason for the architecture. React's core reconciler knows nothing about the DOM; react-dom is a host config implementing about thirty functions — createInstance, appendChild, commitUpdate — and swapping it swaps the platform.

The performance claim, examined

Hand-written DOM code beats React on raw speed, and that is fine

A careful imperative implementation that knows exactly which node to touch will always win against building a tree and diffing it. React's proposition is not speed — it is that the imperative version's maintenance cost grows quadratically with the number of states (J01), and that the version most teams actually write contains an innerHTML rebuild that is far slower than any diff. Signals-based libraries such as Solid make a third choice: track dependencies precisely so no diffing is needed at all, at the cost of a reactive graph you must reason about.

The root, and how it all starts

javascript · from mount to first paint
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
root.render(<App />);

// What happens, in order:
//
// 1 · createRoot builds a FiberRoot and a HostRoot fiber. Nothing is
//     rendered yet; this is the container React will own.
//
// 2 · render() creates the element for <App /> and schedules an update
//     on the root at default priority.
//
// 3 · React begins the RENDER phase: it walks down from the root,
//     calling each component function, building a fiber for each
//     element it finds. This is interruptible (W06).
//
// 4 · Having built a complete tree, React enters the COMMIT phase:
//     it creates the DOM nodes, appends them, and this part is
//     synchronous and uninterruptible (W04).
//
// 5 · The browser paints. Effects run after that.

// createRoot vs the legacy ReactDOM.render: createRoot opts you into
// concurrent features. ReactDOM.render was removed in React 19 —
// automatic batching, transitions and Suspense-for-data all require
// the concurrent root.

root.unmount();   // tears down the tree, running every cleanup

Renderers

RendererHost nodes are
react-domDOM elements
react-dom/serverStrings or streams of HTML (W07)
react-nativeNative views, via a bridge
react-three-fiberthree.js scene objects
inkTerminal output
react-test-rendererPlain objects, for snapshots
The RSC rendererA serialised element stream — the payload a client turns back into a tree (N04)
This is why “learn React, write anywhere” is partly true

The reconciler — components, state, hooks, reconciliation, scheduling — is shared. Only the host config differs, which is the set of functions that create, update and remove a platform's nodes. So the model transfers completely between web, native and a 3D canvas, while the components do not: <div> means nothing to react-native, and styling, layout and gestures are entirely different. The transferable part is large and real; the “write once, run anywhere” version of the claim is not.

Interview follow-up

“What is the virtual DOM?” Answer by correcting the framing: it is a tree of plain JavaScript objects describing the intended UI, recreated on every render and thrown away after React has compared it with the previous one. Then say why it exists, because that is the real question — it is cheap to build and compare, it is serialisable (which is what makes Server Components possible), and it is platform-independent, which is why the same core drives the DOM, native and a 3D canvas. Explicitly reject “it is faster than the real DOM”: diffing is extra work, and React's win is a programming model where you never write state transitions, not raw speed.

W02

Reconciliation: the diffing rules

Comparing two arbitrary trees is O(n³). React does it in O(n) by making two assumptions that are not always true and are almost always close enough. Knowing exactly what those assumptions are explains why keys matter, why a conditional wrapper destroys state, and why moving a component to a different position resets it.

The two heuristics

1 Two elements of different TYPE produce different trees. old: <div><Counter /></div> new: <span><Counter /></span> React does not try to match the Counter inside. It tears down the entire old subtree — unmounting every component, running every cleanup, destroying every piece of state — and builds the new one from scratch. The comparison is oldFiber.type === newElement.type: a reference check for components, a string check for host elements. Which is exactly why a component defined inside another component gets a new reference every render and remounts every time (J06). 2 The developer can mark children as stable with a key. Without a key, children are matched by INDEX. With one, by key. That is the entire mechanism (R03). Everything else in reconciliation follows from those two sentences.

Same type: update in place

javascript · what actually happens
// old
<div className="before" title="hello" />
// new
<div className="after" />

// Same type ('div'), so React keeps the DOM node and diffs the props:
//   className: 'before' → 'after'   → node.className = 'after'
//   title: 'hello' → undefined      → node.removeAttribute('title')
// The node itself, its scroll position, its focus and its identity in
// the document are all preserved.

// For a COMPONENT of the same type, React keeps the fiber — and
// therefore the hooks and their state — and re-runs the function with
// the new props:
// old: <Counter start={0} />  new: <Counter start={5} />
// → the same Counter instance, count preserved, props updated.

// style is diffed per property, not replaced wholesale:
style={{ color: 'red', fontSize: 12 }}
style={{ color: 'blue', fontSize: 12 }}
// → only color is written. fontSize is untouched.

Different type: tear down and rebuild

javascript · the three ways this catches people
// 1 · A conditional wrapper
{isMobile
  ? <Form />
  : <div className="desktop"><Form /></div>}
// Crossing a breakpoint changes the type at that position from Form to
// div, so the Form unmounts: every field resets, focus is lost, and any
// in-flight request in an effect is cancelled by the cleanup.

// Fix: keep the structure constant, change the attribute.
<div className={isMobile ? 'mobile' : 'desktop'}><Form /></div>

// 2 · A component defined inline (J06)
function Parent() {
  const Child = () => <input />;   // NEW function reference every render
  return <Child />;                // type differs → remount, every render
}

// 3 · Switching between two components in the same slot
{tab === 'a' ? <PanelA /> : <PanelB />}
// Different types, so switching tabs unmounts one and mounts the other.
// That is usually what you want. What surprises people is the opposite
// case — same type, different props:
{tab === 'a' ? <Panel id="a" /> : <Panel id="b" />}
// SAME type, same position → React reuses the fiber, so Panel's
// internal state (scroll, expanded rows) carries over between tabs.
// Add distinct keys if they should be separate instances (R03).

Children: the list algorithm

React reconciles children in a single pass, not with a full diff. Phase 1 — walk both lists in order while the keys match. As long as oldChild.key === newChild.key, update in place and advance both. This is the fast path, and it covers "nothing moved, some props changed", which is the overwhelmingly common case. Phase 2 — the remainder. · new list exhausted first → delete the remaining old children · old list exhausted first → insert the remaining new children · both have items left → build a Map of key → oldFiber from the remainder, then for each new child look it up: found → move it (place the existing fiber) missing → create it anything left in the Map at the end is deleted Cost: O(n). The Map makes lookup O(1), and each child is visited a constant number of times. The consequence for moves: React finds the existing fiber and reuses it, so the DOM node, its state and its focus survive — but the node is repositioned with an insertBefore. A list where every item moves is n insertions, which is correct but not free; a list where one item moves is one insertion.
javascript · the two shapes, side by side
// APPENDING — the good case either way.
// old: [a, b, c]   new: [a, b, c, d]
// Phase 1 matches a, b, c. Phase 2 inserts d. One DOM operation.

// PREPENDING — where keys earn their existence.
// old: [a, b, c]   new: [z, a, b, c]

// without keys (index matching):
//   0: a → z   update
//   1: b → a   update
//   2: c → b   update
//   3: —  → c  create
//   → 4 operations, and every component's state stayed at its index
//     while the data shifted past it.

// with keys:
//   z is new           → create + insert at 0
//   a, b, c: matched   → reused, moved
//   → 1 insertion, and state travels with the item.
What “state travels with the item” actually means

The fiber holds the hooks, so reusing a fiber reuses its useState values, its refs, and its DOM node with whatever the browser has attached to it — uncommitted input text, focus, selection, scroll, a CSS transition in flight. That is why an index key on a list of inputs does not merely re-render inefficiently: it leaves the typed text attached to the wrong record, which no amount of re-rendering fixes and which no error reports.

Where the heuristics are wrong

javascript · React accepts these losses knowingly
// 1 · Moving a subtree across parents
// old:  <Left><Editor /></Left><Right />
// new:  <Left /><Right><Editor /></Right>
// A true tree diff would recognise the same Editor and move it.
// React compares per position, so it unmounts and remounts — the
// editor loses its state. A full diff is O(n³); this is the trade.
//
// The escape hatch when you genuinely need it: portals (the DOM node
// moves without the fiber moving), or hoisting the state above both.

// 2 · Type changes that are semantically no-ops
// <div> → <section> rebuilds the subtree, even though nothing about
// the children changed. Rare, and cheap to avoid.

// 3 · Reordering with unstable keys
key={`${item.id}-${item.status}`}
// The key changes when the status changes, so the row is destroyed and
// recreated rather than updated. A key must identify the ITEM, not its
// current contents.

How this differs elsewhere

LibraryHow it updates
ReactRe-run the component, build a new element tree, diff it against the fiber tree
Vue 3Also diffs, but the compiler marks which parts of a template are dynamic, so it skips static subtrees entirely
SvelteNo diffing. The compiler emits imperative DOM updates per reactive value
SolidNo diffing. Fine-grained signals; a component function runs once and only the expressions reading a changed signal re-run
LitTagged templates; only the interpolated holes are updated
The trade React makes, stated fairly

Fine-grained reactivity is measurably faster at the update step and needs no keys for correctness. What React buys by re-running the whole component is a model with no reactive graph: a component is a plain function, values are plain values, and there is no distinction between “a signal” and “a number” to track through your code. That is why React code composes so readily and why its mental model is small — and it is exactly what makes it slower. Being able to describe this as a deliberate trade, rather than as React being behind, is a strong senior-level answer.

Interview follow-up

“How does React decide what to update?” Two heuristics that turn an O(n³) problem into O(n): different element types produce different trees, so React tears down and rebuilds rather than trying to match across them; and children are matched by key, falling back to index. Then give a consequence that shows you have used it — a conditional wrapper changes the type at a position and therefore destroys the subtree's state, which is why toggling a layout can silently reset a form. And name the case React deliberately gets wrong: moving a subtree between parents is an unmount and a remount, because a genuine tree diff is not affordable.

W03

Fiber: the data structure and why it exists

Before React 16, rendering was a recursive function call that could not be stopped. Fiber replaced that recursion with a linked list you can walk, pause and resume — which is what made concurrent rendering, Suspense and transitions possible. It is one data-structure change with very large consequences.

The problem it solved

The old reconciler was recursive: function reconcile(element) { const children = render(element); for (const child of children) reconcile(child); ← the call stack } Once started, it ran to completion. A deep tree meant a long synchronous block, and the browser could not interrupt it: ┌──────────────── 180ms of JavaScript ─────────────────┐ │ render the whole tree │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ▲ ▲ user types user clicks ignored ignored At 60fps a frame is 16.7ms. Anything longer drops frames, and 180ms of blocked main thread is an input delay a user feels as "this page is broken". The fix cannot be "make rendering faster" — some trees are genuinely large. It has to be "make rendering interruptible", which means the work cannot live on the call stack, because you cannot pause and resume a JavaScript call stack. Fiber is a re-implementation of the call stack as data. Each unit of work is an object with pointers to what comes next, so React can do some work, check whether the frame budget is spent, hand control back to the browser, and resume exactly where it stopped.

A fiber node

javascript · the fields that matter
const fiber = {
  // ── identity ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  tag: FunctionComponent,   // HostComponent, HostText, Fragment, …
  type: Counter,            // the function, or 'div'
  key: 'item-42',
  elementType: Counter,     // before memo/lazy unwrapping

  // ── the tree, as a LINKED LIST rather than an array ───────────────
  child: FiberNode,         // FIRST child only
  sibling: FiberNode,       // next sibling
  return: FiberNode,        // parent — "return" because it is where
                            // the traversal returns to, like a stack
                            // frame's return address

  // ── state ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  pendingProps: {…},        // the new props, this render
  memoizedProps: {…},       // the props from the last committed render
  memoizedState: Hook,      // the HEAD of the hooks linked list (W05)
  updateQueue: {…},         // pending state updates

  // ── the host node ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  stateNode: HTMLDivElement,  // the real DOM node, for host components

  // ── work tracking ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  flags: Placement | Update | Deletion,   // what the commit must do
  subtreeFlags: …,          // an OR of descendants' flags, so React can
                            // skip whole subtrees with nothing to do
  lanes: …,                 // priority of pending work (W06)

  // ── double buffering ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  alternate: FiberNode,     // the other version of this same fiber
};
Why a linked list instead of a children array An array needs an index to resume from, and the index is meaningless once you have paused and something has changed. A linked list gives every node an explicit "what is next", so a single pointer is a complete resume point. App │ child ▼ Header ──sibling──▶ Main ──sibling──▶ Footer │ child ▼ List ──sibling──▶ Pager │ ▼ Item ──▶ Item ──▶ Item Traversal order (depth-first, using only these three pointers): App → Header → Main → List → Item → Item → Item → (no child, no sibling: follow return up to List) → Pager → (return to Main) → Footer → (return to App) → done React can stop after ANY node, keep one pointer, and resume.

Double buffering

React keeps two fiber trees at all times. current what is on screen right now workInProgress the one being built Every fiber has an alternate pointer to its counterpart, and React alternates between them rather than allocating a whole new tree — which is where the "buffering" name comes from, borrowed from graphics. current workInProgress ┌────────┐ alternate ┌────────┐ │ App │ ◀─────────▶ │ App' │ └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ ▼ ▼ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ │ Header │ ◀─────────▶ │Header' │ └────────┘ └────────┘ The commit is a single pointer swap: root.current = wip. Three things follow from this: · rendering can be abandoned at any point — throw the workInProgress tree away and nothing on screen was touched. This is what makes interruption safe, and it is why a render must be pure (R02): React may discard your work. · the commit is atomic — the user never sees a half-updated tree, because nothing is visible until the swap. · fibers are reused rather than reallocated, so a re-render of a large tree does not allocate a large tree.

The work loop

javascript · the shape of it, simplified
// The concurrent loop. This is the whole reason fiber exists.
function workLoopConcurrent() {
  while (workInProgress !== null && !shouldYield()) {
    performUnitOfWork(workInProgress);
  }
}

// shouldYield() asks the scheduler whether the time slice is spent —
// roughly 5ms. If so, the loop exits, React schedules a continuation,
// and the browser gets the main thread back to handle input and paint.
// Next time, the loop resumes from `workInProgress` exactly where it
// stopped.

function performUnitOfWork(fiber) {
  // BEGIN: call the component (or create the host instance), producing
  // children. Returns the first child, or null at a leaf.
  const next = beginWork(fiber);

  if (next === null) {
    completeUnitOfWork(fiber);   // walk back up via sibling/return
  } else {
    workInProgress = next;       // walk down
  }
}

// The synchronous loop, used for urgent updates and inside flushSync,
// is the same thing without the yield check:
function workLoopSync() {
  while (workInProgress !== null) {
    performUnitOfWork(workInProgress);
  }
}
Interruptible means your component function can run and be thrown away

If React yields, receives a higher-priority update, and restarts the render, every component it already called during the abandoned attempt ran for nothing — and will be called again. That is why render must be pure: a side effect in the body (mutating a module variable, incrementing a counter, sending analytics) can happen an unpredictable number of times. StrictMode's deliberate double-invoke exists to surface exactly this class of bug in development (R02), because in production it appears only under load, intermittently.

The two sub-phases of a render

beginWork — on the way DOWN · compare pendingProps with memoizedProps · if nothing changed and no pending state, bail out and reuse the whole subtree without walking it · otherwise call the component, reconcile its children (W02), and create or reuse child fibers · set flags: Placement, Update, Deletion completeWork — on the way back UP · create the host instance (the DOM node) if it is new, without attaching it to the document · prepare the property updates, storing them on the fiber · bubble subtreeFlags upward, so a parent knows in O(1) whether anything below it needs committing — this is what lets the commit phase skip entire untouched subtrees Nothing in either sub-phase touches the live DOM. Everything is prepared, and the commit applies it (W04).

What this bought

CapabilityRequires
Time slicing — never blocking input for longPausable work
Transitions (R15, W06)Abandoning an in-progress render for a more urgent one
SuspensePausing a subtree and rendering a fallback instead
Concurrent rendering of two versions of the UITwo trees, only one of which is current
Streaming SSR with selective hydrationCommitting parts of the tree independently (W07)
Error boundaries that can unwindAn explicit parent pointer to walk up
Fiber shipped in React 16 and did nothing visible for three years

The rewrite landed in 2017 as a pure internal change with identical behaviour — no new API, no performance headline. Concurrent features only became usable in React 18, five years later. It is a good example of infrastructure work whose value is entirely in what it makes possible later, and worth remembering when someone asks whether the "virtual DOM" is the interesting part of React's architecture. It is not; the scheduler is.

Interview follow-up

“What is fiber?” A re-implementation of the call stack as a linked data structure, so that rendering can be paused and resumed — which a real call stack cannot be. Each fiber is a unit of work with child, sibling and return pointers, so a single pointer is a complete resume point, and React keeps two trees with the commit being a pointer swap, which makes an in-progress render safe to abandon. Then connect it to something practical, because that is what the question is really testing: this is why render must be pure (abandoned work is re-run), and it is the prerequisite for transitions, Suspense and streaming — none of which the old recursive reconciler could have supported.

W04

The render and commit phases

Everything React does happens in one of two phases with opposite properties. The render phase is interruptible, abandonable and must be pure. The commit phase is synchronous, uninterruptible, and is the only time the DOM is touched. Nearly every rule React asks you to follow is a consequence of that split.

The two phases

Trigger
UpdatesetState, parent render
Phase 1
Renderinterruptible, pure
Phase 2a
Before mutationread the old DOM
Phase 2b
Mutationwrite the DOM
Phase 2c
LayoutuseLayoutEffect
Paint
Browserthen useEffect
Render phaseCommit phase
Can be interruptedYesNo
Can be abandonedYes — the work is thrown awayNo
Can run more than onceYesNo
Touches the DOMNeverYes — this is the only place
Must be pureYesNo — side effects belong here
What runsComponent functions, useMemo, reducers, getDerivedStateFromErrorDOM writes, refs, useLayoutEffect, then useEffect
This is why render must be pure

Not as a matter of taste. React may call a component, yield to the browser, receive a higher-priority update, throw the partial tree away, and call the component again — so a side effect in the render body runs an unpredictable number of times, at unpredictable moments, sometimes for a render nobody ever sees. Mutating a module variable, incrementing a counter, calling an analytics endpoint, or writing to a ref during render are all bugs of this shape, and they appear intermittently under load rather than in tests.

The commit phase in detail

The commit is three sub-phases, in this order, and the ordering is load-bearing. 1 BEFORE MUTATION the DOM is still the OLD one · getSnapshotBeforeUpdate (classes) runs here — the only chance to read layout before it changes, which is how a chat window preserves scroll position when messages are prepended 2 MUTATION the DOM is changed · insert, update and delete host nodes · detach refs for unmounting nodes (ref.current = null) · run useLayoutEffect CLEANUPS for unmounting components · nothing is painted yet — the browser has not regained control 3 LAYOUT the DOM is the NEW one, still unpainted · attach refs (ref.current = node) · run useLayoutEffect setups · a setState here is flushed synchronously, before paint ── the browser paints ── 4 PASSIVE asynchronous, after paint · run useEffect cleanups, then setups · a setState here causes a second render the user may see as a flash Every child's layout effect runs before its parent's, because React walks the effect list bottom-up — so a parent measuring a child in useLayoutEffect finds it already set up.

Why useLayoutEffect exists at all

javascript · the flicker, and its removal
// With useEffect: commit → PAINT → effect → state change → PAINT again.
// The user sees one frame of the wrong position.
function Tooltip({ anchor }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  const [top, setTop] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {                        // ← visible jump
    const h = ref.current.offsetHeight;
    setTop(anchor.top - h);
  }, [anchor]);

  return <div ref={ref} style={{ top }}>…</div>;
}

// With useLayoutEffect: commit → effect → state change → re-render →
// PAINT once, already correct. Nothing intermediate is ever shown.
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const h = ref.current.offsetHeight;
  setTop(anchor.top - h);
}, [anchor]);

// The cost: it BLOCKS painting. A slow layout effect is a dropped
// frame, every time. And it does not run during server rendering,
// which produces a warning — the standard workaround is
const useIsoLayoutEffect =
  typeof window !== 'undefined' ? useLayoutEffect : useEffect;

The order of everything, on a state update

javascript · logged, so you can verify it
function Child() {
  console.log('3  child render');
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    console.log('5  child layout effect');
    return () => console.log('  child layout cleanup');
  });
  useEffect(() => {
    console.log('8  child passive effect');
    return () => console.log('  child passive cleanup');
  });
  return <div />;
}

function Parent() {
  console.log('2  parent render');
  useLayoutEffect(() => console.log('6  parent layout effect'));
  useEffect(() => console.log('9  parent passive effect'));
  return <Child />;
}

// 1  setState called
// 2  parent render          ─┐
// 3  child render            ├─ render phase (interruptible)
// 4  [reconcile, complete]  ─┘
//    ── commit begins, uninterruptible ──
//    refs detached, DOM mutated
// 5  child layout effect    ─┐  bottom-up: children before parents
// 6  parent layout effect   ─┘
// 7  ── browser paints ──
// 8  child passive effect   ─┐  also bottom-up
// 9  parent passive effect  ─┘
//
// On an UPDATE, each effect's cleanup runs immediately before its
// setup — and all cleanups for the whole tree run before any setup,
// so a cleanup never sees a partially re-set-up tree.

Bailouts

javascript · the four ways React does less work
// 1 · Same state value → the update may not even start a render.
setCount(count);          // Object.is equal → bail out (R01)

// 2 · Same element reference → skip the whole subtree in beginWork.
//     This is why passing children from a non-rendering parent works
//     without memo (R02):
function Wrapper({ children }) {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return <><button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)} />{children}</>;
  //                                               ^ same object → skipped
}

// 3 · memo → shallow props comparison before rendering (R14).

// 4 · subtreeFlags → during the COMMIT, a parent whose subtree has no
//     flags set is skipped entirely, in O(1). This is why a commit of a
//     10,000-node tree where one node changed is fast: React never
//     walks the other 9,999.

// What does NOT bail out: a context value change. Consumers are
// scheduled directly and memo does not stop it (R11).
The commit is where the real cost usually is

Render is your JavaScript running — microseconds for a typical component. The commit is DOM writes, followed by the browser recalculating style, layout and paint, which is milliseconds and scales with the number of nodes affected. That is why a component "re-rendering 40 times" is often harmless (identical trees commit nothing) while a single commit that inserts 5,000 rows is a visible freeze that no memoisation will touch. When profiling, read the commit duration first and work backwards.

Layout thrash, and how React avoids it

The browser can batch style and layout recalculation — unless you read a layout property after writing one, which forces a synchronous reflow: for (const el of items) { el.style.width = w + 'px'; write total += el.offsetHeight; READ → forced reflow } ← n reflows React's commit phase separates these by construction: all reads happen in the before-mutation sub-phase, all writes in the mutation sub-phase. You get that for free. You can still reintroduce it, and this is the common way: useLayoutEffect(() => { items.forEach(el => { el.style.height = 'auto'; write setHeight(el.scrollHeight); READ → thrash per item }); }); The fix is the same as in vanilla JS: read everything first, then write everything. const heights = els.map(el => el.scrollHeight); // all reads els.forEach((el, i) => el.style.height = heights[i]); // all writes

Reading the profiler

React DevTools Profiler — a single commit
Commit #4 at 2,140ms    duration 24.1ms

  Render phase   6.2ms
    App                 0.2   Parent rendered
    Dashboard           0.4   Hooks changed
    DataTable           5.1   Props changed (rows)
      Row × 500         …

  Commit phase   17.9ms   ← where the time actually is
    host mutations: 500 insertions
    layout effects: 0.3ms

# Reading this correctly:
#
#   render 6ms, commit 18ms  → the DOM work dominates. memo will not
#                              help; virtualise the list (R03).
#
#   render 40ms, commit 2ms  → a component is doing real work in its
#                              body. Find it and useMemo, or move it.
#
#   many commits, each 1ms   → probably fine. Check whether the user
#                              can perceive anything before optimising.
Interview follow-up

“What is the difference between the render and commit phases?” Render runs your component functions to produce a tree, is interruptible and abandonable, and never touches the DOM; commit applies the result, is synchronous and uninterruptible, and is where refs are attached and effects scheduled. Then draw the conclusion the question is really after: because a render can be discarded and re-run, it must be pure — which is why side effects belong in effects and why useLayoutEffect exists as the escape hatch for the one case where you must read and correct layout before the browser paints. Adding that the commit is usually the expensive half is what turns this into a performance answer as well as a mechanical one.

W05

How hooks actually work

Hooks look like magic because a plain function somehow remembers things between calls. It does not — React does. Each fiber holds a linked list of hook objects, and “which hook is this” is answered by call order. Every rule about hooks, and every confusing error message, follows directly from that.

The mechanism

Before calling your component, React sets a module-level pointer to the fiber being rendered and resets a cursor into its hook list. currentlyRenderingFiber = fiber workInProgressHook = null Each useState, useEffect, useRef call advances the cursor by one and returns that slot's contents. function Profile() { const [name, setName] = useState(''); ← slot 0 const [age, setAge] = useState(0); ← slot 1 const ref = useRef(null); ← slot 2 useEffect(…) ← slot 3 } fiber.memoizedState │ ▼ ┌──────────┐ next ┌──────────┐ next ┌──────────┐ │ state:'' │ ───────▶ │ state: 0 │ ───────▶ │ {current}│ ─▶ … │ queue │ │ queue │ │ │ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ There are no names anywhere. Slot 1 on this render must be the same hook as slot 1 on the last one, and the only thing guaranteeing that is that you called them in the same order. This is also why hooks cannot be called outside a component: the module-level pointer is null, and React throws "Invalid hook call". The same error appears with two copies of React in the bundle, since each copy has its own pointer.
javascript · a toy implementation, to make it concrete
let hooks = [];     // in real React this is a linked list on the fiber
let cursor = 0;

function useState(initial) {
  const i = cursor++;                       // claim THIS slot

  if (hooks[i] === undefined) {             // first render only
    hooks[i] = typeof initial === 'function' ? initial() : initial;
  }

  const setState = (next) => {
    hooks[i] = typeof next === 'function' ? next(hooks[i]) : next;
    scheduleRender();                       // the closure remembers `i`
  };

  return [hooks[i], setState];
}

function render(Component) {
  cursor = 0;                               // reset before every render
  return Component();
}

// Now the rules are obvious rather than arbitrary:
//
//   · a conditional hook shifts every subsequent index by one, so slot
//     2 is suddenly the effect that used to be at slot 3
//   · calling a hook outside render leaves `cursor` undefined
//   · the setter closes over `i`, not over the value — which is why
//     setters are stable across renders and safe in dependency arrays

The error messages, explained

MessageCause
Rendered fewer hooks than expectedA hook was skipped this render — an early return before it, or a condition around it
Rendered more hooks than during the previous renderA hook ran that did not last time — usually a condition that became true
Invalid hook callCalled outside a component, from a plain function, from a class, or there are two copies of React in the bundle
Rendered a different number of hooks after a conditionalSame as the first two; React compares the list length at the end of the render
“Invalid hook call” is a duplicate React about a third of the time

The other causes are obvious from the stack trace; this one is not. It happens when a library bundles its own copy of React, when a monorepo package resolves a different version, or when a linked local package pulls its own node_modules/react. Each copy has its own module-level dispatcher pointer, so a hook called through one copy while the other is rendering sees null. Check with npm ls react, and fix it with a bundler alias or by making React a peer dependency — not by changing your component.

How each hook stores its state

javascript · what lives in a slot
// useState / useReducer
{ memoizedState: currentValue,
  queue: { pending: UpdateCircularList, lastRenderedReducer, … },
  next: Hook }
// The queue is a circular linked list of pending updates. On the next
// render React replays them in order against the last committed value
// — which is why updater functions compose (R01) and why a direct value
// discards earlier queued updates.

// useRef
{ memoizedState: { current: value }, next: Hook }
// One object, created once and never replaced. That is the entire
// implementation — which is why mutating .current does nothing to
// trigger a render: no queue, no scheduling, nothing is watching it.

// useMemo
{ memoizedState: [computedValue, deps], next: Hook }
// On re-render: compare deps with Object.is; equal → return the stored
// value; different → call the factory and store the new pair.

// useCallback — identical, storing the function instead of a result.

// useEffect
{ memoizedState: {
    tag: HasEffect | Passive,
    create: setupFn, destroy: cleanupFn,
    deps: [...], next: Effect },
  next: Hook }
// Effects are ALSO on a per-fiber circular list, so the commit phase
// can walk just the effects rather than the whole tree.

The dispatcher

javascript · why the same hook behaves differently on mount and update
// `useState` imported from 'react' does almost nothing: it delegates to
// whichever dispatcher is currently installed.
function useState(initial) {
  return ReactCurrentDispatcher.current.useState(initial);
}

// React swaps the dispatcher depending on what it is doing:
//
//   HooksDispatcherOnMount     — create the hook, run the initialiser
//   HooksDispatcherOnUpdate    — advance the cursor, replay the queue
//   HooksDispatcherOnRerender  — for a setState DURING render (R09)
//   InvalidNestedHooksDispatcher — inside a useMemo factory, to catch
//                                  hooks called in the wrong place
//   ContextOnlyDispatcher      — when no component is rendering; this
//                                is the one that throws "Invalid hook
//                                call"
//
// This is also how the Server Components renderer offers a DIFFERENT
// set: useState and useEffect simply are not present in the server
// dispatcher, which is why calling them in a Server Component is an
// error rather than a silent no-op (N04).

Why hooks, rather than something named

The obvious alternative — useState('count', 0) with a name — was considered and rejected. The reasons are worth knowing, because they are the real answer to "why is the call-order rule acceptable": · names collide when two custom hooks are composed, and the collision is silent · a hook called in a loop would need generated names · minifiers cannot shorten string keys, so bundles grow · call order is checkable by a LINT RULE, statically, with no runtime cost — and eslint-plugin-react-hooks catches essentially every violation before it runs The trade is a rule you must follow in exchange for an API with no keys, no collisions, and perfect composition: two custom hooks can each use ten hooks internally and never interfere. Compare with the alternatives hooks replaced (R13): mixins had name collisions, HOCs had prop collisions and wrapper hell, render props had nesting. Call order is a smaller price than any of them.

What this means in practice

FactConsequence
Setters are stable for the component's lifetimeSafe to omit from dependency arrays; the linter knows this
useRef returns the same object foreverMutating .current triggers nothing (R10)
Hook state lives on the fiberUnmount the fiber and the state is gone — which is what key exploits (R03)
useMemo is a cache with one entry and no guaranteeReact may discard it; never rely on it for correctness
Custom hooks are ordinary function callsTheir hooks are inlined into the caller's list, in order
Two components calling one hook get separate slotsHooks share logic, never state (R13)
useMemo is a hint, not a guarantee

React reserves the right to throw a memoised value away — for instance to free memory for an offscreen tree — and recompute it on the next render. So useMemo must never be used for anything whose recomputation would be incorrect: creating an object whose identity is semantically meaningful (an ID, a cache key that must not change), or running something with a side effect. For guaranteed-once creation use a ref with a lazy initialiser (R10); for identity that must persist, store it in state.

Interview follow-up

“Why must hooks be called in the same order every render?” Because React stores them in a linked list on the fiber and identifies each one by its position — there are no names anywhere. Skip a hook and every subsequent one reads the previous render's neighbouring slot, so a useEffect starts reading a useState's data. Then answer the question behind the question: names were considered and rejected because they collide when custom hooks compose, they cannot be minified, and call order is statically checkable by a lint rule with zero runtime cost — which is what makes the constraint an acceptable price for an API where two independent hooks can never interfere.

W06

Concurrent rendering: lanes, transitions and priority

Concurrency in React does not mean multiple threads. It means React can work on more than one version of the UI at a time, pause one to do the other, and throw away work that has been superseded. Three user-facing APIs expose it, and all three exist to answer the same question: which of these updates can the user afford to wait for?

The problem

A search box over a large list. Every keystroke does two things: 1 update the input's value — must be instant 2 re-filter and re-render 10,000 results — can lag Without priorities they are one update, so the render for (2) blocks the paint for (1), and typing feels like wading: keypress │████████ render 10k results ████████│ paint ▲ ▲ typed 'a' the 'a' appears, 120ms later Debouncing is the old fix, and it is a poor one: you pick a delay (300ms?) that is too slow on a fast machine and too fast on a slow one, and the list is stale for that whole window regardless. Concurrent rendering fixes it structurally: mark (2) as low-priority, and React renders it in the background, yielding to the browser every few milliseconds and abandoning it entirely if another keystroke arrives. keypress │██│ paint 'a' │▒▒│▒▒│▒▒ background render, abandoned keypress │██│ paint 'ab' │▒▒│▒▒│▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒ … │ paint results No magic number. It adapts to the device, because the unit is "yield when the frame budget is spent", not "wait 300ms".

Lanes

javascript · priority as a bitmask
// React assigns every update a "lane" — a single bit in a 31-bit mask.
// A fiber's pending work is the OR of all lanes with updates on it, so
// "does this subtree have urgent work?" is one bitwise AND.

SyncLane                  // discrete input: click, keydown, flushSync
InputContinuousLane       // continuous input: drag, scroll, hover
DefaultLane               // ordinary setState, network responses
TransitionLanes (×16)     // startTransition, useDeferredValue
RetryLanes                // Suspense retries
IdleLane                  // offscreen work

// Why bits rather than a number? Because React must express "work at
// several priorities is pending at once" and answer questions about
// SETS of them in constant time:
const hasUrgentWork = (fiber.lanes & SyncLane) !== 0;
const isSubsetOf = (a, b) => (a & b) === a;

// Sixteen separate transition lanes exist so that two independent
// transitions — say, two tabs both loading — do not get merged and
// finish as one unit.

// Starvation is handled by EXPIRATION: a lane that has waited too long
// is promoted to synchronous and rendered regardless, so a permanently
// busy page cannot leave a low-priority update unrendered forever.

useTransition

javascript · marking an update as non-urgent
function SearchPage() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [results, setResults] = useState([]);
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function handleChange(e) {
    // URGENT: the input must show the character immediately.
    setQuery(e.target.value);

    // NON-URGENT: this render can be interrupted, and abandoned if
    // another keystroke arrives before it finishes.
    startTransition(() => {
      setResults(filterLargeList(e.target.value));
    });
  }

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={handleChange} />
      {/* A subtle hint, not a spinner. The point of a transition is
          that the OLD content stays usable while the new one prepares. */}
      <div style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
        <Results items={results} />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

// Two rules that catch people:
//
// 1 · The callback must be SYNCHRONOUS. Updates scheduled after an
//     await are no longer part of the transition:
startTransition(async () => {
  await save();        // everything after this is NOT in the transition
  setDone(true);
});
// React 19 added ASYNC transitions, which is how Actions work (N01) —
// but for plain state updates keep the callback synchronous.
//
// 2 · A controlled input's value must NOT be in a transition, or the
//     character the user typed lags behind their keystrokes.

useDeferredValue

javascript · the same idea, for a value you do not control
function Results({ query }) {
  // `query` arrives as a prop, so there is no setState to wrap. Defer
  // the VALUE instead: React renders once with the old value at normal
  // priority, then again with the new one at transition priority.
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query);
  const stale = query !== deferred;

  const items = useMemo(() => filter(deferred), [deferred]);

  return (
    <div style={{ opacity: stale ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
      <List items={items} />
    </div>
  );
}

// React 19 added an initial value, so the first render can show
// something cheap rather than the expensive result:
const deferred = useDeferredValue(query, '');

// useTransition vs useDeferredValue:
//   · you OWN the setState        → useTransition
//   · the value comes from a prop → useDeferredValue
//   · you need an isPending flag  → useTransition
// They are the same mechanism with different ergonomics.

// And both are better than debouncing, because the delay is not a
// number you guessed — it is however long the device actually needs.
A transition is not a delay, and this is the common misreading

React starts the low-priority render immediately. On a fast device with a small list it finishes within the same frame and the user sees no difference at all. What the transition changes is what happens when it cannot finish quickly: React yields to the browser so input stays responsive, and if a newer update arrives it abandons the work instead of completing a render nobody will see. Debouncing always waits; a transition only degrades when the device makes it necessary.

Interruption, concretely

What "abandoning a render" actually means React is building the workInProgress tree (W03). A higher-priority update arrives. · the partially-built tree is discarded — nothing was committed, so nothing on screen changes · every component function already called during that attempt ran for nothing · React renders the urgent update from the current tree · then restarts the abandoned work from the beginning This is the whole reason render must be pure (W04). A component that mutates something outside itself, or fires an analytics event in its body, does so an unpredictable number of times — and only under load, which is when it is hardest to reproduce. StrictMode's double-invoke is a cheap simulation of this in development: if calling your component twice changes the result, it will also break when React abandons a render.

Where concurrency shows up without you asking

FeatureUses
Automatic batching everywhere (React 18)Updates grouped by lane rather than by call site
Suspense without a fallback flashA transition keeps the old content while the new subtree prepares (R15)
Streaming SSR with selective hydrationHydrating a clicked component first, out of document order (W07)
Router navigationsEvery modern React router wraps navigation in a transition
Actions (React 19)An async transition, with pending state managed by React (N01)
<Activity> (19.2)Pre-rendering hidden content at idle priority (N06)
Concurrent rendering makes external stores tear

If React pauses mid-render and an external store changes, two components reading that store in the same commit can see different values — the UI "tears". This is why useSyncExternalStore exists and why every state library now uses it (R09): it forces a synchronous, consistent read and tells React to re-render if the value changed during rendering. A store subscribed to with a plain useEffect is not safe under concurrent rendering, which is the technical reason the ecosystem migrated.

When to reach for it

Use a transition when · an update makes a large, expensive tree re-render · that update is a consequence of an urgent one (type → filter) · the previous content is still useful while the new one prepares · navigating between views that each load data Do not when · the update is the direct visual feedback for an input — a controlled input's own value, a checkbox toggling · the render is already fast; you gain nothing and add an isPending state to reason about · you are using it to "fix" a slow component. It makes the slowness interruptible, not absent — fix the component (R14) The honest summary: most applications need none of this. It matters for large lists, heavy visualisations, and navigations — and for those it is genuinely better than any debounce you could tune by hand.
Interview follow-up

“What does concurrent rendering actually give you?” Not threads — the ability to work on more than one version of the UI and to abandon work that has been superseded. Explain it through the concrete case: typing in a search box produces an urgent update (the character) and a non-urgent one (re-filtering 10,000 rows), and marking the second as a transition lets React yield to the browser and discard it entirely when the next keystroke arrives. Then say why it beats debouncing, because that is the follow-up: a debounce is a fixed number you guessed, while a transition adapts to the device and shows results as soon as it can. Closing with “and it is why render must be pure, because abandoned work is re-run” connects it back to the model.

W07

Server rendering and hydration

React can render to a string or a stream instead of to the DOM, and then “adopt” that HTML in the browser rather than rebuilding it. Hydration is the joint between those two halves, and it is where the majority of server-rendering bugs live — almost all of them from one cause: the server and the client rendered different things.

Why render on the server at all

Client-only rendering request → blank HTML → download JS → parse → execute → fetch data → render → first content · nothing visible until a large bundle has downloaded and run · search engines and link previews see an empty page · slow devices pay the parse cost before anything appears Server rendering request → HTML with content → paint → download JS → hydrate → interactive · content is visible almost immediately · crawlers and social cards get real markup · the JavaScript still ships — it is the same bundle The gap between those two moments is the cost. Content is on screen, and clicking does nothing until hydration finishes. A large app can be visible for a second and dead for another two — which is worse than a spinner, because the user has been told it is ready. That gap is what streaming, selective hydration and ultimately Server Components exist to close.

The server APIs

javascript · renderToString vs the streaming APIs
import { renderToString } from 'react-dom/server';

// The simple one. Synchronous, blocking, no Suspense support: the whole
// tree must render before a single byte is sent.
const html = renderToString(<App />);
res.send(`<div id="root">${html}</div>`);

// The streaming one. Sends HTML as it becomes available, and supports
// Suspense — a boundary that is not ready emits its fallback, and the
// real content is streamed in later and swapped by a tiny inline script.
import { renderToPipeableStream } from 'react-dom/server';   // Node
