import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-dom/server';   // Web streams

const { pipe, abort } = renderToPipeableStream(<App />, {
  bootstrapScripts: ['/main.js'],

  onShellReady() {
    // The shell — everything outside Suspense boundaries — is done.
    // Start sending. The rest arrives later, on the same connection.
    res.statusCode = 200;
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/html');
    pipe(res);
  },

  onShellError(err) {
    // The shell itself failed, so nothing useful can be sent. This is
    // the only point at which you can still change the status code.
    res.statusCode = 500;
    res.send('<h1>Something went wrong</h1>');
  },

  onError(err) {
    // An error inside a Suspense boundary. The shell is already sent,
    // so the client will retry that boundary by rendering it there.
    logger.error(err);
  },
});

// Always set a deadline. A hanging data fetch otherwise holds the
// connection open indefinitely.
setTimeout(abort, 10_000);

Streaming and selective hydration

Streaming — the shell goes out immediately; slow regions follow. <Layout> <Header /> ┐ <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkel />}> │ the SHELL, <Feed /> ← slow query │ sent at once </Suspense> ┘ <Suspense fallback={<SideSkel />}> <Sidebar /> ← slower </Suspense> </Layout> t=0ms header + two skeletons ← paint t=200ms <template> with the feed HTML, plus an inline script that swaps it into place t=400ms the sidebar, the same way Selective hydration — boundaries hydrate independently, and React reprioritises based on what the user touches. · hydration proceeds boundary by boundary, yielding between them, so it never blocks input for long · if the user clicks a component that is not yet hydrated, React hydrates that one first and replays the event · a boundary whose JavaScript has not arrived does not block the rest of the page from becoming interactive Both require the streaming API and a concurrent root. renderToString plus ReactDOM.render gets neither — which is the practical reason to move off the legacy APIs.

Hydration

javascript · adopting existing HTML
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

// NOT createRoot. hydrateRoot walks the existing DOM alongside the
// render, reusing the nodes rather than creating them, and attaching
// event handlers and refs to what is already there.
hydrateRoot(document.getElementById('root'), <App />);

// What hydration does and does not do:
//
//   DOES   attach event handling, run effects, populate refs, and
//          take ownership of the existing nodes
//
//   DOES NOT  re-create the DOM. If the markup matches, not a single
//             node is touched — that is the entire point
//
//   The component functions DO run. Hydration is a full render; it
//   simply reuses the nodes instead of creating them. So a component
//   that is expensive to render is expensive to hydrate.

// Passing server data to the client, which every SSR setup needs:
// serialise it into the HTML, and read it before hydrating.
// <script>window.__DATA__ = {"user":{...}}</script>
hydrateRoot(el, <App initialData={window.__DATA__} />);

// JSON.stringify must be escaped, or a string containing "</script>"
// breaks out of the tag — a real XSS. Use a serialiser such as
// `devalue`, or escape < as \\u003c.

Hydration mismatches

React renders on the client and compares with what the server sent. A difference is a hydration mismatch, and since React 18 the response is to discard the mismatching subtree and re-render it on the client — which is correct, and which silently loses the performance benefit for that region. The five causes, in order of frequency: 1 Time new Date(), "3 minutes ago", a formatted timestamp — the server rendered at one instant and the client at another 2 Randomness Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID(), a generated id that is not stable 3 Browser-only state localStorage, window.matchMedia, navigator, a saved theme — none of which the server has 4 Invalid HTML nesting <div> inside <p>, a <div> inside <tbody>. The browser silently fixes the markup while parsing, so the DOM no longer matches what React sent — and the error points at the wrong place 5 Browser extensions ad blockers and password managers inject attributes and nodes into the document before React hydrates. Unfixable, and a real source of noise
javascript · the three correct fixes
// FIX 1 — render the same thing on both, then update after mount.
// The first client render must MATCH THE SERVER; only after that may it
// differ.
function Theme({ children }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');   // same as the server

  useEffect(() => {
    setTheme(localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? 'light');   // after hydration
  }, []);

  return <div data-theme={theme}>{children}</div>;
}

// FIX 2 — suppressHydrationWarning, for a value that is LEGITIMATELY
// different and unimportant. It suppresses the warning for that element
// only, one level deep, and does not fix anything else.
<time dateTime={iso} suppressHydrationWarning>
  {new Date(iso).toLocaleString()}
</time>

// FIX 3 — do not render it on the server at all, for genuinely
// client-only widgets.
const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false);
useEffect(() => setMounted(true), []);
if (!mounted) return <Placeholder />;    // same on server and first client
return <ClientOnlyWidget />;
// In Next.js: dynamic(() => import('./Widget'), { ssr: false })

// The WRONG fix, seen everywhere: reading localStorage during render and
// suppressing the warning. That still causes a re-render and a visible
// flash — it just hides the message telling you so.
React 19 made mismatch errors readable, and that changed the debugging

Before 19 the message was a generic “Text content does not match” with no indication of where. React 19 prints a diff of the server and client trees with the offending element highlighted, which turns a half-hour hunt into a glance. If you are still seeing the old opaque errors, the version rather than the bug is the first thing to check. React 19.1's Owner Stacks help further by naming the component that created the element rather than the one that rendered it.

The client-only escape hatch, and its cost

javascript · useSyncExternalStore has a server snapshot for this reason
// The reason the hook takes THREE arguments (R09): the third is what
// the server renders, and it must match the client's first render.
const width = useSyncExternalStore(
  subscribe,
  () => window.innerWidth,   // client snapshot
  () => 0,                    // SERVER snapshot — no window exists
);

// A media query, safe under SSR:
function useMediaQuery(query) {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    (cb) => {
      const mql = window.matchMedia(query);
      mql.addEventListener('change', cb);
      return () => mql.removeEventListener('change', cb);
    },
    () => window.matchMedia(query).matches,
    () => false,     // assume "no" on the server, correct after mount
  );
}

// The consequence: a mobile-only component renders as absent on the
// server, then appears after hydration — a layout shift. The better
// answer for layout is CSS media queries, which the server can emit
// and which need no JavaScript at all.

The costs of server rendering

CostDetail
CPU per requestRendering is not cached by default; every request runs your components
Time to interactive can get worseContent appears early and does not respond until hydration completes
Double data fetchingFetched on the server, then again on the client unless you serialise and pass it
No browser APIswindow, document and localStorage are absent; a library touching them at import time crashes the server
Module-scope state is shared across requestsA cache or a "current user" at module scope leaks between users — the most dangerous SSR bug there is (J02)
Operational surfaceA server to run, scale, monitor and keep warm
Hydration is the part that Server Components remove

The whole cost above exists because the same components run twice — once on the server to produce HTML, once on the client to attach behaviour — which means the JavaScript for every component must ship. Server Components change the arrangement: components that never need interactivity run only on the server, are never sent to the browser, and have nothing to hydrate. That is the actual point of RSC, and it is why Part IV follows this chapter rather than preceding it — the problem has to be clear before the solution makes sense.

Interview follow-up

“What is hydration, and why does it fail?” It is the client render that adopts the server's HTML instead of recreating it — the components run, but the existing DOM nodes are reused and event handlers attached. It fails when the two renders disagree, and the causes are almost always the same short list: time, randomness, browser-only state such as localStorage, and invalid HTML nesting that the parser silently corrected. The rule worth stating is that the first client render must match the server exactly, and any divergence has to happen in an effect afterwards — which is also why useSyncExternalStore takes a separate server snapshot.

N01

Actions and form state

React 19's headline change: a function passed to <form action> that React runs as an async transition, managing pending state, errors and sequencing for you. It replaces the four pieces of boilerplate every submit handler contained, and it is the foundation the rest of Part IV builds on.

What it replaces

What React does for you when a function is passed to `action`: · calls preventDefault() — you never write it again · collects the form into a FormData and passes it in · wraps the call in an async transition, so the UI stays responsive while it runs (W06) · exposes pending for the duration · resets the form on success, when the action is uncontrolled · queues concurrent submissions rather than racing them · surfaces a thrown error to the nearest error boundary And crucially: the form works without JavaScript. Because it is a real <form> with a real submit, a browser that has not yet loaded (or cannot run) the bundle posts it natively — which is what makes progressive enhancement possible in a Next.js app (X07).

useActionState

const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(fn, initialState, permalink?) fn(previousState, formData) → nextState
javascript · the full shape, with field errors
function SignupForm() {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(
    async (previous, formData) => {
      const email = formData.get('email');

      const errors = validate({ email });
      if (errors) {
        // Return the submitted values too, or the fields are cleared on
        // a failed submit and the user retypes everything.
        return { errors, values: { email } };
      }

      try {
        await signUp({ email });
        return { success: true };
      } catch (err) {
        return { errors: { form: err.message }, values: { email } };
      }
    },
    { errors: null, values: {} },     // initial state
  );

  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input
        name="email"
        type="email"
        defaultValue={state.values.email}
        aria-invalid={!!state.errors?.email}
        aria-describedby={state.errors?.email ? 'email-err' : undefined}
      />
      {state.errors?.email && (
        <p id="email-err" role="alert">{state.errors.email}</p>
      )}

      <button disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Creating…' : 'Create account'}
      </button>

      {state.errors?.form && <p role="alert">{state.errors.form}</p>}
      {state.success && <p>Check your email.</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

// Note the reducer-like signature: (previousState, formData) → next.
// The previous state is genuinely useful — a retry counter, keeping
// earlier field values, accumulating a list.
Return errors; do not throw them

A thrown error inside an action propagates to the nearest error boundary and replaces the form with the fallback — which is correct for “the database is unreachable” and completely wrong for “that email is already taken”. Validation failures and other expected outcomes should be returned as state, so the form stays on screen with the message attached to the right field. The rule mirrors the one in every other part of this book: expected failures are values, unexpected ones are exceptions.

useFormStatus

javascript · pending state without prop drilling
import { useFormStatus } from 'react-dom';   // note: react-dom, not react

// Reads the status of the nearest <form> ABOVE it in the tree. The
// component does not need the form to pass anything down, which is what
// makes a shared SubmitButton possible.
function SubmitButton({ children }) {
  const { pending, data, method, action } = useFormStatus();

  return (
    <button disabled={pending}>
      {pending ? <Spinner /> : children}
    </button>
  );
}

// Used anywhere, in any form:
<form action={createPost}>
  <input name="title" />
  <SubmitButton>Publish</SubmitButton>   {/* knows it is pending */}
</form>

// THE TRAP: it reads the form ABOVE it. A component that renders the
// form itself always sees pending: false, because there is no form
// above it yet.
function Broken() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();    // ✗ always false
  return <form action={fn}>…</form>;
}
// The button must be a CHILD of the form, in a separate component.

// `data` is the FormData being submitted, which is useful for an
// optimistic preview:
function Preview() {
  const { pending, data } = useFormStatus();
  if (!pending) return null;
  return <p>Posting “{data.get('title')}”…</p>;
}

Actions outside forms

javascript · buttons, and startTransition with async
// A button can carry its own formAction, overriding the form's:
<form action={save}>
  <input name="title" />
  <button>Save</button>
  <button formAction={saveAsDraft}>Save draft</button>
  <button formAction={deletePost}>Delete</button>
</form>

// And React 19 allows ASYNC functions in startTransition, so any
// mutation gets the same pending management without a form at all:
function LikeButton({ postId }) {
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function handleClick() {
    startTransition(async () => {
      await likePost(postId);
      // Updates after the await ARE part of the transition in React 19.
      // In 18 they were not — that is the change that makes this work.
    });
  }

  return (
    <button onClick={handleClick} disabled={isPending}>
      {isPending ? '…' : 'Like'}
    </button>
  );
}

Submission queueing

A user clicks Save three times quickly. Without Actions you get three concurrent requests whose responses can arrive in any order, so the final state is decided by network luck (J04). React queues action calls from the same form: each waits for the previous to settle, so they apply in the order they were made. click 1 ├── request ──┤ click 2 ├── request ──┤ click 3 ├── request ──┤ What this does not do: deduplicate. Three clicks are still three requests, just sequential. If the operation is not idempotent, the button should be disabled while pending — which isPending makes trivial — or the mutation should carry an idempotency key. And it is per form. Two different forms submitting at once run in parallel, which is what you want.

Where Actions fit

UseFor
<form action={fn}>Any form submission. Works without JS if fn is a Server Function (N05)
useActionStateWhen you need the result — errors, a success flag, returned data
useFormStatusA shared submit button or pending indicator, without prop drilling
useOptimisticShowing the result before the server confirms it (N02)
startTransition(async …)Mutations that are not forms — a like button, a delete
A plain onSubmitStill fine. Actions are not mandatory, and a controlled form with live validation may be clearer
Actions push forms back toward uncontrolled

An action receives FormData, so the fields do not need to be in React state — which removes a render per keystroke across the whole form and a large amount of code (R06). Keep individual fields controlled where they genuinely need live behaviour, and let the rest be plain inputs with name attributes. This is a real reversal of the advice that dominated React from 2015 to 2023, and it is worth saying out loud in an interview because it signals you are current.

Interview follow-up

“What problem do Actions solve?” Every submit handler contained the same four things — preventDefault, a pending flag, a try/catch for errors, and a reset — written by hand and slightly differently each time. An action is a function passed to form action that React runs as an async transition, doing all four and additionally queueing concurrent submissions so they cannot race. The part worth volunteering is the progressive-enhancement consequence: it is still a real form element, so with a Server Function behind it the submission works before any JavaScript has loaded, which no onSubmit handler can do.

N02

useOptimistic

Showing the result of an action before the server has confirmed it makes an app feel instant. Doing it by hand means managing a temporary state, reconciling it with the real one, and rolling back on failure — three things that are easy to get subtly wrong. useOptimistic does all of them, and its rollback behaviour is the part worth understanding.

The shape

const [optimisticValue, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(actualValue, updateFn) updateFn(currentValue, optimisticInput) → next value
javascript · a message list
function Thread({ messages, sendMessage }) {
  const [optimisticMessages, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    messages,                                    // the real state
    (current, newText) => [                      // how to apply a guess
      ...current,
      { id: 'temp', text: newText, sending: true },
    ],
  );

  async function formAction(formData) {
    const text = formData.get('message');

    // Applied immediately. The list re-renders with the new message
    // already in it, before any network call.
    addOptimistic(text);

    await sendMessage(text);
    // When the action finishes and `messages` updates with the real
    // value, the optimistic entry disappears automatically.
  }

  return (
    <>
      <ul>
        {optimisticMessages.map(m => (
          <li key={m.id} className={m.sending ? 'pending' : ''}>
            {m.text}
            {m.sending && <span aria-label="Sending">…</span>}
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <form action={formAction}>
        <input name="message" />
        <button>Send</button>
      </form>
    </>
  );
}
The lifecycle, and why no rollback code is needed 1 addOptimistic(x) is called inside an action → React renders the optimistic value immediately 2 the action runs. Throughout, the component reads the optimistic value rather than the real one 3 the action settles → React discards every optimistic update and re-renders with whatever the real state now is That third step is the whole design. Success and failure are the same code path: the optimistic value is thrown away, and the truth is displayed. On success the truth includes your change; on failure it does not, and the UI reverts on its own. So there is no onError and no rollback branch — but there is an obligation: if the action fails, you must tell the user, or their message silently vanishes with no explanation. Return an error from useActionState and render it (N01).
addOptimistic only works inside an action or a transition

Calling it from a plain event handler outside a transition does nothing useful — React has no scope in which the optimistic value is “pending”, so it is applied and immediately discarded on the next render. It must be called inside a form action, inside startTransition, or inside a function passed to useActionState. This is the most common reason people report that “useOptimistic doesn't work”, and the fix is almost always wrapping the mutation in startTransition.

Beyond appending

javascript · the update function can do anything
// A toggle — the most common case after a list append.
const [optimisticLiked, setOptimisticLiked] = useOptimistic(
  post.liked,
  (_current, next) => next,      // just replace
);

function handleLike() {
  startTransition(async () => {
    setOptimisticLiked(!post.liked);
    await toggleLike(post.id);
  });
}

// A counter that moves with the toggle:
const [optimistic, update] = useOptimistic(
  { liked: post.liked, count: post.likeCount },
  (current, liked) => ({
    liked,
    count: current.count + (liked ? 1 : -1),
  }),
);

// A removal, which reads better as a filter than as a flag:
const [optimisticItems, removeOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
  items,
  (current, idToRemove) => current.filter(i => i.id !== idToRemove),
);

// MULTIPLE optimistic updates compose — the reducer is applied once per
// pending update, in order, on top of the real value. Three rapid
// deletions all appear, and all revert together if the batch fails.

When it is the wrong choice

Good fitPoor fit
Likes, reactions, togglesPayments, transfers, anything irreversible
Adding a comment or a messageOperations whose result you cannot predict (a server-assigned price, a generated id you must display)
Reordering a listAnything with a meaningful chance of rejection — a name that may be taken
Marking something read or doneLong operations, where the user will start doing something else before it settles
Deleting, where undo is cheapActions with consequences the user must acknowledge
Optimistic UI is a lie you are promising to keep

You are telling the user something happened before knowing that it did, which is fine when failure is rare and reverting is cheap — a like that un-likes itself is an annoyance. It is not fine when the user will act on the false information: a transfer that appears to succeed, a booking that looks confirmed, a document shown as saved while the user closes the laptop. The test is what happens if the revert goes unnoticed. Where the answer is “they lose something”, show a pending state and wait.

Compared with doing it by hand

Making the pending state visible

javascript · the UI details that make it feel honest
// 1 · Mark optimistic items visually. A message that looks identical to
//     a confirmed one and then vanishes is confusing; one that is
//     slightly dimmed with a "sending" indicator is understood.
<li className={m.sending ? 'opacity-60' : ''}>

// 2 · Announce it to assistive technology, or the change is silent.
<li aria-busy={m.sending}>

// 3 · Keep the input usable. The point of optimistic UI is that the
//     user continues working — disabling the form while it settles
//     undoes the benefit entirely.
<form action={formAction}>
  <input name="message" />   {/* NOT disabled */}
  <button>Send</button>
</form>

// 4 · Surface failures. This is the obligation the automatic rollback
//     creates — without it a message just disappears.
const [error, formAction] = useActionState(async (_prev, fd) => {
  addOptimistic(fd.get('message'));
  try {
    await sendMessage(fd.get('message'));
    return null;
  } catch {
    return 'Could not send. Tap to retry.';
  }
}, null);
Interview follow-up

“How does useOptimistic roll back on failure?” It does not roll back in the usual sense — optimistic updates are layered on top of the real state and discarded wholesale when the action settles, so the component simply re-renders with the truth. Success and failure take the same path, which is why there is no error callback and no reconciliation code. Then name the obligation that creates: because the revert is silent, you must surface the failure yourself, typically by returning an error from useActionState — otherwise the user's message disappears with no explanation, which is a worse experience than not being optimistic at all.

N03

use()

A new primitive that reads a resource — a promise or a context — and is the first thing in React that is deliberately not a hook. It may be called conditionally, inside loops, after an early return. That exemption is not a convenience; it is what makes reading a promise during render possible at all.

Reading a promise

javascript · the component suspends, the boundary shows the fallback
import { use, Suspense } from 'react';

function Comments({ commentsPromise }) {
  // Suspends until the promise resolves; then returns the value.
  // A rejection is thrown, so the nearest error boundary catches it.
  const comments = use(commentsPromise);

  return <ul>{comments.map(c => <li key={c.id}>{c.text}</li>)}</ul>;
}

function Page({ commentsPromise }) {
  return (
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Could not load comments</p>}>
      <Suspense fallback={<CommentsSkeleton />}>
        <Comments commentsPromise={commentsPromise} />
      </Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  );
}

// The component has NO loading state, NO error state, and no effect.
// Those concerns moved to boundaries in the tree, where they can be
// shared by everything beneath them (R15).
The promise must not be created during render

use(fetch('/api/x')) starts a new request on every render, and because suspending re-renders the component, that is an infinite loop of requests. The promise must come from somewhere stable: passed as a prop from a Server Component, returned by a cache that deduplicates by key (React's cache(), or a library), or held in state. This is the single most important rule about use(), and it is the one people hit within five minutes of trying it.

The pattern this enables

Start the request on the server; await it on the client. A Server Component can begin a fetch and pass the unresolved promise across the boundary. The request is already in flight while the HTML streams, and the client component suspends only for whatever time is left. async function Page() { const slow = getSlowData(); ← started, NOT awaited const fast = await getFastData(); return ( <> <Header data={fast} /> ← rendered immediately <Suspense fallback={<Skel />}> <Slow promise={slow} /> ← streams in when ready </Suspense> </> ); } Without this, a client component that needs data must wait for hydration, then start a fetch — a waterfall of "download JS, run, request, wait" (R08). With it, the request started before the HTML was even sent. Promises crossing the boundary are serialisable in the RSC protocol: the streaming format can express "a value that will arrive later", which is the same mechanism that streams Suspense content (W07, N04).

Reading context conditionally

javascript · the second, quieter use of use()
// useContext is a hook, so it obeys the rules: top level, unconditional.
function Panel({ collapsed }) {
  if (collapsed) return <Chevron />;      // early return

  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext); // ✗ never reached on one path
  return <div className={theme}>…</div>;  //   → hook-order error
}

// use() may be called anywhere, so the early return is fine:
function Panel({ collapsed }) {
  if (collapsed) return <Chevron />;

  const theme = use(ThemeContext);        // ✓
  return <div className={theme}>…</div>;
}

// And in a loop, which useContext cannot do:
function Breadcrumbs({ contexts }) {
  return contexts.map(ctx => <span key={ctx.name}>{use(ctx)}</span>);
}

// Why this is allowed: use() does not allocate a hook slot. It reads
// from the fiber's context dependency list or throws a promise — there
// is no positional state to keep aligned, so the call-order rule does
// not apply (W05).

The rules

RuleDetail
Called from a component or a hookNot from an event handler, an effect, or a plain function
May be conditionalThe only React API with this exemption
Takes a promise or a contextNot arbitrary thenables in every case; not observables
The promise must be cached or passed inCreating it during render is an infinite loop
Needs a <Suspense> above itOtherwise the suspension reaches the root and the whole app shows a fallback — or none
Rejections need an error boundaryuse() throws the rejection during render
Works in Server and Client ComponentsIn a Server Component, plain await is usually simpler
In a Server Component, prefer await

use() and await both work in an async Server Component, and await reads better and needs no Suspense boundary to be correct. use() earns its place in two situations: a Client Component consuming a promise handed down from the server, and a case where the read is genuinely conditional. Reaching for use() everywhere because it is new produces code that is harder to follow than the await it replaced.

Caching the promise

javascript · three ways to get a stable promise
// 1 · React's cache(), for Server Components. Deduplicates by argument
//     within a single request, so three components asking for the same
//     user cause one query.
import { cache } from 'react';

const getUser = cache(async (id) => {
  return db.user.findUnique({ where: { id } });
});
// Called from four components with the same id → one database round
// trip. Called on the next request → a fresh call, because the cache is
// per-request (X04).

// 2 · A module-level Map, for a client SPA. Note the SSR caveat from
//     J02: on a server this would be shared across users, so this
//     pattern is client-only.
const cache = new Map();
function getUserPromise(id) {
  if (!cache.has(id)) cache.set(id, fetchUser(id));
  return cache.get(id);
}
function Profile({ id }) {
  const user = use(getUserPromise(id));
  …
}

// 3 · State, when the promise is created by an event.
const [searchPromise, setSearchPromise] = useState(null);

function handleSearch(q) {
  startTransition(() => setSearchPromise(search(q)));
}
{searchPromise && (
  <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
    <Results promise={searchPromise} />
  </Suspense>
)}

Unhandled rejections

javascript · the sharp edge nobody expects
// A promise created on the server and passed to the client may reject
// BEFORE the client component renders and calls use() on it. In Node
// that is an unhandled rejection, which can crash the process.
//
// Attach a no-op catch at creation to mark it handled. use() still
// throws the rejection into the error boundary — the catch only stops
// the runtime-level warning.
async function Page() {
  const dataPromise = getData();
  dataPromise.catch(() => {});     // handled, but not swallowed

  return (
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<Error />}>
      <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
        <Client promise={dataPromise} />
      </Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  );
}

// And always pair Suspense with an error boundary. A promise that
// rejects with no boundary above it unmounts the tree (R15).
Interview follow-up

“Why can use() be called conditionally when no other hook can?” Because it does not occupy a hook slot. Hooks are matched by call order in a linked list on the fiber (W05), so skipping one misaligns every subsequent slot — but use() either reads the fiber's context dependencies or throws a promise to suspend, neither of which is positional state. The follow-up worth reaching first: this exemption is what makes reading a promise during render workable at all, since the read frequently is conditional — and the accompanying rule is that the promise must be created outside the render, or suspending re-renders the component and starts another one, forever.

N04

Server Components

The largest change to React's model since hooks. A Server Component runs only on the server, its code is never sent to the browser, and it can await directly. It is not server-side rendering with a new name — SSR runs your components on the server and again on the client; RSC means some components never reach the client at all.

RSC is not SSR

SSR (W07) server: run every component → HTML string client: download every component's JS → run them all again → hydrate → the whole app ships. SSR improves first paint, not bundle size. RSC server: run the Server Components → a serialised element tree, with holes where Client Components go client: download only the Client Components' JS → render those into the holes → a Server Component's code, and its dependencies, never ship. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ import { marked } from 'marked'; // 40 KB │ │ import sanitizeHtml from 'sanitize-html'; // 60 KB │ │ │ │ export default async function Article({ id }) { server │ │ const post = await db.post.find(id); │ │ return <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ │ │ __html: sanitizeHtml(marked(post.body)) }} />; │ │ } │ │ │ │ → the browser receives the rendered HTML. │ │ 100 KB of libraries, the database client, and the query │ │ are not in the bundle at all. │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ The two are complementary, not alternatives. A typical Next.js page uses RSC to decide what ships, and SSR to turn the resulting tree into HTML for the first paint.

The two environments

Server ComponentClient Component
Marked withNothing — the default'use client' at the top of the file
RunsOn the server, onceServer (for HTML) and client (hydration + updates)
Code shipped to the browserNeverYes
Can be asyncYes — await directlyNo
Can use useState, useEffectNoYes
Can use event handlersNoYes
Can access the database, the filesystem, secretsYesNo
Can use window, localStorageNoYes
Can import the other kindBothOnly Client Components
javascript · app/posts/[id]/page.tsx — a Server Component
// No 'use client' → this runs on the server only.
import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import LikeButton from './LikeButton';      // a Client Component

export default async function PostPage({ params }) {
  const { id } = await params;              // async in Next.js 15+

  // A direct database query, in a component. No API route, no fetch,
  // no serialisation layer — and the credentials never leave the server.
  const post = await db.post.findUnique({
    where: { id },
    include: { author: true },
  });

  if (!post) notFound();

  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{post.title}</h1>
      <p>by {post.author.name}</p>
      <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: post.html }} />

      {/* Only THIS component's JavaScript is sent to the browser. */}
      <LikeButton postId={post.id} initialLikes={post.likes} />
    </article>
  );
}
javascript · app/posts/[id]/LikeButton.tsx — a Client Component
'use client';   // ← the boundary marker. Must be the FIRST line.

import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';
import { likePost } from './actions';

export default function LikeButton({ postId, initialLikes }) {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(initialLikes);
  const [pending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  return (
    <button
      disabled={pending}
      onClick={() => startTransition(async () => {
        setLikes(l => l + 1);
        await likePost(postId);
      })}
    >
      ♥ {likes}
    </button>
  );
}

What 'use client' actually marks

It is not "this component is a client component". It is the boundary of the client bundle. Everything a 'use client' file imports, transitively, is also client code and also ships. page.tsx server └─ Dashboard.tsx server └─ Chart.tsx 'use client' ← boundary ├─ chart-lib ships ├─ utils.ts ships └─ Legend.tsx ships (no directive needed — it is below the boundary) So the directive belongs as LOW in the tree as possible. Putting 'use client' at the top of a layout makes the entire page client-rendered, which throws away the benefit while keeping the complexity — and it is the single most common RSC mistake. The "islands" shape that results: ┌─ server-rendered page ──────────────────────────┐ │ header · article · sidebar · footer │ │ │ │ ┌─ client island ─┐ ┌─ client island ─┐ │ │ │ <LikeButton> │ │ <SearchBox> │ │ │ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The boundary is about serialisation

javascript · what may cross from server to client
// Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component must be
// SERIALISABLE, because they travel through the RSC payload.

// ✓ allowed
<Client
  str="hello" num={1} bool flag={null}
  arr={[1, 2]} obj={{ a: 1 }}
  date={new Date()}          // Dates ARE supported
  map={new Map()} set={new Set()}
  promise={getData()}        // an unresolved promise — for use() (N03)
  element={<ServerThing />}  // a rendered element, as children or a prop
/>

// ✗ not allowed
<Client
  onClick={() => …}          // functions cannot be serialised
  instance={new MyClass()}   // class instances lose their prototype
  symbol={Symbol('x')}
/>
// …with ONE exception: a Server Function, which is passed as a
// reference the client can call back (N05).

// The important pattern: a Server Component can be passed as CHILDREN
// to a Client Component. The server renders it and sends the result;
// the client component just places it.
// app/page.tsx  (server)
<ClientShell>
  <ServerOnlyContent />      {/* rendered on the server */}
</ClientShell>

// ClientShell.tsx  ('use client')
export default function ClientShell({ children }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(true);
  return open ? <div>{children}</div> : null;
  // It renders `children` without ever importing them — so
  // ServerOnlyContent's code never enters the client bundle.
}
The children pattern is the most important RSC technique

A Client Component cannot import a Server Component — that would pull it into the bundle. But it can receive one as children or as a prop, because by then the server has already rendered it to an element tree. This is how you keep interactive shells (tabs, accordions, modals, providers) on the client while their contents stay on the server. Teams that do not learn it end up marking everything 'use client' the first time they need a provider at the root, and lose the whole benefit.

Composition rules

javascript · what can contain what
// server → server      ✓  ordinary
// server → client      ✓  the boundary; props must serialise
// client → client      ✓  ordinary
// client → server      ✗  by IMPORT
//                      ✓  by CHILDREN / props

// The failing case, and its fix:
'use client';
import ServerThing from './ServerThing';   // ✗ pulls it into the bundle
export default function Shell() {
  return <div><ServerThing /></div>;
}

// Fix: accept it instead of importing it.
'use client';
export default function Shell({ children }) {
  return <div>{children}</div>;
}

// Providers are the case everyone meets first. A context provider needs
// 'use client' — but wrapping it around server-rendered children is
// fine, because the children are passed, not imported:
// app/providers.tsx
'use client';
export function Providers({ children }) {
  return <ThemeProvider><QueryProvider>{children}</QueryProvider></ThemeProvider>;
}
// app/layout.tsx  (stays a SERVER component)
export default function Layout({ children }) {
  return <html><body><Providers>{children}</Providers></body></html>;
}

The payload

plaintext · what actually goes over the wire
The server does not send HTML to the React runtime — it sends a
serialised element tree ("the RSC payload" / "flight"), streamed line
by line:

  1:"$Sreact.suspense"
  2:I["./chunks/LikeButton.js","LikeButton"]        ← a client reference
  0:["$","article",null,{"children":[
      ["$","h1",null,{"children":"Hello world"}],
      ["$","$L2",null,{"postId":"p1","initialLikes":4}]   ← the hole
    ]}]

  · "$" entries are elements: [type, key, props]
  · "I" lines register a CLIENT COMPONENT by chunk and export name
  · "$L2" is a reference to that client component — a hole the browser
    fills once the chunk loads
  · rows arrive incrementally, which is how Suspense boundaries stream

Why a custom format rather than JSON: it must express references to
client components, unresolved promises, and rows that arrive later.
JSON can express none of those.

Consequences worth knowing:
  · navigating client-side fetches a NEW payload, not HTML — so the
    client re-renders in place, preserving client state
  · the payload is larger than the equivalent HTML, and is sent in
    addition to it on the first load

What you give up

CostDetail
A server is requiredRSC needs a runtime. It is not a static build output
Two mental modelsEvery file is now “where does this run?”, and the answer is not always local
Serialisation rules at the boundaryA function prop is a build error you will hit repeatedly at first
Framework lock-in, for nowRSC needs a bundler integration; in practice that means Next.js, or Waku, or a Parcel/Vite setup
Harder debuggingA stack trace can span two environments, and errors are redacted in production
Client state resets less predictablyNavigation replaces server-rendered subtrees; what survives depends on the router
RSC is a bet on a shape, and it is reasonable to decline it

If your product is an internal dashboard behind a login, where SEO is irrelevant, first paint is not a business metric and the data is user-specific anyway, then a client-rendered SPA with a query library is simpler and entirely defensible. RSC pays where the content is largely server-owned, where bundle size is a real cost, and where first paint matters — marketing sites, e-commerce, content, dashboards with heavy read paths. Being able to say which side of that line a project falls on is a better answer than advocating either way.

Interview follow-up

“What is the difference between SSR and Server Components?” SSR runs every component on the server to produce HTML and then runs them all again on the client to hydrate, so the whole bundle still ships — it improves first paint, not size. A Server Component runs only on the server and its code is never sent, so its dependencies leave the bundle entirely. Then give the technique that shows practical use: a Client Component cannot import a Server Component, but it can receive one as children, which is how you keep an interactive shell on the client with server-rendered content inside it — and not knowing that is why teams end up marking their root layout 'use client' and losing the benefit.

N05

Server Functions

A function marked 'use server' runs on the server and can be called from the client as if it were local. The bundler replaces it with a reference; React posts the arguments and returns the result. It removes the API layer for mutations — and it creates a public endpoint, which is the part every tutorial underplays.

The mechanism

What the bundler does server side client bundle ────────────────────────── ────────────────────────── 'use server'; // the body is NOT here export async function like(id) { export const like = await db.like(id); createServerReference( } 'a1b2c3#like'); What happens at call time client: like('p1') → POST /current-url Next-Action: a1b2c3#like body: ["p1"] → the server looks up a1b2c3#like in its action manifest, calls it with the deserialised arguments → returns the serialised result, and (in Next.js) an updated RSC payload for any revalidated routes So a Server Function is an RPC endpoint with a generated id. The ergonomics are "just call the function"; the reality is a POST to a URL that anyone can also send. That framing is the whole of the security section below.

Declaring one

javascript · app/posts/actions.ts
'use server';   // file-level: EVERY export here is a server function

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import { auth } from '@/lib/auth';

const CreatePost = z.object({
  title: z.string().trim().min(1).max(200),
  body:  z.string().max(50_000),
});

export async function createPost(prevState, formData) {
  // 1 · AUTHENTICATE. This is a public endpoint (see below).
  const session = await auth();
  if (!session) return { error: 'Not signed in' };

  // 2 · VALIDATE. FormData values are strings from an untrusted source.
  const parsed = CreatePost.safeParse({
    title: formData.get('title'),
    body:  formData.get('body'),
  });
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { errors: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors };
  }

  // 3 · AUTHORISE, scoped by the caller — never by an id from the body.
  const post = await db.post.create({
    data: { ...parsed.data, authorId: session.userId },
  });

  // 4 · Invalidate what is now stale.
  revalidatePath('/posts');

  return { success: true, id: post.id };
}

// The alternative: an inline directive inside a Server Component, for a
// one-off. Anything it closes over is ENCRYPTED into the reference and
// sent to the client, so do not close over secrets.
export default async function Page() {
  const userId = await getUserId();

  async function deletePost(formData) {
    'use server';
    await db.post.delete({ where: { id: formData.get('id'), authorId: userId } });
    revalidatePath('/posts');
  }

  return <form action={deletePost}>…</form>;
}
A Server Function is a public HTTP endpoint

It is not protected by being “only called from this component”. The id is in the client bundle, the request is an ordinary POST, and anyone can send it with any arguments at any time — including arguments your UI would never produce. Treat every one exactly as you would a REST route: authenticate the caller, validate every input against a schema, and scope the authorisation to the session rather than to an id from the request body. db.post.delete({ where: { id } }) without an ownership check lets anyone delete any post, and it looks completely innocuous.

Calling from the client

javascript · three ways
'use client';
import { createPost, likePost } from './actions';

// 1 · As a form action — works without JavaScript (N01)
<form action={createPost}>…</form>

// 2 · With useActionState, when you need the result
function NewPost() {
  const [state, action, pending] = useActionState(createPost, {});
  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="title" defaultValue={state.values?.title} />
      {state.errors?.title && <p role="alert">{state.errors.title[0]}</p>}
      <button disabled={pending}>Publish</button>
    </form>
  );
}

// 3 · Directly, inside a transition — for anything that is not a form
function Like({ id }) {
  const [pending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  return (
    <button onClick={() => startTransition(() => likePost(id))}>♥</button>
  );
}

// Arguments and return values must be SERIALISABLE, same rules as RSC
// props (N04): primitives, plain objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set,
// FormData, and other Server Functions. Not class instances, not
// functions, not Symbols.

// bind() partially applies an argument for a form action — the standard
// way to pass an id alongside the form fields:
const deleteWithId = deletePost.bind(null, post.id);
<form action={deleteWithId}><button>Delete</button></form>
// The bound argument is encrypted by the framework, so it cannot be
// tampered with — but it is still not an authorisation check.

Server Functions versus API routes

Server FunctionRoute Handler / API
Called byYour own React codeAnything — mobile apps, webhooks, scripts
TypesEnd to end, automaticallyHand-written or generated
MethodAlways POSTAny
CachingNone — mutationsFull HTTP caching available
Works without JSYes, via <form action>Only with a plain form action="/api/x"
RevalidationReturns fresh RSC data in the same round tripClient must refetch separately
VersioningNone — ids change between deploysYou control the URL and the contract
Use forMutations from your own UIPublic APIs, webhooks, anything non-React
A Server Function is not an API, and must not become one

The generated id is derived from the build, so it changes whenever the code changes — which means an external consumer that hardcodes it breaks on your next deploy. There is no versioning, no OpenAPI description, no method semantics, and no way to grant a third party access to one endpoint without the whole bundle. If something other than your own React code needs to call it, write a Route Handler. The useful rule: Server Functions for your UI's mutations, Route Handlers for contracts with anyone else.

The mutation round trip

A Server Function in a Next.js app does something an API route cannot: it returns fresh UI alongside its result. click ─▶ POST Next-Action: a1b2#createPost body: FormData ──────────────────────────────────────▶ server: run the function revalidatePath('/posts') re-render the affected Server Components ◀────────────────────────────────────── result + an updated RSC payload React applies both: the returned state, and the new server-rendered tree — in one round trip, without a refetch. With a REST endpoint the same flow is: POST, wait, then a second request to re-read the list, then re-render. Two round trips, and a window where the UI is stale. This is the strongest practical argument for Server Functions, and it is more compelling than the type safety people usually cite.

Revalidation

javascript · telling the framework what is now stale
'use server';
import { revalidatePath, revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';

export async function publishPost(id) {
  await db.post.update({ where: { id }, data: { published: true } });

  // By path — the page and anything under it
  revalidatePath('/posts');
  revalidatePath(`/posts/${id}`);
  revalidatePath('/posts/[id]', 'page');    // a dynamic segment, all ids

  // By tag — anything fetched with { next: { tags: ['posts'] } }.
  // Usually better: the tag describes the DATA, so you do not have to
  // remember every page that reads it (X04).
  revalidateTag('posts');

  // redirect() throws, so it must come last and outside any try/catch —
  // a try/catch around it swallows the redirect and nothing happens.
  redirect(`/posts/${id}`);
}
redirect() throws, and that trips everyone once

It signals the redirect by throwing a special error that the framework catches. So it cannot be inside a try/catch that swallows everything — the redirect is silently cancelled and the function appears to do nothing. Put it after the try/catch, or re-throw anything matching isRedirectError. The same applies to notFound().

The security checklist

For every Server Function, without exception: □ Authenticate — read the session inside the function. Never trust a userId passed as an argument. □ Validate every input with a schema. FormData values are strings from an untrusted source, and a missing field is null rather than an error. □ Authorise by the session, not by an id from the request: db.post.delete({ where: { id } }) ✗ db.post.delete({ where: { id, authorId: session.id } }) ✓ □ Rate limit anything expensive or abusable. It is a public endpoint with no gateway in front of it by default. □ Do not close over secrets in an inline action — closed-over values are encrypted and sent to the client, and encryption is not a reason to send a key at all. □ Never return more than the UI needs. Returning a full user row leaks the password hash into the RSC payload. □ Check the origin for state-changing calls if your framework does not (Next.js verifies Origin against Host by default; confirm it, and configure allowedOrigins behind a proxy). The framing that keeps this right: it is a POST route with a generated name. Everything you would do for one of those, do here.
Interview follow-up

“What is the main risk with Server Actions?” That they look like function calls and are actually public HTTP endpoints — the id is in the client bundle, and anyone can POST arbitrary arguments to it at any time. So every one needs the same treatment as a REST route: authenticate inside the function, validate the input with a schema, and scope authorisation to the session rather than to an id from the request body. The concrete example worth giving is delete({ where: { id } }) versus delete({ where: { id, authorId: session.userId } }) — identical-looking code, and the first lets anyone delete anyone's data.

N06

The rest of React 19, and what it removed

Beyond Actions and Server Components, React 19 is a long list of small changes that each delete some boilerplate. Several of them remove APIs you have written hundreds of times. This chapter covers them, the 19.1 and 19.2 additions, and the removals to check before upgrading.

ref is a prop

javascript · forwardRef is deprecated
// BEFORE — every component that needed to forward a ref was wrapped.
const Input = forwardRef(function Input(props, ref) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...props} />;
});

// REACT 19 — ref arrives in props like anything else.
function Input({ ref, ...props }) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...props} />;
}

// The wrapper also disappears from DevTools, and the typing gets
// simpler: no ForwardedRef<T> generic, just a prop.

// And callback refs may now return a CLEANUP function, which removes
// the null-check dance:
<div ref={(node) => {
  const obs = new ResizeObserver(onResize);
  obs.observe(node);
  return () => obs.disconnect();       // called on detach
}} />

// Before, the same thing needed:
// ref={(node) => { if (node) { … } else { /* cleanup, but of WHAT? */ } }}

Context as a provider

javascript
const Theme = createContext('light');

<Theme.Provider value="dark">…</Theme.Provider>   // still works
<Theme value="dark">…</Theme>                     // React 19

// Context.Consumer is deprecated — use useContext or use() (N03).

Document metadata and resources

javascript · title, meta and link, hoisted automatically
// Rendering these anywhere in the tree hoists them into <head>. No
// react-helmet, no portal, no effect writing document.title.
function BlogPost({ post }) {
  return (
    <article>
      <title>{post.title}</title>
      <meta name="description" content={post.excerpt} />
      <link rel="canonical" href={post.url} />

      <h1>{post.title}</h1>
      …
    </article>
  );
}
// Works in SSR too, so crawlers see the real tags.
// In a Next.js app the `metadata` export is still preferred — it runs
// before rendering and can be async (X10).

// Stylesheets with a precedence are deduplicated and ordered:
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/card.css" precedence="default" />
// Render the same href twice and it is inserted once.

// Async scripts are deduplicated too, so a component can declare its
// own dependency without coordinating with the rest of the app:
<script async src="https://example.com/widget.js" />

// And the preloading APIs, for telling the browser early:
import { preload, preinit, prefetchDNS, preconnect } from 'react-dom';
preconnect('https://api.example.com');
preload('/hero.avif', { as: 'image', fetchPriority: 'high' });
preinit('/analytics.js', { as: 'script' });

The 19.1 and 19.2 additions

AdditionWhat it does
Owner Stacks (19.1)Error messages name the component that created the element, not just the one that rendered it — which is far more useful for a component deep inside a library
<Activity> (19.2)Hide a subtree while preserving its state, tearing down its effects. The proper primitive for tabs and prefetched routes (R04)
useEffectEvent (19.2)A function that always sees current props and state and is explicitly non-reactive, so it is excluded from dependency arrays (R07)
Performance Tracks (19.2)React's own lanes appear in the browser's performance profiler, so you can see scheduling rather than infer it
cacheSignal (19.2)An AbortSignal tied to a cached server render's lifetime
javascript · Activity, and why it is not just display:none
// Three options for a hidden tab, and they differ in what survives:
//
//   {active && <Panel />}        state destroyed, effects torn down
//   <Panel hidden={!active} />    state kept, effects KEEP RUNNING,
//                                 DOM cost kept
//   <Activity mode="hidden">      state kept, effects torn down,
//                                 no DOM cost
//
import { Activity } from 'react';

<Activity mode={tab === 'search' ? 'visible' : 'hidden'}>
  <SearchPanel />   {/* scroll position and query survive the switch,
                         but its polling interval is stopped */}
</Activity>

// It also renders hidden content at IDLE priority, so a likely-next
// route can be prepared without competing with the visible UI.

// useEffectEvent, for the "latest value without re-subscribing" case:
function Chat({ roomId, theme }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    showToast('Connected!', theme);      // always the CURRENT theme
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const conn = connect(roomId);
    conn.on('connected', onConnected);
    return () => conn.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]);      // theme is NOT here — changing it does not reconnect
}

Smaller changes worth knowing

ChangeEffect
Hydration error messagesA diff of server vs client, with the element highlighted (W07)
useDeferredValue(value, initial)Renders something cheap on the very first render
Custom element supportProps are now set as properties when the element defines them, rather than always as attributes
Errors reported oncePreviously logged twice; now one report, plus onCaughtError / onUncaughtError on the root
react-dom/staticprerender and prerenderToNodeStream — await all data, then emit static HTML
Cleanup functions on refsCallback refs may return a teardown
<form> reset on successUncontrolled forms reset automatically after a successful action

What was removed

javascript · check these before upgrading
// ── REMOVED in 19 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ReactDOM.render(…)             → createRoot(el).render(…)
ReactDOM.hydrate(…)            → hydrateRoot(el, …)
ReactDOM.unmountComponentAtNode(el) → root.unmount()
ReactDOM.findDOMNode(inst)     → a ref
React.createFactory(…)         → JSX, or createElement
propTypes / defaultProps on function components
                               → TypeScript, and default parameters
String refs:  ref="myInput"    → useRef, or a callback ref
Legacy Context (contextTypes)  → createContext
module.exports-style factory components

// ── DEPRECATED, still working ────────────────────────────────────────
forwardRef                     → ref as a prop
Context.Consumer               → useContext / use
element.ref                    → element.props.ref

// ── The upgrade path ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
// 1 · Move to React 18.3 first. It is 18.2 plus warnings for everything
//     19 removes — so the warnings ARE the migration checklist.
// 2 · npx codemod@latest react/19/migration-recipe
// 3 · Then 19.

// defaultProps is the one that bites, because the replacement looks
// identical but is not:
function Button({ size = 'md' }) { … }         // undefined → 'md'
Button.defaultProps = { size: 'md' };           // undefined → 'md', same
// …but a default parameter does NOT apply to null, and defaultProps did
// not either — so the behaviour matches. What differs is that
// defaultProps was applied before the component ran, so code reading
// props.size inside a HOC saw the default. Default parameters do not.
Upgrade via 18.3, not straight to 19

React 18.3 is 18.2 with deprecation warnings added and no behavioural change, which makes it a free dry run: install it, run the app, and the console becomes an exact list of what 19 will break. Going directly to 19 turns the same information into runtime errors spread across a large diff. The official codemod handles most of the mechanical work — forwardRef, propTypes, string refs — and what it leaves behind is the part that needed a decision anyway.

The React Compiler

bash · enabling it
# It is a Babel plugin. Works with React 17+ via a runtime shim, and
# natively from 19.
npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest

# Vite
# vite.config.js
#   plugins: [react({ babel: { plugins: ['babel-plugin-react-compiler'] } })]

# Next.js
# next.config.js
#   experimental: { reactCompiler: true }

# The linter reports which components it had to SKIP and why — that
# report is the useful output even before you enable the compiler
# itself, because every skipped component is a rule violation.
npx eslint . --rule 'react-hooks/react-compiler: error'
What the compiler changes about how you write code

Hand-written useMemo, useCallback and memo for referential stability become unnecessary — the compiler inserts equivalent memoisation at a finer granularity than you would (R14). What it does not change is anything structural: waterfalls, oversized lists, over-broad contexts and genuinely expensive work all remain your problem. Its one requirement is that components follow the rules of React, so mutation during render or a ref written in the body causes it to skip that component — and the lint report tells you exactly which, which makes it a useful code-quality tool independently of the performance benefit.

Interview follow-up

“What changed in React 19?” Lead with the three that change how you write code — Actions, which fold pending, error and reset handling into the framework; Server Components, which decide what ships to the browser at all; and use(), which lets a component read a promise during render. Then the ergonomic removals: ref is an ordinary prop so forwardRef is gone, context renders as its own provider, and document metadata hoists automatically so react-helmet is unnecessary. Mentioning that the upgrade path is 18.3 first — because its deprecation warnings are the migration checklist — is a small detail that reads as having actually done it.

X01

Why Next.js, and what “React vs Next.js” actually means

The comparison is not between two alternatives. React is a library for rendering UI; Next.js is a framework that includes React and adds everything React deliberately leaves out. The real question is not which to use — it is whether you need a framework at all, and that has an honest answer in both directions.

What React does not have

Start a React app with nothing else and you must decide, wire up and maintain all of this yourself: routing which URL shows which component, nested layouts, params, navigation, scroll restoration data fetching where it starts, caching, deduplication, invalidation after a mutation server rendering a server, streaming, hydration, the serialisation of initial data bundling a build pipeline, code splitting, tree shaking, asset hashing images resizing, modern formats, lazy loading, preventing layout shift fonts self-hosting, subsetting, avoiding FOUT metadata titles, Open Graph, canonical URLs, sitemaps, robots an API layer if the app talks to a database at all deployment a server, caching headers, a CDN Every one has a good standalone answer — React Router, TanStack Query, Vite, and so on. A framework's proposition is that the integration between them is the expensive part, and that having one set of choices that are known to work together is worth more than picking each one yourself.

The honest comparison

React (+ Vite)Next.js
What it isA UI library plus a build toolA framework that includes React
RoutingAdd React Router or TanStack RouterBuilt in, file-based
RenderingClient-side; SSR is yours to buildServer by default, with static, dynamic and streaming
Server ComponentsNeeds a bundler integration you must assembleThe default
Data fetchingYour choice, on the clientawait in a component, on the server
Backend codeA separate serviceRoute Handlers and Server Functions in the same project
DeploymentStatic files to any hostA Node/edge runtime — or static, if you constrain yourself
Build speedVery fast, and it stays fastSlower; improving with Turbopack
Conceptual loadLower — one environmentHigher — two environments, a caching model, a router with opinions
Lock-inMinimalReal — RSC, the router and the caching are Next-shaped
The question is “do I need a server?”

Everything else follows from it. If your app is behind a login, fetches user-specific data, and has no SEO or first-paint requirement worth paying for — an internal dashboard, an admin tool, a trading terminal — then a client-rendered SPA on a CDN is simpler, cheaper, and has no server to operate. If content must be indexable, first paint is a business metric, or bundle size is a real cost because the audience is on slow devices, then server rendering earns its complexity, and at that point a framework that does it properly beats assembling one.

What Next.js adds, concretely

javascript · the same feature, both ways
// ── React + Vite: a product page ─────────────────────────────────────
// routes.tsx
<Route path="/products/:id" element={<ProductPage />} />

// ProductPage.tsx
function ProductPage() {
  const { id } = useParams();
  const { data: product, isPending } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['product', id],
    queryFn: () => api.get(`/products/${id}`),   // a separate backend
  });

  useEffect(() => { document.title = product?.name ?? 'Loading'; },
            [product]);

  if (isPending) return <Skeleton />;
  return <Product product={product} />;
}
// Ships: React, the router, the query library, the component, and the
// product page's JS — before the request for the product even starts.

// ── Next.js: app/products/[id]/page.tsx ──────────────────────────────
export async function generateMetadata({ params }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const product = await getProduct(id);
  return { title: product.name, openGraph: { images: [product.image] } };
}

export default async function ProductPage({ params }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const product = await getProduct(id);     // the database, directly
  return <Product product={product} />;
}
// No route registration, no query key, no loading state, no effect for
// the title. The HTML arrives with the product in it, and the component
// itself never reaches the browser.

The Pages Router and the App Router

pages/app/
ComponentsAll clientServer by default
Data fetchinggetServerSideProps, getStaticProps — page level onlyawait in any component, at any depth
LayoutsA single _app.tsx, or a per-page hackNested, and preserved across navigation
Loading UIManualloading.tsx → a Suspense boundary
StreamingNoYes
StatusSupported, not receiving new featuresWhere everything new goes
Both routers can coexist, which is what makes migration survivable

A single project can serve some routes from pages/ and others from app/, so a large application can move a route at a time rather than in one commit. The rules are simple — a path may only be defined in one of them, and app/ wins conflicts. The advice for anything new is unambiguous: use the App Router, because the Pages Router receives no new capabilities and every feature in this Part is App Router only. The advice for an existing Pages app is much less urgent: migrate when there is a reason, not on principle.

The alternatives, fairly

ChoiceBest whenTrade
Vite + React RouterAn SPA behind a login, no SEO needYou build any server rendering yourself
Next.jsContent, commerce, anything indexable, mixed static and dynamicComplexity, and a server to run
Remix / React Router 7Web-standards-first; nested routes with loaders and actionsSmaller ecosystem; a different data model to learn
TanStack StartYou already like TanStack Query and Router, want full type safetyYounger; fewer deployment integrations
AstroContent sites with islands of interactivityNot for an app — it is a content-first tool
Vite SSR by handYou have specific requirements and the timeYou own every integration, forever

The costs, stated plainly

Next.js is a real commitment and it is fair to say so: · two environments. Every file is now "where does this run?", and the answer is not always visible in the file itself. · a caching model with several layers that have changed meaningfully between versions, and which is the single largest source of confusion for teams adopting it (X04). · slower builds than Vite, and historically slow dev startup on large apps — the main thing Turbopack addresses. · real lock-in. The router, the caching, the metadata API and the RSC integration are Next-shaped. Moving off is a rewrite of everything except the components themselves. · a hosting story that is easiest on one vendor. It runs anywhere with Node, and self-hosting is documented and viable — but ISR, image optimisation and edge middleware take noticeably more work outside Vercel. None of these is a reason not to use it. They are the things to have weighed before the first sprint rather than during the third.
Interview follow-up

“React or Next.js?” Reject the framing first — Next.js is React, plus routing, server rendering, bundling and a data model. Then give the actual decision: do you need a server? If the app is behind a login with no SEO or first-paint requirement, a Vite SPA is simpler and has nothing to operate. If content must be indexable, first paint matters commercially, or bundle size is a real constraint, server rendering earns its cost and a framework does it better than an assembled stack. Naming the costs unprompted — two environments, a caching model with a learning curve, genuine lock-in — is what makes this read as judgement rather than preference.

X02

The App Router: files, routes and layouts

The routing is the filesystem, and a small set of reserved filenames each map to a React concept — a page, a layout, a Suspense boundary, an error boundary. Learning those six files is most of learning the App Router.

The reserved files

FileIsRuns
page.tsxThe UI for this route. Makes the segment publicly routableserver
layout.tsxWraps this segment and everything below. Preserved across navigationserver
template.tsxLike a layout, but remounted on every navigationserver
loading.tsxA <Suspense> fallback for this segment, added automaticallyserver
error.tsxAn error boundary for this segment. Must be 'use client'client
not-found.tsxRendered by notFound(), and for unmatched URLsserver
route.tsAn HTTP endpoint instead of UI. Cannot coexist with page.tsxserver
default.tsxFallback for an unmatched parallel route slotserver
global-error.tsxCatches errors in the root layout. Must render <html> and <body>client
A directory only becomes a route when it contains a page.tsx or a route.ts. Everything else — components, tests, utilities — can live inside app/ without being reachable, which is what makes colocation safe. app/ ├── layout.tsx / the root layout (required) ├── page.tsx / ├── loading.tsx applies to / and below ├── error.tsx ├── not-found.tsx │ ├── (marketing)/ a ROUTE GROUP — │ ├── layout.tsx not in the URL │ ├── about/page.tsx /about │ └── pricing/page.tsx /pricing │ ├── (app)/ │ ├── layout.tsx a different shell │ ├── dashboard/ │ │ ├── page.tsx /dashboard │ │ ├── loading.tsx │ │ └── _components/ underscore: private, never a route │ │ └── Chart.tsx │ └── settings/ │ ├── layout.tsx nested layout (tabs) │ ├── page.tsx /settings │ └── billing/page.tsx /settings/billing │ ├── posts/ │ ├── page.tsx /posts │ └── [id]/ │ ├── page.tsx /posts/anything dynamic │ └── edit/page.tsx /posts/anything/edit │ ├── docs/[...slug]/page.tsx /docs/a/b/c catch-all ├── shop/[[...filters]]/page.tsx /shop and /shop/a/b optional │ └── api/posts/route.ts /api/posts an endpoint

Layouts

javascript · app/layout.tsx — the root layout is required
import './globals.css';

export const metadata = {
  title: { template: '%s · Quill', default: 'Quill' },
  description: 'A collaborative notebook',
};

// The ROOT layout must render <html> and <body>. It is the only one
// that does.
export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <Providers>{children}</Providers>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

// A nested layout — app/(app)/settings/layout.tsx
export default function SettingsLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <div className="settings">
      <nav>
        <Link href="/settings">Profile</Link>
        <Link href="/settings/billing">Billing</Link>
      </nav>
      <main>{children}</main>
    </div>
  );
}
Layouts do not re-render on navigation, and that is the point

Navigating from /settings to /settings/billing replaces only the page; the settings layout keeps its DOM, its scroll position and any client state inside it. That is what makes a sidebar with a scroll position or an open accordion survive navigation. The consequence people find surprising is that a layout cannot read the current pathname or the route params — it is not re-rendered when they change. Reading them requires a Client Component using usePathname(), or a template.tsx, which is remounted every navigation.

Dynamic segments

javascript · params and searchParams are async in Next.js 15
// app/posts/[id]/page.tsx
export default async function Post({ params, searchParams }) {
  // Both are PROMISES since Next.js 15. Accessing them without await is
  // a build-time error, and the codemod that fixed this on upgrade is
  // the change most teams noticed first.
  const { id } = await params;
  const { page = '1' } = await searchParams;

  const post = await getPost(id);
  if (!post) notFound();              // renders the nearest not-found.tsx

  return <Article post={post} page={Number(page)} />;
}

// Catch-all:  app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx   →  slug: string[]
// /docs/a/b/c  →  { slug: ['a', 'b', 'c'] }

// Optional catch-all: app/shop/[[...filters]]/page.tsx
// /shop        →  { filters: undefined }
// /shop/red/xl →  { filters: ['red', 'xl'] }

// Pre-rendering the known ones at build time:
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany({ select: { id: true } });
  return posts.map(p => ({ id: p.id }));       // strings only
}

// What happens for an id NOT in that list:
export const dynamicParams = true;   // default: render on demand, cache
// export const dynamicParams = false;  // 404 instead — for a fixed set
Reading searchParams makes the page dynamic

A page that awaits searchParams, or calls cookies() or headers(), cannot be statically generated — the answer depends on the request, so Next.js opts the route into dynamic rendering. That is correct, and it surprises people who find their marketing page suddenly rendering per request because a component three levels down read a cookie. Keep request-dependent reads in a small Suspense-wrapped child so only that part is dynamic, which with Partial Prerendering becomes the whole strategy (X05).

Navigation

javascript · Link, and the hooks
import Link from 'next/link';

// Renders a real <a>, so middle-click, open-in-new-tab and crawling all
// work. It also PREFETCHES: in production, the route's payload is
// fetched when the link enters the viewport.
<Link href="/posts/1">Read</Link>
<Link href="/posts/1" prefetch={false}>Read</Link>   // opt out
<Link href="/posts/1" replace scroll={false}>…</Link>

// Programmatic navigation — CLIENT COMPONENTS ONLY
'use client';
import { useRouter, usePathname, useSearchParams, useParams } from 'next/navigation';

const router = useRouter();
router.push('/dashboard');
router.replace('/login');        // no history entry
router.back();
router.refresh();                // re-fetch the server components for
                                 // the current route, keeping client state

const pathname = usePathname();          // '/posts/1'
const params = useParams();              // { id: '1' }
const searchParams = useSearchParams();  // a ReadonlyURLSearchParams

// From a SERVER component, redirect instead:
import { redirect, permanentRedirect, notFound } from 'next/navigation';
redirect('/login');              // 307, and it THROWS — put it last (N05)
useSearchParams opts the whole route into client rendering

It reads a value that only exists at request time, so any component using it must be a Client Component and must be wrapped in <Suspense> — without the boundary, Next.js fails the build with “useSearchParams should be wrapped in a suspense boundary”. The reason is that during static generation there are no search params, so the component has to be deferred to the client. Wrapping just that component keeps the rest of the page static; putting it at the top of a layout makes the entire application dynamic.

Loading and error files

javascript · what they compile to
// app/dashboard/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return <DashboardSkeleton />;
}
// Next.js wraps the segment:  <Suspense fallback={<Loading />}><Page /></Suspense>
// So the layout renders IMMEDIATELY and the page streams in (R15, X05).

// app/dashboard/error.tsx — must be a client component, because an
// error boundary needs componentDidCatch
'use client';

export default function Error({ error, reset }) {
  useEffect(() => { reportError(error); }, [error]);

  return (
    <div role="alert">
      <h2>Something went wrong</h2>
      {/* In production `error.message` is REDACTED to avoid leaking
          server details; `error.digest` is a hash you can match against
          your server logs. */}
      <p>Reference: {error.digest}</p>
      <button onClick={() => reset()}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  );
}

// error.tsx catches errors in its segment and BELOW — but NOT in its
// own layout, because the boundary is rendered inside that layout.
// Catching a root layout error needs app/global-error.tsx.

Route groups, parallel and intercepting routes

javascript · the three advanced conventions
// ── ROUTE GROUPS: (folder) ───────────────────────────────────────────
// Organise files and apply different layouts without affecting the URL.
// app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx  →  /about
// app/(app)/dashboard/page.tsx    →  /dashboard
// Each group can have its own layout.tsx, which is the usual reason.

// ── PARALLEL ROUTES: @slot ───────────────────────────────────────────
// Render several independent subtrees in one layout, each with its own
// loading and error states.
// app/dashboard/@analytics/page.tsx
// app/dashboard/@team/page.tsx
export default function Layout({ children, analytics, team }) {
  return (
    <>
      {children}
      <div className="grid">{analytics}{team}</div>
    </>
  );
}
// Each slot streams separately — one slow panel does not block the
// other. A slot needs default.tsx for URLs where it has no match.

// ── INTERCEPTING ROUTES: (.)folder ───────────────────────────────────
// Show a route in a modal when navigated to from within the app, and as
// a full page on direct load or refresh. This is the photo-in-a-modal
// pattern, and it is genuinely hard to build by hand.
// app/feed/page.tsx
// app/feed/@modal/(.)photo/[id]/page.tsx   ← intercepts /photo/[id]
// app/photo/[id]/page.tsx                  ← the real page
//
//   (.)  same level      (..)  one up
//   (..)(..)  two up     (...)  from the app root
Colocation is the feature that makes app/ pleasant

Because only page.tsx and route.ts create routes, everything else can live beside them — components, tests, helper functions, the SQL for that page. A folder prefixed with an underscore (_components) is explicitly private and never routable even if it somehow contained a page file. That means a feature's code lives in one directory rather than being scattered across components/, hooks/, lib/ and pages/, and deleting a feature is deleting a folder.

Interview follow-up

“What is the difference between a layout and a template in Next.js?” A layout persists across navigations within its segment — its DOM, its state and its scroll position survive, which is what makes a sidebar keep its position — while a template is remounted on every navigation, so its state resets and its effects re-run. The consequence worth volunteering is that a layout therefore cannot react to the current path or params, because it is not re-rendered when they change; reading those requires a Client Component with usePathname. Templates exist for the cases where the reset is what you want: per-route enter animations, or an analytics effect that must fire on every navigation.

X03

Server and Client Components in practice
