N04 covered the model. This chapter is the day-to-day: where to put the boundary, the errors you will hit in the first week, how to use a provider without turning the whole app into a Client Component, and the mistakes that quietly cost you the entire benefit.

The default, and how to move the boundary down

Everything in app/ is a Server Component until a file says 'use client'. The skill is keeping that marker as low in the tree as possible. The instinct that ruins it: app/layout.tsx 'use client' ← needed a theme provider → EVERY component below is now client code. The whole app ships. The benefit is gone, and the complexity of two environments remains. The fix is almost always the children pattern (N04): the client component receives server-rendered content rather than importing it. app/layout.tsx server └─ <Providers> 'use client' └─ {children} still server A practical ordering when you are unsure: 1 write it as a Server Component 2 hit an error — useState, onClick, useEffect, a browser API 3 extract only that piece into a 'use client' file 4 pass it the data it needs as props Step 3 is where the discipline is. Extracting the button is right; marking the page is the shortcut that costs the benefit.

The errors you will hit

ErrorCauseFix
useState only works in a Client ComponentState in a Server Component'use client' on the smallest piece that needs it
Event handlers cannot be passed to Client Component propsAn onClick crossing the boundaryMove the handler into the client component; pass data, not functions
Functions cannot be passed directlyAny non-serialisable propPass primitives, or a Server Function (N05)
You're importing a component that needs useStateA client-only library imported into a Server ComponentWrap it in a 'use client' file of your own
window is not definedA browser API at module scope, or during renderMove it into an effect, or dynamic(..., { ssr: false })
useSearchParams should be wrapped in a suspense boundaryRequest-time data in a statically rendered routeWrap just that component in <Suspense> (X02)
Hydration failedServer and client rendered differentlyW07 — usually time, randomness, or localStorage

Providers, without the cascade

javascript · app/providers.tsx
'use client';

import { ThemeProvider } from 'next-themes';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useState } from 'react';

export function Providers({ children }) {
  // A NEW QueryClient per component instance, created lazily. A module-
  // level client would be shared across every request on the server —
  // one user's cached data served to another (J02). This is the single
  // most dangerous SSR bug there is.
  const [queryClient] = useState(() => new QueryClient({
    defaultOptions: { queries: { staleTime: 60_000 } },
  }));

  return (
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <ThemeProvider attribute="class">{children}</ThemeProvider>
    </QueryClientProvider>
  );
}
javascript · app/layout.tsx — stays a Server Component
import { Providers } from './providers';

export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        {/* Providers is a client component, but `children` was rendered
            on the SERVER and passed in — so every page below remains a
            Server Component. The provider only wraps them. */}
        <Providers>{children}</Providers>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
Module-scope state on the server is shared between users

A module is evaluated once per server process and lives for the lifetime of that process — so a QueryClient, a cache Map, or a “current user” variable at module scope is shared by every concurrent request. In the browser that is per-tab and harmless; on the server it is a cross-request data leak, and it is the most damaging category of bug in server-rendered React. The rule: module scope holds constants, compiled regexes and connection pools. Anything request-specific is created inside a component, a request handler, or React's cache().

Keeping server-only code on the server

javascript · make the mistake a build error
// lib/db.ts
import 'server-only';   // ← a package whose only job is to fail the
                        //   build if this file ends up in a client bundle

import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';
export const db = new PrismaClient();

// Now an accidental import from a 'use client' file is a BUILD ERROR
// rather than a runtime failure — or worse, a database URL shipped to
// the browser. It costs one line and it is worth putting in every file
// that touches secrets, the database, or the filesystem.

// The mirror image, for code that must NOT run on the server:
import 'client-only';

// And the environment-variable rule, which is the other half:
process.env.DATABASE_URL          // server only — undefined on the client
process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL   // inlined into the bundle at BUILD time
// NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are PUBLIC. They are string-replaced into the
// JavaScript, so anyone can read them. Never put a secret behind that
// prefix, and remember they are baked at build time — changing one
// requires a rebuild, not just a restart.

Client-only libraries

javascript · three techniques
// 1 · A library that touches window at import time cannot be server-
//     rendered at all. Disable SSR for it.
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic';

const Map = dynamic(() => import('./Map'), {
  ssr: false,                     // never rendered on the server
  loading: () => <MapSkeleton />, // and a placeholder while it loads
});
// NOTE: ssr: false is only allowed in a CLIENT component. In a Server
// Component it is a build error — wrap it in a small client file.

// 2 · A library that only needs the browser at RUNTIME can render on
//     the server and initialise after mount:
'use client';
export function Editor() {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    let editor;
    import('@editor/lib').then(({ create }) => {
      editor = create(ref.current);
    });
    return () => editor?.destroy();
  }, []);
  return <div ref={ref} />;
}

// 3 · A third-party component with no 'use client' of its own. Wrap it:
// components/Carousel.tsx
'use client';
export { Carousel } from 'some-carousel-library';
// One line, and now Server Components can import YOUR file.

The composition patterns

javascript · the four that cover almost everything
// 1 · SERVER DATA → CLIENT INTERACTIVITY
//     Fetch on the server, hand the result to a small client island.
export default async function Page() {
  const products = await getProducts();      // server
  return <ProductFilter products={products} />;   // 'use client'
}

// 2 · CLIENT SHELL → SERVER CONTENT
//     The interactive wrapper is client; what it wraps is not.
<Accordion>                    {/* 'use client' */}
  <ServerRenderedDetails />    {/* server — passed as children */}
</Accordion>

// 3 · SERVER FUNCTION AS A PROP
//     The one non-serialisable value that MAY cross the boundary.
import { deleteItem } from './actions';       // 'use server'
<DeleteButton onDelete={deleteItem} />        // 'use client'

// 4 · PROMISE AS A PROP  (N03)
//     Start the request on the server; let the client suspend on it.
export default function Page() {
  const commentsPromise = getComments();      // NOT awaited
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
      <Comments promise={commentsPromise} />  {/* use() on the client */}
    </Suspense>
  );
}

Auditing the boundary

finding out what is actually shipping
$ npx @next/bundle-analyzer      # or ANALYZE=true next build

Route (app)                         Size     First Load JS
┌ ○ /                               1.2 kB        94.3 kB
├ ○ /about                          182 B         88.1 kB
├ ƒ /dashboard                      48.7 kB      142 kB   ← look here
└ ● /posts/[id]                     2.1 kB        91.4 kB
+ First Load JS shared by all                     87.9 kB

○  Static     prerendered at build time
●  SSG        prerendered with generateStaticParams
ƒ  Dynamic    server-rendered on demand

# Reading this:
#
#   · "shared by all" is the framework plus your root layout's client
#     code. If it grows, something got marked 'use client' too high.
#
#   · a route much larger than its neighbours has a client boundary
#     that is too wide, or a heavy library inside one.
#
#   · a route showing ƒ that you expected to be ○ has picked up a
#     dynamic API — cookies(), headers(), searchParams — somewhere
#     below it (X05).

$ grep -rl "use client" app/ | wc -l
# A rough health check. A hundred of them in a fifty-route app is
# normal. Five, all in layouts, means the boundary is in the wrong place.
The two mistakes that cost the whole benefit

Marking a layout 'use client' — usually to add a provider or read the pathname — which makes every page below it client code. Use the children pattern, or extract just the interactive bit. And fetching on the client out of habit: a useQuery in a Client Component inside a server-rendered page reintroduces exactly the waterfall RSC removed, because the request cannot start until the bundle has downloaded and hydrated. Both look harmless in review and are visible immediately in the bundle analyser, which is why it belongs in CI.

Interview follow-up

“Where do you put 'use client'?” As low in the tree as possible, because the directive marks a boundary — everything it imports transitively also ships. Then give the technique that makes that achievable: a Client Component cannot import a Server Component, but it can receive one as children, which is how a provider or an interactive shell stays on the client while its contents stay on the server. The failure mode worth naming is marking the root layout 'use client' to add a theme provider, which quietly converts the entire application to client rendering while keeping every bit of RSC's complexity.

X04

Data fetching and the caching model

This is the part of Next.js that confuses everyone, and the confusion is earned: there are four independent caches with different lifetimes, different invalidation, and defaults that changed in version 15. Learning them as four named things with one sentence each is the fastest route out.

Fetching is just await

javascript · in the component, at any depth
// No hook, no effect, no loading state. It runs on the server, so it
// can talk to the database directly — there is no API layer in between
// unless you want one.
export default async function Page({ params }) {
  const { id } = await params;

  const post = await db.post.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  if (!post) notFound();

  return <Article post={post} />;
}

// PARALLEL, not sequential. Two awaits in a row are two round trips;
// Promise.all is one wait (R08).
const [user, posts, stats] = await Promise.all([
  getUser(id), getPosts(id), getStats(id),
]);

// Fetching further down the tree is fine and often better — the
// component that needs the data asks for it, and Suspense lets it
// stream independently (X05):
export default async function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />
      <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
        <Feed />      {/* awaits its own data */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The four caches

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 1 · REQUEST MEMOIZATION React, per request │ │ Two identical fetches during ONE render → one request. │ │ Lifetime: the render. Not configurable. Always on. │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 2 · DATA CACHE Next.js, across requests │ │ Persists fetch results on the server, across users and │ │ deploys. Opt-IN since Next 15. │ │ Invalidated by: revalidate, revalidateTag, revalidatePath │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 3 · FULL ROUTE CACHE Next.js, build/request │ │ The rendered HTML and RSC payload for a static route. │ │ Invalidated by: a redeploy, or revalidation │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 4 · ROUTER CACHE the browser, in memory │ │ Visited route payloads, so Back is instant. │ │ Lifetime: the session. Cleared by router.refresh(), a │ │ Server Function, or a full reload. │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ They are independent. A stale page can come from any one of them, and "I revalidated and it did not update" is nearly always the wrong layer — most often the client Router Cache, which revalidatePath on the server does not touch until the next navigation.
The defaults changed in Next.js 15, and most tutorials predate it

In 14, fetch was cached indefinitely by default, GET Route Handlers were cached, and the client Router Cache held page segments for 30 seconds. All three surprised people by serving stale data. In 15 the defaults inverted: fetch is no-store, GET handlers are not cached, and the Router Cache's staleTime for page segments is 0. Caching is now opt-in, which is far less surprising — and it means any article showing cache: 'no-store' as the fix for staleness is describing a version you are probably not running.

1 · Request memoization

javascript · why prop drilling data is unnecessary
// Three components in one render, all asking for the same user.
async function Layout()  { const u = await getUser(id); … }
async function Header()  { const u = await getUser(id); … }
async function Sidebar() { const u = await getUser(id); … }

// With fetch: automatic. React dedupes identical (url, options) pairs
// for the duration of the render.
async function getUser(id) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${id}`);
  return res.json();
}                                          // → ONE request

// With a database client or any non-fetch source: wrap it in React's
// cache(), which memoises by arguments for the same render pass.
import { cache } from 'react';

export const getUser = cache(async (id) => {
  return db.user.findUnique({ where: { id } });
});                                        // → ONE query

// This is why you should NOT thread data down through props "to avoid
// refetching". Each component asking for what it needs is clearer, and
// the deduplication makes it free.

2 · The Data Cache

javascript · opting in, and choosing how it expires
// Not cached — the Next.js 15 default.
await fetch(url);

// Cached indefinitely, until revalidated.
await fetch(url, { cache: 'force-cache' });

// Time-based: serve from cache for 60s, then revalidate in the
// background (stale-while-revalidate).
await fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } });

// TAGGED — the important one. The tag describes the DATA, so a mutation
// can invalidate it without knowing which pages read it.
await fetch(url, { next: { tags: ['posts', `post:${id}`] } });

// For anything that is not fetch — a database, an SDK, a file read:
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

export const getPopularPosts = unstable_cache(
  async () => db.post.findMany({ orderBy: { views: 'desc' }, take: 10 }),
  ['popular-posts'],                    // the cache key parts
  { revalidate: 300, tags: ['posts'] },
);

// Then, from a Server Function (N05):
revalidateTag('posts');        // every entry tagged 'posts', everywhere
revalidateTag(`post:${id}`);   // one post
revalidatePath('/posts');      // by route instead

// cache() vs unstable_cache(): cache() is PER REQUEST (deduplication);
// unstable_cache() is ACROSS requests (a real cache). Confusing them is
// common — the first does not survive the response.
Tag by data, not by route

revalidatePath('/posts') requires the mutation to know every page that displays posts — the index, the author page, the sidebar on the home page, the RSS feed. Miss one and it serves stale content indefinitely. revalidateTag('posts') requires only that each fetch declares what it reads, which is local information the fetch already has. Tag granularly (posts plus post:${id}) so a single edit does not invalidate the whole index, and reserve revalidatePath for cases where the route genuinely is the unit.

3 · The Full Route Cache

At build time, Next.js renders every route it can and stores the HTML and the RSC payload. A request for such a route is a file read. A route is static unless something makes it dynamic. The things that make it dynamic: · cookies(), headers(), draftMode() · reading searchParams in a page · connection() · an uncached fetch (which, since 15, is the default) · export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' Forcing it, per route: export const dynamic = 'force-static'; // ignore dynamic APIs export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'; // never cache export const dynamic = 'error'; // FAIL THE BUILD if this // route cannot be static export const revalidate = 3600; // ISR: regenerate hourly export const fetchCache = 'default-cache'; dynamic = 'error' is underused and excellent: it turns "a component someone added three levels down reads a cookie, so the marketing page now renders per request" from an invisible regression into a failed build.

4 · The Router Cache

javascript · the one that causes "it did not update"
// The browser keeps RSC payloads for routes you have visited, so Back
// is instant and prefetched links render without a round trip.
//
// Next.js 15 defaults:
//   page segments   staleTime 0    → refetched on navigation
//   layouts         cached         → not refetched (they rarely change)
//   back/forward    always from cache, for instant history navigation

// Configurable:
// next.config.js
experimental: {
  staleTimes: { dynamic: 30, static: 180 },
}

// Clearing it from the client:
router.refresh();      // refetch the current route's server components,
                       // KEEPING client state and scroll position

// A Server Function that calls revalidatePath/Tag also returns a fresh
// payload, so the router cache updates in the same round trip (N05) —
// which is why mutations through actions do not need a manual refresh.

// The diagnosis, when data looks stale:
//   1 · is it the Data Cache?        → revalidateTag / revalidatePath
//   2 · is it the Full Route Cache?  → revalidate, or a redeploy
//   3 · is it the Router Cache?      → router.refresh(), or navigate away
//   4 · is it a CDN in front?        → check the Cache-Control headers
// Test with a hard reload in an incognito window: that eliminates 3 and
// tells you whether the problem is on the server or the client.

Putting it together

DataStrategy
Marketing copy from a CMSrevalidate: 3600 plus a webhook calling revalidateTag on publish
A product catalogueStatic with generateStaticParams, tagged, revalidated on change
A user's dashboardDynamic — it reads cookies, so caching is neither possible nor wanted
A price that changes hourlyrevalidate: 3600; the first request after expiry serves stale and refreshes behind it
A live stock levelUncached, in a Suspense boundary so the rest of the page is still static (X05)
Search resultsDynamic by definition — it reads searchParams
An expensive reportunstable_cache with a long revalidate and an explicit tag

The mistakes

Three more that cost real performance

Sequential awaits that could be Promise.all — two 200 ms queries become 400 ms for no reason. Fetching in a Client Component inside a server-rendered page, which reintroduces the waterfall RSC removed: the request cannot start until the bundle downloads and hydrates. And one uncached fetch in a shared layout, which makes every route beneath it dynamic — the most common cause of “why is nothing static any more”, and exactly what dynamic = 'error' catches.

Where this is heading

The 'use cache' direction

The framework is moving toward an explicit 'use cache' directive that marks a function, component or file as cacheable, with cacheLife and cacheTag to configure it — replacing the implicit coupling between “does this route use a dynamic API” and “is it cached”. It is behind a flag at the time of writing and the details are still moving, so build against the model in this chapter and treat the directive as the direction rather than the current API. The underlying concepts — request deduplication, a persistent data cache, tag-based invalidation — are stable and transfer either way.

Interview follow-up

“Explain Next.js caching.” Name the four layers with one sentence each: request memoization dedupes identical fetches within a single render; the Data Cache persists fetch results across requests and is opt-in since 15; the Full Route Cache stores rendered static routes; and the client Router Cache keeps visited payloads so Back is instant. Then add the two things that show practical experience — that the defaults inverted in version 15, so most articles you will find describe the opposite behaviour; and that “I revalidated and it did not update” is usually the client Router Cache, which a server-side revalidateTag does not touch until the next navigation.

X05

Rendering strategies: static, dynamic, ISR and streaming

The same component tree can be turned into HTML at four different moments, and the choice is per route rather than per application. Getting it right is the largest single performance lever in a Next.js app — and the newest option, partial prerendering, removes the need to choose for the whole page at all.

The four moments

STATIC rendered at build time, served as a file fastest possible. Content is fixed until the next deploy or revalidation. → marketing, docs, blog posts ISR static, plus regenerate after N seconds the first request after expiry serves the stale copy and triggers a refresh behind it, so nobody waits. → catalogues, CMS content, anything with a tolerable staleness window DYNAMIC rendered per request required when the output depends on cookies, headers or search params. → dashboards, personalised pages, search PPR static shell + dynamic holes, in one response the cached shell streams immediately; the personalised parts stream in behind it. → the answer to "this page is 90% static and 10% personalised, so all of it is dynamic" ┌──────────────── time to first byte ──────────────────────────────┐ │ static ▏ │ │ ISR ▏ │ │ PPR ▏▏▏ shell instant, holes stream │ │ dynamic ████████████ waits for the slowest query │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Static, and pre-rendering the ids

javascript · app/posts/[slug]/page.tsx
// Which pages to build. Returning [] builds none up front and renders
// each on demand the first time it is requested.
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany({
    where: { published: true },
    select: { slug: true },
  });
  return posts.map(p => ({ slug: p.slug }));   // string values only
}

// What happens for a slug NOT in that list:
export const dynamicParams = true;   // render on demand, then cache
// export const dynamicParams = false;  // 404 — for a genuinely fixed set

export default async function Post({ params }) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const post = await getPost(slug);
  if (!post) notFound();
  return <Article post={post} />;
}

// For a very large catalogue, build the popular ones and let the tail
// render on demand — a 50,000-page build takes hours and most of it is
// never requested.
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const top = await db.post.findMany({
    orderBy: { views: 'desc' }, take: 500, select: { slug: true },
  });
  return top.map(p => ({ slug: p.slug }));
}

ISR

javascript · time-based and on-demand
// Time-based, for the whole route:
export const revalidate = 3600;      // seconds

// Or per fetch, which is finer-grained:
await fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } });

// The behaviour is stale-while-revalidate, and this is the part worth
// understanding:
//
//   t=0     request → build, cache, serve            (fresh)
//   t=30    request → serve from cache               (fresh)
//   t=90    request → serve the STALE copy AND       (stale, refreshing)
//                     regenerate in the background
//   t=91    request → serve the NEW copy             (fresh)
//
// So nobody ever waits for a regeneration. The trade is that the
// request immediately after expiry sees old content.

// ON-DEMAND is usually better than a timer: revalidate when the data
// actually changes, from a webhook or a Server Function.
// app/api/revalidate/route.ts
export async function POST(req) {
  const secret = req.headers.get('x-webhook-secret');
  if (secret !== process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET) {
    return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
  }
  const { slug } = await req.json();
  revalidateTag(`post:${slug}`);
  return Response.json({ revalidated: true });
}
// A CMS publish now updates the site in seconds, with no polling and
// no arbitrary staleness window.
Prefer on-demand revalidation to a timer

A revalidate: 60 on a page that changes twice a day regenerates it 1,440 times a day for two useful updates, and still shows stale content for up to a minute after each real change. A webhook calling revalidateTag updates it within seconds of the actual edit and does no work in between. Use a timer as a safety net with a long interval — an hour, a day — and let the webhook do the real work, so a missed webhook self-corrects rather than leaving the site stale indefinitely.

Dynamic

javascript · what forces it, and how to contain it
// Any of these anywhere in the route's tree makes the WHOLE route
// dynamic:
import { cookies, headers, draftMode, connection } from 'next/headers';

const store = await cookies();       // async since Next.js 15
const h = await headers();
// …or reading searchParams in a page, or an uncached fetch.

export default async function Dashboard() {
  const session = await getSession();     // reads cookies
  const data = await getUserData(session.userId);
  return <Charts data={data} />;
}

// THE CONTAINMENT PATTERN, which is the important technique here:
// keep the dynamic read in a small child behind Suspense, so the rest
// of the page stays static and streams immediately.
export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <Hero />              {/* static */}
      <Features />          {/* static */}

      <Suspense fallback={<GreetingSkeleton />}>
        <PersonalGreeting />  {/* reads cookies — only THIS is dynamic */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}
// With PPR enabled this is exactly the shape that produces a cached
// shell with a streamed hole.

Streaming

javascript · one slow query should not block the page
// WITHOUT streaming: the whole page waits for the slowest await.
export default async function Page() {
  const user = await getUser();        //  50ms
  const feed = await getFeed();        // 800ms  ← everyone waits
  const recs = await getRecs();        // 400ms
  return <>…</>;                       // TTFB ≈ 1250ms
}

// WITH streaming: the shell goes out immediately and each region
// arrives when it is ready.
export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />                       {/* instant */}

      <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
        <Feed />                       {/* awaits inside */}
      </Suspense>

      <Suspense fallback={<RecsSkeleton />}>
        <Recommendations />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}
// TTFB ≈ 50ms. Feed appears at 800ms, recommendations at 400ms —
// independently, in whatever order they finish.

// loading.tsx does this automatically for a whole segment:
// app/dashboard/loading.tsx  →  <Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>

// The parallel-vs-sequential rule still applies INSIDE a boundary:
async function Feed() {
  const [posts, authors] = await Promise.all([getPosts(), getAuthors()]);
  //     ^ not two sequential awaits
}
Streaming does not make anything faster — it changes what waits

The slow query still takes 800 ms. What changes is that the user sees the header, the navigation and the page structure at 50 ms instead of staring at a white screen for 1.25 seconds. That is a large perceived-performance win and it is not a real one: total time to complete content is the same or slightly worse. So streaming is not a substitute for fixing a slow query — and a page split into eight boundaries that all pop in at different moments can feel worse than one that arrives at once. Put boundaries where the content is genuinely independent, and fix the query.

Partial prerendering

The problem PPR solves: one dynamic read makes the whole route dynamic, so a page that is 95% marketing copy and 5% "Hi, Masud" is rendered from scratch on every request. PPR splits the response: build time render everything that can be static, stopping at each Suspense boundary that contains a dynamic read. Store that shell. request serve the cached shell immediately, then stream the dynamic holes into it on the same connection. ┌── one HTTP response ─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ <nav> … </nav> ← from the cache, at t=0 │ │ <h1>Products</h1> ← from the cache │ │ <div>[cart skeleton]</div> ← placeholder │ │ … │ │ <template><CartCount count={3} /></template> ← at t=120ms │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Enabling it (experimental at the time of writing): // next.config.js experimental: { ppr: 'incremental' } // app/products/page.tsx export const experimental_ppr = true; The mental shift: stop asking "is this page static or dynamic" and start asking "which PARTS of it are". The Suspense boundary becomes the unit, which is the same boundary you would already draw for streaming.

Choosing

PageStrategyWhy
Landing, docs, aboutStaticSame for everyone; changes on deploy
Blog, CMS contentISR + webhookStatic speed, updated when the editor publishes
Product page with live stockPPR, or static + a client islandThe description is static; the stock is not
Search resultsDynamicDepends entirely on searchParams
User dashboardDynamic + streamingPer-user; stream the slow panels
CheckoutDynamic, uncachedMust never serve another user's state
An admin tool behind a loginDynamic, or a client SPANo SEO, no first-paint value — the simplest thing wins
Check what you actually got, in the build output

next build prints a symbol per route: ○ static, ● prerendered with params, ƒ dynamic, ◐ partially prerendered. A route you expected to be ○ showing ƒ has picked up a dynamic API somewhere in its tree, often three components down and often accidentally. Read that table on every build, and add export const dynamic = 'error' to the routes that must stay static so the regression fails CI rather than quietly doubling your server cost.

Interview follow-up

“When would you use ISR over SSR?” When the content is the same for every user and a bounded staleness window is acceptable — a catalogue, a blog, a docs site. ISR gives static-file performance with a refresh path, and the refresh is stale-while-revalidate so no user ever waits for the regeneration. Then improve the answer twice: prefer on-demand revalidation via a webhook over a timer, because a timer regenerates constantly and is still stale after a real edit; and note that the static-or-dynamic choice is being replaced by partial prerendering, where a cached shell streams immediately and only the genuinely request-dependent parts are rendered per request.

X06

Route Handlers: the API layer

A route.ts file exports functions named after HTTP methods and receives a standard Request, returning a standard Response. It is the escape hatch for everything Server Components and Server Functions cannot do — webhooks, public APIs, file downloads, anything a non-React client calls.

The shape

javascript · app/api/posts/route.ts
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import { z } from 'zod';

// Web-standard Request and Response. No req/res objects, no framework
// abstraction — the same API a Service Worker or Deno would give you.
export async function GET(request) {
  const { searchParams } = new URL(request.url);
  const page = Number(searchParams.get('page') ?? '1');

  const posts = await db.post.findMany({
    take: 20, skip: (page - 1) * 20,
  });

  return Response.json({ posts, page });
}

const CreatePost = z.object({
  title: z.string().trim().min(1).max(200),
  body: z.string().max(50_000),
});

export async function POST(request) {
  // AUTHENTICATE. A route handler is a public endpoint; nothing about
  // being in your app protects it.
  const session = await auth();
  if (!session) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Unauthorized' }, { status: 401 });
  }

  // VALIDATE. Bound the body first, or a client can send gigabytes.
  let body;
  try {
    body = await request.json();
  } catch {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Invalid JSON' }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const parsed = CreatePost.safeParse(body);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: 'Validation failed', fields: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors },
      { status: 422 },
    );
  }

  const post = await db.post.create({
    data: { ...parsed.data, authorId: session.userId },
  });

  revalidateTag('posts');     // the RSC cache is now stale (X04)

  return Response.json(post, {
    status: 201,
    headers: { Location: `/api/posts/${post.id}` },
  });
}

// Every method is a named export. Anything not exported returns 405
// automatically.
export async function PATCH(request) { … }
export async function DELETE(request) { … }
export async function OPTIONS() { … }
route.ts and page.tsx cannot coexist

A segment is either UI or an endpoint, not both — putting both files in one directory is a build error. That is why API routes conventionally live under app/api/, but the location is a convention rather than a rule: app/sitemap.xml/route.ts serving /sitemap.xml is perfectly valid and often the tidiest place for it.

When to use one, and when not to

Use a Route HandlerDo not
Webhooks — Stripe, GitHub, a CMSTo fetch data for your own Server Component — call the function directly (X04)
A public API for mobile apps or third partiesFor a mutation from your own UI — use a Server Function (N05)
File downloads, generated images, PDFsAs a wrapper around a single database query your page already makes
OAuth callbacks and auth endpointsBecause “that is how APIs work” — the extra hop is real cost
Anything needing a method other than POST
Streaming responses, SSE
Endpoints with a stable, versioned contract

Dynamic segments, cookies and headers

javascript · app/api/posts/[id]/route.ts
export async function GET(request, { params }) {
  const { id } = await params;          // async since Next.js 15 (X02)

  const post = await db.post.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  if (!post) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Not found' }, { status: 404 });
  }
  return Response.json(post);
}

// Cookies and headers, from next/headers or from the Request itself:
import { cookies, headers } from 'next/headers';

export async function GET(request) {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const theme = cookieStore.get('theme')?.value;

  const h = await headers();
  const ua = h.get('user-agent');

  // Or straight from the standard Request:
  const auth = request.headers.get('authorization');

  // Setting a cookie needs NextResponse:
  const res = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
  res.cookies.set('theme', 'dark', {
    httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge: 31536000,
  });
  return res;
}

Caching

javascript · not cached by default since Next.js 15
// In Next 14 a GET handler with no dynamic APIs was cached at build
// time, which surprised people whose "live" endpoint returned the same
// value forever. In 15 it is dynamic by default.

// Opt in explicitly:
export const dynamic = 'force-static';
export const revalidate = 3600;

// Or set the headers yourself, which is clearer for an endpoint a CDN
// will also see:
export async function GET() {
  const data = await getExpensiveThing();
  return Response.json(data, {
    headers: {
      'Cache-Control': 'public, s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=86400',
    },
  });
}

// A handler that reads cookies, headers or the request URL's search
// params is dynamic regardless — it cannot be cached, because the
// answer depends on the request.

Streaming and non-JSON responses

javascript · the cases that need a Route Handler
// Server-sent events — a long-lived response the client reads
// incrementally.
export async function GET() {
  const encoder = new TextEncoder();

  const stream = new ReadableStream({
    async start(controller) {
      const unsubscribe = events.subscribe((event) => {
        controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(`data: ${JSON.stringify(event)}\n\n`));
      });
      // Clean up when the client disconnects, or the subscription leaks
      // for the lifetime of the process.
      request.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => {
        unsubscribe();
        controller.close();
      });
    },
  });

  return new Response(stream, {
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream',
      'Cache-Control': 'no-cache, no-transform',
      Connection: 'keep-alive',
    },
  });
}

// A generated file:
export async function GET() {
  const pdf = await renderInvoice(id);
  return new Response(pdf, {
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/pdf',
      'Content-Disposition': 'attachment; filename="invoice.pdf"',
    },
  });
}

// An LLM-style token stream, piping an upstream response straight
// through without buffering it:
export async function POST(req) {
  const upstream = await fetch(LLM_URL, { … });
  return new Response(upstream.body, {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain; charset=utf-8' },
  });
}

Webhooks

javascript · app/api/webhooks/stripe/route.ts
export async function POST(request) {
  // 1 · The RAW body is required for signature verification. Parsing it
  //     as JSON first and re-stringifying will NOT match, because key
  //     order and whitespace change. This is the classic webhook bug.
  const payload = await request.text();
  const signature = request.headers.get('stripe-signature');

  let event;
  try {
    event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(
      payload, signature, process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET,
    );
  } catch (err) {
    // Never process an unverified webhook. The endpoint is public.
    return new Response('Invalid signature', { status: 400 });
  }

  // 2 · IDEMPOTENCY. Providers retry on any non-2xx, and occasionally
  //     deliver twice on success. Record the event id and ignore
  //     duplicates, in the same transaction as the effect.
  const inserted = await db.webhookEvent.createMany({
    data: { id: event.id }, skipDuplicates: true,
  });
  if (inserted.count === 0) return new Response('Already processed');

  // 3 · Acknowledge FAST. Long work here causes the provider to time
  //     out and retry, so queue it rather than doing it inline.
  switch (event.type) {
    case 'checkout.session.completed':
      await fulfilOrder(event.data.object);
      break;
  }

  revalidateTag('orders');
  return new Response('ok');
}

// Verify the raw body is genuinely raw: middleware or a proxy that
// rewrites the request can break the signature in ways that only
// reproduce in production.
Three webhook rules, all learned the hard way

Verify the signature against the raw body — reserialising JSON changes the bytes and the signature will never match. Be idempotent, because every provider retries and occasionally double-delivers; a unique constraint on the event id claimed in the same transaction as the effect is the whole mechanism. And respond quickly: providers time out in seconds and retry, so a handler that does thirty seconds of work turns one event into five. Queue the work and return 200.

CORS, for an endpoint others call

javascript
const ALLOWED = new Set(['https://app.example.com']);

function corsHeaders(origin) {
  // An ALLOWLIST. Reflecting whatever Origin arrives, together with
  // credentials, lets any site call your API as a logged-in user.
  if (!ALLOWED.has(origin)) return {};
  return {
    'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': origin,
    'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials': 'true',
    'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'GET, POST, OPTIONS',
    'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': 'Content-Type, Authorization',
    Vary: 'Origin',        // or a shared cache serves one origin's
  };                       // response to another
}

export async function OPTIONS(request) {
  return new Response(null, {
    status: 204,
    headers: corsHeaders(request.headers.get('origin')),
  });
}

export async function GET(request) {
  const data = await getData();
  return Response.json(data, {
    headers: corsHeaders(request.headers.get('origin')),
  });
}
Interview follow-up

“When would you use a Route Handler rather than a Server Function?” When the caller is not your own React code. Server Functions are RPC with a build-generated id, always POST, unversioned, and they change identity on every deploy — which is fine for your UI's mutations and unusable for anything external. Route Handlers give you a stable URL, real HTTP methods, cache headers and streaming, so webhooks, public APIs, file downloads and OAuth callbacks all belong there. The anti-pattern worth naming is the opposite direction: a Server Component fetching from your own Route Handler, which adds a network hop and a serialisation round trip to call a function that was already on the same machine.

X07

Server Actions: mutations, revalidation and security

N05 covered what Server Functions are and how they work. This chapter is the Next.js production version: the file layout, the validation pipeline, the revalidation that makes the UI update, redirects, cookies — and the security model, which is the part people get wrong in ways that are genuinely dangerous.

The complete shape

javascript · app/posts/actions.ts
'use server';

import { z } from 'zod';
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';

const CreatePost = z.object({
  title: z.string().trim().min(1, 'Title is required').max(200),
  body:  z.string().trim().min(1, 'Body is required').max(50_000),
  tags:  z.array(z.string().max(30)).max(10).default([]),
});

export async function createPost(prevState, formData) {
  // 1 · AUTHENTICATE — every action, every time. There is no
  //     inherited protection from where it was imported.
  const session = await auth();
  if (!session) return { error: 'You must be signed in.' };

  // 2 · VALIDATE — formData is attacker-controlled.
  const parsed = CreatePost.safeParse({
    title: formData.get('title'),
    body:  formData.get('body'),
    tags:  formData.getAll('tags'),
  });
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return {
      error: 'Please fix the errors below.',
      fields: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors,
      // Echo the submitted values back so the form is not wiped —
      // the page re-renders on the server and uncontrolled inputs
      // would otherwise lose everything the user typed.
      values: Object.fromEntries(formData),
    };
  }

  // 3 · AUTHORISE — is THIS user allowed to do THIS?
  if (!(await canCreatePost(session.userId))) {
    return { error: 'Your plan does not allow more posts.' };
  }

  // 4 · MUTATE, with errors turned into state rather than crashes.
  let post;
  try {
    post = await db.post.create({
      data: { ...parsed.data, authorId: session.userId },
    });
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.code === 'P2002') return { error: 'That title is already taken.' };
    console.error(err);                       // log the real thing
    return { error: 'Something went wrong. Please try again.' };
  }

  // 5 · REVALIDATE — otherwise the list still shows the old data.
  revalidateTag('posts');

  // 6 · REDIRECT — throws internally, so it must be OUTSIDE try/catch
  //     (see the warning below) and nothing after it runs.
  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`);
}
redirect() inside a try block silently breaks

redirect and notFound work by throwing a special error that the framework catches. A try { … } catch {} around them swallows that error, so the redirect never happens and your catch block reports a failure for an operation that succeeded. Always call them after the try/catch, in the normal flow. Since Next.js 15 redirect in a Server Action issues a 303 so the browser follows with a GET; and note it must be called during the action, not returned as a value.

Wiring it to the form

javascript · app/posts/new/post-form.tsx
'use client';

import { useActionState } from 'react';
import { useFormStatus } from 'react-dom';
import { createPost } from '../actions';

function Submit() {
  // Must be in a CHILD of the form — it reads the nearest form's
  // context, and a component that renders <form> cannot see it (N01).
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();
  return (
    <button disabled={pending}>
      {pending ? 'Publishing…' : 'Publish'}
    </button>
  );
}

export function PostForm() {
  const [state, action] = useActionState(createPost, {});

  return (
    <form action={action}>
      {state.error && <p role="alert" className="err">{state.error}</p>}

      <label htmlFor="title">Title</label>
      <input
        id="title" name="title"
        defaultValue={state.values?.title}
        aria-invalid={!!state.fields?.title}
        aria-describedby={state.fields?.title ? 'title-err' : undefined}
      />
      {state.fields?.title &&
        <p id="title-err" className="err">{state.fields.title[0]}</p>}

      <label htmlFor="body">Body</label>
      <textarea id="body" name="body" defaultValue={state.values?.body} />

      <Submit />
    </form>
  );
}
// This form WORKS WITH JAVASCRIPT DISABLED. The browser posts it,
// the server runs the action, the page re-renders with the errors.
// Progressive enhancement, for free, which is the main reason to use
// a form action rather than an onClick handler.

Passing an id without putting it in the DOM

javascript · bind, and why a hidden input is not enough
// bind prepends arguments. They are serialised into the payload, not
// rendered as form fields:
'use server';
export async function deletePost(id, formData) {
  const session = await auth();
  const post = await db.post.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  // STILL CHECK OWNERSHIP. bind is not a security boundary — the
  // bound value travels through the client and can be tampered with.
  if (post?.authorId !== session?.userId) throw new Error('Forbidden');
  await db.post.delete({ where: { id } });
  revalidateTag('posts');
}

// In the component:
<form action={deletePost.bind(null, post.id)}>
  <button>Delete</button>
</form>

// The alternative is a hidden input, which is equivalent in security
// terms (both are client-supplied) but visible in the HTML:
<form action={deletePost}>
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value={post.id} />
  <button>Delete</button>
</form>

// Inline actions close over server-side variables, which IS a real
// difference — the value never reaches the client at all:
export default async function Page({ params }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  async function publish() {
    'use server';
    // `id` came from the URL on the server; the client cannot alter it.
    // You still authorise, because the URL is also user input.
    await db.post.update({ where: { id }, data: { published: true } });
    revalidatePath(`/posts/${id}`);
  }
  return <form action={publish}><button>Publish</button></form>;
}

The security model

A Server Action is a public HTTP endpoint. The build gives it an opaque id and React posts to it. Anyone who can read your JavaScript bundle can extract that id and POST to it directly, with any body. curl https://you.com/any-page \ -H "Next-Action: 7f9a2e4c…" \ -H "Content-Type: multipart/form-data; …" \ --data-binary @crafted-payload So these are not protections: ✗ the button is only rendered for admins ✗ the action is only imported by an admin page ✗ the id is obfuscated ✗ the argument was bound with .bind() ✗ a Client Component validated the input first Every action does all four, itself: 1 · AUTHENTICATE who is calling? 2 · VALIDATE is the input well-formed and bounded? 3 · AUTHORISE may this user do this to this resource? 4 · RATE LIMIT for anything expensive or abusable The framework gives you one thing for free: Origin/Host checking on the POST, which blocks classic cross-site form CSRF. It gives you nothing else.
Never export a non-action from a 'use server' file

The directive applies to the whole module: every export becomes a callable endpoint. A helper you exported for testing, a constant, a utility that takes a raw SQL fragment — all of them become reachable from the internet. Keep 'use server' files to actions only, put helpers in a separate module, and use import 'server-only' on modules that must never be reachable at all. The mirror-image mistake is equally bad: leaving 'use server' off a file whose functions you pass to client components, which fails loudly rather than silently and is therefore the safer error.

An authorised-action helper

javascript · lib/safe-action.ts — removing the chance to forget
// Writing auth + validation by hand in twenty actions means forgetting
// it in one. Make the safe path the default path.
import 'server-only';

export function authedAction(schema, handler) {
  return async function (prevState, formData) {
    const session = await auth();
    if (!session) return { error: 'Not signed in.' };

    const input = Object.fromEntries(formData);
    const parsed = schema.safeParse(input);
    if (!parsed.success) {
      return {
        error: 'Please fix the errors below.',
        fields: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors,
        values: input,
      };
    }

    const { allowed, retryAfter } = await rateLimit(
      `action:${session.userId}`, { limit: 20, window: 60 },
    );
    if (!allowed) return { error: `Too many requests. Try again in ${retryAfter}s.` };

    try {
      return (await handler(parsed.data, session)) ?? { ok: true };
    } catch (err) {
      console.error(err);
      return { error: 'Something went wrong.' };
    }
  };
}

// Usage — the action is now the business logic and nothing else:
'use server';
export const renameNotebook = authedAction(
  z.object({ id: z.string().ulid(), name: z.string().trim().min(1).max(80) }),
  async ({ id, name }, session) => {
    const n = await db.notebook.findUnique({ where: { id } });
    if (n?.ownerId !== session.userId) return { error: 'Not found.' };
    await db.notebook.update({ where: { id }, data: { name } });
    revalidateTag(`notebook:${id}`);
  },
);
// Libraries such as next-safe-action package this pattern with typed
// inputs and middleware if you would rather not hand-roll it.

Cookies, headers and revalidation

javascript
'use server';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';

export async function signIn(prevState, formData) {
  const user = await verifyCredentials(formData);
  if (!user) return { error: 'Invalid email or password.' };

  const store = await cookies();
  // Actions CAN set cookies — Server Components cannot, which is why
  // session creation must happen in an action, a route handler or
  // middleware.
  store.set('session', await createSessionToken(user.id), {
    httpOnly: true,               // not readable from JS
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production',
    sameSite: 'lax',
    path: '/',
    maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24 * 7,
  });

  redirect('/dashboard');
}

// WHAT REVALIDATION ACTUALLY DOES in an action:
// the response carries both the action's return value AND a fresh RSC
// payload for the current route. So the UI updates in one round trip —
// no refetch, no router.refresh(), no client cache to invalidate.
//
//   revalidateTag('posts')        every fetch tagged 'posts'
//   revalidateTag(`post:${id}`)   one post
//   revalidatePath('/posts')      one route
//   revalidatePath('/posts/[id]', 'page')   a dynamic route's pages
//   revalidatePath('/', 'layout')  everything under the root layout —
//                                  a sledgehammer; measure before using

Actions from event handlers

javascript · not everything is a form
'use client';
import { useTransition, useOptimistic } from 'react';

export function LikeButton({ postId, likes, liked }) {
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  const [optimistic, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    { likes, liked },
    (state) => ({ likes: state.likes + (state.liked ? -1 : 1), liked: !state.liked }),
  );

  return (
    <button
      disabled={isPending}
      onClick={() => startTransition(async () => {
        // useOptimistic requires an action or transition context —
        // outside one, the optimistic value reverts immediately (N02).
        addOptimistic(null);
        await toggleLike(postId);
      })}
    >
      {optimistic.liked ? '♥' : '♡'} {optimistic.likes}
    </button>
  );
}
// Without startTransition the await blocks and the button feels dead;
// with it, React knows a mutation is in flight and keeps the UI
// responsive.
Actions run in series, and that matters for lists

React queues Server Actions from the same client and runs them one at a time, so a fast third click waits behind a slow first one. That prevents interleaved writes, which is usually what you want for a single form — but in a list of twenty toggle buttons it makes the last one feel broken. For independent per-row mutations, either accept the queue and show per-row pending state, or use a Route Handler where parallelism is yours to control.

Interview follow-up

“How do you secure a Server Action?” Start by stating the threat model, because that is what the question is really testing: an action is a public POST endpoint with a build-generated id, so anyone who can read your bundle can call it with any payload. Therefore every action authenticates, validates its input with a schema, authorises the specific resource, and rate-limits if it is expensive — and none of “the button is hidden”, “it is only imported by the admin page” or “the id was bound” counts as any of those. Finish with the module-scope trap: 'use server' applies to every export in the file, so a stray exported helper becomes an internet-reachable endpoint.

X08

Navigation, loading, errors and not-found

The App Router turns three things that are hand-rolled in most apps — the loading state, the error boundary and the 404 — into files. Each has rules that are not obvious from the name, and the interactions between them cause most of the “why is my loading state not showing” questions.

How navigation works

A <Link> click does not reload the document. 1 · prefetch when the link enters the viewport, Next.js fetches that route's RSC payload in the background (production only — it is off in dev, which is why dev navigation feels slower) 2 · click React starts a transition 3 · fetch the RSC payload, if not already prefetched 4 · reconcile the new tree is diffed against the old one; shared layouts are preserved, so their state, scroll position and any open panels survive 5 · commit the URL updates and the new page paints Consequences worth internalising: · a layout does not re-render on navigation within it · client state in a layout survives; client state in a page does not · the RSC payload is JSON-ish, not HTML — the browser never parses a new document, so there is no flash and no script re-execution · prefetching means most navigations have zero network latency, and also means you are fetching routes the user may never visit

Link and the navigation APIs

javascript
import Link from 'next/link';

<Link href="/posts">Posts</Link>
<Link href={{ pathname: '/posts', query: { tag: 'react' } }}>React</Link>

<Link href="/posts" prefetch={false}>   {/* a heavy, rarely-clicked route */}
<Link href="/posts" replace>            {/* no history entry */}
<Link href="/posts" scroll={false}>     {/* keep scroll position */}

// Programmatic — client components only:
'use client';
import { useRouter, usePathname, useSearchParams, useParams } from 'next/navigation';
// NOTE: next/navigation, not next/router. Importing the Pages Router's
// hook in the App Router throws at runtime, and the error message is
// not obvious.

const router = useRouter();
router.push('/posts');
router.replace('/posts');
router.back();
router.refresh();      // refetch the server components for this route,
                       // KEEPING client state and scroll — the correct
                       // tool after a mutation done outside an action

const pathname = usePathname();          // '/posts/123'
const params   = useParams();            // { id: '123' }
const search   = useSearchParams();      // a ReadonlyURLSearchParams

// On the server, use redirect() instead:
import { redirect, permanentRedirect } from 'next/navigation';
redirect('/login');                       // 307 / 303 from an action
permanentRedirect('/new-home');           // 308
useSearchParams forces client rendering, and needs a Suspense boundary

Search params are only known per request, so a component calling useSearchParams cannot be prerendered. Next.js handles this by requiring the nearest parent <Suspense> — without one, next build fails with “useSearchParams() should be wrapped in a suspense boundary”, and if the page is static the whole route silently opts out of prerendering. Wrap the component that reads them, not the page, so the rest of the route stays static. On a server page, read the searchParams prop instead — it is a promise in Next 15 and it does not have this problem.

An active-link component

javascript · app/components/nav-link.tsx
'use client';
import Link from 'next/link';
import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation';

export function NavLink({ href, children, exact = false }) {
  const pathname = usePathname();
  const active = exact
    ? pathname === href
    : pathname === href || pathname.startsWith(href + '/');
    //                     ^ the '/' matters: without it '/post' would
    //                       match '/posts' too

  return (
    <Link href={href} aria-current={active ? 'page' : undefined}
          className={active ? 'nav-link active' : 'nav-link'}>
      {children}
    </Link>
  );
}
// This is the standard reason a nav bar is a Client Component while
// everything around it is a Server Component — and it is the smallest
// possible client boundary, which is the point (X03).

loading.tsx

javascript · app/dashboard/loading.tsx
// Automatically wraps page.tsx in a Suspense boundary. Shown while the
// server renders the segment — on first load AND on navigation into it.
export default function Loading() {
  // A SKELETON, not a spinner. It reserves the right space, which
  // avoids layout shift, and it tells the user what is coming.
  return (
    <div className="dash" aria-busy="true" aria-live="polite">
      <div className="skel skel-title" />
      <div className="skel skel-chart" />
      <div className="skel skel-row" />
      <div className="skel skel-row" />
      <span className="sr-only">Loading dashboard</span>
    </div>
  );
}

// WHY IT MIGHT NOT APPEAR:
//   · the route is static — there is nothing to wait for
//   · the data resolved faster than React's throttle
//   · the await is in the LAYOUT, not the page — loading.tsx only
//     covers the page and below
//   · a parent segment's loading.tsx caught it first
//
// For finer control, skip loading.tsx and place <Suspense> boundaries
// exactly where you want them (X05) — loading.tsx is the coarse,
// whole-segment version of the same mechanism.

error.tsx

javascript · app/dashboard/error.tsx
'use client';   // REQUIRED. An error boundary needs componentDidCatch,
                // which is a class-component lifecycle and therefore
                // client-only. Forgetting this is the most common
                // error.tsx mistake.

import { useEffect } from 'react';

export default function Error({ error, reset }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    // error.message is REDACTED in production for server errors, to
    // avoid leaking internals. error.digest is a hash you can grep for
    // in your server logs to find the real stack.
    reportError(error, { digest: error.digest });
  }, [error]);

  return (
    <div role="alert">
      <h2>Something went wrong</h2>
      {error.digest && <p className="mono">Reference: {error.digest}</p>}
      <button onClick={reset}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  );
}
// reset() re-renders the segment. It only helps for transient failures;
// for a deterministic bug it will fail again immediately.

// WHAT IT DOES NOT CATCH:
//   · errors in the LAYOUT of the same segment — the boundary sits
//     inside that layout. Use the PARENT segment's error.tsx.
//   · errors in the root layout — use app/global-error.tsx, which
//     replaces the whole document and must render <html> and <body>
//   · errors in event handlers and async callbacks (R15)
//   · errors thrown after a response has started streaming
javascript · app/global-error.tsx
'use client';

// The last resort. It replaces the root layout, so it must render the
// document shell itself — and it is only used in production.
export default function GlobalError({ error, reset }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <h1>Application error</h1>
        <button onClick={reset}>Reload</button>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

not-found.tsx

javascript
// app/posts/[slug]/page.tsx
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';

export default async function Post({ params }) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const post = await getPost(slug);
  if (!post) notFound();          // throws; sends a real 404 status
  return <Article post={post} />;
}

// app/posts/not-found.tsx — rendered for notFound() thrown anywhere in
// this segment's subtree, and for unmatched URLs under it.
export default function NotFound() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Post not found</h2>
      <Link href="/posts">Back to all posts</Link>
    </div>
  );
}

// Returning a "not found" component instead of calling notFound()
// gives a 200 status, which tells search engines the page exists and
// is a genuine SEO bug — one that is easy to ship and hard to notice.

The file hierarchy, and what wraps what

For one segment, Next.js composes the files like this: <Layout> <ErrorBoundary fallback={error.tsx}> <Suspense fallback={loading.tsx}> <NotFoundBoundary fallback={not-found.tsx}> <Page /> </NotFoundBoundary> </Suspense> </ErrorBoundary> </Layout> Read the nesting and the rules fall out: · error.tsx is INSIDE layout.tsx → it cannot catch layout errors · loading.tsx is INSIDE the error boundary → an error during loading shows the error UI, not a stuck skeleton · these nest per segment, so a deeper error.tsx handles a deeper failure and leaves the surrounding chrome intact template.tsx, rarely needed, sits between layout and children and creates a new instance on every navigation — so its state resets and its effects re-run. Use it for per-page enter animations or a per-page analytics effect; use layout.tsx for everything else.

Optimistic navigation feedback

javascript · useLinkStatus, React 19 + Next 15
'use client';
import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link';

// Rendered as a CHILD of Link — same context rule as useFormStatus.
function Spinner() {
  const { pending } = useLinkStatus();
  return pending ? <span className="spin" aria-hidden /> : null;
}

<Link href="/reports">Reports <Spinner /></Link>

// For a general "navigating" indicator, useTransition around a
// programmatic push works too:
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
<button onClick={() => startTransition(() => router.push('/reports'))}>
  {isPending ? 'Opening…' : 'Open reports'}
</button>
Give every route a loading state and an error state

A route with no loading.tsx and a slow server render appears frozen — the browser has committed to the navigation but nothing changes on screen, and users click the link again. A route with no error.tsx escalates a single failed query to the nearest ancestor boundary, often blanking the entire application for a problem confined to one panel. Both files are five lines. Add them at each meaningful segment as a matter of course, and put a shared skeleton component behind them so it is not twenty copies of the same markup.

Interview follow-up

“Why does error.tsx need 'use client'?” Because an error boundary is implemented with componentDidCatch / getDerivedStateFromError, which only exist on class components and only run on the client — there is no equivalent server hook. Follow it with the boundary placement, which is the part that shows you have actually used it: error.tsx is rendered inside its own segment's layout, so it cannot catch an error thrown by that layout; for that you need the parent segment's error.tsx, or global-error.tsx for the root layout, which replaces the entire document and must render <html> and <body> itself.

X09

Middleware, authentication and the edge

Middleware runs before every matched request, in a constrained runtime, with the power to rewrite, redirect and set headers. It is the right place for a cheap cookie check and the wrong place for your authorisation logic — a distinction that a well-known 2025 CVE made expensive for people who got it backwards.

The file

javascript · middleware.ts — at the project root, beside app/
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';

export function middleware(request) {
  const { pathname } = request.nextUrl;

  // CONTINUE
  const res = NextResponse.next();
  res.headers.set('x-request-id', crypto.randomUUID());
  return res;

  // REDIRECT — changes the URL in the browser
  // return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url));

  // REWRITE — serves different content at the same URL
  // return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/maintenance', request.url));

  // RESPOND directly
  // return new NextResponse('Forbidden', { status: 403 });
}

// The matcher is evaluated at BUILD time, so it must be statically
// analysable — no variables, no computed values.
export const config = {
  matcher: [
    // Everything except static assets, the image optimiser and metadata
    // files. Without an exclusion like this, middleware runs on every
    // .js chunk and every image, which is pure latency.
    '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|.*\\.(?:svg|png|jpg|webp)$).*)',
  ],
};

The runtime is not Node

Middleware runs on the Edge runtime by default: a V8 isolate with web APIs, not a Node process. available fetch, Request/Response, URL, Headers, crypto.subtle, TextEncoder, streams missing fs, net, child_process, most of node:*, and therefore most database drivers, bcrypt, jsonwebtoken, Prisma's default client limits small code size budget, short execution time, no persistent connections between invocations This is why the auth pattern below only reads the cookie. You cannot query your database from middleware, and you should not want to — it runs on every single request, so anything you put there is paid for by every page load in the application. Node runtime for middleware exists (export const runtime = 'nodejs') and has been stabilising; check whether your deployment target supports it before relying on it.

The authentication pattern that is correct

javascript · middleware.ts — optimistic only
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import { jwtVerify } from 'jose';        // jose works on the edge;
                                         // jsonwebtoken does not

const PUBLIC = ['/', '/login', '/signup', '/pricing', '/blog'];

export async function middleware(request) {
  const { pathname } = request.nextUrl;
  if (PUBLIC.some(p => pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + '/'))) {
    return NextResponse.next();
  }

  const token = request.cookies.get('session')?.value;
  if (!token) {
    const url = new URL('/login', request.url);
    url.searchParams.set('from', pathname);   // so login can send them back
    return NextResponse.redirect(url);
  }

  try {
    // Verifying the SIGNATURE is cheap and stateless. It proves the
    // token was issued by you and has not expired. It does NOT prove
    // the session is still valid — revocation lives in the database.
    await jwtVerify(token, new TextEncoder().encode(process.env.JWT_SECRET));
  } catch {
    const res = NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url));
    res.cookies.delete('session');
    return res;
  }

  return NextResponse.next();
}
javascript · and the real check, where the data is
// lib/auth.ts
import 'server-only';
import { cache } from 'react';

export const requireUser = cache(async () => {
  const token = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value;
  if (!token) redirect('/login');

  const claims = await verify(token);
  // The database lookup middleware could not do: is the session
  // revoked? was the user deleted, suspended, downgraded?
  const user = await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id: claims.sub } });
  if (!user || user.suspended) redirect('/login');
  return user;
});

// Every protected page, layout and action calls this. cache() means
// twenty components calling it costs one query (X04).
export default async function Dashboard() {
  const user = await requireUser();
  return <Charts userId={user.id} />;
}

// And AUTHORISATION — "may this user touch this resource" — is checked
// at the data layer, per resource, every time:
export async function getNotebook(id, user) {
  const n = await db.notebook.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  if (!n) return null;
  if (n.ownerId !== user.id && !(await hasAccess(n.id, user.id))) return null;
  return n;                      // 404, not 403 — do not confirm
}                                // that a resource exists
Middleware is not a security boundary — CVE-2025-29927

A vulnerability disclosed in March 2025 let an attacker skip middleware entirely by sending a crafted x-middleware-subrequest header. Applications whose only authorisation check lived in middleware were fully exposed: every protected page became public. Patched versions exist and you should be on one — but the lesson outlives the CVE. Middleware is a routing optimisation that saves a render for obviously-unauthenticated requests; it is a filter, not a gate. Every page, layout, Server Function and Route Handler must independently verify the session and the permission, close to the data. If deleting middleware.ts would expose anything, the architecture is wrong.

What middleware is genuinely good for

UseWhy it fits
Redirecting unauthenticated users away from /app/*Saves rendering a page the user cannot see; the real check still runs
i18n: detect locale, rewrite to /{locale}/…Needs the Accept-Language header before routing
A/B tests and feature flags by cookieRewrite to a variant without changing the URL
Security headers, CSP noncesMust be set on every response, uniformly
Multi-tenant subdomain → path rewritingRouting decision from the Host header
Bot and geo blockingCheap, request-level, no app logic needed
Maintenance modeOne env var, every route

Composing several concerns

javascript · one middleware export, several behaviours
export async function middleware(request) {
  const { pathname } = request.nextUrl;
  const host = request.headers.get('host') ?? '';

  // 1 · Maintenance
  if (process.env.MAINTENANCE === '1' && !pathname.startsWith('/maintenance')) {
    return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/maintenance', request.url));
  }

  // 2 · Multi-tenant: acme.example.com/settings → /tenants/acme/settings
  const sub = host.split('.')[0];
  if (sub && !['www', 'app', 'localhost:3000'].includes(host)) {
    const url = request.nextUrl.clone();
    url.pathname = `/tenants/${sub}${pathname}`;
    return withHeaders(NextResponse.rewrite(url));
  }

  // 3 · Locale
  if (!/^\/(en|fr|de)(\/|$)/.test(pathname)) {
    const locale = pickLocale(request.headers.get('accept-language'));
    return withHeaders(
      NextResponse.redirect(new URL(`/${locale}${pathname}`, request.url)));
  }

  return withHeaders(NextResponse.next());
}

// 4 · Security headers on every response, including the rewrites above
function withHeaders(res) {
  const nonce = crypto.randomUUID();
  res.headers.set('Content-Security-Policy',
    `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'; ` +
    `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self';`);
  res.headers.set('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff');
  res.headers.set('Referrer-Policy', 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin');
  res.headers.set('Permissions-Policy', 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()');
  res.headers.set('x-nonce', nonce);      // read it in the root layout
  return res;
}
// Pattern: each concern either RETURNS a response or falls through to
// the next. Keep the whole file fast — it runs on every request.

Passing data from middleware to the app

javascript
// Middleware cannot mutate the request body or pass objects. The
// channel is REQUEST headers, which the app reads with headers().
export function middleware(request) {
  const headers = new Headers(request.headers);
  headers.set('x-tenant', resolveTenant(request));
  headers.set('x-nonce', nonce);
  return NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } });
}

// app/layout.tsx
import { headers } from 'next/headers';

export default async function RootLayout({ children }) {
  const nonce = (await headers()).get('x-nonce') ?? undefined;
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>{children}</body>
      <script nonce={nonce} … />
    </html>
  );
}
// Calling headers() makes the route dynamic (X05) — so doing this in
// the ROOT layout makes the entire application dynamic. That is a real
// cost; read the header only where you need it.
Three middleware performance traps

No matcher, so it runs for every JS chunk, font and image — often five times more invocations than page views. An await fetch inside it, which adds its latency to every request in the application; if you must, cache aggressively and set a short timeout. And a heavy import: the edge bundle has a small size budget, and pulling in a date library or a validation schema to make one decision will either blow the limit or slow cold starts. Middleware should be tens of lines and reach nothing but cookies, headers and the URL.

Interview follow-up

“Where do you put auth in a Next.js app?” In layers, and be explicit that middleware is the outermost and weakest one: it does a cheap cookie and signature check to redirect obvious anonymous traffic, because it cannot reach your database and it runs on every request. The authoritative session check goes in the page, layout or action via a cache()-wrapped helper that queries the database; authorisation goes at the data layer, per resource, returning 404 rather than 403 so you do not confirm that a record exists. Then name CVE-2025-29927 as the reason this layering is not paranoia — a header-spoofing bug let attackers bypass middleware entirely, and only the apps with checks below it were safe.

X10

Images, fonts, metadata and SEO

These four are the least glamorous part of Next.js and the largest share of a Lighthouse score. Images and fonts are where Largest Contentful Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift are won or lost; metadata is where a page either shows up correctly in search results and social cards, or does not show up at all.

next/image

javascript
import Image from 'next/image';
import hero from '@/public/hero.jpg';

// STATIC IMPORT — the best case. Width, height and a blur placeholder
// are derived at build time, so there is zero layout shift and no
// dimensions to get wrong.
<Image src={hero} alt="Two people reviewing a document" priority placeholder="blur" />

// REMOTE — you must supply dimensions, because the build cannot know
// them and without them the browser reserves no space (that is CLS).
<Image
  src={product.imageUrl}
  alt={product.name}
  width={800}
  height={600}
  sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw"
/>

// FILL — for a container of unknown size. The parent must be
// positioned, or the image escapes it.
<div style={{ position: 'relative', aspectRatio: '16/9' }}>
  <Image src={url} alt="" fill sizes="100vw" style={{ objectFit: 'cover' }} />
</div>

// next.config.js — remote hosts must be allowlisted, or the optimiser
// becomes an open image proxy that anyone can point at any URL.
module.exports = {
  images: {
    remotePatterns: [
      { protocol: 'https', hostname: 'cdn.example.com', pathname: '/images/**' },
    ],
    formats: ['image/avif', 'image/webp'],
    // For an external optimiser (Cloudinary, imgix) or a static export:
    // loader: 'custom', loaderFile: './image-loader.js',
    // unoptimized: true,
  },
};
priority and sizes are the two that actually matter

Every next/image is lazy-loaded by default, including the hero — so without priority on your LCP image, the browser does not even start fetching it until layout runs, and LCP suffers by hundreds of milliseconds. Set priority on exactly the one or two above-the-fold images and nothing else; marking everything priority is the same as marking nothing. Then sizes: without it a responsive image defaults to 100vw, so a phone downloads the full-width desktop asset for a thumbnail. sizes describes the rendered width at each breakpoint, and it is what lets the browser pick the right entry from srcset.

next/font

javascript · app/layout.tsx
import { Inter, JetBrains_Mono } from 'next/font/google';
import localFont from 'next/font/local';

// Downloaded and SELF-HOSTED at build time. No request to Google at
// runtime — which removes a third-party round trip, removes a privacy
// problem, and removes a single point of failure.
const inter = Inter({
  subsets: ['latin'],
  display: 'swap',
  variable: '--font-sans',
  // Metric overrides are computed automatically so the fallback font
  // occupies the same space — this is what eliminates the font-swap
  // layout shift that used to be unavoidable.
});

const mono = JetBrains_Mono({ subsets: ['latin'], variable: '--font-mono' });

const brand = localFont({
  src: [
    { path: './Brand-Regular.woff2', weight: '400', style: 'normal' },
    { path: './Brand-Bold.woff2',    weight: '700', style: 'normal' },
  ],
  variable: '--font-brand',
  display: 'swap',
});

export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" className={`${inter.variable} ${mono.variable} ${brand.variable}`}>
      <body>{children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}

/* globals.css */
/* body { font-family: var(--font-sans), system-ui, sans-serif; } */

// Call the font loader at MODULE SCOPE, with literal arguments — it is
// a build-time transform, not a runtime function. Calling it inside a
// component, or with a variable, fails the build.

Static metadata

javascript · app/layout.tsx
export const metadata = {
  // Required for og:image and other absolute URLs to resolve. Without
  // it, relative image paths in cards are silently dropped.
  metadataBase: new URL('https://example.com'),

  title: {
    default: 'Acme — project tracking that stays out of the way',
    template: '%s · Acme',      // child pages fill in %s
  },
  description: 'Plan, track and ship. Under 60 seconds to your first board.',
  applicationName: 'Acme',
  authors: [{ name: 'Acme', url: 'https://example.com' }],
  openGraph: {
    type: 'website',
    siteName: 'Acme',
    locale: 'en_GB',
    images: [{ url: '/og.png', width: 1200, height: 630, alt: 'Acme' }],
  },
  twitter: { card: 'summary_large_image', site: '@acme' },
  robots: {
    index: true, follow: true,
    googleBot: { index: true, follow: true, 'max-image-preview': 'large' },
  },
  alternates: {
    canonical: '/',
    languages: { 'en-GB': '/en', 'fr-FR': '/fr' },
  },
  icons: { icon: '/favicon.ico', apple: '/apple-touch-icon.png' },
};
// Metadata merges down the layout chain: a child overrides individual
