// fields and inherits the rest. It is only read from layout.tsx and
// page.tsx — never from a component.

Dynamic metadata

javascript · app/posts/[slug]/page.tsx
export async function generateMetadata({ params }, parent) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  // This fetch is deduped against the page's own fetch of the same
  // post (X04), so it costs nothing extra.
  const post = await getPost(slug);
  if (!post) return { title: 'Not found' };

  const previousImages = (await parent).openGraph?.images ?? [];

  return {
    title: post.title,                          // → "Title · Acme"
    description: post.excerpt,
    alternates: { canonical: `/posts/${slug}` },
    openGraph: {
      type: 'article',
      publishedTime: post.publishedAt.toISOString(),
      authors: [post.author.name],
      images: [post.ogImage, ...previousImages],
    },
  };
}

// STREAMING NOTE: Next.js does not block the response on
// generateMetadata. The shell streams, and the tags are inserted when
// it resolves. So a slow generateMetadata does not hurt TTFB — but it
// must not be slower than the crawler's patience.

Generated OG images

javascript · app/posts/[slug]/opengraph-image.tsx
import { ImageResponse } from 'next/og';

export const alt = 'Post preview';
export const size = { width: 1200, height: 630 };
export const contentType = 'image/png';

export default async function Image({ params }) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const post = await getPost(slug);

  // JSX rendered to a PNG with Satori. A SUBSET of CSS: flexbox only,
  // no grid, no float, and every element with more than one child needs
  // an explicit display:flex. Debug by opening the route directly.
  return new ImageResponse(
    (
      <div style={{
        width: '100%', height: '100%', display: 'flex',
        flexDirection: 'column', justifyContent: 'center',
        padding: 80, background: '#111019', color: '#fff',
      }}>
        <div style={{ fontSize: 64, fontWeight: 700, lineHeight: 1.1 }}>
          {post.title}
        </div>
        <div style={{ fontSize: 28, marginTop: 24, opacity: 0.7 }}>
          {post.author.name} · {post.readingTime} min read
        </div>
      </div>
    ),
    { ...size },
  );
}
// Cached like any other route, so it is generated once per post rather
// than per share.

Sitemap, robots and structured data

javascript · app/sitemap.ts and app/robots.ts
// app/sitemap.ts → /sitemap.xml
export default async function sitemap() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany({
    where: { published: true },
    select: { slug: true, updatedAt: true },
  });

  return [
    { url: 'https://example.com',        lastModified: new Date(), priority: 1 },
    { url: 'https://example.com/pricing', lastModified: new Date(), priority: 0.8 },
    ...posts.map(p => ({
      url: `https://example.com/posts/${p.slug}`,
      lastModified: p.updatedAt,
      changeFrequency: 'weekly',
      priority: 0.6,
    })),
  ];
}
// Over 50,000 URLs: export generateSitemaps() to split into indexed
// chunks — a single oversized sitemap is ignored.

// app/robots.ts → /robots.txt
export default function robots() {
  return {
    rules: [{ userAgent: '*', allow: '/', disallow: ['/api/', '/admin/'] }],
    sitemap: 'https://example.com/sitemap.xml',
  };
}
javascript · JSON-LD, in the page body
export default async function Post({ params }) {
  const post = await getPost((await params).slug);

  const jsonLd = {
    '@context': 'https://schema.org',
    '@type': 'Article',
    headline: post.title,
    datePublished: post.publishedAt.toISOString(),
    author: { '@type': 'Person', name: post.author.name },
  };

  return (
    <>
      <script
        type="application/ld+json"
        // The content is yours, not user input — but if any field can
        // contain user text, escape '<' or an injected </script> ends
        // the block early.
        dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{
          __html: JSON.stringify(jsonLd).replace(/</g, '\\u003c'),
        }}
      />
      <Article post={post} />
    </>
  );
}

The SEO checklist

ItemWhere
A unique title and description per pagegenerateMetadata
metadataBase set onceRoot layout — without it OG images break
A canonical URL on every indexable pagealternates.canonical
Real 404s, not 200s with a “not found” messagenotFound() (X08)
One h1, in document orderThe page itself
Content in the HTML, not injected after hydrationServer Components
lang on <html>Root layout
Sitemap, robots, structured datasitemap.ts, robots.ts, JSON-LD
Preview staging with noindexrobots: { index: false } behind an env check
Verify what the crawler sees, not what the browser shows

curl -s https://yoursite.com/page | grep -i '<title' shows the HTML as delivered. If the title, description or main content is missing there but visible in the browser, it is being added after hydration and a crawler may never see it — the commonest cause is content rendered inside a Client Component that fetches in an effect. Check a deployed preview rather than dev, since some metadata behaviour differs, and remember that a staging site indexed by accident competes with production for the same keywords.

Interview follow-up

“How does next/image improve performance?” Four mechanisms, and naming all four separates a real answer from a memorised one: it serves modern formats (AVIF/WebP) and correctly-sized variants via srcset, so phones do not download desktop assets; it reserves space from known width and height, so there is no layout shift; it lazy-loads below-the-fold images; and it can show a blur placeholder generated at build time. Then add the two props people get wrong — priority on the LCP image, because the default lazy loading applies to the hero too, and sizes, because without it a responsive image assumes it is full-width at every breakpoint.

X11

Performance: bundles, waterfalls and Core Web Vitals

Performance work fails when it is guesswork. This chapter is a procedure: measure the three metrics that are actually scored, find which of four specific causes is responsible, apply the fix for that cause, measure again. Most Next.js performance problems are one of four things, and you can tell them apart from the build output alone.

The three metrics

LCP Largest Contentful Paint good ≤ 2.5s When the biggest element above the fold finishes painting. Usually the hero image or the headline. Caused by: a slow server render, an unoptimised or lazy-loaded hero image, a render-blocking resource, no CDN. INP Interaction to Next Paint good ≤ 200ms The worst input-to-paint delay across the whole visit. Replaced FID in March 2024 and is much harder to pass, because it measures the full interaction, not just the first input's delay. Caused by: long tasks on the main thread, an expensive re-render on every keystroke, a huge hydration cost. CLS Cumulative Layout Shift good ≤ 0.1 How much content jumps around after it appears. Caused by: images without dimensions, fonts swapping, banners injected above existing content, ads. Measure with field data (real users, Vercel Analytics, CrUX) not just lab data (Lighthouse). A Lighthouse score of 100 on your laptop tells you very little about a mid-range Android on 4G.

Read the build output first

next build
$ next build

Route (app)                          Size     First Load JS
┌ ○ /                                1.8 kB          94 kB
├ ○ /about                           0.4 kB          92 kB
├ ● /posts/[slug]                    2.1 kB          95 kB
├ ƒ /dashboard                      148 kB         242 kB   ← look here
└ ƒ /api/posts                       0 kB            0 kB
+ First Load JS shared by all                        91.4 kB
  ├ chunks/framework-a1b2.js                         45.2 kB
  ├ chunks/main-c3d4.js                              31.8 kB
  └ other shared chunks                              14.4 kB

○  (Static)              prerendered as static content
●  (SSG)                 prerendered with generateStaticParams
ƒ  (Dynamic)             server-rendered on demand
Three questions to ask of that table

Which routes are ƒ that should be ○? Each one is a render you are paying for on every request, usually because a component deep in the tree reads a cookie (X05). Which route's First Load JS is an outlier? 242 kB against a 91 kB baseline means ~150 kB of route-specific client code — find out what. Is the shared baseline creeping up? Everything in the shared chunk is downloaded by every visitor on every route, so a library imported into the root layout is the most expensive import in the application. Record these numbers in CI and fail the build on a regression.

Cause 1 — too much client JavaScript

bash · find out what is in the bundle
npm i -D @next/bundle-analyzer

# next.config.js
# const withBundleAnalyzer = require('@next/bundle-analyzer')({
#   enabled: process.env.ANALYZE === 'true',
# });
# module.exports = withBundleAnalyzer({});

ANALYZE=true npm run build      # opens a treemap per bundle
javascript · the four fixes, in order of effect
// 1 · MOVE IT TO THE SERVER. A markdown renderer, a syntax highlighter,
//     a date formatter, a heavy schema — if it runs on data you already
//     have on the server, it does not belong in the bundle at all.
//     This is the single largest lever RSC gives you (N04).

// 2 · IMPORT NARROWLY.
import debounce from 'lodash/debounce';       // 2 kB
// import { debounce } from 'lodash';         // 70 kB unless tree-shaken
// optimizePackageImports handles many libraries automatically:
//   experimental: { optimizePackageImports: ['lodash', 'date-fns', 'lucide-react'] }

// 3 · LOAD IT LATER. Anything below the fold or behind an interaction.
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic';

const Editor  = dynamic(() => import('@/components/editor'),
  { loading: () => <EditorSkeleton />, ssr: false });
const Chart   = dynamic(() => import('@/components/chart'));

// Or truly on demand, so it is not even in the initial graph:
async function onExport() {
  const { exportToPdf } = await import('@/lib/pdf');   // 400 kB, once
  await exportToPdf(data);
}

// 4 · CHOOSE A SMALLER DEPENDENCY. moment (70 kB) → date-fns subset or
//     Intl.DateTimeFormat (0 kB). A full charting library for one
//     sparkline → an inline SVG.

// SCRIPTS: third-party tags are often larger than your whole app.
import Script from 'next/script';
<Script src="https://analytics.example.com/s.js" strategy="lazyOnload" />
// afterInteractive (default) · lazyOnload (idle) · beforeInteractive
// (blocking — almost never correct) · worker (experimental, off-thread)

Cause 2 — waterfalls

Server waterfall — sequential awaits await getUser() ████ 200ms await getPosts() ████ 200ms await getStats() ████ 200ms total 600ms Promise.all([…]) ████ 200ms total 200ms Client waterfall — the one RSC was designed to remove HTML ██ JS bundle ██████ hydrate ███ useEffect fetch ████ render ██ total ~1.2s Server Component: data fetched during the render, before the HTML is sent. total ~0.3s Nested-component waterfall — subtle and common <Page> awaits user └ <Profile> awaits profile ← cannot start until the parent's └ <Posts> awaits posts await resolves Fix: hoist the fetches and pass promises down, or wrap the children in separate Suspense boundaries so they render in parallel (X05).

Cause 3 — an expensive render

javascript · the INP killers
// A. A large list re-rendering on every keystroke.
//    useDeferredValue keeps typing responsive by letting the list lag
//    behind the input (R14, W06).
const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
const deferred = useDeferredValue(query);
const results = useMemo(() => filter(items, deferred), [items, deferred]);

// B. Context that changes on every render, re-rendering every consumer.
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, signOut }), [user, signOut]);   // R11

// C. Thousands of DOM nodes. Virtualise — nothing else works.
//    react-window / @tanstack/react-virtual render ~20 rows for 10,000.

// D. A long synchronous task blocking the main thread. Anything over
//    50ms is a "long task" and directly harms INP. Chunk it, move it
//    to a Worker, or do it on the server.

// E. Hydrating far more than necessary. A page that is 95% static
//    content inside one big 'use client' boundary pays full hydration
//    cost for markup that will never change (X03).

// MEASURE, do not guess:
//   React DevTools Profiler        which component, how long
//   Performance panel → Long tasks what blocks the main thread
//   Lighthouse → "Avoid long main-thread tasks"

Cause 4 — a slow server

javascript
// The framework cannot make a 2-second query fast. Check, in order:
//
// 1 · N+1 queries. A list of 50 posts each fetching its author is 51
//     queries. Use a join or a dataloader.
// 2 · Missing indexes. EXPLAIN the query.
// 3 · Region mismatch. A server in Frankfurt and a database in Ohio
//     pays ~100ms per round trip — and a page making six sequential
//     queries pays it six times. Co-locate them; this is the single
//     most common "Next.js is slow" cause that is not Next.js.
// 4 · Cold starts. Serverless functions that are rarely called pay
//     initialisation on the first request.
// 5 · Connection exhaustion. Serverless + a connection-per-instance
//     database client exhausts the pool under load — use a pooler
//     (PgBouncer, Prisma Accelerate, Neon's serverless driver).

// Then cache what is cacheable (X04):
export const revalidate = 300;
const getStats = unstable_cache(fetchStats, ['stats'], { revalidate: 300 });

// And stream what cannot be cached, so the slow part does not hold up
// the page (X05).

A worked example

1
Measure. Field data shows LCP 4.1s, INP 380ms on the dashboard. Build output: ƒ /dashboard · 242 kB.
2
Analyse. The treemap shows a 180 kB charting library and moment in the route bundle. The page has one 'use client' at the top.
3
Lower the boundary. Header, filters and summary cards become Server Components; only the interactive chart stays client. Route bundle: 242 → 198 kB.
4
Defer and replace. The chart becomes a dynamic import with a skeleton; moment is replaced with Intl.DateTimeFormat. First Load JS: 198 → 96 kB.
5
Fix the waterfall. Four sequential queries become one Promise.all; the slow report moves behind a Suspense boundary. TTFB 1.4s → 220ms.
6
Re-measure. LCP 1.6s, INP 140ms. Record both numbers in CI so the next feature cannot quietly undo it.
Do not optimise in dev

The development server is deliberately slow: no minification, no prefetching, on-demand compilation, source maps, React in development mode with extra checks and doubled effect invocation. A route that takes 900 ms in next dev may take 40 ms in production. Always measure against next build && next start, and preferably against a real deployment — otherwise you will spend an afternoon optimising the dev compiler.

Interview follow-up

“A Next.js page is slow. How do you debug it?” Give a procedure, not a list of tips. First determine which slow: TTFB (server), LCP (first paint), or INP (interaction) — they have disjoint causes. Read the build output for the route's First Load JS and its static/dynamic marker. Then narrow: bundle analyser for JavaScript weight, the network waterfall for sequential fetches, the React Profiler for render cost, and database timings for the server. Apply the fix that matches the cause — lower the client boundary, Promise.all the queries, cache or stream, virtualise the list — and measure in production, since dev is unrepresentative by design.

X12

Building, deploying and operating a Next.js app

A Next.js build produces several different kinds of output — static files, serverless handlers, an image optimiser, a cache — and where they can run determines your hosting options. This chapter covers the build, the deployment targets, configuration, observability and the operational details that only appear once real traffic arrives.

What the build produces

next build → .next/ static/ hashed JS, CSS, fonts, images → any CDN server/app/ a rendering function per route → Node runtime plus prerendered .html and .rsc for static routes cache/ the Data Cache and ISR artefacts → needs to be shared and persistent (image optimiser) resizes on demand → needs a runtime This is why hosting a Next.js app is not the same as hosting a SPA. Unless every route is static, you need a Node runtime, somewhere to keep the cache that all instances can see, and something to serve optimised images. output: 'standalone' in next.config.js traces exactly the node_modules files the server needs and emits a self-contained directory — a ~1 GB image becomes ~150 MB. output: 'export' emits pure static HTML. No SSR, no ISR, no image optimisation, no Route Handlers, no middleware — it is the "this is really a static site" option, not a deployment strategy for a dynamic app.

Docker

dockerfile · a standalone multi-stage build
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
# NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are INLINED into the client bundle at build time.
# They are baked into the image; changing them needs a rebuild, not a
# restart. Never put a secret in one.
ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL
ENV NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
RUN addgroup -g 1001 nodejs && adduser -u 1001 -G nodejs -S nextjs

# standalone traces only the files the server actually imports
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public
COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/.next/static ./.next/static

USER nextjs
EXPOSE 3000
ENV PORT=3000 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Multiple instances need a shared cache

The default ISR cache is the local filesystem. Run three containers behind a load balancer and you have three independent caches: a revalidateTag handled by instance A leaves B and C serving stale content indefinitely, and a page regenerates three times instead of once. Configure a shared cache handler (cacheHandler in next.config.js, backed by Redis or S3) before scaling past one instance — or accept that ISR is per-instance and use short revalidate windows. On Vercel this is handled for you, which is precisely why the problem surprises people the first time they self-host.

Deployment targets

TargetFitWatch for
VercelEverything works, day one: ISR, PPR, image optimiser, edge middleware, preview deploysCost at scale; some features land here first and are awkward elsewhere
Docker / KubernetesFull control, any cloud, existing platformShared cache handler, image optimiser CPU, no edge middleware by default
Node on a VMSimple, predictable, cheapYou own TLS, the CDN, restarts and log shipping
Netlify / Cloudflare / AWS AmplifyGood support via adaptersFeature lag; verify ISR and middleware behaviour for your version
Static exportDocs and marketing sites on any static hostNo SSR, ISR, handlers, middleware or image optimisation

Environment variables

javascript · the rule that causes real leaks
// NEXT_PUBLIC_*  → inlined into the CLIENT bundle at BUILD time.
//                  Public. Permanent. Baked into the image.
// everything else → server only, read at runtime.

// A single character's difference between a secret and a leak:
NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY=phc_...       // fine, it is a public key
NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_SECRET=sk_live_... // SHIPPED TO EVERY BROWSER

// Validate at startup so a missing variable fails the boot rather than
// the first request that needs it:
// lib/env.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

const server = z.object({
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
  SESSION_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: z.string().startsWith('sk_'),
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']),
});

export const env = server.parse(process.env);
// Import it in next.config.js too, so `next build` fails fast in CI
// when a variable is missing from the deployment environment.

// Reading process.env with a computed key defeats the inlining:
const url = process.env[`NEXT_PUBLIC_${name}`];   // undefined at runtime
const url = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL;      // works

Health checks and instrumentation

javascript · instrumentation.ts and a readiness endpoint
// instrumentation.ts — runs once per server process, before anything
// else. The right place for tracing, and for error reporting that must
// catch startup failures.
export async function register() {
  if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'nodejs') {
    await import('./instrumentation.node');   // OpenTelemetry, Sentry…
  }
}

// Server-side error reporting hook (Next 15):
export function onRequestError(err, request, context) {
  reportToSentry(err, {
    path: request.path,
    method: request.method,
    routerKind: context.routerKind,      // 'App Router' | 'Pages Router'
    renderSource: context.renderSource,  // where it failed
  });
}

// app/api/health/route.ts — LIVENESS: is the process up?
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';
export async function GET() {
  return Response.json({ ok: true, commit: process.env.GIT_SHA });
}

// app/api/ready/route.ts — READINESS: can it serve traffic?
export async function GET() {
  try {
    await db.$queryRaw`SELECT 1`;
    return Response.json({ ok: true });
  } catch {
    return Response.json({ ok: false }, { status: 503 });
  }
}
// Keep them separate: a failed readiness check should stop new traffic
// being routed here; a failed liveness check should restart the pod.
// Conflating them turns a brief database blip into a restart storm.

A CI pipeline

yaml · .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci

      - run: npx tsc --noEmit          # types
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test -- --coverage

      # Cache the Next.js build cache between runs — this is usually
      # the single largest CI speed-up for a Next.js repo.
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: .next/cache
          key: next-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}-${{ hashFiles('**/*.[jt]s?(x)') }}
          restore-keys: next-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}-

      - run: npm run build
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}

      # Fail the PR if the bundle grew
      - run: npx bundlesize

      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npm run test:e2e

Operating it

ConcernWhat to do
ErrorsSentry via instrumentation.ts and onRequestError; correlate client reports with error.digest (X08)
TracingOpenTelemetry — Next.js emits spans for render, fetch and route handling
Web VitalsuseReportWebVitals, or a provider's analytics — field data, not Lighthouse (X11)
LogsStructured JSON to stdout; never log request bodies or cookies
RollbackImmutable deploys with an instant previous-version switch; test it before you need it
MigrationsExpand–migrate–contract, so old and new code both run during the rollout
Stale assetsHandle chunk-load failures — a user on an old tab requests a hashed chunk that no longer exists; catch it and reload
The deploy-time bug nobody tests for

After a deploy, a browser tab open on the old version still holds references to hashed chunk filenames that are no longer on the CDN. The next navigation that needs a lazily-loaded chunk throws ChunkLoadError and the app appears to break for no reason — and it only happens to users who had the site open across a release, which is exactly nobody in your test suite. Catch it in error.tsx: if the message matches a chunk-load failure, prompt a reload. Keeping the previous build's static assets available for a grace period after deploy avoids it entirely.

Interview follow-up

“What is involved in self-hosting Next.js?” Name the parts a SPA does not have: a Node runtime for SSR and Route Handlers, a shared and persistent cache for ISR (otherwise every instance has its own and revalidation only reaches one of them), something to serve optimised images, and a CDN in front of .next/static. Mention output: 'standalone' as the mechanism that makes the container small by tracing only the modules the server imports, and be honest about the gaps — edge middleware and some newer features are easiest on Vercel, so self-hosting means checking feature support against your version rather than assuming parity.

T01

Why TypeScript, and what it actually is

TypeScript is JavaScript plus a type annotation syntax and a compiler that checks it. That is the whole product. It adds no runtime, changes no semantics, and every line of valid JavaScript is already valid TypeScript — which is why adoption can be gradual and why the honest case for it is narrower and more interesting than “types are good”.

What it is, precisely

TypeScript = JavaScript + types, erased at build time. your.ts ──[ tsc / SWC / esbuild ]──▶ your.js │ └── types are DELETED, not compiled Three consequences that answer most beginner questions: 1 · There is no runtime. Types do not exist when the code runs. You cannot check a type at runtime, you cannot switch on one, and a value arriving from an API is whatever the server actually sent regardless of what you declared. 2 · The type system is structural, not nominal. Two types with the same shape are the same type. A class does not need to `implement` an interface to satisfy it. 3 · It is deliberately unsound. There are holes — `any`, assertions, array index access, mutable covariance — that exist because closing them would reject too much correct JavaScript. TypeScript optimises for usefulness on real code, not for proving correctness. So: TypeScript catches mistakes at the moment you write them. It does not make your program safe. Everything crossing a boundary — an API response, a form submission, localStorage, an env var — must still be validated at runtime.

JavaScript vs TypeScript, on the same code

The honest case for it

What you getWhy it matters more than it sounds
Autocomplete that is always rightThe most-used feature by a wide margin. Not having to remember whether it is user.name or user.fullName compounds over every line you write.
Refactoring you can trustRenaming a field or changing a signature shows you every call site. In plain JavaScript this is a grep and a prayer, which is why large JS codebases accumulate code nobody dares touch.
Types as documentation that cannot driftA comment saying a parameter is optional goes stale. A ? cannot.
Null and undefined tracked explicitlyUnder strictNullChecks, the single most common JavaScript runtime error becomes a compile error.
ExhaustivenessAdd a case to a union and every switch that handles it incompletely fails to compile (T05).
A shared vocabularyOn a team, a type is a precise statement of what a function expects, which is otherwise negotiated in review comments.
And the costs, stated plainly

A build step, and a slower one — type checking a large project takes seconds to minutes, and it is separate from bundling since esbuild and SWC strip types without checking them. A learning curve with a long tail: generics, conditional types and variance are genuinely hard, and a badly-typed codebase is harder to work in than an untyped one. Dependency friction when a library ships no types or bad ones. And a real temptation to over-engineer — the type-level programming in T06 is powerful enough that people build cathedrals where a plain interface would do. Weigh these honestly: for a throwaway script or a tiny site, TypeScript is overhead. For anything a team maintains for more than a few months, it pays for itself quickly.

The claim it does not support

typescript · types are not validation
interface User { id: string; email: string; age: number }

async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  return res.json();      // res.json() returns `any`
}
// This compiles. It is also a LIE — the annotation asserts a shape
// that nothing has checked. If the API returns { id, emailAddress }
// then `user.email` is undefined at runtime and TypeScript said
// nothing, because the type was a promise you made, not a fact.

// The fix is a runtime schema that PRODUCES the type, so there is one
// source of truth and it is the one that actually runs:
import { z } from 'zod';

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  age: z.number().int().min(0),
});
export type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;   // derived, never drifts

async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status);
  return UserSchema.parse(await res.json());     // throws if it lies
}

// The rule: VALIDATE AT EVERY BOUNDARY, INFER THE TYPE FROM THE
// SCHEMA. Boundaries are API responses, form data, URL params,
// localStorage, environment variables, webhooks, and anything from
// a third-party SDK.
Where the type system is deliberately unsound

Knowing these is what separates someone who uses TypeScript from someone who trusts it blindly. any disables checking entirely and spreads silently through everything it touches. Type assertions (as) are you overriding the compiler, correct or not. Array index access is typed as T, not T | undefined, so arr[99] on a three-element array type-checks and returns undefined — fixable with noUncheckedIndexedAccess. Object property access on an index signature has the same hole. Function parameter bivariance on method syntax lets an unsafe callback through. And mutable array covariance means a Dog[] is assignable to Animal[], which can then have a Cat pushed into it. Each is a considered trade so that ordinary JavaScript patterns keep working.

Your first file

typescript · the syntax, in one page
// ANNOTATIONS go after a colon. Most of the time you should omit them
// and let inference do the work — see T02.
let name: string = 'Sam';
let age = 41;                       // inferred as number; do not annotate

// FUNCTIONS: annotate parameters, usually let the return type infer.
function greet(name: string, greeting = 'Hello'): string {
  return `${greeting}, ${name}`;
}
const double = (n: number) => n * 2;       // returns number, inferred

// OBJECTS
interface Order {
  id: string;
  total: number;
  note?: string;            // optional: string | undefined
  readonly createdAt: Date; // cannot be reassigned after creation
}

// UNIONS — the workhorse of the whole language.
type Status = 'draft' | 'published' | 'archived';
type Id = string | number;

// ARRAYS
const tags: string[] = [];
const pair: [number, number] = [0, 0];      // tuple, fixed length

// The three things to actually learn, in order:
//   1 · unions and narrowing        (T02, T05)
//   2 · generics                    (T04)
//   3 · the utility types           (T06)
// Everything else can be looked up.

Should you use it?

A React or Next.js application a team maintains
Yes, without hesitation. The ecosystem assumes it, the props-and-state model benefits enormously, and the refactoring safety is worth the build step on its own.
A library you publish
Yes. Consumers expect types, and shipping them from source is far more reliable than hand-written declaration files.
A prototype you will throw away
Probably not, and that is a legitimate answer. The value is in maintenance, and there is none.
An existing large JavaScript codebase
Incrementally — allowJs, then file by file, starting with the shared utilities everything imports (T09). A big-bang conversion is how these migrations fail.
A small script or a build tool
JSDoc type annotations in a .js file give you most of the editor benefit with no build step at all, and Node can now strip TypeScript types natively — so the gap has narrowed.
Interview follow-up

“Why use TypeScript?” The weak answer is “it catches errors”. The strong one names what it catches and what it does not: it catches mistakes at the moment of writing — wrong argument counts, misspelled properties, unhandled null, missing switch cases — and it makes refactoring mechanical rather than archaeological, which is the benefit that actually scales with team size. Then volunteer the limit, because it is what shows experience: types are erased at build time, so nothing is checked at runtime, and an annotation on a fetch result is a promise you made rather than a fact. Real safety at a boundary needs a runtime schema, with the TypeScript type inferred from it so the two cannot drift apart.

T02

The type system: inference, unions and literals

Two ideas carry most of TypeScript's value, and beginners typically discover them late. The first is that you should annotate far less than you think — inference is better at this than you are. The second is that a union of literal types is the most useful construct in the language, because it lets you make illegal states impossible to write down.

The primitives, and the special ones

typescript
// The ordinary ones mirror JavaScript:
string  number  boolean  bigint  symbol  null  undefined

// `number` covers integers and floats — there is no int type, because
// JavaScript has none. `bigint` is separate and does not mix with it.

// THE SPECIAL ONES, in order of how much trouble they cause:

let a: any;        // ✗ CHECKING OFF. Every operation is allowed, and
                   //   the looseness spreads to everything it touches.
a.whatever.deeply.nested();   // compiles. crashes.

let u: unknown;    // ✓ The safe `any`. Accepts anything, but you must
                   //   narrow before using it.
u.toUpperCase();              // ✗ Error — good.
if (typeof u === 'string') u.toUpperCase();   // ✓

function fail(m: string): never {   // never = this never returns
  throw new Error(m);               // also: the type of an impossible
}                                   // value, used for exhaustiveness (T05)

function log(): void { }            // void = the return is not usable

// `null` and `undefined` are only meaningful under strictNullChecks,
// which you should always have on (T09). Without it they are
// assignable to everything and the compiler's most valuable check is
// switched off.
any is contagious, and that is why it is worse than it looks

One any does not stay local. Anything it touches becomes any — property access, function results, array elements — so a single as any in a data-loading function can silently disable checking across a whole feature, and nothing reports it. Use unknown instead whenever you genuinely do not know the type: it accepts any value on the way in but forces you to narrow before use, which is exactly the discipline you want at a boundary. Turn on noImplicitAny so accidental ones are errors, and treat an explicit any as a comment-worthy decision rather than a shrug.

Inference: annotate less

The rule: annotate boundaries, infer interiors

Annotate function parameters, because there is nothing to infer them from. Annotate the return type of an exported function when you want the signature to be a deliberate contract rather than whatever the body happens to produce — it also gives better error locations, since a mistake is reported inside the function instead of at every call site. Annotate a variable initialised as empty (const items: Item[] = []), or it infers any[]. Everything else should be inferred. Over-annotation is not extra safety; it is a second copy of the truth that can disagree with the first.

Literal types and widening

typescript · why const and let infer differently
let   a = 'hello';       // string      — widened, because it can change
const b = 'hello';       // 'hello'     — a literal type, it cannot

// This matters constantly:
type Method = 'GET' | 'POST';
function request(url: string, method: Method) { }

const m = 'POST';
request('/api', m);           // ✓ m is the literal type 'POST'

let m2 = 'POST';
request('/api', m2);          // ✗ Argument of type 'string' is not
                              //   assignable to parameter of type 'Method'

// Objects widen their properties too:
const config = { method: 'POST' };        // { method: string }
request('/api', config.method);           // ✗ same error

// THREE FIXES, in ascending order of preference:
const config1 = { method: 'POST' as const };          // one property
const config2 = { method: 'POST' } as const;          // the whole object,
                                                      // deeply readonly
const config3: { method: Method } = { method: 'POST' }; // annotate

// `as const` is the one to reach for. It also turns arrays into
// readonly tuples of literals, which is how you derive a union from a
// runtime value:
const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = typeof ROLES[number];      // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'
// One source of truth: the array is iterable at runtime AND produces
// the type. Declaring both separately is how they drift apart.

Unions: the workhorse

typescript · making illegal states unrepresentable
// ✗ Three independent booleans permit eight states, four of which are
//   nonsense — loading AND error, success with no data, and so on.
//   Every consumer must handle combinations that should not exist.
interface BadState {
  isLoading: boolean;
  isError: boolean;
  data?: User[];
  error?: Error;
}

// ✓ A DISCRIMINATED UNION permits exactly four states, and each one
//   carries precisely the data that state has.
type RequestState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: User[] }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error };

function render(state: RequestState) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':    return null;
    case 'loading': return <Spinner />;
    // Inside this branch, TypeScript KNOWS `data` exists. You cannot
    // read it in the error branch, and you cannot forget to check.
    case 'success': return <List users={state.data} />;
    case 'error':   return <Error message={state.error.message} />;
  }
}

// The same technique models anything with variants:
type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
  | { kind: 'rect'; width: number; height: number };

type Result<T, E = Error> =
  | { ok: true; value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

type Action =
  | { type: 'added'; text: string }
  | { type: 'toggled'; id: string }
  | { type: 'cleared' };
// This is why useReducer and TypeScript fit so well together (R12):
// the action union makes every dispatch checked and every reducer
// branch exhaustive.

Intersections, and where they differ from extends

typescript
type WithId = { id: string };
type WithTimestamps = { createdAt: Date; updatedAt: Date };

type Entity = WithId & WithTimestamps;      // all properties of both
type User = Entity & { email: string };

// A union is "one OR the other"; an intersection is "both at once".
// Reading `&` as "and" and `|` as "or" is correct for object types —
// though note that for primitives an intersection is usually `never`,
// since nothing is both a string and a number.
type Impossible = string & number;          // never

// CONFLICTING properties produce never rather than an error, which is
// a confusing failure mode:
type A = { v: string } & { v: number };     // { v: never } — unusable

// An intersection is the composable alternative to interface
// inheritance, and it works with unions on either side:
type ButtonProps = BaseProps & (
  | { as: 'button'; onClick: () => void }
  | { as: 'a'; href: string }
);
// Now `href` is required when as='a' and forbidden otherwise — a
// pattern used constantly in React component APIs (T07).

Arrays, tuples and readonly

typescript
const names: string[] = [];
const grid: number[][] = [];
const mixed: (string | number)[] = [];        // note the parentheses
const arrays: string[] | number[] = [];       // DIFFERENT: one or the
                                              // other, not a mix

// TUPLES — fixed length, positional types. This is what useState
// returns, which is why destructuring it works:
const point: [number, number] = [0, 0];
const entry: [key: string, value: number] = ['a', 1];   // named, for
                                                        // readability only
type UseState<T> = [T, (v: T) => void];

// READONLY prevents mutation at compile time. It costs nothing at
// runtime and catches accidental sorts and pushes:
const frozen: readonly string[] = ['a'];
frozen.push('b');                  // ✗ Property 'push' does not exist
const sorted = [...frozen].sort(); // ✓ copy first (R03)

// Prefer readonly for function parameters you do not intend to
// mutate — it documents the contract and prevents a whole class of
// bug where a helper quietly sorts its caller's array in place.
function longest(items: readonly string[]) { … }
Array access lies by default

const arr: string[] = []; const first = arr[0]; gives first the type string — but at runtime it is undefined. TypeScript assumes every index is in bounds, which is unsound and is the source of a large share of “cannot read property of undefined” errors that survive into a typed codebase. Turn on noUncheckedIndexedAccess and the type becomes string | undefined, forcing a check. It is noisy on an existing codebase, which is why it is not part of strict — turn it on for new projects, where the cost is small and the payoff is exactly the errors you were hoping types would catch. The same applies to index signatures: Record<string, User> claims every key exists.

Interview follow-up

“What is the difference between any and unknown?” Both accept any value, but any turns checking off for everything downstream — property access, calls, arithmetic all compile — while unknown accepts the value and then refuses every operation until you narrow it. So unknown is what you want at a boundary: parsing JSON, a caught error, a third-party callback. The deeper point worth adding is that any is contagious — one of them can silently disable checking across a whole module — which is why noImplicitAny matters and why an explicit any should be a deliberate, commented decision rather than a way past an error message.

T03

Objects, interfaces and structural typing

TypeScript's type system is structural: a type is a description of a shape, and anything with that shape satisfies it. No implements, no inheritance, no registration. This one decision explains most of the behaviour that surprises people coming from Java or C#, including why two unrelated types can be interchangeable and why excess properties are sometimes an error and sometimes not.

Structural typing

typescript · shape is identity
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
interface Vector { x: number; y: number }

let p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 };
let v: Vector = p;           // ✓ identical shapes, interchangeable

// A class satisfies an interface without declaring that it does:
class Position { constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {} }
const q: Point = new Position(1, 2);       // ✓

// EXTRA properties are fine when the value arrives through a variable,
// because the object still HAS everything Point requires:
const labelled = { x: 1, y: 2, label: 'origin' };
const r: Point = labelled;                 // ✓

// …but NOT when it is an object literal assigned directly. This is
// EXCESS PROPERTY CHECKING, a deliberate exception to structural
// typing that exists to catch typos:
const s: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: 'origin' };
// ✗ Object literal may only specify known properties,
//   and 'label' does not exist in type 'Point'.

// Which is why this is caught:
const t: Point = { x: 1, Y: 2 };    // ✗ 'Y' does not exist … did you
                                    //   mean to write 'y'?
// and this is not:
function draw(p: Point) {}
draw(labelled);                     // ✓ — the check applies to
                                    //   literals, not to variables
Structural typing is why TypeScript fits JavaScript

JavaScript code passes object literals around constantly and rarely builds class hierarchies, so a nominal system — where a type must be explicitly declared to relate to another — would reject most correct code. Structural typing means a function asking for { name: string } accepts anything with a name, which is exactly how the underlying language behaves. The trade-off is that two semantically different things with the same shape are interchangeable: a UserId and a PostId are both string, so passing one where the other is expected compiles. When that distinction matters, brand the type — the technique at the end of this chapter.

interface or type?

interfacetype
Object shapesYesYes
UnionsNoYes
Primitives, tuples, functionsNoYes
Mapped and conditional typesNoYes
Declaration mergingYesNo
Extendingextends&
Error messagesShows the nameOften expands the shape
Recursive definitionsYesYes
typescript · the practical answer
// Use `interface` for object shapes that might be extended, and for
// anything public in a library — the error messages are better and
// consumers can augment it.
interface ButtonProps extends React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> {
  variant?: 'primary' | 'ghost';
}

// Use `type` for everything else — which in practice is most things,
// because unions are everywhere.
type Status = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'done';
type Handler = (e: Event) => void;
type Pair = [number, number];
type Nullable<T> = T | null;

// DECLARATION MERGING is the one capability only interfaces have. Two
// declarations of the same name combine, which is how you augment a
// third-party type:
declare global {
  interface Window { analytics?: { track(e: string): void } }
}
window.analytics?.track('signup');       // now typed

// It is also a footgun in application code: two interfaces with the
// same name in one scope silently merge instead of erroring, so a
// duplicated name produces a type nobody wrote. A duplicated `type`
// is a clear error.

// Pick one for consistency and stop arguing about it in review — the
// difference is small enough that the convention matters more than
// the choice.

Optional, readonly, and index signatures

typescript
interface Config {
  url: string;
  timeout?: number;            // number | undefined, and MAY BE ABSENT
  readonly key: string;        // cannot be reassigned after creation
}

// `?` and `| undefined` are NOT the same thing, and the difference
// bites under exactOptionalPropertyTypes:
interface A { x?: number }              // may be missing entirely
interface B { x: number | undefined }   // must be present, may be undefined

const a: A = {};             // ✓
const b: B = {};             // ✗ Property 'x' is missing

// INDEX SIGNATURES describe objects with dynamic keys:
interface Dictionary { [key: string]: string }
const d: Dictionary = { a: '1' };
d.anything.toUpperCase();    // ✓ compiles — and crashes, because the
                             // index signature claims every key exists

// Record is the same thing, more readable, and it accepts a key union:
type Scores = Record<string, number>;
type ByRole = Record<'admin' | 'editor', User[]>;   // exhaustive keys

// For genuinely dynamic keys, either turn on noUncheckedIndexedAccess
// or model the absence explicitly:
type Dictionary2 = Record<string, string | undefined>;
const value = d2[key];       // string | undefined — forces a check

// And for real dynamic key/value data, a Map is often the better
// structure: it has a genuine `has`, it does not inherit prototype
// keys, and its types are honest.
const cache = new Map<string, User>();
cache.get(id)?.email;        // get() returns User | undefined

Classes, briefly

typescript
class Account {
  // Parameter properties: declare and assign in one place.
  constructor(
    public readonly id: string,
    private balance: number,
    protected currency = 'GBP',
  ) {}

  // `private` is compile-time only — erased at build, so the field is
  // readable at runtime. `#private` is a real JavaScript private field
  // and is genuinely inaccessible. Prefer `#` when it matters.
  #pin: string = '';

  deposit(amount: number): this {
    if (amount <= 0) throw new RangeError('Amount must be positive');
    this.balance += amount;
    return this;                 // `this` type enables chaining in
  }                              // subclasses too

  get formatted(): string {
    return new Intl.NumberFormat('en-GB', {
      style: 'currency', currency: this.currency,
    }).format(this.balance);
  }
}

// `implements` is CHECKED but not required — structural typing means
// a class satisfies an interface by shape regardless. Use it to get
// an error at the class rather than at every use site.
class Repo implements UserRepository {
  async find(id: string) { … }
}

// In React codebases classes are rare: components are functions, and
// state lives in hooks. They still earn their place for domain
// objects with invariants, and for error subclasses (J09).

Branded types

typescript · making two strings different types
// The problem structural typing creates: these are the same type, so
// nothing stops you passing one where the other is expected.
function transfer(from: string, to: string, amount: number) {}
transfer(userId, amount, accountId);      // ✓ compiles. Wrong order.

// A BRAND is a phantom property that exists only in the type system —
// it is erased at build time and costs nothing at runtime.
declare const brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly [brand]: B };

type UserId = Brand<string, 'UserId'>;
type AccountId = Brand<string, 'AccountId'>;
type Cents = Brand<number, 'Cents'>;

function transfer(from: AccountId, to: AccountId, amount: Cents) {}

const u = 'usr_1' as UserId;
transfer(u, acct, cents);   // ✗ Type 'UserId' is not assignable to
                            //   type 'AccountId'.

// The only way to create one is through a constructor that validates,
// which makes the type a proof that validation happened:
function toCents(pounds: number): Cents {
  if (!Number.isFinite(pounds)) throw new RangeError('Not a number');
  return Math.round(pounds * 100) as Cents;
}

// Use this sparingly — for ids that get mixed up, for money, for
// values where the unit matters (Seconds vs Milliseconds), and for
// "this string has been sanitised". Branding everything is exactly the
// over-engineering T01 warned about.
Type assertions are not conversions

value as Type tells the compiler to stop checking; it performs no conversion and no validation. "5" as unknown as number compiles and gives you a string at runtime that every later operation treats as a number. Assertions are legitimate in exactly three places: narrowing something you genuinely know more about than the compiler does (a DOM query result, a branded constructor), satisfying an API whose types are wrong, and in tests. Everywhere else, prefer narrowing (T05) or a schema parse. The double assertion through unknown should be a strong smell — it is the syntax TypeScript requires precisely because it wants you to notice.

Interview follow-up

“interface or type?” The honest answer is that for object shapes they are nearly interchangeable and the team convention matters more than the choice — but show you know the real differences: only type can express unions, tuples, primitives, and mapped or conditional types, which is most of what you write; only interface supports declaration merging, which is how you augment Window or a third-party module and also a subtle hazard, since two same-named interfaces merge silently instead of erroring. If they push on structural typing, the point to make is that it is what makes TypeScript fit JavaScript — a function asking for { name: string } accepts anything with a name — and that when you need two same-shaped things to be genuinely distinct, branding with a phantom property is the technique.

T04

Functions and generics

Generics are where most people stall, usually because they are introduced as “type parameters” without saying what they are for. They exist to preserve a relationship: when the output type depends on the input type, a generic is how you say so, and the alternative is losing all type information at the boundary.

Function types

typescript
// Parameters need annotations; the return type usually infers.
function add(a: number, b: number) { return a + b; }        // : number

// Optional and default parameters — note that a default makes the
// parameter optional automatically, so `?` with a default is an error.
function greet(name: string, greeting = 'Hello', title?: string) {}

// Rest parameters are an array:
function sum(...nums: number[]) { return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }

// Function TYPES, for parameters and variables:
type Comparator = (a: string, b: string) => number;
type Handler = { (e: Event): void; cancel(): void };   // callable + props

// CONTEXTUAL TYPING is why callbacks rarely need annotations — the
// parameter types come from where the function is used:
['a', 'b'].map((s) => s.toUpperCase());   // s is string, inferred
window.addEventListener('click', (e) => e.clientX);   // MouseEvent

// OVERLOADS, for a function whose return type depends on its
// arguments in a way a single signature cannot express:
function parse(input: string): object;
function parse(input: string, raw: true): string;
function parse(input: string, raw?: boolean): object | string {
  return raw ? input : JSON.parse(input);
}
// The implementation signature is NOT callable — only the overloads
// above it are. Prefer a union or a generic where possible; overloads
// do not narrow well and are easy to get subtly wrong.

Why generics exist

The one-sentence rule for when to use a generic

Use a generic when a type appears in more than one place in a signature and those places must agree — input to output, or one parameter to another. If a type parameter is used only once, it is doing nothing that unknown would not do, and it is usually a sign of cargo-culting. function log<T>(value: T): void is just function log(value: unknown): void with extra syntax; function map<T, U>(arr: T[], fn: (t: T) => U): U[] earns every one of its parameters.

Constraints

typescript · extends narrows what T can be
// Unconstrained, you can do nothing with a T except pass it around:
function longest<T>(a: T, b: T) {
  return a.length > b.length ? a : b;   // ✗ Property 'length' does not
}                                        //   exist on type 'T'

// `extends` here means "T must be assignable to this":
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T) {
  return a.length > b.length ? a : b;   // ✓ and the return keeps T
}
longest('hello', 'hi');                  // string
longest([1, 2], [1, 2, 3]);              // number[]
longest(1, 2);                           // ✗ number has no length

// The classic: a key of an object, with the value type following.
function getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}
const user = { name: 'Sam', age: 41 };
getProperty(user, 'name');       // string
getProperty(user, 'age');        // number
getProperty(user, 'emial');      // ✗ not assignable to 'name' | 'age'

// DEFAULTS, so common cases need no explicit argument:
type ApiResult<T = unknown, E = Error> =
  | { ok: true; data: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

// Generics on types and classes work the same way:
interface Repository<T extends { id: string }> {
  find(id: string): Promise<T | null>;
  save(entity: T): Promise<T>;
}
class Queue<T> {
  #items: T[] = [];
  push(item: T) { this.#items.push(item); }
  pop(): T | undefined { return this.#items.shift(); }
}

Inference, and when to help it

typescript
// Usually you never write the type argument — it is inferred from the
// values you pass:
const nums = first([1, 2, 3]);              // T = number

// Specify it explicitly only when there is nothing to infer from, or
// when inference produces something too wide:
const empty = first<string>([]);            // T could not be inferred
const state = useState<User | null>(null);  // otherwise T = null

// A frequent trap — inference widens literals:
function pick<T>(options: T[]): T { return options[0]; }
const choice = pick(['a', 'b']);            // string, not 'a' | 'b'

// Fix with a constraint that keeps the literal type:
function pick2<const T extends string>(options: T[]): T { return options[0]; }
const choice2 = pick2(['a', 'b']);          // 'a' | 'b'
// `const` type parameters (TS 5.0) do what `as const` at the call site
// used to be needed for.

// PARTIAL INFERENCE IS ALL-OR-NOTHING: you cannot specify one type
// argument and infer the rest. A common workaround is currying:
const createStore = <S>() => <A extends Action>(reducer: (s: S, a: A) => S) => …;
createStore<AppState>()(reducer);      // S given, A inferred

Typing async functions

typescript
// An async function always returns a Promise, so annotate the RESOLVED
// type — TypeScript wraps it for you.
async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  return UserSchema.parse(await res.json());
}

// Errors are NOT in the type. TypeScript has no checked exceptions, so
// a function's signature says nothing about what it throws — which is
// one reason to return expected failures as values (J09):
async function getUser2(id: string): Promise<Result<User, 'not-found'>> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  if (res.status === 404) return { ok: false, error: 'not-found' };
  return { ok: true, value: UserSchema.parse(await res.json()) };
}
// Now the failure mode is visible in the signature and the caller
// cannot forget it.

// A caught error is `unknown` under useUnknownInCatchVariables (part
// of strict), because JavaScript can throw anything:
try { await getUser(id); }
catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return err.status;
  if (err instanceof Error) report(err.message);
  throw err;
}

// Awaited<T> unwraps nested promises — useful when deriving a type
// from an existing async function:
type User2 = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof getUser>>;   // User

A worked example

typescript · a typed fetch wrapper, built up
import { z } from 'zod';

// The schema is the single source of truth: it validates at runtime
// AND produces the type, so the two cannot drift (T01).
export async function apiGet<S extends z.ZodTypeAny>(
  path: string,
  schema: S,
  init?: RequestInit,
): Promise<z.infer<S>> {
  //        ^ the return type is DERIVED from the schema argument.
  //          This is the relationship a generic exists to express.
  const res = await fetch(path, init);
  if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status, await res.text());
  return schema.parse(await res.json());
}

const UserSchema = z.object({ id: z.string(), email: z.string().email() });

const user = await apiGet('/api/me', UserSchema);
//    ^ { id: string; email: string } — inferred, validated, and there
//      is exactly one place to change if the shape changes.

// Compare the non-generic version, which forces every caller to
// annotate and to trust that annotation:
async function apiGetBad(path: string): Promise<unknown> { … }
const user2 = await apiGetBad('/api/me') as User;   // a hope, not a check
Do not reach for generics to look sophisticated

The most common failure in typed React codebases is not missing generics; it is unnecessary ones. A type parameter used once, a wrapper generic over a type that is always the same, a helper with four parameters where one interface would do — each makes the signature harder to read, the error messages longer, and the code harder to change. Write the concrete version first. Add a type parameter only when you find yourself writing the same function twice for two types, or when a caller is forced to assert because information was lost. Generics are a tool for preserving type information, not for signalling seniority.

Interview follow-up

“What are generics for?” Say what they preserve rather than what they are: when the type of the output depends on the type of the input, a generic keeps that relationship, and without one you either fall back to any — which turns checking off everywhere downstream — or to unknown, which forces every caller to narrow. Give first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined as the minimal example and getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] as the one that shows constraints. Then add the discipline point: a type parameter used only once is doing nothing unknown would not do, so the rule is that a generic earns its place when the same type appears in two positions that must agree.

T05

Narrowing, discriminated unions and exhaustiveness

Narrowing is TypeScript following your control flow. You write an ordinary if, and inside the branch the compiler knows more than it did outside. Combined with discriminated unions and a never check, it gives you the single most valuable guarantee in the language: add a case and every place that fails to handle it stops compiling.

The narrowing operators

typescript · control flow analysis, in full
function handle(value: string | number | string[] | null | Date) {
  // typeof — for primitives
  if (typeof value === 'string') value.toUpperCase();
  if (typeof value === 'number') value.toFixed(2);

  // Array.isArray — the built-in guard for arrays
  if (Array.isArray(value)) value.join(', ');

  // instanceof — for classes and built-ins
  if (value instanceof Date) value.getTime();

  // TRUTHINESS — convenient, and a trap: it also excludes '' and 0,
  // which are usually valid values.
  if (value) { /* excludes null, '', 0, NaN */ }
  if (value !== null) { /* excludes null only — usually what you want */ }
  if (value != null) { /* excludes null AND undefined, using == */ }
}

// `in` — for object shapes without a discriminant
type Fish = { swim(): void };
type Bird = { fly(): void };
function move(animal: Fish | Bird) {
  if ('swim' in animal) animal.swim();
  else animal.fly();
}

// EQUALITY narrows both sides:
function compare(a: string | number, b: string | boolean) {
  if (a === b) {
    // both must be string, since that is the only overlap
    a.toUpperCase(); b.toUpperCase();
  }
}

// ASSIGNMENT narrows too — the declared type constrains what is
// allowed, but the CURRENT type follows the last assignment:
let x: string | number = 'hello';
x.toUpperCase();         // ✓ x is string here
x = 42;
x.toFixed();             // ✓ x is number here

Discriminated unions

typescript · the pattern that makes narrowing mechanical
// A DISCRIMINANT is a literal-typed property shared by every member
// with a different value in each. Switching on it narrows perfectly.
type Shape =
  | { kind: 'circle'; radius: number }
  | { kind: 'square'; size: number }
  | { kind: 'rect'; width: number; height: number };

function area(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
    case 'square': return shape.size ** 2;
    case 'rect':   return shape.width * shape.height;
  }
}
// Inside each branch, only that member's properties exist. Reading
// `shape.radius` in the 'square' case is an error, and you cannot
// forget which fields belong to which variant.

// The discriminant must be a LITERAL type, which is why this fails:
type Bad =
  | { kind: string; radius: number }      // ✗ not a literal
  | { kind: string; size: number };       //   no narrowing possible

// It does not have to be called `kind` — `type`, `status`, `ok` and
// `state` are all common, and a boolean works for two variants:
type Result<T, E> =
  | { ok: true; value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

function unwrap<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>): T {
  if (r.ok) return r.value;        // narrowed by a boolean literal
  throw r.error;
}

Exhaustiveness with never

typescript · the guarantee worth the whole chapter
function assertNever(value: never, message = 'Unhandled case'): never {
  // `never` is the type with no values. If the compiler can reach this
  // line, it means some union member was not handled — and it tells
  // you exactly which one, by name, in the error.
  throw new Error(`${message}: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

function area(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
    case 'square': return shape.size ** 2;
    case 'rect':   return shape.width * shape.height;
    default:       return assertNever(shape);
  }
}

// NOW add a member to Shape:
//   | { kind: 'triangle'; base: number; height: number }
//
// ✗ Argument of type '{ kind: "triangle"; … }' is not assignable to
//   parameter of type 'never'.
//
// Every switch in the codebase that does not handle triangles fails
// to compile, pointing at the exact line. That is the property that
// makes unions safe to extend in a large codebase — and it is
// impossible to get from a `string` type or an enum of strings you
// switch on loosely.

// The same works with if/else chains and with a mapped lookup:
const AREA: Record<Shape['kind'], (s: any) => number> = {
  circle: (s) => Math.PI * s.radius ** 2,
  square: (s) => s.size ** 2,
  rect:   (s) => s.width * s.height,
};
// Record over a key union is exhaustive by construction: omit a key
// and it does not compile. Often cleaner than a switch, and it is how
// you build a handler table.
This is the argument for unions over enums

A union of string literals gives you exhaustiveness, autocompletion, zero runtime cost (it erases completely), and values that are just strings — so they serialise, compare and log naturally. A TypeScript enum emits a runtime object, has confusing numeric-enum reverse mapping, is nominally typed in a structurally typed language, and const enum breaks under isolated-modules transpilers such as esbuild and SWC, which is what most build tools now use. If you want a runtime list as well, use as const on an array and derive the union from it (T02) — one source of truth, both capabilities.

Type predicates

typescript · teaching the compiler your own guards
// A normal boolean function does NOT narrow:
function isString(v: unknown) { return typeof v === 'string'; }
if (isString(x)) x.toUpperCase();     // ✗ x is still unknown

// `v is T` makes it a type predicate — the compiler trusts it:
function isString(v: unknown): v is string { return typeof v === 'string'; }
if (isString(x)) x.toUpperCase();     // ✓

// The classic use — filtering out nullish values, which TypeScript
// cannot narrow through `filter` on its own:
const maybe: (User | null)[] = [user1, null, user2];

const bad = maybe.filter((u) => u !== null);      // still (User | null)[]
const good = maybe.filter((u): u is User => u !== null);   // User[]
// TypeScript 5.5 infers this for simple predicates, so `bad` now works
// in newer versions — but the explicit form is still needed for
// anything the inference cannot follow.

// A guard for a discriminated union member:
function isError<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>): r is Extract<Result<T, E>, { ok: false }> {
  return !r.ok;
}

// ASSERTION FUNCTIONS narrow for the rest of the scope rather than a
// branch — note they require an explicit type annotation on the
// declaration, not just an arrow function:
function assertIsUser(v: unknown): asserts v is User {
  if (!UserSchema.safeParse(v).success) throw new TypeError('Not a User');
}
assertIsUser(data);
data.email;        // ✓ narrowed from here on

// ⚠ A predicate is an UNCHECKED PROMISE. Nothing verifies that the
// body actually implements the check, so a wrong one is a silent lie:
function isUser(v: unknown): v is User { return v !== null; }   // ✗ lies
// Prefer deriving guards from a schema, where the check and the type
// come from the same definition.

Where narrowing gets lost

typescript · the four cases that surprise people
// 1 · A CALLBACK RESETS IT. The compiler cannot know whether the
//     callback runs now or later, or whether something reassigned the
//     variable in between.
function f(value: string | null) {
  if (value === null) return;
  value.toUpperCase();                    // ✓
  setTimeout(() => value.toUpperCase());  // ✓ for a const/param…
  items.forEach(() => value.toUpperCase());
}
// …but for a `let` that is reassigned anywhere, narrowing is
// discarded inside closures. The fix is a const:
const v = value;   // narrowed and immutable

// 2 · OPTIONAL PROPERTY ACCESS does not persist across statements when
//     the object could have changed:
if (obj.user) {
  obj.user.name;                 // ✓ same expression, still narrowed
  doSomething();
  obj.user.name;                 // ✓ still fine — TS assumes no mutation
}
// But through a function boundary or a getter, it is not:
if (getUser()) getUser().name;   // ✗ two separate calls

// 3 · ARRAY ACCESS IS NOT NARROWED by a length check:
if (arr.length > 0) arr[0].toUpperCase();
// ✓ under default settings, ✗ under noUncheckedIndexedAccess —
// and the strict version is correct, because the check does not
// prove the element is defined. Use `const first = arr[0]; if (first)`.

// 4 · DESTRUCTURING BREAKS DISCRIMINATION in older versions — you
//     cannot destructure the discriminant and the payload separately
//     and still narrow. TypeScript 4.6+ handles the common case:
const { kind, ...rest } = shape;
if (kind === 'circle') rest.radius;   // ✗ — narrow first, then use
if (shape.kind === 'circle') { const { radius } = shape; }   // ✓

A React example

typescript · the request state from T02, made exhaustive
type State<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error; retry: () => void };

export function Async<T>({ state, children }: {
  state: State<T>;
  children: (data: T) => React.ReactNode;
}) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
      return null;
    case 'loading':
      return <Skeleton />;
    case 'error':
      // `retry` exists only here, so it cannot be called in a state
      // where it would be undefined.
      return <ErrorPanel message={state.error.message} onRetry={state.retry} />;
    case 'success':
      // `data` exists only here, and is typed as T.
      return <>{children(state.data)}</>;
    default:
      return assertNever(state);
  }
}

// Add a 'refreshing' status later and this component — and every other
// consumer of State — fails to compile until it is handled. That is
// the refactoring safety people mean when they say TypeScript scales.
Interview follow-up

“What is a discriminated union and why use one?” A union whose members share a literal-typed property with a distinct value in each, so switching on it narrows to exactly one member and you can only access the fields that member actually has. The reason to use one is that it makes illegal states unrepresentable — three booleans permit eight combinations, half of them nonsense, while a four-member union permits four. Then take it further with the part that wins the point: add a default: assertNever(value) branch, and because never has no values, adding a new member causes every incomplete switch in the codebase to fail compilation, naming the unhandled case. That is the property that makes a union safe to extend, and it is also the main reason to prefer string-literal unions to enum.

T06

Utility types and type-level programming

TypeScript's type system is itself a small functional language: you can map over types, branch on them, and pull pieces out of them. Most days you need only the dozen built-in utilities. The machinery underneath is worth understanding because it explains why they work — and because knowing when not to use it is the more valuable skill.

The utilities you will actually use

UtilityDoesTypical use
Partial<T>All properties optionalA patch or update payload
Required<T>All properties requiredAfter filling defaults
Readonly<T>All properties readonlyFrozen config, props
Pick<T, K>Keep only these keysA narrow view of a model
Omit<T, K>Remove these keysStrip id for a create payload
Record<K, V>Object with keys K, values VLookup tables, handler maps
Exclude<U, M>Remove members from a unionNarrow a union of literals
Extract<U, M>Keep matching membersPull one variant out
NonNullable<T>Remove null and undefinedAfter a guard
ReturnType<F>What F returnsDeriving from existing code
Parameters<F>F's parameters, as a tupleWrapping a function
Awaited<T>Unwrap a promiseAsync return types
typescript · in practice
interface User {
  id: string; email: string; name: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer';
  createdAt: Date;
}

// Derive, do not duplicate. Every one of these stays correct when
// User changes.
type NewUser = Omit<User, 'id' | 'createdAt'>;
type UserPatch = Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>;
type UserSummary = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>;
type Role = User['role'];                        // indexed access
type Privileged = Exclude<Role, 'viewer'>;       // 'admin' | 'editor'
type UsersByRole = Record<Role, User[]>;

// Derive from VALUES too — often better than declaring a type and
// hoping the implementation matches it:
const DEFAULTS = { pageSize: 20, sort: 'createdAt', dir: 'desc' } as const;
type Params = typeof DEFAULTS;                   // the value's type
type SortDir = typeof DEFAULTS['dir'];           // 'desc'

type User2 = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof getUser>>;
type LoadArgs = Parameters<typeof loadPage>;
Omit does not check its keys, and that is a real bug source

Omit<User, 'emial'> compiles happily and silently omits nothing, so a typo leaves the property in place and nobody notices until runtime. Pick does check, because its keys are constrained to keyof T; Omit's are deliberately not, to support some library patterns. If it matters, use a checked version — type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> — and note the same looseness in Exclude, which quietly returns the original union when nothing matches.

keyof, typeof and indexed access

typescript · the three building blocks
// keyof — the union of an object type's keys
type UserKey = keyof User;         // 'id' | 'email' | 'name' | 'role' | …

// typeof (in type position) — the type of a VALUE
const config = { retries: 3, timeout: 5000 };
type Config = typeof config;       // { retries: number; timeout: number }

// Indexed access — look up a property's type
type Email = User['email'];        // string
type Either = User['email' | 'name'];   // string
type Values = User[keyof User];    // the union of ALL value types

// Arrays: index with `number` to get the element type
const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = typeof ROLES[number];  // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'
// ↑ the single most useful idiom in this chapter: one array that is
// both iterable at runtime and the source of the type.

// Together they give you the canonical typed-getter signature (T04):
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { return obj[key]; }

Mapped types

typescript · transforming every property
// This is how Partial and Readonly are defined — there is no magic:
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type MyReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };

// Modifiers can be REMOVED with a minus sign:
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type Concrete<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };     // this is Required

// KEY REMAPPING with `as` builds new names:
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};
type UserGetters = Getters<Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>>;
// { getName: () => string; getEmail: () => string }

// Mapping to `never` FILTERS keys out:
type OnlyStrings<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K];
};
type StringFields = OnlyStrings<User>;   // { email: string; name: string;
                                          //   role: … }

// A genuinely useful one — deep readonly for config objects:
type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (infer R)[]
  ? readonly DeepReadonly<R>[]
  : T extends object
    ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
    : T;

Conditional types and infer

typescript · branching at the type level
// `T extends U ? X : Y` — read `extends` as "is assignable to".
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type A = IsString<'hello'>;        // true
type B = IsString<42>;             // false

// `infer` captures a type from a position, like a destructuring
// pattern for types. This is how ReturnType is defined:
type MyReturnType<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type MyElement<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type MyAwaited<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? MyAwaited<V> : T;

// DISTRIBUTION: a conditional over a NAKED type parameter applies to
// each union member separately, which is how Exclude works…
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
type C = MyExclude<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'b'>;    // 'a' | 'c'

// …and is also the behaviour that surprises people. Wrap in a tuple
// to switch it off:
type IsUnion<T> = [T] extends [string] ? 'all strings' : 'mixed';

// TEMPLATE LITERAL TYPES do string manipulation:
type EventName<T extends string> = `on${Capitalize<T>}`;
type Handlers = EventName<'click' | 'focus'>;      // 'onClick' | 'onFocus'

type Route = `/users/${string}`;
type CssVar = `--${string}`;

// Parsing with infer + template literals:
type PathParams<P extends string> =
  P extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | PathParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : P extends `${string}:${infer Last}` ? Last : never;

type Params = PathParams<'/users/:userId/posts/:postId'>;
// 'userId' | 'postId'  — a typed router in a dozen characters

A realistic example

typescript · a typed event emitter
// The payload type follows the event name — the kind of relationship
// generics exist for (T04), expressed with a mapped type.
type Events = {
  'user:signed-in': { userId: string; at: Date };
  'cart:item-added': { productId: string; qty: number };
  'app:error': { error: Error };
};

class Emitter<E extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  #handlers: { [K in keyof E]?: Set<(payload: E[K]) => void> } = {};

  on<K extends keyof E>(event: K, handler: (payload: E[K]) => void) {
    (this.#handlers[event] ??= new Set()).add(handler);
    return () => this.#handlers[event]!.delete(handler);
  }

  emit<K extends keyof E>(event: K, payload: E[K]) {
    this.#handlers[event]?.forEach((h) => h(payload));
  }
}

const bus = new Emitter<Events>();

bus.on('user:signed-in', (p) => p.userId);      // p is fully typed
bus.emit('cart:item-added', { productId: 'p1', qty: 2 });   // ✓
bus.emit('cart:item-added', { productId: 'p1' });           // ✗ missing qty
bus.emit('user:signd-in', { … });                            // ✗ typo caught

Knowing when to stop

Type-level programming has a real cost, and it is paid by everyone else

A clever conditional type produces error messages that fill the screen and name types nobody wrote, so a junior colleague hitting it has no path forward. Deeply recursive types slow the compiler measurably and can hit the instantiation-depth limit in a way that only appears as the codebase grows. And a type that encodes a rule the runtime does not enforce gives false confidence. The test before writing one: would a plain interface, a union, or a runtime check do the job? If yes, do that. Type-level machinery earns its place in a library's public API, where one difficult type buys ergonomics for thousands of call sites — and rarely in application code, where the same effort is better spent on a Zod schema that also checks at runtime.

Two practical habits
