Derive, do not duplicate. Anywhere you would write a second type that must match a first, use Pick, Omit, ReturnType, typeof or z.infer instead, so the two cannot drift. Name your intermediate types. A chain of four inline conditionals is unreadable and produces unreadable errors; three named aliases with one step each are as fast to compile and can be hovered individually in the editor. And when you do reach for something exotic, leave a comment saying what it does — it is the one place in a TypeScript codebase where a comment is almost always warranted.

Interview follow-up

“What are conditional types and infer?” A conditional type branches on assignability — T extends U ? X : Y — and infer captures a type from a position inside the pattern, the way destructuring captures a value. Show ReturnType being defined in one line, since that demonstrates both at once. Then add distribution, which is the behaviour that separates people who have read about this from people who have debugged it: a conditional over a naked type parameter applies to each union member individually, which is how Exclude works and also why a type you expected to return one thing returns a union — and wrapping both sides in a tuple turns it off. Finish with judgement: this machinery belongs in library APIs, and in application code a plain union plus a runtime schema is almost always the better trade.

T07

TypeScript with React

React and TypeScript fit together well, and the friction points are few and specific: how to type props so a component's API is honest, which hooks need help from you, how to type events and refs without importing the wrong thing, and the two or three patterns — polymorphic components, discriminated props — that come up in every component library.

Props

typescript · components/button.tsx
import { type ComponentPropsWithoutRef, type ReactNode } from 'react';

// EXTEND THE UNDERLYING ELEMENT. This gives you every native
// attribute — onClick, disabled, aria-*, data-*, form, name — with
// correct types, without listing any of them.
interface ButtonProps extends ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> {
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost';
  size?: 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg';
  loading?: boolean;
  icon?: ReactNode;
}

export function Button({
  variant = 'primary', size = 'md', loading, icon,
  children, className, disabled, ...rest
}: ButtonProps) {
  return (
    <button
      className={cn('btn', `btn-${variant}`, `btn-${size}`, className)}
      disabled={disabled || loading}
      {...rest}
    >
      {loading ? <Spinner /> : icon}
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

// ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>  — props, no ref
// ComponentPropsWithRef<'button'>     — props including ref
// ComponentProps<typeof MyComponent>  — another component's props
//
// In React 19 `ref` is an ordinary prop (N06), so
// ComponentPropsWithRef is the one you usually want for a component
// that forwards a ref — and forwardRef is no longer needed.

// DO NOT USE React.FC. It adds nothing, historically forced an
// implicit `children`, and interferes with generic components.
const Bad: React.FC<Props> = ({ … }) => …;      // ✗
function Good({ … }: Props) { … }                // ✓

Children and the node types

typescript · which one to use
interface Props {
  children: React.ReactNode;        // ✓ almost always this: anything
                                    //   renderable — string, number,
                                    //   element, array, null, boolean
  header: React.ReactElement;       // exactly one element, not a string
  render: (item: Item) => React.ReactNode;    // a render prop
  icon: React.ComponentType<{ size?: number }>;  // a COMPONENT, to be
                                                  // rendered by you
}

// Optional children — a component that may or may not wrap content:
interface CardProps { children?: React.ReactNode }

// `JSX.Element` is narrower than ReactNode and excludes strings,
// numbers, null and arrays — so it rejects perfectly valid children.
// Use ReactNode unless you specifically need a single element.

// A component that renders another component, not an element:
function Field({ as: Component = 'input', ...rest }: {
  as?: React.ElementType;
} & ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'input'>) {
  return <Component {...rest} />;
}

Hooks

typescript · the four that need help
// useState — inferred from the initial value, so annotate only when
// the initial value is narrower than the state will be.
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);                 // number ✓
const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);   // needed: else null
const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([]);        // needed: else never[]
const [state, setState] = useState<State>({ status: 'idle' });
//     ↑ annotate with the union so later statuses are assignable (T05)

// useRef has three distinct forms and the difference matters:
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);   // a DOM ref —
                                                   // readonly .current
const timerRef = useRef<number | undefined>(undefined);  // a mutable box
const countRef = useRef(0);                        // mutable, inferred

inputRef.current?.focus();      // always optional-chain: null until
                                // the commit phase, and null after
                                // unmount (R10)

// useReducer — annotate through the reducer, not the hook. Given a
// typed reducer, state and dispatch both follow:
type Action =
  | { type: 'added'; text: string }
  | { type: 'toggled'; id: string };

function reducer(state: State, action: Action): State { … }
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);
dispatch({ type: 'added', text: 'x' });     // ✓ checked
dispatch({ type: 'addd', text: 'x' });      // ✗ typo caught

// useContext — the null-check boilerplate, solved once:
const ThemeContext = createContext<Theme | null>(null);

export function useTheme() {
  const ctx = useContext(ThemeContext);
  // This throw is also a TYPE NARROWING: the return type is Theme,
  // not Theme | null, so no consumer needs a null check.
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useTheme must be used within ThemeProvider');
  return ctx;
}

// Custom hooks — return a tuple `as const` so destructuring names are
// free and the types stay positional rather than widening to a union:
function useToggle(initial = false) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = useCallback(() => setOn((v) => !v), []);
  return [on, toggle] as const;        // readonly [boolean, () => void]
}
const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle();
Three hook typing traps

useState([]) infers never[], so pushing anything into it is an error with a confusing message — annotate the element type. useRef<T>(null) versus useRef<T | null>(null): the first is the DOM-ref form and gives a readonly current that React assigns; the second is a mutable box you assign yourself. Using the first and then writing to .current is an error, and using the second on a JSX ref attribute works but loses the intent. The useState updater takes the previous state, so setUser(u => ({ ...u, name })) fails when u can be null — narrow first, or model the state so it cannot be.

Events

typescript · let them infer, annotate when you must
// INLINE handlers are contextually typed — never annotate these:
<button onClick={(e) => e.currentTarget.blur()} />       // e inferred
<input onChange={(e) => setValue(e.target.value)} />     // e inferred

// EXTRACTED handlers need the type, and these are the ones to know:
function onClick(e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) {}
function onChange(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {}
function onSubmit(e: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {}
function onKeyDown(e: React.KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {}
function onFocus(e: React.FocusEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {}

// Or derive it from the element, which never goes out of date:
type ClickHandler = React.ComponentProps<'button'>['onClick'];

// target vs currentTarget — a real distinction, not a synonym:
//   currentTarget  the element the handler is ATTACHED to (typed)
//   target         the element that was actually clicked (EventTarget,
//                  so it needs narrowing — a click on a button may
//                  originate on a span inside it)
function onClick(e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) {
  e.currentTarget.disabled = true;      // ✓ typed as the button
  (e.target as HTMLElement).closest('li');   // target needs narrowing
}

// FormData from a submit, which is the idiomatic uncontrolled read:
function onSubmit(e: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const data = new FormData(e.currentTarget);
  const email = data.get('email');       // FormDataEntryValue | null
  const parsed = LoginSchema.parse(Object.fromEntries(data));   // ✓ typed
}

Generic components

typescript · a list that keeps its item type
interface ListProps<T> {
  items: readonly T[];
  getKey: (item: T) => string;
  renderItem: (item: T, index: number) => React.ReactNode;
  empty?: React.ReactNode;
}

// A plain function declaration takes type parameters naturally. This
// is another reason not to use React.FC, which cannot express this.
export function List<T>({ items, getKey, renderItem, empty }: ListProps<T>) {
  if (items.length === 0) return <>{empty ?? <p>Nothing here yet.</p>}</>;
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item, i) => <li key={getKey(item)}>{renderItem(item, i)}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}

// T is inferred from `items`, and flows into both callbacks:
<List
  items={users}
  getKey={(u) => u.id}            // u: User
  renderItem={(u) => u.email}     // u: User
/>

// In a .tsx file, `const List = <T,>(props) => …` needs the trailing
// comma, or the parser reads <T> as a JSX tag. A function declaration
// avoids the problem entirely.

Discriminated props

typescript · making an invalid combination unwritable
// The problem: a component that is sometimes a link and sometimes a
// button. With optional props, both `href` and `onClick` are always
// allowed, and the invalid combinations compile.
type BadProps = { href?: string; onClick?: () => void };   // ✗

// A UNION makes the relationship explicit (T02, T05):
type ActionProps =
  | { as: 'button'; onClick: () => void; href?: never }
  | { as: 'a'; href: string; onClick?: never };
//                            ^ `never` explicitly FORBIDS the other
//                              variant's prop, which is what produces
//                              a clear error rather than silence

function Action(props: ActionProps & { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  if (props.as === 'a') return <a href={props.href}>{props.children}</a>;
  return <button onClick={props.onClick}>{props.children}</button>;
}

<Action as="a" href="/x">Go</Action>              // ✓
<Action as="button" onClick={fn}>Go</Action>      // ✓
<Action as="a" onClick={fn}>Go</Action>           // ✗ good

// Same technique for a controlled/uncontrolled API, or for a
// component where one prop unlocks others:
type InputProps =
  | { multiline: true; rows?: number }
  | { multiline?: false; rows?: never };

Polymorphic components

typescript · the `as` prop, done properly
// A component that can render as any element and still accept that
// element's props. This is the one genuinely advanced pattern in
// React typing, and it appears in every design system.
type PolymorphicProps<E extends React.ElementType, P> = P & {
  as?: E;
} & Omit<React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<E>, keyof P | 'as'>;
//    ^ Omit prevents a collision when the element has a prop of the
//      same name as one of yours

interface TextOwnProps {
  size?: 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg';
  weight?: 'normal' | 'bold';
}

export function Text<E extends React.ElementType = 'span'>({
  as, size = 'md', weight = 'normal', ...rest
}: PolymorphicProps<E, TextOwnProps>) {
  const Component = as ?? 'span';
  return <Component className={cn(`text-${size}`, `font-${weight}`)} {...rest} />;
}

<Text>default span</Text>
<Text as="h1" size="lg">A heading</Text>
<Text as="a" href="/about">A link</Text>      // href is valid only here
<Text as="span" href="/about">nope</Text>     // ✗ correctly rejected

// Worth knowing, worth using sparingly: the error messages when it
// goes wrong are long, and a simple union of two concrete components
// is often the better trade (T06).
Type the props, let everything else infer

The productive default in a React codebase is: annotate the props interface, annotate a useState only when its initial value is narrower than its eventual type, and annotate nothing else. Return types of components, event parameters on inline handlers, callback parameters passed to map, and the results of hooks all infer correctly. Every additional annotation is a second copy of the truth that can disagree with the first — and in React, where a component's real contract is its props, the props interface is the one place a deliberate annotation genuinely earns its keep.

Interview follow-up

“How do you type a React component's props?” Define an interface and extend the underlying element's props — interface ButtonProps extends ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> — so every native attribute, ARIA prop and data attribute comes through correctly without listing any of them. Then say why you do not use React.FC: it adds nothing, historically forced an implicit children, and cannot express a generic component. If they push for something harder, the discriminated-props pattern is the best thing to show — modelling “either href or onClick, never both” as a union with never on the opposing branch, so an invalid combination is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise.

T08

End-to-end type safety in Next.js

A Next.js app has four or five boundaries where data enters: the URL, a form, an API response, a webhook, and the environment. Each is where a type annotation becomes a lie. This chapter is about pushing real, runtime-checked types across all of them so that a rename in the database surfaces as a compile error in the component.

The chain

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ DATABASE Prisma / Drizzle / Kysely generate types │ │ ↓ from the schema — inferred, not written │ │ DATA LAYER functions return those types │ │ ↓ │ │ SERVER COMPONENT await → fully typed, no boundary at all │ │ ↓ │ │ CLIENT COMPONENT props — checked, but must be serializable│ │ ↓ │ │ SERVER FUNCTION FormData is UNTYPED → parse with a schema│ │ ↓ │ │ DATABASE │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Two of these links are free and three are not. Free: database → data layer → Server Component → props. The App Router's biggest typing win is that there is no serialization boundary to re-declare: a Server Component awaits a typed function and passes typed props (N04). NOT free, because the value arrives as `unknown` or as strings: · URL params and searchParams · FormData in a Server Function · fetch() responses from anything you do not own · process.env · webhooks At each of those, parse — do not assert. The schema produces the type; the annotation does not produce the data (T01).

The schema is the source of truth

typescript · lib/schemas.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const CreatePostSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().trim().min(1, 'Title is required').max(200),
  body: z.string().trim().min(1).max(50_000),
  tags: z.array(z.string().max(30)).max(10).default([]),
  publishAt: z.coerce.date().optional(),
  // coerce is what turns a form's string into a Date, a number or a
  // boolean — FormData values are always strings.
});

// ONE declaration, used three ways:
export type CreatePost = z.infer<typeof CreatePostSchema>;
//   ↑ the TypeScript type, derived
//   → CreatePostSchema.parse()  validates on the server
//   → the same schema validates on the client for instant feedback
//
// Declaring `interface CreatePost` separately and hoping it matches
// the schema is exactly the drift this avoids.

// Input vs output types differ when you use defaults or transforms:
type Input = z.input<typeof CreatePostSchema>;    // tags optional
type Output = z.infer<typeof CreatePostSchema>;   // tags: string[]
// Use `input` for what a caller may send and `infer` for what your
// code receives after parsing.

Typed Server Functions

typescript · app/posts/actions.ts
'use server';

// The return type is a discriminated union, so the client cannot read
// `fields` without checking that it failed (T05, X07).
export type ActionState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string; fields?: Record<string, string[]>;
      values?: Record<string, string> }
  | { status: 'success'; id: string };

export async function createPost(
  _prev: ActionState,
  formData: FormData,
): Promise<ActionState> {
  const session = await auth();
  if (!session) return { status: 'error', message: 'You must be signed in.' };

  // FormData is entirely untyped — every value is a string or a File.
  // safeParse returns a discriminated union, so narrowing is automatic.
  const parsed = CreatePostSchema.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return {
      status: 'error',
      message: 'Please fix the errors below.',
      fields: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors,
      values: Object.fromEntries(formData) as Record<string, string>,
    };
  }

  // parsed.data is CreatePost — validated, coerced and typed.
  const post = await db.post.create({
    data: { ...parsed.data, authorId: session.userId },
  });
  revalidateTag('posts');
  return { status: 'success', id: post.id };
}
typescript · the client side, fully typed
'use client';
import { useActionState } from 'react';
import { createPost, type ActionState } from './actions';

export function PostForm() {
  // useActionState infers the state type from the action's signature,
  // so `state` is ActionState with no annotation needed.
  const [state, action, isPending] = useActionState<ActionState, FormData>(
    createPost,
    { status: 'idle' },
  );

  return (
    <form action={action}>
      {/* Narrowing means `message` is only accessible here */}
      {state.status === 'error' && <p role="alert">{state.message}</p>}

      <input name="title" defaultValue={
        state.status === 'error' ? state.values?.title : undefined
      } />
      {state.status === 'error' && state.fields?.title &&
        <p className="err">{state.fields.title[0]}</p>}

      <button disabled={isPending}>{isPending ? 'Publishing…' : 'Publish'}</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Route params and search params

typescript · app/posts/[slug]/page.tsx
// In Next.js 15 both are Promises (X02), and both are UNVALIDATED
// user input — a `params.id` is whatever was in the URL.
export default async function Page({
  params,
  searchParams,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
  searchParams: Promise<Record<string, string | string[] | undefined>>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;

  // Parse search params rather than reading them raw: this gives you
  // defaults, coercion, and protection against a hand-edited URL.
  const SearchSchema = z.object({
    page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
    sort: z.enum(['newest', 'oldest', 'popular']).default('newest'),
    tag: z.string().max(30).optional(),
  });
  const query = SearchSchema.parse(await searchParams);
  //    ↑ { page: number; sort: 'newest' | …; tag?: string }

  const post = await getPost(slug);       // typed by the data layer
  if (!post) notFound();
  return <Article post={post} query={query} />;
}

// TYPED ROUTES catch broken links at build time — a genuinely
// valuable Next.js feature that is off by default:
// next.config.ts →  { typedRoutes: true }
<Link href="/posts/hello">      // ✓
<Link href="/postz/hello">      // ✗ not assignable to type 'Route'

// And `next typegen` / the generated .next/types give you PageProps
// helpers so the param shape is derived from the folder structure
// rather than hand-written.

Route handlers and external data

typescript · app/api/posts/route.ts
export async function POST(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  // request.json() returns `any` — the most dangerous return type in
  // the standard library, because it silently disables checking
  // downstream (T02).
  let raw: unknown;
  try {
    raw = await request.json();
  } catch {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Invalid JSON' }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const parsed = CreatePostSchema.safeParse(raw);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: 'Validation failed', fields: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors },
      { status: 422 },
    );
  }
  const post = await db.post.create({ data: parsed.data });
  return Response.json(post, { status: 201 });
}

// Consuming an API you do NOT control — the annotation is a lie, the
// parse is a fact:
async function getRates(): Promise<Rates> {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/rates');
  if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status);
  return RatesSchema.parse(await res.json());
  //     ↑ if they rename a field, this throws HERE with a clear
  //       message, instead of producing undefined four components away
}

Environment variables

typescript · lib/env.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

// process.env is Record<string, string | undefined> — every value is
// possibly undefined and always a string, which is why `PORT * 2` is
// a type error and `FEATURE_X === 'true'` is a string comparison.
const server = z.object({
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
  SESSION_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: z.string().startsWith('sk_'),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000),
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']),
});

const client = z.object({
  NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL: z.string().url(),
});

// Parse at module load, so a missing variable fails the BOOT rather
// than the first request that happens to need it (X12).
export const env = {
  ...server.parse(process.env),
  ...client.parse({ NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL }),
};
// NEXT_PUBLIC_ values must be referenced by their full literal name or
// the build-time inlining does not happen (X12) — which is why the
// client object is spelled out rather than spread from process.env.

// Import this from next.config.ts too, so `next build` fails in CI
// when a deployment environment is missing something.
import 'server-only';   // and make sure the server half never ships
The rule that makes all of this work: parse, don't assert

as User tells the compiler to stop asking questions. UserSchema.parse(data) tells the program to check. They look similar in the editor and they are opposites in production: the assertion produces a type that is true only if you were right, while the parse produces a type that is true because it was verified. Every as on data that crossed a network, a form, a URL or a storage API is a place where a backend rename becomes a silent undefined three components away instead of a clear error at the boundary. The cost is a few kilobytes of schema library and a few microseconds per request; the benefit is that your types stop being a hope.

Typed data access

typescript · let the ORM generate the types
// Prisma generates types from the schema, and the SELECTION shapes
// the result — so a query selecting three columns returns a type with
// exactly those three, not the full model with the rest undefined.
const post = await db.post.findUnique({
  where: { slug },
  select: {
    id: true, title: true, body: true,
    author: { select: { name: true, avatarUrl: true } },
  },
});
// post: { id: string; title: string; body: string;
//         author: { name: string; avatarUrl: string | null } } | null

// Derive the type instead of re-declaring it, so it follows the query:
type PostWithAuthor = NonNullable<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof getPost>>>;

export async function getPost(slug: string) { … }

// In the component, no annotation at all:
export default async function Page({ params }) {
  const post = await getPost((await params).slug);
  if (!post) notFound();
  return <Article post={post} />;     // Article's props: PostWithAuthor
}

// Drizzle and Kysely do the same with `$inferSelect` / `Selectable<T>`.
// The principle is identical: the database schema is the origin of the
// types, and every layer above derives from it. Rename a column and
// the error appears at every use site — which is the whole point.
Interview follow-up

“What does end-to-end type safety mean in practice?” That a change at one end — a renamed database column, a changed API field — produces a compile error at the other, rather than an undefined at runtime. Then be specific about where it is free and where it is not: in the App Router, database → data layer → Server Component → props is genuinely checked end to end, because there is no serialization boundary to re-declare. The links that are not free are the ones where data arrives untyped — URL params, FormData, response.json(), process.env, webhooks — and at each of those the rule is parse, don't assert: define a schema, infer the TypeScript type from it, and validate at the boundary, so there is one source of truth and the one that runs is the one that checks.

T09

Configuration, strictness and migrating a codebase

Two thirds of the value of TypeScript is decided by tsconfig.json. A project with strict off is running a fundamentally weaker checker — null is assignable to everything, implicit any is everywhere — and most complaints that “TypeScript did not catch it” trace back to a flag.

A working config

json · tsconfig.json for a Next.js app
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "lib": ["DOM", "DOM.Iterable", "ES2022"],
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",

    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "noUnusedParameters": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,

    "jsx": "preserve",
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,

    "noEmit": true,
    "incremental": true,
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] },
    "plugins": [{ "name": "next" }]
  },
  "include": ["next-env.d.ts", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", ".next/types/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules"]
}

What strict actually turns on

FlagCatches
strictNullChecksThe important one. Without it null and undefined are assignable to every type, so the most common runtime error in JavaScript is invisible.
noImplicitAnyA parameter or variable the compiler could not infer, silently becoming any
strictFunctionTypesUnsafe callback parameter variance (function-type syntax only, not methods)
strictBindCallApplyWrong arguments to bind, call and apply
strictPropertyInitializationA class field never assigned in the constructor
noImplicitThisthis of unknown type in a standalone function
useUnknownInCatchVariablesTreating a caught error as any — it becomes unknown (J09)
alwaysStrictEmits "use strict"
The three flags outside strict that are worth it

noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes arr[i] and record[key] return T | undefined, which is the truth — by default TypeScript assumes every index is in bounds, and that single assumption accounts for a large share of the “cannot read property of undefined” errors that survive into typed code. It is noisy to adopt, which is why it is not in strict; turn it on for new projects. exactOptionalPropertyTypes distinguishes “absent” from “present and undefined”, which matters when you spread a patch object over a record. verbatimModuleSyntax forces import type for type-only imports, which prevents a whole class of bundler bug where an import kept alive purely for its types drags a module into the runtime build.

Module resolution and import type

typescript
// moduleResolution: "bundler" is what you want for anything built by
// Vite, webpack, esbuild or Next.js — it follows package `exports`
// maps and does not require file extensions in imports.
// "node16"/"nodenext" is for code Node runs directly, and it DOES
// require extensions and respects the package `type` field.

// verbatimModuleSyntax makes this distinction load-bearing:
import type { User } from './types';        // erased entirely
import { parseUser } from './parse';         // kept at runtime
import { type Config, loadConfig } from './config';   // mixed

// Why it matters: without the `type` keyword, a bundler cannot always
// tell that an import exists only for types, so it keeps the module in
// the graph. On the server that can pull a database client into a
// client bundle; in Next.js it can turn a Server Component's helper
// into a build error about `fs` not being available in the browser.

// isolatedModules requires each file to be transpilable ALONE, which
// is what esbuild and SWC do. It bans a few things:
export { SomeType };              // ✗ ambiguous — is it a type?
export type { SomeType };         // ✓
const enum Direction { Up }       // ✗ needs cross-file information

Declaration files

typescript · types/global.d.ts
// A .d.ts file declares types with no implementation. You need one
// for three things.

// 1 · A LIBRARY THAT SHIPS NO TYPES. Try @types/<name> first; only
//     write this if it does not exist.
declare module 'untyped-legacy-lib' {
  export function doThing(input: string): Promise<number>;
  const _default: { version: string };
  export default _default;
}
// The lazy escape hatch, when you only need it to compile:
declare module 'some-lib';        // everything from it is `any`

// 2 · NON-CODE IMPORTS your bundler handles:
declare module '*.svg' {
  const content: React.FC<React.SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>>;
  export default content;
}

// 3 · AUGMENTING an existing type. This uses declaration merging,
//     which is why these must be `interface` (T03):
declare global {
  interface Window {
    analytics?: { track(event: string, props?: Record<string, unknown>): void };
  }
  namespace NodeJS {
    interface ProcessEnv {
      DATABASE_URL: string;       // prefer the zod approach in T08 —
    }                              // this only makes the type nicer,
  }                                // it does not check anything
}

// Augmenting a third-party module — adding a field to a session type:
declare module 'next-auth' {
  interface Session { user: { id: string; role: 'admin' | 'user' } }
}

export {};    // REQUIRED in a .d.ts that uses `declare global` inside
              // a module — without an import or export the file is a
              // script and `declare global` is an error.

Migrating a JavaScript codebase

Do not rewrite. Convert, file by file, with the build green the whole way. 1 · Turn it on, permissively "allowJs": true, "checkJs": false, "strict": false Rename nothing yet. The build must still pass. 2 · Type the shared foundations first The utilities and models that everything imports. Typing a leaf component first gives you almost nothing; typing the API client gives every caller autocomplete immediately. 3 · Rename .js → .ts, one file per pull request Fix what the compiler finds. Use `any` freely at this stage — an `any` you can grep for later is better than a stalled migration. Mark them: // TODO(ts): tighten 4 · Turn on strict flags one at a time, repo-wide noImplicitAny first, then strictNullChecks — which is the expensive one and also the one worth the most. A per-file escape hatch exists: // @ts-nocheck at the top. 5 · Ratchet Add "strict": true only once the count reaches zero, then forbid regressions in CI. A lint rule banning new `any` and new `@ts-ignore` is what makes the gains permanent. JSDoc as a stepping stone — full type checking in .js files, no build step, and it survives if the migration stalls: /** @param {string} id @returns {Promise<User>} */ export async function getUser(id) { … } /** @type {import('./types').Config} */ const config = { … };

Escape hatches, ranked

typescript · least bad to worst
// 1 · NARROW IT. Almost always possible, and always the right answer.
if (typeof value === 'string') value.toUpperCase();

// 2 · A SCHEMA PARSE. At a boundary, this is not an escape hatch at
//     all — it is the correct solution (T08).
const user = UserSchema.parse(data);

// 3 · A TYPE ASSERTION, with a comment saying why you know better.
const input = e.target as HTMLInputElement;   // the handler is on the
                                              // input itself

// 4 · NON-NULL ASSERTION. Fine when the invariant is local and
//     obvious; a landmine when it is three files away.
document.getElementById('root')!;             // mounted in index.html

// 5 · @ts-expect-error — better than @ts-ignore, ALWAYS. It errors if
//     the line stops failing, so it cleans itself up after an upgrade.
// @ts-expect-error — upstream types are wrong, see issue #412
legacyLib.doThing(input);

// 6 · `any`. Contagious (T02). If you must, contain it in one function
//     with a typed signature so the looseness cannot spread:
function parseLegacy(raw: unknown): Config {
  const data = raw as any;                 // one place, one line
  return { url: String(data.url), retries: Number(data.retries) };
}

// NEVER: @ts-nocheck on a file you are actively developing, and
// "strict": false to make an error go away.
skipLibCheck: true is almost always correct, and worth understanding

It skips type-checking .d.ts files in node_modules. That sounds unsafe and is not: your own code is still fully checked against those types. What it skips is checking the libraries' declarations against each other, which in a real dependency tree means conflicts between two versions of the same @types package — errors you cannot fix and that have nothing to do with your code. It is in the default Next.js config, it dramatically speeds up compilation, and turning it off is a well-known way to spend an afternoon on other people's type definitions.

Keeping type checking fast

ProblemFix
Slow full checksincremental: true plus a cached tsBuildInfoFile in CI
Editor lag on a large repoProject references, splitting the app into composite projects
One file takes secondsUsually a deeply recursive or heavily unioned type (T06) — name intermediates, or simplify
Slow buildsThey are separate concerns: esbuild and SWC strip types without checking, so run tsc --noEmit in CI and let the bundler transpile
Finding the culprittsc --generateTrace, or --extendedDiagnostics for a summary
Regressions creeping intsc --noEmit as a required CI check, plus a lint rule against new any
Interview follow-up

“What does strict do, and would you turn it on?” Yes, always, on any new project — and name the flag that matters most: strictNullChecks, because without it null and undefined are assignable to every type and TypeScript's single most valuable check is switched off. List two or three of the others, then show judgement about the ones outside strict: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is correct and noisy, so it belongs in new projects rather than as a day-one change to a large existing one. If the question turns to migration, the answer is incremental — allowJs, convert the shared foundations first, rename one file per pull request, enable strict flags one at a time repo-wide, and ratchet with a CI check so the gains cannot regress.

T10

The TypeScript interview

TypeScript questions sort candidates faster than React questions do, because there is a clear line between people who have used it and people who understand it. The line is almost always the same: knowing that types are erased at build time, and reasoning correctly from that fact.

The dividing question

The core questions

“any vs unknown vs never.”
any switches checking off and is contagious — everything it touches becomes any, so one of them can silently disable a module. unknown is the safe top type: it accepts any value but permits no operation until you narrow, which is exactly what you want for parsed JSON or a caught error. never is the bottom type, with no values: the return type of a function that always throws, and the tool for exhaustiveness checks. (T02)
“interface or type?”
For object shapes, nearly interchangeable — say that first, because pretending there is a big difference is a tell. Only type can express unions, tuples, primitives and mapped or conditional types, which is most of what you write. Only interface supports declaration merging, which is how you augment Window or a third-party module — and which is also why two same-named interfaces merge silently instead of erroring. (T03)
“What is structural typing?”
A type is a shape, so anything with that shape satisfies it — no implements, no inheritance, no registration. It is what makes TypeScript fit JavaScript, where object literals are passed around constantly. The consequence worth naming is that two semantically different things with the same shape are interchangeable — a UserId and a PostId are both string — and branding with a phantom property is how you separate them when it matters. (T03)
“What is a discriminated union and why use one?”
A union whose members share a literal-typed property with a distinct value in each, so switching on it narrows to exactly one member. It makes illegal states unrepresentable: three booleans permit eight combinations, half nonsense, while a four-member union permits four. Then go further — a default: assertNever(x) branch means adding a member breaks every incomplete switch at compile time, naming the case. (T05)
“What are generics for?”
Preserving a relationship: when the output type depends on the input type, a generic says so, and without one you lose the information to any or push narrowing onto every caller. Give first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined, then getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] for constraints. Add the discipline: a type parameter used only once does nothing unknown would not do. (T04)
“Explain keyof, typeof and indexed access.”
keyof T is the union of T's keys; typeof value (in type position) is the type of a value; T['key'] looks up a property's type. The idiom worth showing is const ROLES = [...] as const; type Role = typeof ROLES[number] — one array that is both iterable at runtime and the source of the union, so the two cannot drift. (T06)
“What are conditional types and infer?”
T extends U ? X : Y branches on assignability; infer captures a type from a position inside the pattern. Define ReturnType in one line to show both. Then mention distribution — a conditional over a naked type parameter applies to each union member separately, which is how Exclude works and also why a type unexpectedly returns a union; wrapping both sides in a tuple turns it off. (T06)
“How do you type a React component?”
An interface extending the underlying element's props — extends ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> — so every native attribute and ARIA prop comes through typed without listing any. Not React.FC: it adds nothing, historically forced an implicit children, and cannot express a generic component. The advanced answer is discriminated props: modelling “either href or onClick, never both” as a union. (T07)
“How do you handle data from an API?”
Parse, do not assert. res.json() returns any, so annotating the return type is a claim nothing verified — if the backend renames a field you get undefined three components away rather than an error at the boundary. Define a schema, validate at the boundary, and infer the TypeScript type from the schema so there is one source of truth and it is the one that runs. (T01, T08)
“What does strict do?”
Enables eight flags, of which strictNullChecks is the one that matters most — without it null and undefined are assignable to every type, which disables the check that catches the most common runtime error in JavaScript. Show judgement about what is not in strict: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is correct but noisy, so it belongs in new projects rather than as a day-one change to a large existing one. (T09)

The unsoundness question

“Can TypeScript be wrong about a type?” — say yes, and list the holes

This is the question that most reliably separates depth from familiarity, because the expected answer is “no, that is the point”. The correct answer is that TypeScript is deliberately unsound, because closing the holes would reject too much correct JavaScript. any and type assertions are you overriding the checker. Array and index-signature access is typed as T rather than T | undefined, so arr[99] on a three-element array type-checks — fixed by noUncheckedIndexedAccess. Method-syntax parameter bivariance lets an unsafe callback through. Mutable array covariance means a Dog[] is assignable to Animal[], which can then have a Cat pushed into it. And anything crossing a runtime boundary is whatever actually arrived. Each is a considered trade, and knowing them is what lets you decide where a runtime check is genuinely needed.

Exercises that come up

typescript · write these on a whiteboard
// 1 · Implement the common utility types. These test whether you know
//     mapped and conditional types, and they are short.
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type MyRequired<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };
type MyOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = MyPick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>;
type MyReturnType<F> = F extends (...a: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;

// 2 · A deep readonly / deep partial — tests recursion and the array
//     case, which most candidates forget.
type DeepPartial<T> = T extends (infer E)[]
  ? DeepPartial<E>[]
  : T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } : T;

// 3 · Type a function whose return depends on an argument.
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { return obj[key]; }

// 4 · Exhaustiveness — they will add a variant and expect a compile
//     error, not a runtime one.
function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error(`Unhandled: ${x}`); }

// 5 · Make an invalid prop combination impossible.
type Props =
  | { variant: 'link'; href: string; onClick?: never }
  | { variant: 'button'; onClick: () => void; href?: never };

// 6 · Type a debounce that preserves the wrapped function's signature —
//     tests Parameters, ReturnType and `this`.
function debounce<F extends (...args: any[]) => void>(fn: F, ms: number) {
  let t: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>;
  return function (this: ThisParameterType<F>, ...args: Parameters<F>) {
    clearTimeout(t);
    t = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), ms);
  };
}

The mixed-up pairs

ConfusedThe distinction
unknown vs anyBoth accept anything; only any permits every operation afterwards
never vs voidnever never returns at all; void returns, with an unusable value
x?: T vs x: T | undefinedMay be absent vs must be present, possibly undefined
as vs a schema parseOverriding the compiler vs actually checking
enum vs a literal unionRuntime object, nominal, breaks isolated modules vs erased, structural, exhaustive
Pick vs OmitPick checks its keys; Omit silently accepts a typo
extends in a constraint vs in a conditional“Must be assignable to” vs “is assignable to?”
type import vs value importErased vs kept in the bundle — matters for client/server boundaries
Declaring a type vs inferring oneTwo sources of truth that can disagree vs one

What they are really testing

Behind the specific questions, four things: 1 · Do you know types are erased? Everything about validation, boundaries and runtime safety follows from this one fact. 2 · Can you model data so bad states cannot exist? Unions over booleans, narrow types over `string`, derived types over duplicated ones. 3 · Do you know when to stop? A candidate who reaches for a recursive conditional type where an interface would do is a liability, not an asset. Saying "I'd just use a union here" scores well. 4 · Can you work with imperfect types? Real codebases have untyped libraries, wrong @types, and legacy `any`. Knowing @ts-expect-error over @ts-ignore, and containing an `any` inside a typed function, shows you have shipped something.
The strongest single thing you can say

When a question touches data coming from anywhere outside your own code, say: “I would define a Zod schema, validate at the boundary, and infer the TypeScript type from the schema.” It answers the question, demonstrates that you know types are erased, removes the drift between a declared type and the real shape, and shows you have thought about where safety actually comes from. It is one sentence and it covers API responses, forms, URL params, environment variables and webhooks.

Questions worth asking them

“Is strict on, and are there files with @ts-nocheck?” tells you whether the types are real or decorative. “How do you validate API responses?” tells you whether they know the difference between an annotation and a check. “Is the type checker a required CI step?” tells you whether errors accumulate. And “how did the migration go, if there was one?” is the question that gets you an honest description of the codebase's health — nobody describes a painless migration, so the answer is usually candid.

B01

useLocalStorage, done properly

Every codebase has one of these and most of them are wrong in the same five ways. It is a good first implementation chapter because the naive version looks obviously correct, works in development, and then fails in private browsing, on the server, and in a second tab.

The naive version, and what breaks

javascript · five bugs in nine lines
function useLocalStorage(key, initial) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(
    JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key)) ?? initial    // 1, 2, 3
  );
  useEffect(() => {
    localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value));   // 4
  }, [key, value]);
  return [value, setValue];                             // 5
}

// 1 · READS ON EVERY RENDER. useState's argument is evaluated each
//     time and thrown away after the first — a synchronous disk read
//     per render.
// 2 · THROWS ON BAD JSON. One malformed value (a half-written entry, a
//     value written by an older version) and the component crashes on
//     mount, permanently, until the user clears site data.
// 3 · CRASHES ON THE SERVER. `localStorage` is undefined in Node, so
//     this breaks SSR entirely — and in the browser it can still throw
//     in private mode or with site data blocked.
// 4 · WRITES ON MOUNT. The first effect run writes the value it just
//     read, which is pointless, and it also writes the fallback for a
//     key the user never set.
// 5 · NO CROSS-TAB SYNC. Two tabs drift apart silently, and whichever
//     writes last wins with no indication to the other.

The corrected version

javascript · hooks/use-local-storage.ts
import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';

export function useLocalStorage(key, initialValue, {
  serialize = JSON.stringify,
  deserialize = JSON.parse,
} = {}) {
  // LAZY INITIALISER: runs once. And it must return the SAME value the
  // server rendered, or hydration mismatches — see the note below.
  const [value, setValue] = useState(() => read(key, initialValue, deserialize));

  // Keep the key in a ref so the setter does not need it as a
  // dependency and therefore stays referentially stable.
  const keyRef = useRef(key);
  useEffect(() => { keyRef.current = key; }, [key]);

  const set = useCallback((update) => {
    setValue((prev) => {
      // Support the updater form, exactly like useState.
      const next = typeof update === 'function' ? update(prev) : update;
      try {
        if (next === undefined) {
          window.localStorage.removeItem(keyRef.current);
        } else {
          window.localStorage.setItem(keyRef.current, serialize(next));
        }
        // The `storage` event fires only in OTHER tabs, never the one
        // that wrote. Dispatch our own so same-tab subscribers of the
        // same key stay in sync too.
        window.dispatchEvent(new StorageEvent('storage', {
          key: keyRef.current,
          newValue: next === undefined ? null : serialize(next),
        }));
      } catch (err) {
        // QuotaExceededError, private mode, blocked site data. The
        // in-memory value is still correct; only persistence failed.
        console.warn(`useLocalStorage: could not write "${keyRef.current}"`, err);
      }
      return next;
    });
  }, [serialize]);

  // Re-read when the key changes, and subscribe to changes from
  // anywhere — other tabs via the native event, this tab via ours.
  useEffect(() => {
    setValue(read(key, initialValue, deserialize));

    const onStorage = (e) => {
      // e.key === null means the whole store was cleared.
      if (e.key !== null && e.key !== key) return;
      setValue(read(key, initialValue, deserialize));
    };
    window.addEventListener('storage', onStorage);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('storage', onStorage);
  }, [key]);   // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

  return [value, set];
}

function read(key, fallback, deserialize) {
  // Guard for SSR and for environments where access itself throws.
  if (typeof window === 'undefined') return fallback;
  try {
    const raw = window.localStorage.getItem(key);
    return raw === null ? fallback : deserialize(raw);
  } catch {
    return fallback;      // corrupt JSON or blocked storage: fall back
  }                       // rather than crash the component
}
The hydration problem, and the only honest fixes

With SSR, the server has no access to the user's storage, so it must render the fallback. If the client's first render reads the stored value instead, the two trees differ and React reports a hydration mismatch — and in React 18 it would discard and re-render the whole subtree. There are exactly two correct approaches. Two-pass: render the fallback on the first client render too, then update in an effect — correct, but the user sees a flash of the default (light theme, collapsed sidebar). Blocking inline script: a tiny script in <head> that reads storage and sets a class or data attribute on <html> before first paint, with CSS doing the work — no flash, no mismatch, because React never renders the difference. Themes should use the second; almost everything else is fine with the first.

The useSyncExternalStore version

javascript · the modern, tear-free implementation
import { useCallback, useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';

// localStorage IS an external store, so React has a purpose-built hook
// for it. This version cannot tear under concurrent rendering, and
// getServerSnapshot makes the SSR contract explicit rather than
// accidental.
const listeners = new Set();
const cache = new Map();          // key -> last parsed value

function emit(key) {
  cache.delete(key);
  listeners.forEach((l) => l());
}

function subscribe(listener) {
  listeners.add(listener);
  const onStorage = () => { cache.clear(); listener(); };
  window.addEventListener('storage', onStorage);
  return () => {
    listeners.delete(listener);
    window.removeEventListener('storage', onStorage);
  };
}

export function useLocalStorageSync(key, initialValue) {
  // getSnapshot MUST return a referentially stable value when nothing
  // changed, or React re-renders in an infinite loop. That is what the
  // cache Map is for — JSON.parse returns a new object every call.
  const getSnapshot = useCallback(() => {
    if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
    let parsed = initialValue;
    try {
      const raw = window.localStorage.getItem(key);
      parsed = raw === null ? initialValue : JSON.parse(raw);
    } catch { /* fall through to the default */ }
    cache.set(key, parsed);
    return parsed;
  }, [key, initialValue]);

  const getServerSnapshot = useCallback(() => initialValue, [initialValue]);

  const value = useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot);

  const set = useCallback((update) => {
    const next = typeof update === 'function' ? update(getSnapshot()) : update;
    try {
      next === undefined
        ? window.localStorage.removeItem(key)
        : window.localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(next));
    } catch (err) {
      console.warn('useLocalStorage: write failed', err);
    }
    emit(key);                    // notify this tab immediately
  }, [key, getSnapshot]);

  return [value, set];
}
The getSnapshot infinite loop

This is the one bug this version introduces if you are careless. useSyncExternalStore calls getSnapshot on every render and compares the result with Object.is; if it differs, it re-renders. JSON.parse returns a new object every time, so an uncached snapshot function means every render produces a different value, which schedules another render, forever — React will eventually throw “The result of getSnapshot should be cached”. Cache the parsed value and invalidate the cache only when storage actually changes, exactly as above.

Versioning and migration

javascript · because the shape you persist today is not the shape you want next year
// Stored data outlives your code. A user who last visited six months
// ago has whatever shape you were writing then, and it will arrive in
// your component as though it were current.
const MIGRATIONS = {
  1: (old) => ({ ...old, density: 'comfortable' }),      // v0 -> v1
  2: (old) => ({ ...old, columns: old.cols ?? [], cols: undefined }),
};
const CURRENT = 2;

function readVersioned(key, fallback) {
  try {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
    if (!raw) return fallback;
    let { version = 0, data } = JSON.parse(raw);
    while (version < CURRENT) {
      version += 1;
      data = MIGRATIONS[version](data);
    }
    return data;
  } catch {
    localStorage.removeItem(key);      // unrecoverable: discard it
    return fallback;
  }
}

// And VALIDATE what comes back, because storage is user-writable —
// anyone can open devtools and put anything in there:
const parsed = PreferencesSchema.safeParse(readVersioned(key, defaults));
const prefs = parsed.success ? parsed.data : defaults;

When not to use it

SituationUse insteadWhy
Auth tokens, session statehttpOnly cookiesReadable by any script on the page — an XSS becomes a full account takeover
Anything the server must readA cookieStorage is never sent with requests; the server cannot see it
More than a few hundred KBIndexedDB~5 MB origin limit, and every access is synchronous — large reads block the main thread
Data that must survive reliablyThe serverCleared by private mode, storage pressure, and the user's cleanup tools
Per-tab statesessionStorageLocal storage is shared across every tab on the origin
Anything personal or sensitiveDo not persist itIt survives logout and stays on shared machines
Good uses are small, non-authoritative and disposable

A collapsed sidebar, a chosen theme, a table's column widths, a dismissed banner, a draft comment, the last-used filter. The test is simple: if the value vanished, would the user lose anything more than a small convenience? If the answer is yes, it belongs on the server. Treat local storage as a cache of preferences, never as a database.

Interview follow-up

“Write useLocalStorage.” Write the straightforward version, then walk through its failure modes before being asked — the lazy initialiser so it does not read on every render, try/catch on both read and write because malformed JSON and blocked storage both throw, an SSR guard, and the storage event for cross-tab sync with the detail that it does not fire in the tab that wrote. If they push further, the strong finish is hydration: the server cannot know the stored value, so either you accept a flash and update in an effect, or you set a class on <html> from a blocking inline script before first paint.

B02

useWindowSize and responsive rendering

Tracking the viewport in JavaScript is easy to write and easy to write badly: a resize listener that fires two hundred times a second, a server render that crashes on window, and a hydration mismatch because the server guessed desktop and the user is on a phone. The chapter also argues for doing less of this — most responsive behaviour belongs in CSS.

The hook

javascript · hooks/use-window-size.ts
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export function useWindowSize() {
  // SSR: there is no window, so start undefined and let the first
  // effect fill it in. Do NOT read window during render — it crashes
  // on the server and it makes the component impure.
  const [size, setSize] = useState({ width: undefined, height: undefined });

  useEffect(() => {
    let frame = 0;

    const measure = () => {
      // rAF-throttle: resize fires far faster than the browser paints,
      // and setting state per event means dozens of wasted renders per
      // frame. One update per frame is the most that can ever be seen.
      cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
      frame = requestAnimationFrame(() => {
        setSize((prev) =>
          // Bail out if nothing changed, so a resize that ends on the
          // same width does not re-render the tree.
          prev.width === window.innerWidth && prev.height === window.innerHeight
            ? prev
            : { width: window.innerWidth, height: window.innerHeight });
      });
    };

    measure();                          // initial read, after mount
    window.addEventListener('resize', measure, { passive: true });
    window.addEventListener('orientationchange', measure);

    return () => {
      cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
      window.removeEventListener('resize', measure);
      window.removeEventListener('orientationchange', measure);
    };
  }, []);

  return size;
}
The first render is always “unknown”, and your UI must handle it

Because the server cannot know the viewport, width is undefined on the server and on the client's first render. Branching on it — width < 768 ? <MobileNav/> : <DesktopNav/> — means the server renders one tree, the client hydrates with the same one, and then an effect swaps it: a visible flash, a layout shift, and a wasted mount of the wrong component. Either render both and let CSS hide one, or render a neutral placeholder of the correct height until width is defined. A hook like this is for behaviour that genuinely cannot be expressed in CSS, not for choosing which component to render.

Prefer matchMedia for breakpoints

javascript · hooks/use-media-query.ts
import { useSyncExternalStore, useCallback } from 'react';

// A breakpoint question does not need the pixel count. matchMedia
// fires only when the ANSWER changes — twice while dragging a window
// across 768px, not four hundred times.
export function useMediaQuery(query, serverValue = false) {
  const subscribe = useCallback((onChange) => {
    const mql = window.matchMedia(query);
    mql.addEventListener('change', onChange);
    return () => mql.removeEventListener('change', onChange);
  }, [query]);

  const getSnapshot = useCallback(() => window.matchMedia(query).matches, [query]);
  const getServerSnapshot = useCallback(() => serverValue, [serverValue]);

  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot);
}

// Usage:
const isDesktop = useMediaQuery('(min-width: 1024px)');
const reduceMotion = useMediaQuery('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');
const isDark = useMediaQuery('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)');
const isCoarse = useMediaQuery('(pointer: coarse)');   // touch, not width
const canHover = useMediaQuery('(hover: hover)');

// `pointer` and `hover` are the right questions for "is this a touch
// device" — a narrow desktop window is not a phone, and a tablet with
// a keyboard is not a phone either. Width is a poor proxy for input
// capability, and this is where most device detection goes wrong.

// Boolean snapshots are primitives, so there is no getSnapshot caching
// problem here (B01) — true and false are always referentially equal.

Element size, which is usually what you actually want

javascript · hooks/use-element-size.ts
import { useState, useCallback, useRef, useEffect } from 'react';

// A chart, a virtualised list, a truncating label — these care about
// the size of THEIR BOX, not the window. An element can change size
// because a sibling appeared, a font loaded, or a panel collapsed,
// none of which fire a window resize event.
export function useElementSize() {
  const [size, setSize] = useState({ width: 0, height: 0 });
  const observerRef = useRef(null);

  // A CALLBACK REF, not useRef + useEffect: this runs the moment the
  // node attaches, and again if it is replaced — a ref object's
  // assignment triggers nothing (R10).
  const ref = useCallback((node) => {
    observerRef.current?.disconnect();
    if (!node) return;

    const ro = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
      // contentBoxSize is the modern field; contentRect is the
      // fallback. Read from the entry rather than calling
      // getBoundingClientRect, which forces a synchronous layout.
      const box = entry.contentBoxSize?.[0];
      const width = box ? box.inlineSize : entry.contentRect.width;
      const height = box ? box.blockSize : entry.contentRect.height;
      setSize((p) => (p.width === width && p.height === height
        ? p : { width, height }));
    });
    ro.observe(node);
    observerRef.current = ro;
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => () => observerRef.current?.disconnect(), []);

  return [ref, size];
}

// Usage:
const [ref, { width }] = useElementSize();
return <div ref={ref}>{width > 600 ? <WideChart /> : <NarrowChart />}</div>;

// ResizeObserver loop warning: if the callback changes the size of the
// element it observes, the browser logs "ResizeObserver loop completed
// with undelivered notifications". Setting React state is fine — it
// happens on the next render — but synchronously writing a style to
// the observed node is not.

The mobile viewport, which lies

javascript · visualViewport and the 100vh problem
// On mobile, `100vh` is the viewport with the browser chrome HIDDEN,
// so a full-height element is taller than the screen and the bottom is
// cut off. The CSS fix came first and is better:
//    height: 100dvh;    /* dynamic — shrinks with the address bar   */
//    height: 100svh;    /* small  — always the smallest possible    */
//    height: 100lvh;    /* large  — always the largest              */

// For the on-screen keyboard, which does not change innerHeight on
// iOS, use visualViewport:
export function useVisualViewport() {
  const [vp, setVp] = useState({ height: 0, offsetTop: 0, keyboardOpen: false });

  useEffect(() => {
    const v = window.visualViewport;
    if (!v) return;
    const onChange = () => setVp({
      height: v.height,
      offsetTop: v.offsetTop,
      // A crude but reliable heuristic: the visual viewport is much
      // shorter than the layout viewport.
      keyboardOpen: window.innerHeight - v.height > 150,
    });
    onChange();
    v.addEventListener('resize', onChange);
    v.addEventListener('scroll', onChange);
    return () => {
      v.removeEventListener('resize', onChange);
      v.removeEventListener('scroll', onChange);
    };
  }, []);

  return vp;
}
// The usual reason to need this: a fixed bottom toolbar that must sit
// above the keyboard rather than behind it.

Do it in CSS where you can

Reach for a hook only when CSS genuinely cannot answer the question

CSS handles it correctly on the first paint, with no JavaScript, no re-render and no hydration concern — and container queries mean a component can respond to its own box rather than the window, which is what most “responsive component” code was trying to approximate. Use a hook when the decision is behavioural rather than visual: how many rows a virtualised list should render, whether to open a drawer or a modal, whether to enable a drag interaction on a coarse pointer, or how many items to fetch. Those cannot be expressed as a stylesheet.

Interview follow-up

“Write a hook that tracks the window size.” Write it, then improve it unprompted: throttle with requestAnimationFrame because resize fires faster than the browser paints, bail out when the value is unchanged, guard for SSR, and clean up both listeners. The senior signal is what you say next — that for a breakpoint you should use matchMedia, which only fires when the answer changes; that for an element you should use ResizeObserver, because a window listener misses a sibling collapsing; and that most of the time the right answer is a media or container query in CSS, which is correct on the first paint and costs no JavaScript at all.

B03

useFetch and a query cache from scratch

This is the most-written custom hook in React and the one most likely to be subtly broken. We will build it in three stages — a correct single-request hook, then deduplication and caching, then revalidation — and finish with an honest account of what is still missing, which is the argument for not writing it yourself.

Stage 1 — one request, correctly

javascript · hooks/use-fetch.ts
import { useState, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react';

export function useFetch(url, { enabled = true, ...init } = {}) {
  // ONE status field, not three booleans. Three booleans permit
  // impossible states — loading AND error at once — and every consumer
  // then has to handle combinations that should never exist.
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: enabled ? 'loading' : 'idle' });
  const [attempt, setAttempt] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!enabled) { setState({ status: 'idle' }); return; }

    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState((s) => (s.status === 'success'
      // Keep the old data visible while refetching, so the UI does not
      // flash back to a skeleton on every revalidation.
      ? { ...s, status: 'refreshing' }
      : { status: 'loading' }));

    fetch(url, { ...init, signal: controller.signal })
      .then(async (res) => {
        // fetch does NOT reject on 4xx or 5xx (J09). Without this
        // check, a 500 returning an HTML error page becomes a JSON
        // parse error somewhere far away.
        if (!res.ok) {
          const body = await res.text().catch(() => '');
          const err = new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
          err.status = res.status; err.body = body;
          throw err;
        }
        return res.status === 204 ? null : res.json();
      })
      .then((data) => setState({ status: 'success', data }))
      .catch((error) => {
        // An abort is not a failure — it is us cancelling. Showing an
        // error for it produces a flash of "something went wrong" on
        // every navigation.
        if (error.name === 'AbortError') return;
        setState({ status: 'error', error });
      });

    // THE RACE GUARD. Without this, type "rea" then "react": if the
    // first response is slower it lands last and the screen shows
    // results for the wrong query. Intermittent, and never
    // reproducible locally.
    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [url, enabled, attempt]);   // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

  const refetch = useCallback(() => setAttempt((a) => a + 1), []);

  return {
    ...state,
    isLoading: state.status === 'loading',
    isError: state.status === 'error',
    refetch,
  };
}
Three things this already gets right that most versions do not

The res.ok check — fetch only rejects on network failure, CORS or abort, so a 404 flows straight into .json(). Ignoring AbortError — cancelling is normal, and treating it as an error means every navigation flashes a failure message. Keeping data during a refetch — jumping back to a skeleton whenever the data revalidates is jarring, and a separate refreshing status lets you show a subtle indicator instead. Beyond that, the init object being in the closure but not in the dependency array is a deliberate compromise: an inline options object would re-run the effect every render. A real library solves this with an explicit key, which is the next stage.

Stage 2 — a cache with deduplication

javascript · lib/query-cache.ts
// The problem with stage 1: three components mounting at once fire
// three identical requests, and navigating away and back refetches
// from scratch. Both are fixed by a cache keyed by request identity.

const cache = new Map();      // key -> entry
const subs  = new Map();      // key -> Set of listeners

const now = () => Date.now();

function getEntry(key) {
  if (!cache.has(key)) {
    cache.set(key, { status: 'idle', data: undefined, error: undefined,
                     updatedAt: 0, promise: null });
  }
  return cache.get(key);
}

function notify(key) {
  subs.get(key)?.forEach((fn) => fn());
}

export function subscribe(key, listener) {
  if (!subs.has(key)) subs.set(key, new Set());
  subs.get(key).add(listener);
  return () => {
    const set = subs.get(key);
    set.delete(listener);
    // Garbage collection: drop cached data nobody is watching, after a
    // grace period, so navigating back within a few minutes is instant
    // but memory does not grow without bound.
    if (set.size === 0) {
      setTimeout(() => { if (subs.get(key)?.size === 0) cache.delete(key); },
                 5 * 60_000);
    }
  };
}

export function getSnapshot(key) {
  return getEntry(key);          // a STABLE object reference — required
}                                // by useSyncExternalStore (B01)

export function fetchQuery(key, fetcher, { staleTime = 0, force = false } = {}) {
  const entry = getEntry(key);

  // DEDUPLICATION: an identical request already in flight? Return the
  // same promise instead of starting another.
  if (entry.promise) return entry.promise;

  // Fresh enough? Do nothing at all.
  if (!force && entry.status === 'success' && now() - entry.updatedAt < staleTime) {
    return Promise.resolve(entry.data);
  }

  const controller = new AbortController();
  entry.status = entry.status === 'success' ? 'refreshing' : 'loading';
  entry.abort = () => controller.abort();
  notify(key);

  entry.promise = Promise.resolve(fetcher({ signal: controller.signal }))
    .then((data) => {
      cache.set(key, { ...entry, status: 'success', data, error: undefined,
                       updatedAt: now(), promise: null });
      notify(key);
      return data;
    })
    .catch((error) => {
      if (error.name === 'AbortError') { entry.promise = null; return; }
      cache.set(key, { ...entry, status: 'error', error, promise: null });
      notify(key);
      throw error;
    });

  return entry.promise;
}

export function invalidate(prefix) {
  // Invalidate by key PREFIX, so a mutation can say "anything about
  // posts is now stale" without listing every page and filter.
  for (const key of cache.keys()) {
    if (key.startsWith(prefix)) {
      const e = cache.get(key);
      cache.set(key, { ...e, updatedAt: 0 });
      if (subs.get(key)?.size) fetchQuery(key, e.fetcher, { force: true });
      else notify(key);
    }
  }
}

export function setQueryData(key, updater) {
  const e = getEntry(key);
  const data = typeof updater === 'function' ? updater(e.data) : updater;
  cache.set(key, { ...e, status: 'success', data, updatedAt: now() });
  notify(key);                   // the basis of optimistic updates
}

The hook on top of it

javascript · hooks/use-query.ts
import { useSyncExternalStore, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react';
import { subscribe, getSnapshot, fetchQuery, invalidate } from '@/lib/query-cache';

export function useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn, staleTime = 30_000, enabled = true }) {
  // The KEY is the cache identity. Serialising it means an object of
  // params works and order does not matter if you sort it.
  const key = JSON.stringify(queryKey);

  const sub = useCallback((l) => subscribe(key, l), [key]);
  const snap = useCallback(() => getSnapshot(key), [key]);
  const entry = useSyncExternalStore(sub, snap, snap);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (enabled) fetchQuery(key, queryFn, { staleTime });
  }, [key, enabled]);   // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

  // REVALIDATE ON FOCUS AND RECONNECT: a tab left open for an hour is
  // showing stale data, and the user's first action is usually to
  // trust it. This single behaviour is why libraries feel "live".
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!enabled) return;
    const revalidate = () => {
      if (document.visibilityState === 'visible') {
        fetchQuery(key, queryFn, { staleTime });
      }
    };
    window.addEventListener('visibilitychange', revalidate);
    window.addEventListener('online', revalidate);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('visibilitychange', revalidate);
      window.removeEventListener('online', revalidate);
    };
  }, [key, enabled]);   // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

  return {
    data: entry.data,
    error: entry.error,
    status: entry.status,
    isPending: entry.status === 'loading',
    isRefreshing: entry.status === 'refreshing',
    refetch: () => fetchQuery(key, queryFn, { force: true }),
  };
}

// Usage — and note the shape is now deliberately TanStack-compatible,
// so replacing this with the real thing is a single import change.
const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['posts', { tag, page }],
  queryFn: ({ signal }) => getPosts({ tag, page, signal }),
  staleTime: 60_000,
});

Mutations, with rollback

javascript
export function useMutation({ mutationFn, onMutate, onError, onSettled }) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle' });

  const mutate = useCallback(async (vars) => {
    setState({ status: 'loading' });
    // onMutate returns a rollback context — the snapshot to restore if
    // the request fails. Without it, a failed optimistic update leaves
    // the wrong thing on screen forever.
    const ctx = await onMutate?.(vars);
    try {
      const data = await mutationFn(vars);
      setState({ status: 'success', data });
      return data;
    } catch (error) {
      onError?.(error, vars, ctx);
      setState({ status: 'error', error });
      throw error;
    } finally {
      onSettled?.();
    }
  }, [mutationFn, onMutate, onError, onSettled]);

  return { ...state, mutate, isPending: state.status === 'loading' };
}

const { mutate } = useMutation({
  mutationFn: createPost,
  onMutate: (draft) => {
    const key = JSON.stringify(['posts']);
    const previous = getSnapshot(key).data;
    setQueryData(key, (old = []) => [{ ...draft, id: 'temp', pending: true }, ...old]);
    return { previous, key };
  },
  onError: (_e, _v, ctx) => setQueryData(ctx.key, ctx.previous),
  onSettled: () => invalidate('["posts"'),
});

What is still missing

Roughly 200 lines in, and these remain unsolved: · structural sharing — returning the same object identity for unchanged nested data, so memoised children do not re-render after every refetch · paginated and infinite queries with placeholder data, so changing page does not flash a skeleton · retry with backoff, and knowing which errors are retryable · request cancellation on unmount vs keeping the request alive for other subscribers of the same key · offline queueing and resuming paused mutations · SSR hydration — serialising the server's cache into the client without refetching everything · garbage collection tuned per query rather than one timer · devtools showing every key's state, which is how you debug any of the above So: build this once, to understand it. Then use TanStack Query. The hook above is about 8 kB of your code to maintain forever; the library is about 13 kB and has all of the above, tested. And in the App Router, ask first whether you need any of it: data needed for the initial view should be fetched in a Server Component (X04), where caching and deduplication are the framework's problem. Client fetching is for what happens after load — polling, infinite scroll, live filters.
The `use()` alternative in React 19

If the data is fetched on the server and only read on the client, you do not need any of this. A Server Component can start a request without awaiting it, pass the promise down as a prop, and a Client Component reads it with use(promise) inside a Suspense boundary — no status field, no effect, no race guard, because there is only ever one request and React handles the suspension. Reserve the full hook for data whose lifecycle the client genuinely owns.

Interview follow-up

“Write a useFetch hook.” The four things being scored are a single status field rather than three booleans, the res.ok check because fetch does not reject on 4xx, an AbortController in the cleanup with AbortError ignored, and every parameter in the dependency array. Then earn the senior mark by saying what you have not built — deduplication of identical in-flight requests, staleness, background revalidation on focus, retry, and cache garbage collection — and that in production this is a solved problem, so the interesting question is whether the data should be fetched on the client at all.

B04

Infinite scroll and virtualized lists

These are two different problems that get solved together. Infinite scroll is about fetching more as the user descends; virtualization is about rendering only what is visible. You can need either alone, and a list of ten thousand rows needs both — plus the accessibility work that almost every implementation skips.

Infinite scroll with IntersectionObserver

javascript · hooks/use-infinite-scroll.ts
import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

// Do NOT use a scroll listener with scrollTop + offsetHeight
// arithmetic. It fires constantly, forces a synchronous layout on
// every call, and breaks the moment the list is inside a scrolling
// container rather than the window. IntersectionObserver is the
// purpose-built API and it runs off the main thread.
export function useInfiniteScroll({ onLoadMore, hasMore, isLoading, rootMargin = '400px' }) {
  const observerRef = useRef(null);
  // Keep the callback in a ref so changing it does not tear down and
  // rebuild the observer on every render.
  const cbRef = useRef(onLoadMore);
  useEffect(() => { cbRef.current = onLoadMore; });

  // CALLBACK REF: fires when the sentinel node attaches or is
  // replaced. A ref object would never tell us the node had arrived.
  const sentinelRef = useCallback((node) => {
    observerRef.current?.disconnect();
    if (!node || !hasMore || isLoading) return;

    observerRef.current = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
      if (entry.isIntersecting) cbRef.current();
    }, {
      // rootMargin pre-loads BEFORE the sentinel is visible, so the
      // next page is usually there by the time the user arrives.
      rootMargin,
      threshold: 0,
    });
    observerRef.current.observe(node);
  }, [hasMore, isLoading, rootMargin]);

  useEffect(() => () => observerRef.current?.disconnect(), []);

  return sentinelRef;
}
javascript · components/feed.tsx
export function Feed() {
  const [pages, setPages] = useState([]);
  const [cursor, setCursor] = useState(null);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('idle');
  const hasMore = cursor !== undefined;      // undefined = exhausted

  const loadMore = useCallback(async () => {
    // THE DOUBLE-FIRE GUARD. Without it, the observer fires again while
    // the first request is in flight — a fast scroll can trigger four
    // page loads and render duplicates.
    if (status === 'loading' || !hasMore) return;
    setStatus('loading');
    try {
      const page = await getFeed({ cursor, limit: 20 });
      setPages((p) => [...p, page.items]);
      setCursor(page.nextCursor ?? undefined);
      setStatus('idle');
    } catch (err) {
      setStatus('error');
    }
  }, [cursor, hasMore, status]);
