  const sentinelRef = useInfiniteScroll({ onLoadMore: loadMore, hasMore,
                                          isLoading: status === 'loading' });
  const items = pages.flat();

  return (
    <>
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)}
      </ul>

      {/* ACCESSIBILITY: announce arrivals, and always provide a real
          button. Keyboard and screen-reader users may never trigger an
          intersection, and "load more" must not be scroll-only. */}
      <div aria-live="polite" className="sr-only">
        {status === 'idle' && `${items.length} items loaded`}
      </div>

      {hasMore && (
        <div ref={sentinelRef}>
          <button onClick={loadMore} disabled={status === 'loading'}>
            {status === 'loading' ? 'Loading…' : 'Load more'}
          </button>
        </div>
      )}
      {status === 'error' && (
        <p role="alert">Could not load more. <button onClick={loadMore}>Retry</button></p>
      )}
      {!hasMore && items.length > 0 && <p>That is everything.</p>}
    </>
  );
}
Use cursor pagination, not page=2

Offset pagination is wrong for an infinite feed: if three items are inserted at the top between loading page 1 and page 2, every item shifts down by three and the user sees the last three of page 1 again. Delete items instead and they skip content entirely. A cursor — an opaque token meaning “everything after this record in this sort order” — is stable under insertion and deletion, and it is also faster, because OFFSET 10000 makes the database count and discard ten thousand rows while WHERE (created_at, id) < (…) uses an index. The tell that a feed uses offsets is duplicate items on a busy timeline.

Why memoization cannot save a long list

10,000 rows in the DOM. What each fix actually does: React.memo on Row skips React's reconciliation for unchanged rows. The 10,000 DOM nodes still exist. → helps updates, not the initial cost useMemo on the array avoids rebuilding an array. Irrelevant. virtualization renders ~20 nodes instead of 10,000. → the only thing that works The cost of 10,000 nodes is not React. It is browser layout, paint, memory, and the accessibility tree — all of which grow with node count no matter what the framework does. Thresholds, roughly: < 100 rows do nothing 100–1,000 memo the row; check the profiler > 1,000 virtualize > 50 columns virtualize horizontally too

A fixed-height virtualizer

javascript · components/virtual-list.tsx
export function VirtualList({ items, rowHeight = 48, height = 600,
                              overscan = 5, renderRow }) {
  const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0);
  const containerRef = useRef(null);

  const total = items.length * rowHeight;

  // The whole algorithm is three lines of arithmetic.
  const start = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight) - overscan);
  const visibleCount = Math.ceil(height / rowHeight) + overscan * 2;
  const end = Math.min(items.length, start + visibleCount);
  const slice = items.slice(start, end);

  // OVERSCAN matters: without extra rows above and below, a fast
  // scroll shows blank space for a frame because rendering has not
  // caught up. Five is usually enough; more costs render time.

  const onScroll = useCallback((e) => {
    // rAF-throttle: scroll fires far more often than the browser
    // paints, and each setState is a render (B02).
    const top = e.currentTarget.scrollTop;
    requestAnimationFrame(() => setScrollTop(top));
  }, []);

  return (
    <div
      ref={containerRef}
      onScroll={onScroll}
      style={{ height, overflowY: 'auto', position: 'relative' }}
      // The scroll container is the list; rows inside are presentational
      role="list"
      aria-rowcount={items.length}
    >
      {/* A spacer of the FULL height, so the scrollbar is the right
          size and the scroll position is meaningful. */}
      <div style={{ height: total, position: 'relative' }}>
        {/* One translated container rather than absolutely positioning
            every row: fewer style writes, and it composites on the GPU. */}
        <div style={{ transform: `translateY(${start * rowHeight}px)` }}>
          {slice.map((item, i) => (
            <div
              key={item.id}
              role="listitem"
              aria-posinset={start + i + 1}
              aria-setsize={items.length}
              style={{ height: rowHeight }}
            >
              {renderRow(item, start + i)}
            </div>
          ))}
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Variable heights

javascript · measure, cache, and correct
// Fixed heights are simple because position is `index * rowHeight`.
// Variable heights need a running total, and you cannot know a row's
// height until it has rendered — so you estimate, measure, and adjust.
function useVariableVirtual({ items, estimate = 60, height, overscan = 5 }) {
  const measured = useRef(new Map());        // index -> measured height
  const [, forceUpdate] = useReducer((n) => n + 1, 0);
  const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0);

  // Prefix sums, recomputed when a measurement changes. For very large
  // lists a Fenwick tree makes this O(log n) instead of O(n).
  const offsets = useMemo(() => {
    const acc = [0];
    for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
      acc.push(acc[i] + (measured.current.get(i) ?? estimate));
    }
    return acc;
  }, [items.length, estimate, measured.current.size]);

  const find = (y) => {                       // binary search
    let lo = 0, hi = items.length - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
      const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
      offsets[mid + 1] <= y ? (lo = mid + 1) : (hi = mid);
    }
    return lo;
  };

  const start = Math.max(0, find(scrollTop) - overscan);
  let end = start;
  while (end < items.length && offsets[end] < scrollTop + height) end++;
  end = Math.min(items.length, end + overscan);

  // Each rendered row reports its real height once.
  const measureRef = (index) => (node) => {
    if (!node) return;
    const h = node.getBoundingClientRect().height;
    if (measured.current.get(index) !== h) {
      measured.current.set(index, h);
      forceUpdate();
    }
  };

  return { start, end, offsets, measureRef, setScrollTop,
           totalHeight: offsets[items.length] };
}
// The visible artefact of this approach is scrollbar drift: as real
// heights replace estimates, the total height changes and the
// scrollbar jumps slightly. Libraries reduce it by anchoring to the
// first visible item and correcting scrollTop after measurement.

Combining both

javascript · infinite + virtual, without a sentinel
// A sentinel element does not work inside a virtualizer — it is not
// rendered until it is already in view, which defeats the pre-load.
// Trigger from the visible RANGE instead.
useEffect(() => {
  if (end >= items.length - 10 && hasMore && !isLoading) loadMore();
}, [end, items.length, hasMore, isLoading, loadMore]);

// And preserve scroll position when prepending (a chat log loading
// older messages). Measure before, restore after:
const el = containerRef.current;
const before = el.scrollHeight;
await loadOlder();
requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  el.scrollTop += el.scrollHeight - before;   // or the view jumps
});

The accessibility problem

Infinite scroll is hostile by default, and it is fixable

There is no way to reach the footer — every attempt loads more content. Screen reader users get no announcement that anything arrived. Keyboard users who tab past the last rendered row find nothing. The browser's Find-in-page only searches rendered rows, so virtualized content is invisible to it. And leaving and returning loses the position entirely. The mitigations are concrete: always render a real Load more button, so scrolling is an enhancement rather than the mechanism; announce new content in an aria-live="polite" region; put the footer content somewhere reachable such as a sidebar; keep the URL in sync with the page so back and refresh restore position; and supply aria-posinset, aria-setsize and aria-rowcount so assistive technology knows the real list size rather than the twenty rows in the DOM.

When to use a library

NeedReach for
Fixed-height rows, simple listThe 40-line version above
Variable heights, grids, horizontal@tanstack/react-virtual
Windowing with a long historyreact-window
Infinite + cache + dedupeuseInfiniteQuery from TanStack Query
Sticky headers, sections, sortable virtual tablesA library — the edge cases multiply fast
Interview follow-up

“Build infinite scroll.” Use IntersectionObserver, not a scroll listener, and say why — no layout thrash, works in any scroll container, runs off the main thread. Then volunteer the three things candidates usually miss: the in-flight guard, because a fast scroll fires the observer repeatedly and loads four pages; cursor rather than offset pagination, because insertions shift offsets and produce duplicates; and the accessibility fallback, because a scroll-only trigger excludes keyboard and screen-reader users and makes the footer unreachable. If they follow up with performance, the answer is that memoization does not help ten thousand rows — only virtualization does, because the cost is browser layout and paint rather than React.

B05

A data table: sorting, filtering and pagination

The table is where the URL-as-state argument earns its keep. Sort, filter and page are exactly the values a user expects to survive a reload, a back button and a link sent to a colleague — and the moment they live in useState instead, all three break silently.

The first decision: client or server

CLIENT-SIDE — fetch everything once, sort and filter in memory ✓ instant interaction, trivially simple ✗ the whole dataset crosses the wire and sits in memory → up to a few thousand rows SERVER-SIDE — every change is a request with query params ✓ scales to any size; the database does the work it is for ✗ a round trip per interaction; needs indexes on sort columns → beyond a few thousand rows, or when the data is sensitive enough that you should not ship rows the user cannot see HYBRID — server-paginates, client-sorts the current page ✗ usually wrong, and the mistake is subtle: sorting one page of 20 out of 10,000 rows sorts the wrong 20. The user sees a sorted page that is not the top of the sorted dataset. Whichever you choose, the URL is the source of truth: /orders?q=acme&status=open&sort=total&dir=desc&page=3 shareable · bookmarkable · survives reload · back button works · server-renderable · and no state synchronisation code at all.

URL state

javascript · hooks/use-table-params.ts
'use client';
import { useRouter, usePathname, useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation';
import { useCallback, useMemo } from 'react';

export function useTableParams(defaults = { sort: 'createdAt', dir: 'desc', page: 1 }) {
  const router = useRouter();
  const pathname = usePathname();
  const searchParams = useSearchParams();

  const params = useMemo(() => ({
    q: searchParams.get('q') ?? '',
    status: searchParams.get('status') ?? 'all',
    sort: searchParams.get('sort') ?? defaults.sort,
    dir: searchParams.get('dir') === 'asc' ? 'asc' : 'desc',
    page: Math.max(1, Number(searchParams.get('page')) || 1),
  }), [searchParams, defaults.sort]);

  const setParams = useCallback((patch, { replace = false } = {}) => {
    const next = new URLSearchParams(searchParams);
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(patch)) {
      // Keep the URL clean: drop empty and default values rather than
      // accumulating ?q=&status=all&dir=desc on every interaction.
      if (v === '' || v == null || v === 'all') next.delete(k);
      else next.set(k, String(v));
    }
    // ANY change other than the page itself resets to page 1 —
    // otherwise filtering to 3 results while on page 7 shows nothing.
    if (!('page' in patch)) next.delete('page');

    // scroll:false keeps the viewport where it is; replace:true for
    // rapid changes such as typing, so the back button does not have
    // to walk through every keystroke.
    router[replace ? 'replace' : 'push'](`${pathname}?${next}`, { scroll: false });
  }, [router, pathname, searchParams]);

  return [params, setParams];
}
Two details that cause bug reports

Reset the page on any filter or sort change. A user on page 7 who types a search that matches four rows lands on an empty page and reports the search as broken. Use replace for typing and push for discrete actions. A search box that pushes a history entry per keystroke makes the back button useless — thirty presses to leave the page. Debounce the input, then replace; use push for clicking a sort header or a page number, which are the navigations a user expects to be able to undo.

Sorting

javascript · comparators that do not lie
const collator = new Intl.Collator(undefined, { numeric: true, sensitivity: 'base' });

function comparatorFor(type) {
  switch (type) {
    case 'string':
      // NOT a.localeCompare(b) per call — creating a collator for
      // every comparison is dramatically slower on large arrays. And
      // never a < b, which sorts "Zebra" before "apple" by code point
      // and mis-sorts every accented character.
      return (a, b) => collator.compare(a ?? '', b ?? '');
    case 'number':
      return (a, b) => (a ?? -Infinity) - (b ?? -Infinity);
    case 'date':
      return (a, b) => new Date(a ?? 0) - new Date(b ?? 0);
    case 'boolean':
      return (a, b) => Number(b) - Number(a);
    default:
      return (a, b) => collator.compare(String(a ?? ''), String(b ?? ''));
  }
}

function sortRows(rows, columns, sort, dir) {
  const col = columns.find((c) => c.id === sort);
  if (!col) return rows;
  const cmp = comparatorFor(col.type);
  const sign = dir === 'asc' ? 1 : -1;

  // Copy first: Array.prototype.sort MUTATES, and mutating the array
  // you got as a prop or from a query cache is a real bug.
  return [...rows].sort((a, b) => {
    const r = cmp(col.accessor(a), col.accessor(b)) * sign;
    // TIE-BREAK on a unique key. Array.sort is stable in modern
    // engines, but a stable sort of a list that arrived in a different
    // order last time still looks random to the user.
    return r !== 0 ? r : collator.compare(a.id, b.id);
  });
}

// Null handling deserves a decision rather than an accident: above,
// nulls sort first ascending. Many tables want them last regardless of
// direction, which needs an explicit pre-check rather than a sentinel.

The accessible table

javascript · components/data-table.tsx
export function DataTable({ columns, rows, total, params, setParams }) {
  const toggleSort = (id) => setParams({
    sort: id,
    dir: params.sort === id && params.dir === 'asc' ? 'desc' : 'asc',
  });

  return (
    <div className="table-wrap" tabIndex={0} role="region"
         aria-labelledby="orders-caption">
      {/* tabIndex on the scroll container so keyboard users can scroll
          a wide table horizontally. Without it, the overflow is
          mouse-only. */}
      <table>
        <caption id="orders-caption" className="sr-only">
          Orders, sorted by {params.sort}, {params.dir}ending.
          Page {params.page} of {Math.ceil(total / 20)}.
        </caption>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            {columns.map((col) => {
              const active = params.sort === col.id;
              return (
                <th
                  key={col.id}
                  scope="col"
                  // aria-sort is how a screen reader announces the
                  // current order. It goes on the th, not the button,
                  // and only ONE column may be other than "none".
                  aria-sort={active ? (params.dir === 'asc' ? 'ascending' : 'descending')
                                    : 'none'}
                >
                  {col.sortable === false ? col.label : (
                    // A real BUTTON inside the th — not an onClick on
                    // the th itself, which is not focusable and not
                    // announced as interactive.
                    <button type="button" onClick={() => toggleSort(col.id)}>
                      {col.label}
                      <span aria-hidden="true">
                        {active ? (params.dir === 'asc' ? ' ▲' : ' ▼') : ' ⇅'}
                      </span>
                    </button>
                  )}
                </th>
              );
            })}
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          {rows.length === 0 ? (
            <tr><td colSpan={columns.length}>
              <EmptyState hasFilters={!!params.q || params.status !== 'all'}
                          onClear={() => setParams({ q: '', status: 'all' })} />
            </td></tr>
          ) : rows.map((row) => (
            <tr key={row.id}>
              {columns.map((col) => (
                <td key={col.id}>{col.render ? col.render(row) : col.accessor(row)}</td>
              ))}
            </tr>
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <div aria-live="polite" className="sr-only">
        {total} results, page {params.page}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}
Two empty states, not one

“No orders yet” and “No orders match these filters” are different situations needing different UI. The first wants an explanation and a call to action — create your first order. The second wants a Clear filters button, because the user has done something and the fastest fix is to undo it. Shipping one generic “No results” for both is the commonest reason a user concludes the data is missing when in fact a filter three fields away is excluding it.

Pagination

javascript · components/pagination.tsx
function pageWindow(current, last, span = 1) {
  const pages = new Set([1, last]);
  for (let i = current - span; i <= current + span; i++) {
    if (i > 1 && i < last) pages.add(i);
  }
  const sorted = [...pages].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  // Insert gap markers where the sequence jumps: 1 … 4 5 6 … 20
  return sorted.flatMap((p, i) =>
    i > 0 && p - sorted[i - 1] > 1 ? ['gap', p] : [p]);
}

export function Pagination({ page, pageSize, total, onChange }) {
  const last = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(total / pageSize));
  if (last === 1) return null;

  return (
    <nav aria-label="Pagination">
      <button onClick={() => onChange(page - 1)} disabled={page === 1}>
        Previous
      </button>

      {pageWindow(page, last).map((p, i) =>
        p === 'gap'
          ? <span key={`g${i}`} aria-hidden="true">…</span>
          : <button
              key={p}
              onClick={() => onChange(p)}
              // aria-current, not just a CSS class — otherwise a
              // screen reader cannot tell which page it is on.
              aria-current={p === page ? 'page' : undefined}
              aria-label={`Page ${p}`}
            >{p}</button>)}

      <button onClick={() => onChange(page + 1)} disabled={page === last}>
        Next
      </button>
    </nav>
  );
}
// Note `disabled` rather than hiding the button: a control that
// disappears shifts the layout and moves the other buttons under the
// user's cursor mid-click.

The server side

javascript · app/orders/page.tsx
const SORTABLE = { createdAt: 'created_at', total: 'total_cents', customer: 'customer_name' };

export default async function OrdersPage({ searchParams }) {
  const sp = await searchParams;

  // VALIDATE. These values come from the URL, which is user input —
  // interpolating `sort` into SQL directly is an injection, and an
  // unbounded pageSize is a denial-of-service.
  const page = Math.max(1, Number(sp.page) || 1);
  const pageSize = Math.min(100, Number(sp.pageSize) || 20);
  const sortColumn = SORTABLE[sp.sort] ?? 'created_at';   // allowlist
  const dir = sp.dir === 'asc' ? 'ASC' : 'DESC';

  const [rows, total] = await Promise.all([
    db.order.findMany({
      where: buildWhere(sp),
      orderBy: { [sortColumn]: dir.toLowerCase() },
      skip: (page - 1) * pageSize,
      take: pageSize,
    }),
    // COUNT(*) over a large filtered table is often slower than the
    // page query itself. Options: cache it, use an estimate above a
    // threshold, or switch to cursor pagination and drop the total.
    db.order.count({ where: buildWhere(sp) }),
  ]);

  return <OrdersTable rows={rows} total={total} />;
}
// Index the sort columns. An unindexed ORDER BY on a large table sorts
// the entire filtered set for every page request.

Row selection

javascript · the indeterminate checkbox
const [selected, setSelected] = useState(() => new Set());

const allOnPage = rows.length > 0 && rows.every((r) => selected.has(r.id));
const someOnPage = rows.some((r) => selected.has(r.id)) && !allOnPage;

// `indeterminate` is a DOM PROPERTY with no HTML attribute, so it can
// only be set imperatively — via a ref or a callback ref.
<input
  type="checkbox"
  checked={allOnPage}
  ref={(el) => { if (el) el.indeterminate = someOnPage; }}
  onChange={(e) => setSelected((prev) => {
    const next = new Set(prev);
    rows.forEach((r) => e.target.checked ? next.add(r.id) : next.delete(r.id));
    return next;
  })}
  aria-label={`Select all ${rows.length} rows on this page`}
/>

// Be explicit about scope. "Select all" on a paginated table means the
// page, not the dataset — so when a selection is made, offer the other
// option rather than guessing:
{allOnPage && total > rows.length && (
  <p role="status">
    {rows.length} on this page selected.{' '}
    <button onClick={selectAllMatching}>Select all {total} matching</button>
  </p>
)}
Selection and pagination interact badly unless you decide the rule

Does a selection survive changing page? Changing a filter? Sorting? Each answer is defensible, but an undecided implementation does something arbitrary and users then delete the wrong records. The safe default: selection persists across sort and page, because the rows still exist and the user's intent is intact, and is cleared on filter change, because the selected rows may no longer be visible and a bulk action on invisible rows is dangerous. Whatever you choose, always show the count — “3 selected” — so nothing acts on rows the user has forgotten about.

Interview follow-up

“Build a sortable, paginated table.” Lead with where the state lives: sort, filter and page go in the URL, because they must survive reload and be shareable, and that also makes the whole thing server-renderable with no synchronisation code. Then the details that mark experience — reset the page when filters change, allowlist the sort column before it reaches SQL, copy the array before sorting because sort mutates, use a single Intl.Collator rather than localeCompare per comparison, and put aria-sort on the header with a real <button> inside it. If asked about scale, the answer is server-side sorting with indexed columns, and that COUNT(*) is often the slowest part of the request.

B06

A multi-step form: the checkout wizard

The wizard is a state-shape exercise disguised as a UI exercise. Nearly every bad implementation makes the same first decision — a piece of state per step — and then spends the rest of its life fighting the consequences: data lost going back, validation that cannot see other steps, and a submit that has to reassemble everything.

The state shape

The reducer

javascript · checkout/reducer.ts
export const STEPS = [
  { id: 'contact',  label: 'Contact',  schema: ContactSchema },
  { id: 'shipping', label: 'Shipping', schema: ShippingSchema },
  { id: 'payment',  label: 'Payment',  schema: PaymentSchema },
  { id: 'review',   label: 'Review',   schema: null },
];

export const initialState = {
  step: 0,
  data: {},
  errors: {},
  furthest: 0,          // the deepest step reached, for the stepper
  status: 'editing',    // editing | submitting | error | done
};

export function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'change':
      return {
        ...state,
        data: { ...state.data, [action.field]: action.value },
        // Clear the field's error as soon as the user edits it.
        // Leaving a stale error under a field they are fixing is the
        // single most irritating form behaviour there is.
        errors: { ...state.errors, [action.field]: undefined },
      };

    case 'next': {
      const schema = STEPS[state.step].schema;
      const result = schema ? schema.safeParse(state.data) : { success: true };
      if (!result.success) {
        return { ...state, errors: result.error.flatten().fieldErrors };
      }
      const step = Math.min(state.step + 1, STEPS.length - 1);
      return { ...state, step, errors: {}, furthest: Math.max(state.furthest, step) };
    }

    case 'back':
      // NEVER validate on back, and never clear data. The user is
      // going back precisely because something is wrong.
      return { ...state, step: Math.max(0, state.step - 1), errors: {} };

    case 'goto': {
      // Guard jumps: you may return to a completed step, but you may
      // not skip forward past one that has not been validated.
      if (action.step > state.furthest) return state;
      return { ...state, step: action.step, errors: {} };
    }

    case 'submitting': return { ...state, status: 'submitting', errors: {} };
    case 'failed':
      return {
        ...state,
        status: 'error',
        errors: action.errors ?? {},
        // Send the user back to the step that owns the failing field,
        // rather than showing an error on the review page next to
        // nothing they can edit.
        step: action.step ?? state.step,
      };
    case 'done': return { ...state, status: 'done' };
    case 'reset': return initialState;
    default: throw new Error(`Unknown action: ${action.type}`);
  }
}

Schemas per step, and one for the whole thing

javascript · checkout/schema.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const ContactSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string().trim().toLowerCase().email('Enter a valid email address'),
  phone: z.string().trim().optional(),
});

export const ShippingSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().trim().min(1, 'Required').max(100),
  line1: z.string().trim().min(1, 'Required'),
  city: z.string().trim().min(1, 'Required'),
  postcode: z.string().trim().min(1, 'Required'),
  country: z.string().length(2),
});

export const PaymentSchema = z.object({
  method: z.enum(['card', 'paypal', 'invoice']),
  // CROSS-FIELD rules are why one flat data object matters: this
  // cannot be expressed if each step owns its own state.
  poNumber: z.string().optional(),
}).refine((d) => d.method !== 'invoice' || !!d.poNumber, {
  message: 'A purchase order number is required for invoice payment',
  path: ['poNumber'],
});

// The composite schema is what the SERVER validates. Step schemas are
// a convenience for the client; they are not a security boundary,
// because nothing stops a caller posting straight to the endpoint.
export const CheckoutSchema = ContactSchema
  .merge(ShippingSchema)
  .and(PaymentSchema);
Never store card details in your own state

The moment raw card numbers pass through your JavaScript, your React state, or your server, you are inside PCI DSS scope and the compliance burden is substantial. Use the payment provider's hosted fields or element — Stripe Elements, Checkout, or the equivalent — which render in a cross-origin iframe you cannot read, and give you back a token. Your wizard's data object holds that token and nothing else. The same principle applies to any regulated data the form collects: keep the field out of your state entirely rather than trying to scrub it later.

The step in the URL

javascript · so back, refresh and links all work
// A wizard whose step lives only in React state has a broken back
// button: pressing it leaves the checkout entirely, losing everything.
// Put the step in the URL and the browser's own navigation becomes the
// step navigation.
const router = useRouter();
const pathname = usePathname();
const stepId = useSearchParams().get('step') ?? STEPS[0].id;
const step = Math.max(0, STEPS.findIndex((s) => s.id === stepId));

function goTo(index) {
  if (index > furthest) return;                 // guard, as in the reducer
  router.push(`${pathname}?step=${STEPS[index].id}`, { scroll: false });
}

// FOCUS MANAGEMENT. A step change is a navigation: without moving
// focus, a keyboard user stays on the Next button that no longer
// exists, and a screen reader announces nothing at all.
const headingRef = useRef(null);
useEffect(() => {
  headingRef.current?.focus();
  window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'instant' });
}, [step]);

<h2 ref={headingRef} tabIndex={-1}>{STEPS[step].label}</h2>
{/* tabIndex={-1} makes it programmatically focusable without adding
    it to the tab order. */}

Persisting the draft

javascript · surviving an accidental reload
const STORAGE_KEY = 'checkout-draft-v2';

// Restore once, on mount. Validate what comes back — storage is
// user-writable, and it may have been written by an older version of
// this form (B01).
useEffect(() => {
  const saved = readVersioned(STORAGE_KEY, null);
  if (saved) dispatch({ type: 'restore', state: saved });
}, []);

// Save on change, debounced so a fast typist does not write to
// storage on every keystroke (J10).
const save = useMemo(() => debounce((data) => {
  try {
    // NEVER persist payment tokens, CVCs, or anything you would not
    // want left on a shared machine.
    const { paymentToken, cvc, ...safe } = data;
    localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify({ version: 2, data: safe }));
  } catch { /* quota or blocked storage — the form still works */ }
}, 500), []);

useEffect(() => { save(state.data); }, [state.data, save]);
useEffect(() => save.cancel, [save]);

// Clear it on success, or the next visit restores a completed order.
// And warn on leaving with unsaved work:
useEffect(() => {
  if (state.status === 'done' || !Object.keys(state.data).length) return;
  const onBeforeUnload = (e) => { e.preventDefault(); e.returnValue = ''; };
  window.addEventListener('beforeunload', onBeforeUnload);
  return () => window.removeEventListener('beforeunload', onBeforeUnload);
}, [state.status, state.data]);

The step component and the submit

javascript · checkout/wizard.tsx
export function Wizard() {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);
  const current = STEPS[state.step];
  const isLast = state.step === STEPS.length - 1;

  async function onSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (!isLast) { dispatch({ type: 'next' }); return; }

    dispatch({ type: 'submitting' });
    const result = await placeOrder(state.data);     // a Server Function
    if (!result.ok) {
      // Map the server's field errors back to the step that owns them,
      // so the user lands somewhere they can actually fix it.
      const field = Object.keys(result.fields ?? {})[0];
      const owning = STEPS.findIndex((s) => s.schema?.shape?.[field]);
      dispatch({ type: 'failed', errors: result.fields,
                 step: owning >= 0 ? owning : state.step });
      return;
    }
    localStorage.removeItem(STORAGE_KEY);
    dispatch({ type: 'done' });
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={onSubmit} noValidate>
      {/* noValidate turns off the browser's own bubbles so your
          messages are the only ones — but keep type="email" and
          inputMode for the keyboards they produce. */}

      <Stepper steps={STEPS} current={state.step} furthest={state.furthest}
               onGoTo={(i) => dispatch({ type: 'goto', step: i })} />

      {/* Each step is ONE form element, submitted with Enter. Nested
          forms are invalid HTML — never put a <form> per step inside
          an outer form. */}
      <StepFields step={current.id} data={state.data} errors={state.errors}
                  onChange={(field, value) => dispatch({ type: 'change', field, value })} />

      {state.status === 'error' && (
        <p role="alert">Something went wrong. Please check the highlighted fields.</p>
      )}

      <div className="actions">
        <button type="button" onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'back' })}
                disabled={state.step === 0}>Back</button>
        <button type="submit" disabled={state.status === 'submitting'}>
          {state.status === 'submitting' ? 'Placing order…'
            : isLast ? 'Place order' : 'Continue'}
        </button>
      </div>
    </form>
  );
}

The stepper

javascript · an ordered list, not a row of divs
function Stepper({ steps, current, furthest, onGoTo }) {
  return (
    <nav aria-label="Checkout progress">
      <ol>
        {steps.map((s, i) => {
          const done = i < current;
          const isCurrent = i === current;
          return (
            <li key={s.id} aria-current={isCurrent ? 'step' : undefined}>
              <button type="button" onClick={() => onGoTo(i)}
                      disabled={i > furthest}>
                <span aria-hidden="true">{done ? '✓' : i + 1}</span>
                {s.label}
                {/* Visually the tick carries the meaning; a screen
                    reader needs the word. */}
                {done && <span className="sr-only"> (completed)</span>}
              </button>
            </li>
          );
        })}
      </ol>
      <p className="sr-only" aria-live="polite">
        Step {current + 1} of {steps.length}: {steps[current].label}
      </p>
    </nav>
  );
}
Validate on the server, again, over the whole object

Step schemas run in the browser and are a convenience for the user. Nothing prevents a caller posting directly to your endpoint with any payload, so the submit handler must parse the composite schema server-side before touching the database — and it must re-check anything that could have changed while the user was filling the form: stock levels, prices, whether the discount code is still valid, whether the address is deliverable. A wizard is slow by nature, which makes it the form most likely to submit against conditions that no longer hold.

Interview follow-up

“Build a multi-step form.” The answer is decided in the first thirty seconds: one step index plus one flat data object, not state per step. Say why — cross-step validation becomes possible, persisting a draft is one JSON.stringify, and going back cannot lose anything because nothing was ever partitioned. Then the details interviewers listen for: never validate on Back, clear a field's error the moment it is edited, put the step in the URL so the browser's back button works, move focus to the step heading on change, guard forward jumps against unvalidated steps, and validate the whole object again on the server because step schemas are client-side convenience rather than a boundary.

B07

A Kanban board: drag-and-drop that works

Drag-and-drop is the interview exercise where the visible part is easy and everything around it is hard: the ordering scheme that survives concurrent edits, the optimistic update that rolls back, and the keyboard alternative without which the feature is unusable for a significant number of people.

The data model

javascript · normalized, with explicit order
// NOT nested arrays of card objects inside column objects. Normalized
// state means moving a card touches two small arrays instead of
// rebuilding a deep tree, and a card's content can update without
// re-rendering every column.
const board = {
  columnOrder: ['todo', 'doing', 'done'],
  columns: {
    todo:  { id: 'todo',  title: 'To do',       cardIds: ['c1', 'c4', 'c9'] },
    doing: { id: 'doing', title: 'In progress', cardIds: ['c2'] },
    done:  { id: 'done',  title: 'Done',        cardIds: ['c3', 'c7'] },
  },
  cards: {
    c1: { id: 'c1', title: 'Write the spec', assignee: 'sam', rank: 'a0' },
    // …
  },
};

// The move, as a pure function. Note it is the only place the rules
// live — the DOM events just call it.
function moveCard(board, { cardId, from, to, index }) {
  if (from === to) {
    const ids = [...board.columns[from].cardIds];
    const currentIndex = ids.indexOf(cardId);
    ids.splice(currentIndex, 1);
    // Reordering within a column: removing first shifts every later
    // index down by one, so a drop targeting index 5 from index 2 must
    // land at 4. Splicing after removal handles this automatically —
    // computing the index before removal is the classic off-by-one.
    ids.splice(index, 0, cardId);
    return { ...board, columns: { ...board.columns,
      [from]: { ...board.columns[from], cardIds: ids } } };
  }

  const fromIds = board.columns[from].cardIds.filter((id) => id !== cardId);
  const toIds = [...board.columns[to].cardIds];
  toIds.splice(index, 0, cardId);

  return {
    ...board,
    columns: {
      ...board.columns,
      [from]: { ...board.columns[from], cardIds: fromIds },
      [to]:   { ...board.columns[to],   cardIds: toIds },
    },
  };
}

Persisting order without renumbering everything

The naive scheme: an integer `position` column, 0..n. Move one card and every card after it in both columns needs a new position — an UPDATE over potentially hundreds of rows for a single drag, and two users dragging at once produce a mess. The fix: fractional ranking. Store an ORDERABLE STRING and compute a value strictly between the two neighbours. before [ "a0" , , "a1" ] insert "a0V" ← between, no other row changes ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ UPDATE cards SET rank = 'a0V', column_id = 'doing' │ │ WHERE id = 'c4'; │ │ ONE row. Always. │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Sort by (rank, id). The trailing id breaks ties when two clients independently generate the same rank, so the order is still deterministic for everyone. Keys always divide, so they grow slowly in length; a background job can rebalance a column whose keys have grown long. The published implementations are LexoRank (Jira) and fractional-indexing — use one rather than writing your own, because the edge cases around equal neighbours and the first and last positions are fiddly.

The pointer-based drag

javascript · hooks/use-drag.ts — why not HTML5 drag-and-drop
// The native HTML5 API (draggable, dragstart, dragover) has real
// problems: it does not work on touch devices at all, the drag image
// is hard to control, dragover must call preventDefault on every event
// to permit a drop, and the dataTransfer payload is unreadable during
// dragover on most browsers. Pointer events work everywhere and give
// you full control.

export function useDrag({ onDrop }) {
  const [drag, setDrag] = useState(null);   // { id, from, x, y, w, h }

  const start = useCallback((e, { id, from }) => {
    // Ignore secondary buttons, and let interactive children through
    // so a button inside a card is still clickable.
    if (e.button !== 0) return;
    if (e.target.closest('button, a, input, [data-no-drag]')) return;

    const rect = e.currentTarget.getBoundingClientRect();
    // setPointerCapture routes every subsequent pointer event to this
    // element, even outside it — without it, moving fast loses the
    // drag the moment the cursor leaves the card.
    e.currentTarget.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);

    setDrag({
      id, from,
      offsetX: e.clientX - rect.left,
      offsetY: e.clientY - rect.top,
      x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY,
      w: rect.width, h: rect.height,
      moved: false,
    });
  }, []);

  const move = useCallback((e) => {
    setDrag((d) => {
      if (!d) return d;
      // A 5px threshold distinguishes a drag from a click. Without it,
      // every click on a card is a one-pixel drag and the card's own
      // onClick never feels reliable.
      const moved = d.moved || Math.hypot(e.clientX - d.x, e.clientY - d.y) > 5;
      return { ...d, x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY, moved };
    });
  }, []);

  const end = useCallback((e) => {
    setDrag((d) => {
      if (d?.moved) {
        // elementFromPoint tells us what is under the pointer. The
        // dragged preview must have pointer-events: none, or it is
        // always the answer.
        const target = document.elementFromPoint(e.clientX, e.clientY)
          ?.closest('[data-column]');
        if (target) {
          onDrop({
            cardId: d.id,
            from: d.from,
            to: target.dataset.column,
            index: indexFromPoint(target, e.clientY),
          });
        }
      }
      return null;
    });
  }, [onDrop]);

  return { drag, handlers: { onPointerDown: start, onPointerMove: move,
                             onPointerUp: end, onPointerCancel: () => setDrag(null) } };
}

// Where in the column did they drop? Compare against each card's
// midpoint — above the midpoint means before it.
function indexFromPoint(columnEl, y) {
  const cards = [...columnEl.querySelectorAll('[data-card]')];
  for (let i = 0; i < cards.length; i++) {
    const r = cards[i].getBoundingClientRect();
    if (y < r.top + r.height / 2) return i;
  }
  return cards.length;
}
Three CSS lines that make or break the feel

touch-action: none on the draggable element, or the browser scrolls the page instead of letting you drag on touch devices — this is the number one reason a drag works on desktop and does nothing on a phone. user-select: none while dragging, or the pointer selects text across the board as it moves. And pointer-events: none on the floating preview, or elementFromPoint returns the preview itself and every drop is computed against the wrong element. Also render the preview with position: fixed and a translate, never by animating top and left, so it composites on the GPU instead of triggering layout on every frame.

Optimistic move with rollback

javascript · the board must feel instant
const [board, setBoard] = useState(initial);

async function handleDrop({ cardId, from, to, index }) {
  const previous = board;                        // the rollback snapshot
  const next = moveCard(board, { cardId, from, to, index });
  setBoard(next);                                // 1 · optimistic, instant

  // 2 · compute the persistent rank from the card's new neighbours
  const ids = next.columns[to].cardIds;
  const pos = ids.indexOf(cardId);
  const rank = generateKeyBetween(
    pos > 0 ? next.cards[ids[pos - 1]].rank : null,
    pos < ids.length - 1 ? next.cards[ids[pos + 1]].rank : null,
  );

  try {
    const saved = await moveCardAction({ cardId, columnId: to, rank });
    // 3 · reconcile with the server's answer rather than assuming ours
    //     was right — another user may have moved something too.
    setBoard((b) => ({ ...b, cards: { ...b.cards, [cardId]: saved } }));
  } catch (err) {
    setBoard(previous);                          // 4 · roll back
    toast.error('Could not move the card. It has been put back.');
  }
}

// If the board is multiplayer, the rollback is not enough on its own —
// a websocket or polling update must be able to overwrite local state,
// and the optimistic value has to lose gracefully when it does. That
// is why the server's response replaces the card rather than being
// ignored on success.

The keyboard alternative, which is not optional

javascript · a drag-only board is unusable for many people
function Card({ card, columnId, index, onMove }) {
  const [grabbed, setGrabbed] = useState(false);

  function onKeyDown(e) {
    // Space or Enter picks up and puts down. Arrows move while held.
    if (e.key === ' ' || e.key === 'Enter') {
      e.preventDefault();
      setGrabbed((g) => !g);
      announce(grabbed
        ? `${card.title} dropped in ${columnId}, position ${index + 1}`
        : `${card.title} grabbed. Use arrow keys to move, space to drop, escape to cancel.`);
      return;
    }
    if (e.key === 'Escape' && grabbed) { setGrabbed(false); announce('Move cancelled'); return; }
    if (!grabbed) return;

    const moves = {
      ArrowUp:    { index: index - 1 },
      ArrowDown:  { index: index + 1 },
      ArrowLeft:  { column: -1 },
      ArrowRight: { column: +1 },
    };
    const m = moves[e.key];
    if (!m) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    onMove(m);
    announce(describePosition(card, m));
  }

  return (
    <li
      data-card
      // A real button role, in the tab order, with state exposed.
      tabIndex={0}
      role="button"
      aria-roledescription="draggable card"
      aria-grabbed={grabbed}          // deprecated in ARIA 1.1 but
                                      // still the clearest signal; pair
                                      // it with the live region below
      aria-describedby="dnd-help"
      onKeyDown={onKeyDown}
      className={grabbed ? 'card grabbed' : 'card'}
    >
      {card.title}
    </li>
  );
}

// ONE live region for the whole board, updated imperatively. Rendering
// announcements as React state causes them to be announced twice in
// some screen readers.
<div id="dnd-live" role="status" aria-live="assertive" className="sr-only" />
<p id="dnd-help" className="sr-only">
  Press space to pick up a card, arrow keys to move it, space to drop,
  escape to cancel.
</p>

function announce(message) {
  document.getElementById('dnd-live').textContent = message;
}
Use a library — and this is the reason

Everything above is the straightforward half. What remains: auto-scrolling a column when the pointer nears its edge, and scrolling the page when it nears the viewport edge; collision detection that feels right when cards are different heights; animating the gap that opens for the card; nested scroll containers; multi-select drag; touch long-press to disambiguate from scrolling; and making all of it work with a virtualized list, where the drop target may not be rendered. dnd-kit handles these, ships the keyboard sensor and live-region announcements described above, and is accessible by default. Build this once to understand the model; then use the library. Note that react-beautiful-dnd is no longer maintained — its successor is @atlaskit/pragmatic-drag-and-drop.

Interview follow-up

“Build a drag-and-drop Kanban board.” Start with the data model — normalized columns holding ordered card ids — and the moveCard pure function, because that is where the off-by-one lives when reordering within a column. Then raise the three things that distinguish a real implementation: ordering, where an integer position column means updating every row after the insertion point and a fractional rank means updating exactly one; optimism, where the UI updates instantly and rolls back to a snapshot on failure; and keyboard access, where space picks up, arrows move, escape cancels, and a live region announces each change. Finish by naming the auto-scroll and collision-detection edge cases as the reason production code uses dnd-kit.

B08

An interactive file explorer

The tree is the classic recursion exercise, and the naive recursive component is the right answer right up until the tree has ten thousand nodes or needs keyboard navigation. Then it needs to be flattened — which turns out to make everything else easier too.

Two representations

NESTED — what the API returns, and what recursion wants { id:'src', type:'folder', children:[ { id:'app', type:'folder', children:[…] }, { id:'index.ts', type:'file' } ] } ✓ trivial to render recursively ✗ cannot virtualize — you cannot slice a tree ✗ keyboard nav needs the flat visual order, which recursion does not give you ✗ "what is the next visible row" is a tree walk every keypress FLAT — what the UI actually renders [ { id:'src', depth:0, isFolder:true, expanded:true }, { id:'app', depth:1, isFolder:true, expanded:false }, { id:'index.ts', depth:1, isFolder:false } ] ✓ it is a LIST, so virtualization is the usual windowing ✓ keyboard nav is index +/- 1 ✓ depth becomes a padding value, not a nesting level ✓ type-ahead search is a linear scan So: keep the tree as the source of truth, and derive the flat visible rows from it plus the set of expanded ids. The derivation is the memoised computation; nothing is stored twice.

The flattening

javascript · hooks/use-tree.ts
import { useMemo, useState, useCallback } from 'react';

export function useTree(root, { defaultExpanded = [] } = {}) {
  // A Set of ids, not an `expanded` boolean on each node. Keeping it
  // outside the data means the tree can be refetched and replaced
  // without losing the user's expansion state.
  const [expanded, setExpanded] = useState(() => new Set(defaultExpanded));
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState(null);

  const rows = useMemo(() => {
    const out = [];
    // ITERATIVE, with an explicit stack. A recursive walk of a deep
    // tree can exhaust the call stack, and a symlink cycle in a real
    // filesystem makes it infinite — which is what the `seen` set
    // guards against.
    const seen = new Set();
    const stack = [{ node: root, depth: 0 }];

    while (stack.length) {
      const { node, depth } = stack.pop();
      if (seen.has(node.id)) continue;
      seen.add(node.id);

      const isFolder = node.type === 'folder';
      const isOpen = isFolder && expanded.has(node.id);
      out.push({ id: node.id, name: node.name, depth, isFolder,
                 expanded: isOpen, node });

      if (isOpen && node.children) {
        // Folders first, then alphabetical — and push in reverse
        // because the stack pops last-in-first-out.
        const sorted = [...node.children].sort((a, b) =>
          (a.type === b.type ? 0 : a.type === 'folder' ? -1 : 1) ||
          a.name.localeCompare(b.name, undefined, { numeric: true }));
        for (let i = sorted.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
          stack.push({ node: sorted[i], depth: depth + 1 });
        }
      }
    }
    return out;
  }, [root, expanded]);

  const toggle = useCallback((id) => setExpanded((prev) => {
    const next = new Set(prev);
    next.has(id) ? next.delete(id) : next.add(id);
    return next;
  }), []);

  return { rows, expanded, toggle, selected, setSelected, setExpanded };
}

Lazy-loading children

javascript · a real filesystem is not sent in one payload
// A folder starts as { id, name, type:'folder', children: undefined },
// meaning "not loaded yet" — distinct from children: [], meaning
// "loaded, and empty". Conflating the two produces a folder that
// re-fetches forever or one that can never be opened.
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(() => new Set());

async function openFolder(node) {
  toggle(node.id);
  if (node.children !== undefined || loading.has(node.id)) return;

  setLoading((s) => new Set(s).add(node.id));
  try {
    const children = await listDirectory(node.path);
    setRoot((r) => updateNode(r, node.id, (n) => ({ ...n, children })));
  } catch {
    // Collapse again on failure, so the disclosure arrow does not lie
    // about having content.
    toggle(node.id);
    toast.error(`Could not open ${node.name}`);
  } finally {
    setLoading((s) => { const n = new Set(s); n.delete(node.id); return n; });
  }
}

// Immutable update of one node in a nested tree, by path recursion:
function updateNode(node, id, fn) {
  if (node.id === id) return fn(node);
  if (!node.children) return node;
  const children = node.children.map((c) => updateNode(c, id, fn));
  // Return the SAME reference when nothing beneath changed, so
  // memoised subtrees do not re-render (W02).
  return children.every((c, i) => c === node.children[i])
    ? node : { ...node, children };
}

The ARIA tree, and roving tabindex

javascript · components/file-tree.tsx
export function FileTree({ root }) {
  const { rows, toggle, selected, setSelected, setExpanded } = useTree(root);
  const [focusIndex, setFocusIndex] = useState(0);
  const listRef = useRef(null);

  // ROVING TABINDEX: the tree is ONE tab stop. Tab moves past it;
  // arrows move within it. Giving every node tabIndex={0} would mean
  // a thousand tab presses to get past a large tree.
  function onKeyDown(e) {
    const row = rows[focusIndex];
    const move = (i) => {
      const next = Math.max(0, Math.min(rows.length - 1, i));
      setFocusIndex(next);
      listRef.current?.querySelector(`[data-index="${next}"]`)?.focus();
    };

    switch (e.key) {
      case 'ArrowDown': e.preventDefault(); move(focusIndex + 1); break;
      case 'ArrowUp':   e.preventDefault(); move(focusIndex - 1); break;

      case 'ArrowRight':
        e.preventDefault();
        // Closed folder → open it. Open folder → move to first child.
        if (row.isFolder && !row.expanded) toggle(row.id);
        else if (row.isFolder) move(focusIndex + 1);
        break;

      case 'ArrowLeft':
        e.preventDefault();
        // Open folder → close it. Otherwise → jump to the PARENT,
        // which in a flat list is the nearest earlier row with a
        // smaller depth.
        if (row.isFolder && row.expanded) toggle(row.id);
        else {
          for (let i = focusIndex - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            if (rows[i].depth < row.depth) { move(i); break; }
          }
        }
        break;

      case 'Home': e.preventDefault(); move(0); break;
      case 'End':  e.preventDefault(); move(rows.length - 1); break;

      case 'Enter': case ' ':
        e.preventDefault();
        row.isFolder ? toggle(row.id) : setSelected(row.id);
        break;

      case '*':
        // Expand every sibling at this level — a real tree-view
        // convention that almost nobody implements.
        e.preventDefault();
        setExpanded((prev) => {
          const next = new Set(prev);
          rows.filter((r) => r.depth === row.depth && r.isFolder)
              .forEach((r) => next.add(r.id));
          return next;
        });
        break;

      default:
        // TYPE-AHEAD: a printable character jumps to the next row
        // starting with it, wrapping around.
        if (e.key.length === 1 && !e.metaKey && !e.ctrlKey) {
          const k = e.key.toLowerCase();
          const order = [...rows.slice(focusIndex + 1), ...rows.slice(0, focusIndex + 1)];
          const hit = order.find((r) => r.name.toLowerCase().startsWith(k));
          if (hit) move(rows.indexOf(hit));
        }
    }
  }

  return (
    <ul ref={listRef} role="tree" aria-label="Files" onKeyDown={onKeyDown}>
      {rows.map((row, i) => (
        <li
          key={row.id}
          role="treeitem"
          data-index={i}
          // aria-level is 1-based; aria-expanded must be ABSENT on a
          // leaf, not false — false announces "collapsed" and implies
          // it contains something.
          aria-level={row.depth + 1}
          aria-expanded={row.isFolder ? row.expanded : undefined}
          aria-selected={selected === row.id}
          tabIndex={i === focusIndex ? 0 : -1}
          onFocus={() => setFocusIndex(i)}
          onClick={() => (row.isFolder ? toggle(row.id) : setSelected(row.id))}
          // Indent with padding on the ROW, not by nesting lists —
          // the flat structure is what makes virtualization possible.
          style={{ paddingInlineStart: `${row.depth * 16 + 8}px` }}
        >
          <span aria-hidden="true">{row.isFolder ? (row.expanded ? '▾' : '▸') : ' '}</span>
          <Icon type={row.isFolder ? 'folder' : extname(row.name)} aria-hidden="true" />
          {row.name}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
A flat role="tree" is valid, and it is what makes this work

The ARIA spec does not require treeitem elements to be physically nested — aria-level, aria-setsize and aria-posinset communicate the hierarchy explicitly. That is exactly why the flat representation is the right one: you get a single flat list that can be windowed, whose keyboard navigation is index arithmetic, and which still announces correctly as a tree. If you nest <ul> elements instead, virtualization becomes impossible and “move to the next visible row” becomes a tree walk on every arrow press.

Inline rename

javascript
function RenameField({ initial, onCommit, onCancel }) {
  const ref = useCallback((node) => {
    if (!node) return;
    node.focus();
    // Select the basename only, leaving the extension — the behaviour
    // every file manager has and users notice when it is missing.
    const dot = initial.lastIndexOf('.');
    node.setSelectionRange(0, dot > 0 ? dot : initial.length);
  }, [initial]);

  return (
    <input
      ref={ref}
      defaultValue={initial}
      aria-label="New name"
      onKeyDown={(e) => {
        // Stop the tree's own handler seeing these keys, or typing a
        // name triggers type-ahead navigation.
        e.stopPropagation();
        if (e.key === 'Enter') onCommit(e.currentTarget.value.trim());
        if (e.key === 'Escape') onCancel();
      }}
      onBlur={(e) => onCommit(e.currentTarget.value.trim())}
    />
  );
}
// Validate before committing: not empty, no path separators, not a
// duplicate among siblings, within the length limit. And commit
// optimistically with a rollback, as in B07.

Scaling up

SizeWhat to do
< 500 visible rowsRender them all; memoise the row component
> 500 visible rowsVirtualize the flat list — the windowing from B04 applies unchanged
Deep or unknown treesLazy-load children on expand; show a spinner on the row
Huge folders (10k files)Paginate within the folder, with a “show more” row
Search across the treeQuery the server; show results as a flat list, not a filtered tree
Memoise the row, and key by id

Every expand or collapse rebuilds the flat array, so without memo on the row component every visible row re-renders on every toggle. Key rows by their stable node id rather than by index, or expanding a folder near the top reuses the wrong DOM nodes for everything below it — the same failure as an index-keyed list (R03), and here it manifests as an inline rename field suddenly attached to a different file.

Interview follow-up

“Build a file tree.” Write the recursive version first, since it is what they expect, then say why production code flattens: a flat array of { id, depth, expanded } makes the list virtualizable, makes keyboard navigation index arithmetic instead of a tree walk, and is still a valid role="tree" because aria-level carries the hierarchy. Keep expansion in a Set of ids outside the data so a refetch does not collapse everything. Then the keyboard details that show you have read the pattern: right arrow opens a closed folder but moves into an open one, left arrow closes an open folder but jumps to the parent otherwise, and aria-expanded must be absent on leaves rather than false.

B09

Modal dialogs, properly

A modal is the component most often shipped broken, because the broken version looks identical to the correct one. Focus escapes behind it, Escape does nothing, the page scrolls underneath, the layout shifts when the scrollbar disappears, and a screen reader reads the whole page as though the dialog were not there. Most of this is now solved by a native element.

Start with <dialog>

javascript · the browser does the hard parts
export function NativeDialog({ open, onClose, title, children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el) return;
    // showModal() is what makes it modal: Escape closes it, focus is
    // trapped, everything behind becomes inert to both pointer and
    // assistive technology, and it renders in the TOP LAYER — above
    // every z-index on the page, outside every overflow and transform
    // containing block. No portal needed.
    if (open && !el.open) el.showModal();
    if (!open && el.open) el.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog
      ref={ref}
      aria-labelledby="dlg-title"
      // The browser fires `close` for Escape too, so this is the one
      // handler that covers every dismissal path.
      onClose={onClose}
      onClick={(e) => {
        // Backdrop clicks: the ::backdrop pseudo-element is not a
        // separate node, so a click on it targets the dialog itself.
        // Compare against the bounding box to tell them apart.
        const r = e.currentTarget.getBoundingClientRect();
        const inside = e.clientX >= r.left && e.clientX <= r.right &&
                       e.clientY >= r.top && e.clientY <= r.bottom;
        if (!inside) e.currentTarget.close();
      }}
    >
      <h2 id="dlg-title">{title}</h2>
      {children}
      {/* method="dialog" closes the dialog on submit with no JS, and
          returnValue carries the button's value to the close handler. */}
      <form method="dialog">
        <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
        <button value="confirm">Confirm</button>
      </form>
    </dialog>
  );
}
css · the styling you must add yourself
dialog {
  /* UA styles centre it with a fixed width; reset before styling. */
  padding: 0;
  border: none;
  max-width: min(32rem, calc(100vw - 2rem));
  max-height: calc(100dvh - 2rem);   /* dvh, not vh, for mobile (B02) */
  overflow: auto;
  border-radius: 12px;
  background: var(--surface);
  color: var(--ink);
}

dialog::backdrop {
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);
  backdrop-filter: blur(2px);
}

/* Animating a dialog needs `display` and `overlay` in the transition,
   plus @starting-style for the entry — otherwise it pops in and the
   exit never plays because display:none applies immediately. */
dialog {
  opacity: 0;
  translate: 0 8px;
  transition: opacity .2s, translate .2s, overlay .2s allow-discrete,
              display .2s allow-discrete;
}
dialog[open] { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; }
@starting-style { dialog[open] { opacity: 0; translate: 0 8px; } }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  dialog { transition-duration: 0.01ms; }
}

/* The scroll lock the native element does NOT do for you: */
body:has(dialog[open]) {
  overflow: hidden;
  /* Compensate for the removed scrollbar, or the whole page shifts
     sideways by ~15px when the modal opens. scrollbar-gutter on the
     html element from the start is the cleaner fix. */
  padding-right: var(--scrollbar-width, 0px);
}
html { scrollbar-gutter: stable; }
What showModal() gives you free, and what it does not

Free: the top layer, so no z-index wars and no portal; a real focus trap; Escape to close; inert on the rest of the document, so background content is unreachable by pointer, keyboard and screen reader; and ::backdrop. Not free: scroll locking the body, returning focus to a sensible place when the trigger has been removed from the DOM, distinguishing a backdrop click from a content click, and transitions, which need allow-discrete and @starting-style. Note that <dialog open> as an attribute is not modal — it renders inline with none of the above. Always call showModal().

The React portal version

javascript · when you need full control over the mechanics
export function Modal({ open, onClose, title, description, children,
                        initialFocus, closeOnBackdrop = true }) {
  const panelRef = useRef(null);
  const restoreRef = useRef(null);
  const titleId = useId();
  const descId = useId();

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!open) return;

    // 1 · REMEMBER where focus was, so it can go back. Capture the
    //     element, not just a selector — the trigger may be in a list
    //     that re-renders.
    restoreRef.current = document.activeElement;

    // 2 · MOVE focus in. Prefer an explicitly requested element,
    //     otherwise the first focusable, otherwise the panel itself.
    const target = initialFocus?.current
      ?? panelRef.current?.querySelector(FOCUSABLE)
      ?? panelRef.current;
    target?.focus();

    // 3 · TRAP Tab inside the panel.
    function onKeyDown(e) {
      if (e.key === 'Escape') { e.stopPropagation(); onClose(); return; }
      if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;

      const items = [...panelRef.current.querySelectorAll(FOCUSABLE)]
        .filter((el) => el.offsetParent !== null);   // skip hidden ones
      if (items.length === 0) { e.preventDefault(); return; }

      const first = items[0], last = items[items.length - 1];
      // Wrap in both directions. Without the shift-tab branch, focus
      // escapes backwards into the page behind — the single most
      // common focus-trap bug.
      if (!e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) {
        e.preventDefault(); first.focus();
      } else if (e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) {
        e.preventDefault(); last.focus();
      }
    }
    document.addEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown, true);

    // 4 · LOCK scroll, compensating for the scrollbar.
    const scrollbar = window.innerWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth;
    const prev = {
      overflow: document.body.style.overflow,
      paddingRight: document.body.style.paddingRight,
    };
    document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden';
    document.body.style.paddingRight = `${scrollbar}px`;

    // 5 · HIDE the rest of the app from assistive technology. Without
    //     this, a screen reader can still read the page behind, which
    //     is the difference between a dialog and a floating div.
    const appRoot = document.getElementById('__next') ?? document.body.firstElementChild;
    appRoot?.setAttribute('inert', '');

    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown, true);
      document.body.style.overflow = prev.overflow;
      document.body.style.paddingRight = prev.paddingRight;
      appRoot?.removeAttribute('inert');
      // 6 · RESTORE focus — but only if the element still exists and
      //     is still in the document, or focus silently lands on
      //     <body> and keyboard users start from the top of the page.
      const el = restoreRef.current;
      if (el && document.contains(el)) el.focus();
    };
  }, [open, onClose, initialFocus]);

  if (!open) return null;

  return createPortal(
    <div className="overlay" onMouseDown={(e) => {
      // mouseDown, not click: a click that STARTS inside the panel and
      // ends on the backdrop — a text selection dragged outward —
      // would otherwise close the dialog and lose the user's work.
      if (closeOnBackdrop && e.target === e.currentTarget) onClose();
    }}>
      <div
        ref={panelRef}
        role="dialog"
        aria-modal="true"
        aria-labelledby={titleId}
        aria-describedby={description ? descId : undefined}
        tabIndex={-1}
        className="panel"
      >
        <h2 id={titleId}>{title}</h2>
        {description && <p id={descId}>{description}</p>}
        {children}
        <button onClick={onClose} aria-label="Close dialog">×</button>
      </div>
    </div>,
    document.body,
  );
}

const FOCUSABLE = [
  'a[href]', 'button:not([disabled])', 'input:not([disabled])',
  'select:not([disabled])', 'textarea:not([disabled])',
  '[tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])', 'audio[controls]', 'video[controls]',
  '[contenteditable]:not([contenteditable="false"])',
].join(',');

A promise-based confirm

javascript · because `if (confirm(...))` reads better than modal state
const ConfirmContext = createContext(null);

export function ConfirmProvider({ children }) {
  const [request, setRequest] = useState(null);

  const confirm = useCallback((options) => {
    // withResolvers (J08) is exactly the deferred pattern this needs.
    const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
    setRequest({ ...options, resolve });
    return promise;
  }, []);

  const settle = (value) => { request?.resolve(value); setRequest(null); };

  return (
    <ConfirmContext.Provider value={confirm}>
      {children}
      <Modal
        open={!!request}
        onClose={() => settle(false)}
        title={request?.title ?? ''}
        description={request?.body}
      >
        <button onClick={() => settle(false)}>{request?.cancelLabel ?? 'Cancel'}</button>
        <button onClick={() => settle(true)} className={request?.destructive ? 'danger' : ''}>
          {request?.confirmLabel ?? 'Confirm'}
        </button>
      </Modal>
    </ConfirmContext.Provider>
  );
}

export const useConfirm = () => useContext(ConfirmContext);

// At the call site, the flow reads linearly:
const confirm = useConfirm();
async function onDelete() {
  const ok = await confirm({
    title: 'Delete this notebook?',
    body: 'All 42 notes will be permanently removed. This cannot be undone.',
    confirmLabel: 'Delete notebook',
    destructive: true,
  });
  if (!ok) return;
  await deleteNotebook(id);
}
// Note the wording: name the object, state the consequence, and label
// the button with the VERB rather than "OK" — a user skimming reads
// only the button.

The checklist

□ focus moves INTO the dialog on open □ Tab and Shift+Tab both wrap inside it □ Escape closes it □ focus returns to the trigger on close — and falls back sensibly if the trigger no longer exists □ the background is inert to pointer, keyboard AND screen reader □ body scroll is locked, with the scrollbar width compensated □ role="dialog" + aria-modal="true" □ aria-labelledby points at the visible title □ the close button has an accessible name □ a backdrop click that STARTED inside the panel does not close it □ transitions respect prefers-reduced-motion □ it renders above everything — top layer, or a portal to body □ on mobile it fits: 100dvh, and it does not sit under the keyboard □ nested dialogs stack, and Escape closes only the topmost Fourteen items. This is why the honest recommendation is to use <dialog> for the mechanics, or Radix Dialog / React Aria when you need more — and to write the above only to understand what they are doing for you.
Do not put a modal in a modal unless you must

Nested dialogs stack correctly in the top layer and Escape closes only the topmost, so the mechanics work — but the experience rarely does. A confirmation inside a form inside a wizard means the user has three levels of context to hold and no clear sense of what cancelling will discard. Prefer replacing the dialog's content, promoting the second step to its own route, or using an inline confirmation within the existing panel. If you genuinely need nesting, keep it to two levels and make each level's cancel action explicit about what it abandons.

Interview follow-up

“Build an accessible modal.” Open by saying you would use <dialog> with showModal(), because the browser gives you the focus trap, Escape, the top layer and inert on the background — then implement the React version anyway, since that is what they are asking for. The scored details are: focus in on open and back to the trigger on close, a Tab trap that wraps both ways, role="dialog" with aria-modal and aria-labelledby, body scroll lock with scrollbar-width compensation so the page does not jump, and a portal so no ancestor's overflow or z-index can clip it. The detail almost nobody mentions is using mousedown rather than click for the backdrop, so dragging a text selection out of the panel does not dismiss it.

B10

The OTP input

Six boxes, one digit each. It looks like the smallest component in this part and it has the most edge cases: paste, backspace across boundaries, mobile keyboards, SMS autofill, and the fact that a screen reader encountering six unlabelled single-character inputs has no idea what is being asked.

One input, or six?

SIX INPUTS — the conventional approach ✓ obvious visual affordance; each digit has its own box ✗ paste must be distributed by hand ✗ backspace across boundaries needs explicit handling ✗ SMS autofill often fills only the first box ✗ six controls in the tab order and six things to label ONE INPUT — visually segmented with CSS ✓ paste, autofill, undo, selection and IME all just work ✓ one label, one control, one value ✓ `autocomplete="one-time-code"` fills correctly on iOS/Android ✗ rendering the boxes takes some CSS work ✗ a caret between segments needs care Recommendation: one real input, with the boxes drawn behind it. Every platform affordance is inherited rather than reimplemented, and the failure mode most users hit — pasting a code from their messages app — works without a single line of code. We will build both, because interviews usually ask for six.

The six-input version

javascript · components/otp-input.tsx
export function OtpInput({ length = 6, value, onChange, onComplete, disabled }) {
  const refs = useRef([]);

  // The VALUE is one string; the boxes are derived. Keeping six
  // separate state variables makes paste, clear and validation
  // needlessly hard, and makes the parent's job worse.
  const digits = value.padEnd(length, ' ').slice(0, length).split('');

  const setAt = (index, char) => {
    const next = digits.map((d, i) => (i === index ? char : d)).join('').trimEnd();
    onChange(next);
    return next;
  };

  const focusAt = (i) => {
    const el = refs.current[Math.max(0, Math.min(length - 1, i))];
    el?.focus();
    el?.select();       // select so typing replaces rather than appends
  };

  function handleChange(e, index) {
    // Take the LAST character typed, not the first: typing into a box
    // that already has a digit should replace it, and on Android the
    // input event can deliver the whole field's contents.
    const raw = e.target.value.replace(/\D/g, '');
    if (!raw) return;

    if (raw.length > 1) { distribute(raw, index); return; }   // autofill

    const next = setAt(index, raw);
    if (index < length - 1) focusAt(index + 1);
    if (next.length === length) onComplete?.(next);
  }

  function handleKeyDown(e, index) {
    switch (e.key) {
      case 'Backspace':
        e.preventDefault();
        if (digits[index].trim()) {
          setAt(index, ' ');            // clear this box, stay put
        } else if (index > 0) {
          // THE BOUNDARY CASE: backspace in an empty box moves back
          // AND clears the previous one, which is what users expect
          // and what most implementations get wrong.
          setAt(index - 1, ' ');
          focusAt(index - 1);
        }
        break;
      case 'Delete':
        e.preventDefault();
        setAt(index, ' ');
        break;
      case 'ArrowLeft':  e.preventDefault(); focusAt(index - 1); break;
      case 'ArrowRight': e.preventDefault(); focusAt(index + 1); break;
      case 'Home':       e.preventDefault(); focusAt(0); break;
      case 'End':        e.preventDefault(); focusAt(length - 1); break;
      default:
        // Block non-digits before they reach the field, so no flash of
        // an invalid character. Allow shortcuts through.
        if (e.key.length === 1 && !/\d/.test(e.key) && !e.metaKey && !e.ctrlKey) {
          e.preventDefault();
        }
    }
  }

  function distribute(text, startIndex = 0) {
    const chars = text.replace(/\D/g, '').slice(0, length - startIndex).split('');
    const next = [...digits];
    chars.forEach((c, i) => { next[startIndex + i] = c; });
    const joined = next.join('').trimEnd();
    onChange(joined);
    focusAt(Math.min(startIndex + chars.length, length - 1));
    if (joined.length === length) onComplete?.(joined);
  }

  return (
    // A group with ONE accessible name. Six unlabelled inputs announce
    // as six anonymous text fields and give no indication of the task.
    <div
      role="group"
      aria-labelledby="otp-label"
      aria-describedby="otp-help"
      onPaste={(e) => {
        // THE BIG ONE. Without this, pasting "482913" puts all six
        // characters in one box, or only the first. Paste is how most
        // people actually enter a code.
        e.preventDefault();
        distribute(e.clipboardData.getData('text'), 0);
      }}
    >
      {Array.from({ length }, (_, i) => (
        <input
          key={i}
          ref={(el) => { refs.current[i] = el; }}
          value={digits[i].trim()}
          onChange={(e) => handleChange(e, i)}
          onKeyDown={(e) => handleKeyDown(e, i)}
          onFocus={(e) => e.target.select()}
          disabled={disabled}

          // MOBILE. inputMode drives the on-screen keyboard: numeric
          // gives a digit pad without the +*# of type="tel", and
          // type="text" avoids the spinner and the scroll-to-change
          // behaviour of type="number".
          type="text"
          inputMode="numeric"
          pattern="[0-9]*"
          maxLength={1}
          autoComplete={i === 0 ? 'one-time-code' : 'off'}
          // iOS offers the SMS code above the keyboard for the first
          // field only; when accepted it arrives as a multi-character
          // change event, which handleChange redirects to distribute.

          aria-label={`Digit ${i + 1} of ${length}`}
          className="otp-box"
        />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}
Paste is the requirement, not an enhancement

Watch anyone enter a verification code: they switch to their messages app, copy the code, switch back, and paste. An OTP field that does not handle paste correctly is broken for the majority path, not an edge case. The onPaste handler must go on the container, not each input — pasting while focused on box 3 should still fill from box 1 if the code is complete — and it must strip non-digits, because copying from a message often brings spaces, a trailing full stop, or the surrounding words.

The single-input version

javascript · one real field, boxes drawn behind it
export function OtpField({ length = 6, value, onChange, onComplete }) {
  const [focused, setFocused] = useState(false);
  const digits = value.split('');
  const activeIndex = Math.min(value.length, length - 1);

  return (
    <div className="otp-wrap">
      <label htmlFor="otp" className="sr-only">
        Enter the {length}-digit code we sent you
      </label>

      {/* ONE input. Transparent, stretched over the boxes, caret
          hidden. Paste, autofill, undo, select-all and IME all work
          because it is an ordinary text field. */}
      <input
        id="otp"
        value={value}
        onChange={(e) => {
          const next = e.target.value.replace(/\D/g, '').slice(0, length);
          onChange(next);
          if (next.length === length) onComplete?.(next);
        }}
        onFocus={() => setFocused(true)}
        onBlur={() => setFocused(false)}
        // Keep the caret at the end: clicking the middle of the field
        // would otherwise insert digits where the user clicked.
        onSelect={(e) => {
          const end = e.currentTarget.value.length;
          e.currentTarget.setSelectionRange(end, end);
        }}
        type="text"
        inputMode="numeric"
        autoComplete="one-time-code"
        maxLength={length}
        className="otp-real"
        aria-describedby="otp-help"
      />

      {/* The boxes are presentation only. */}
      <div className="otp-boxes" aria-hidden="true">
        {Array.from({ length }, (_, i) => (
          <span key={i}
                className={`otp-box ${focused && i === activeIndex ? 'active' : ''}`}>
            {digits[i] ?? ''}
          </span>
        ))}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}
css
.otp-wrap { position: relative; display: inline-block; }

.otp-real {
  position: absolute; inset: 0;
  width: 100%; height: 100%;
  opacity: 0;                 /* invisible but still a real input:    */
  caret-color: transparent;   /* focusable, autofillable, pasteable   */
  font-size: 16px;            /* under 16px iOS zooms the page on focus */
}

.otp-boxes { display: flex; gap: .5rem; pointer-events: none; }

.otp-box {
  width: 3rem; height: 3.5rem;
  display: grid; place-items: center;
  font: 600 1.5rem/1 var(--font-mono);
  border: 2px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: 10px;
}
.otp-box.active {
  border-color: var(--accent);
  animation: blink 1s step-end infinite;   /* a fake caret */
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .otp-box.active { animation: none; } }

The surrounding flow

javascript · resend timer, errors, and the WebOTP API
function VerifyForm({ email }) {
  const [code, setCode] = useState('');
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle' });
  const [cooldown, setCooldown] = useState(0);

  // WebOTP (Chrome on Android): reads the code from an SMS formatted
