  // with a final line of `@example.com #123456`, with no user action.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!('OTPCredential' in window)) return;
    const ac = new AbortController();
    navigator.credentials
      .get({ otp: { transport: ['sms'] }, signal: ac.signal })
      .then((otp) => otp && setCode(otp.code))
      .catch(() => {});          // user dismissed, or unsupported
    return () => ac.abort();
  }, []);

  // Resend cooldown, because the button is otherwise hammered.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (cooldown <= 0) return;
    const t = setTimeout(() => setCooldown((c) => c - 1), 1000);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);
  }, [cooldown]);

  async function submit(value) {
    setState({ status: 'verifying' });
    const res = await verifyCode({ email, code: value });
    if (!res.ok) {
      setState({ status: 'error', message: res.message, attemptsLeft: res.attemptsLeft });
      setCode('');               // clear so they can retype immediately
      return;
    }
    setState({ status: 'done' });
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); submit(code); }}>
      <h1 id="otp-label">Enter your code</h1>
      <p id="otp-help">We sent a 6-digit code to {maskEmail(email)}.</p>

      <OtpField length={6} value={code} onChange={setCode} onComplete={submit} />
      {/* Auto-submit on completion: the user has typed six digits,
          asking them to click Verify as well is friction. Keep the
          button for keyboard users and for retries. */}

      <div role="alert">
        {state.status === 'error' && (
          <p>{state.message}
            {state.attemptsLeft != null && ` ${state.attemptsLeft} attempts remaining.`}</p>
        )}
      </div>

      <button type="submit" disabled={code.length < 6 || state.status === 'verifying'}>
        {state.status === 'verifying' ? 'Verifying…' : 'Verify'}
      </button>

      <button type="button" disabled={cooldown > 0}
              onClick={() => { resend(email); setCooldown(30); }}>
        {cooldown > 0 ? `Resend in ${cooldown}s` : 'Resend code'}
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}
The security half lives on the server, and the client cannot help

A six-digit code has a million possibilities, which is nothing without rate limiting: the server must cap attempts per code (five, then invalidate), cap requests per account and per IP with a sliding window (J10), expire codes in five to ten minutes, and enforce single use — a code that still works after a successful login is a replay vulnerability. Compare in constant time, store a hash rather than the code itself, and invalidate every outstanding code when a new one is issued, or a user who clicks Resend three times has three valid codes in flight. None of this can be done in the component; the client-side cooldown is a courtesy that any attacker bypasses by calling the endpoint directly.

Interview follow-up

“Build an OTP input.” Hold the value as one string and derive the boxes, rather than six pieces of state — that single decision makes paste, clear and validation straightforward. Then volunteer the cases that separate implementations: paste handled on the container and stripped of non-digits, because that is how most people actually enter a code; backspace in an empty box moving back and clearing the previous digit; inputMode="numeric" with autoComplete="one-time-code" for mobile keyboards and SMS autofill; and a role="group" with one accessible name, since six unlabelled single-character fields tell a screen reader user nothing. If there is time, mention that a single visually-segmented input inherits all of this from the platform for free.

B11

Tabs and accordions: the compound component

These two share an implementation shape — a parent holding selection state, children reading it through context — and they are the standard exercise for compound components. They also have precise, published keyboard and ARIA contracts that almost no hand-rolled version implements correctly.

The compound pattern

Tabs

javascript · components/tabs.tsx
const TabsContext = createContext(null);
const useTabs = () => {
  const ctx = useContext(TabsContext);
  // Fail loudly rather than reading undefined three renders later.
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('Tab components must be used inside <Tabs>');
  return ctx;
};

export function Tabs({ children, value, defaultValue, onValueChange,
                       activation = 'automatic', orientation = 'horizontal' }) {
  // CONTROLLED OR UNCONTROLLED, the standard dual API: use the prop
  // when it is provided, internal state otherwise.
  const [internal, setInternal] = useState(defaultValue);
  const isControlled = value !== undefined;
  const selected = isControlled ? value : internal;

  const setSelected = useCallback((next) => {
    if (!isControlled) setInternal(next);
    onValueChange?.(next);
  }, [isControlled, onValueChange]);

  // useId gives ids that match between server and client, so the
  // aria-controls / aria-labelledby wiring survives hydration (R10).
  const baseId = useId();
  const tabsRef = useRef([]);           // registered tab values, in order

  const ctx = useMemo(() => ({
    selected, setSelected, baseId, tabsRef, activation, orientation,
  }), [selected, setSelected, baseId, activation, orientation]);

  return <TabsContext.Provider value={ctx}>{children}</TabsContext.Provider>;
}

export function TabList({ children, label }) {
  const { tabsRef, selected, setSelected, activation, orientation } = useTabs();

  function onKeyDown(e) {
    const values = tabsRef.current;
    const i = values.indexOf(selected);
    const next = orientation === 'vertical'
      ? { ArrowDown: i + 1, ArrowUp: i - 1 }
      : { ArrowRight: i + 1, ArrowLeft: i - 1 };

    let target = next[e.key];
    if (e.key === 'Home') target = 0;
    if (e.key === 'End') target = values.length - 1;
    if (target === undefined) return;

    e.preventDefault();
    // WRAP AROUND — required by the ARIA pattern, and the thing
    // hand-rolled versions usually clamp instead.
    const wrapped = (target + values.length) % values.length;
    const value = values[wrapped];

    // AUTOMATIC activation selects on arrow; MANUAL only moves focus
    // and requires Enter or Space. Use manual when a panel is
    // expensive or fetches data — otherwise arrowing through five tabs
    // fires five requests.
    document.getElementById(`tab-${value}`)?.focus();
    if (activation === 'automatic') setSelected(value);
  }

  return (
    <div role="tablist" aria-label={label} aria-orientation={orientation}
         onKeyDown={onKeyDown}>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

export function Tab({ value, children, disabled }) {
  const { selected, setSelected, baseId, tabsRef } = useTabs();
  const isSelected = selected === value;

  // Register in render order so the keyboard handler knows the
  // sequence. An effect would run after the first keypress is
  // possible, and children may be reordered.
  if (!tabsRef.current.includes(value)) tabsRef.current.push(value);
  useEffect(() => () => {
    tabsRef.current = tabsRef.current.filter((v) => v !== value);
  }, [value, tabsRef]);

  return (
    <button
      type="button"
      role="tab"
      id={`tab-${value}`}
      aria-selected={isSelected}
      aria-controls={`panel-${value}`}
      // ROVING TABINDEX: the tablist is one tab stop. Tab enters it and
      // Tab leaves it; arrows move between tabs. Without this, a
      // ten-tab interface costs ten Tab presses to walk past.
      tabIndex={isSelected ? 0 : -1}
      disabled={disabled}
      onClick={() => setSelected(value)}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

export function TabPanel({ value, children, keepMounted = false }) {
  const { selected } = useTabs();
  const isSelected = selected === value;
  if (!isSelected && !keepMounted) return null;

  return (
    <div
      role="tabpanel"
      id={`panel-${value}`}
      aria-labelledby={`tab-${value}`}
      // The panel itself is focusable so that Tab from the tablist
      // lands in the content — required when the panel has no
      // focusable children of its own.
      tabIndex={0}
      hidden={!isSelected}
    >
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}
Unmounting a panel destroys its state — and that is sometimes the bug

The default above unmounts hidden panels, which is right for a heavy panel you do not want rendering in the background. But it means a half-filled form, a scroll position, or an expanded section is lost every time the user switches away and back. keepMounted with hidden preserves everything at the cost of rendering all panels — and note that hidden must be a real attribute, not display:none applied by a class, so the content is also hidden from assistive technology and removed from the tab order. React 19's <Activity> is the proper answer to this trade-off: state and DOM are preserved while effects are suspended and rendering drops to low priority.

Persisting the tab in the URL

javascript · because a shared link should open the same tab
// Tabs that represent meaningfully different views — Overview,
// Activity, Settings — belong in the URL, exactly like a table's sort
// (B05). Tabs that are a minor detail toggle do not.
const searchParams = useSearchParams();
const router = useRouter();
const pathname = usePathname();
const tab = searchParams.get('tab') ?? 'overview';

<Tabs
  value={tab}
  onValueChange={(v) => {
    const next = new URLSearchParams(searchParams);
    v === 'overview' ? next.delete('tab') : next.set('tab', v);
    // replace, not push: a user tabbing through four tabs should not
    // need four back presses to leave the page.
    router.replace(`${pathname}?${next}`, { scroll: false });
  }}
>

// In the App Router, parallel routes are the heavier alternative: each
// tab becomes a real route segment with its own loading and error
// states, and the content is server-rendered (X02).

The accordion, which is a different pattern

javascript · components/accordion.tsx
// An accordion is NOT tabs. It is a set of disclosure widgets: no
// tablist, no roving tabindex, no arrow keys required — each header is
// an ordinary button in the tab order, and Tab moves between them.
// Using role="tab" on an accordion header is a common and incorrect
// substitution.

const AccordionContext = createContext(null);

export function Accordion({ children, type = 'single', defaultValue,
                            collapsible = true }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(() =>
    new Set(defaultValue ? [defaultValue].flat() : []));

  const toggle = useCallback((value) => {
    setOpen((prev) => {
      const next = new Set(prev);
      if (next.has(value)) {
        // `collapsible: false` means one section is always open —
        // useful for a settings panel where a blank state is odd.
        if (type === 'single' && !collapsible) return prev;
        next.delete(value);
      } else {
        if (type === 'single') next.clear();
        next.add(value);
      }
      return next;
    });
  }, [type, collapsible]);

  const ctx = useMemo(() => ({ open, toggle }), [open, toggle]);
  return <AccordionContext.Provider value={ctx}>{children}</AccordionContext.Provider>;
}

export function AccordionItem({ value, title, children }) {
  const { open, toggle } = useContext(AccordionContext);
  const id = useId();
  const isOpen = open.has(value);

  return (
    <div className="acc-item">
      {/* The button must be INSIDE a heading, so the document outline
          is navigable — screen reader users jump by heading. */}
      <h3>
        <button
          type="button"
          id={`acc-trigger-${id}`}
          aria-expanded={isOpen}
          aria-controls={`acc-panel-${id}`}
          onClick={() => toggle(value)}
        >
          {title}
          <ChevronIcon aria-hidden="true" data-open={isOpen} />
        </button>
      </h3>

      <div
        id={`acc-panel-${id}`}
        role="region"
        aria-labelledby={`acc-trigger-${id}`}
        className="acc-panel"
        data-state={isOpen ? 'open' : 'closed'}
      >
        {/* Keep it mounted and hide with CSS so the height can animate
            and the content is findable by Ctrl+F when open. */}
        <div className="acc-inner" inert={!isOpen || undefined}>
          {children}
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}
css · animating to auto height, without measuring
/* height: auto has never been animatable, which is why accordions
   historically measured scrollHeight in an effect and wrote a pixel
   value. grid-template-rows 0fr -> 1fr animates to content height with
   no JavaScript at all. */
.acc-panel {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-rows: 0fr;
  transition: grid-template-rows .22s ease;
}
.acc-panel[data-state='open'] { grid-template-rows: 1fr; }

.acc-inner {
  overflow: hidden;      /* required — the child must be clippable */
  min-height: 0;         /* or the grid row refuses to shrink      */
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .acc-panel { transition: none; }
}

/* Newer browsers can do this directly, with a fallback above:
   .acc-panel { interpolate-size: allow-keywords; }              */
Consider <details> before writing any of this

<details> and <summary> give you a disclosure widget with correct semantics, keyboard support and Ctrl+F searchability for free, and <details name="group"> now makes an exclusive accordion where opening one closes the others — natively, with no JavaScript. Reach for the React version when you need controlled state, animation beyond what the element supports, or an onValueChange to persist. For an FAQ or a settings list, the native element is less code and behaves better.

Which pattern for which problem

SituationUseWhy
Alternative views of one subjectTabsOnly one is relevant at a time; comparison is not needed
Sections a user may want open togetherAccordion (multiple)Tabs cannot show two panels at once
FAQ, long-form disclosure<details>Native, searchable, zero JavaScript
Steps in a required orderA wizard (B06)Tabs imply free navigation; steps do not
More than about seven tabsA list or a selectA tablist that wraps or scrolls is hard to scan
Content that must be printed or found with Ctrl+FNeither — render it allHidden content is not findable or printable
Panels that are separate URLs conceptuallyRoutes, or parallel routesDeep-linkable, server-rendered, own loading states
Interview follow-up

“Build a tabs component.” Use the compound pattern with context, and say why: the consumer owns the markup, so you are not adding a prop for every visual variation. Then the ARIA contract, which is what is actually being tested — role="tablist", tab and tabpanel; aria-selected and aria-controls wired with useId so hydration matches; and roving tabindex so the whole tablist is one tab stop with arrow keys moving between tabs and wrapping at the ends. Two details score highly: manual versus automatic activation, because arrowing through tabs that fetch data fires a request per tab; and that unmounting a hidden panel loses its state, which is a deliberate trade rather than an oversight. Close by noting that an accordion is a disclosure pattern, not tabs — plain buttons with aria-expanded, no roving tabindex.

B12

An image carousel

The carousel has a reputation for being the component most often built with JavaScript that should have been built with CSS. Scroll-snap gives you momentum, touch, keyboard and accessibility for nothing; the JavaScript you add on top is for the controls and the active-slide indicator, not for the scrolling itself.

Start with CSS

css · a working carousel with no JavaScript at all
.carousel {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  overflow-x: auto;
  scroll-snap-type: x mandatory;

  /* Hide the scrollbar visually but keep the element scrollable —
     never `overflow: hidden`, which removes keyboard scrolling too. */
  scrollbar-width: none;
  -ms-overflow-style: none;
}
.carousel::-webkit-scrollbar { display: none; }

.slide {
  flex: 0 0 100%;
  scroll-snap-align: center;
  /* stop prevents the user flicking past several slides at once;
     `normal` allows it. Use stop for a gallery, normal for a long
     product strip. */
  scroll-snap-stop: always;
}

/* Smooth programmatic scrolling for the prev/next buttons — and turn
   it off for users who ask, or a carousel becomes motion sickness. */
.carousel { scroll-behavior: smooth; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .carousel { scroll-behavior: auto; scroll-snap-type: none; }
}

/* Native scroll-driven indicators, no observer needed, where
   supported: */
@supports (animation-timeline: scroll(self inline)) {
  .progress {
    animation: grow linear both;
    animation-timeline: scroll(self inline);
  }
}
What this already gives you

Touch swiping with native momentum and rubber-banding that no JavaScript implementation matches. Trackpad and shift-scroll on desktop. Keyboard scrolling when the container is focusable. Correct behaviour with a screen reader, because the slides are ordinary content in the DOM rather than transformed off-screen. And zero bundle cost. A transform-based carousel reimplements all of it, usually worse — the most common symptom being a swipe that feels weightless because it has no momentum model. Add JavaScript for the buttons, the dots and the active index; leave the scrolling to the browser.

The React component

javascript · components/carousel.tsx
export function Carousel({ slides, label = 'Gallery', autoPlay = false,
                           interval = 5000 }) {
  const trackRef = useRef(null);
  const [active, setActive] = useState(0);
  const [paused, setPaused] = useState(false);
  const reduceMotion = useMediaQuery('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');  // B02

  // ACTIVE SLIDE via IntersectionObserver rather than scroll maths.
  // A scroll handler would need to compute which slide is nearest the
  // centre on every event; the observer tells you directly, off the
  // main thread.
  useEffect(() => {
    const track = trackRef.current;
    if (!track) return;

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
      // With several slides partly visible, take the most visible one.
      const best = entries
        .filter((e) => e.isIntersecting)
        .sort((a, b) => b.intersectionRatio - a.intersectionRatio)[0];
      if (best) setActive(Number(best.target.dataset.index));
    }, { root: track, threshold: [0.5, 0.75, 1] });

    track.querySelectorAll('[data-index]').forEach((el) => observer.observe(el));
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [slides.length]);

  const goTo = useCallback((index) => {
    const track = trackRef.current;
    const target = track?.querySelector(`[data-index="${index}"]`);
    if (!target) return;
    // scrollIntoView on the child, not scrollLeft arithmetic — it
    // works with variable slide widths, gaps, and RTL layouts, none of
    // which a hand-computed offset handles.
    target.scrollIntoView({ behavior: reduceMotion ? 'auto' : 'smooth',
                            block: 'nearest', inline: 'center' });
  }, [reduceMotion]);

  // AUTOPLAY, with all four of the conditions that make it tolerable.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!autoPlay || paused || reduceMotion) return;

    const tick = () => {
      // Pause when the tab is hidden: otherwise a background tab burns
      // CPU and the user returns to slide 47.
      if (document.visibilityState !== 'visible') return;
      setActive((i) => {
        const next = (i + 1) % slides.length;
        goTo(next);
        return next;
      });
    };
    const id = setInterval(tick, interval);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, [autoPlay, paused, reduceMotion, interval, slides.length, goTo]);

  return (
    <section
      // roledescription tells a screen reader this is a carousel
      // rather than a generic region, so it can announce it usefully.
      aria-roledescription="carousel"
      aria-label={label}
      // Pause on hover AND on focus — a keyboard user tabbing through
      // slides needs the same reprieve as a mouse user hovering.
      onMouseEnter={() => setPaused(true)}
      onMouseLeave={() => setPaused(false)}
      onFocusCapture={() => setPaused(true)}
      onBlurCapture={() => setPaused(false)}
    >
      <div
        ref={trackRef}
        className="carousel"
        // Focusable so the container can be scrolled with arrow keys,
        // with a label so it is not an anonymous scroll region.
        tabIndex={0}
        role="group"
        aria-label={`${slides.length} slides`}
        onKeyDown={(e) => {
          if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') { e.preventDefault(); goTo(Math.min(active + 1, slides.length - 1)); }
          if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft')  { e.preventDefault(); goTo(Math.max(active - 1, 0)); }
          if (e.key === 'Home')       { e.preventDefault(); goTo(0); }
          if (e.key === 'End')        { e.preventDefault(); goTo(slides.length - 1); }
        }}
      >
        {slides.map((slide, i) => (
          <div
            key={slide.id}
            data-index={i}
            className="slide"
            role="group"
            aria-roledescription="slide"
            aria-label={`${i + 1} of ${slides.length}`}
            // Do NOT set aria-hidden on off-screen slides: they are
            // genuinely in the document and reachable by scrolling, and
            // hiding them breaks Find-in-page and sequential reading.
          >
            <Image
              src={slide.src}
              alt={slide.alt}
              width={1200}
              height={675}
              sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 60vw"
              // Only the first slide is above the fold (X10).
              priority={i === 0}
              loading={i === 0 ? undefined : 'lazy'}
            />
            {slide.caption && <p className="caption">{slide.caption}</p>}
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>

      <div className="controls">
        <button onClick={() => goTo(active - 1)} disabled={active === 0}
                aria-label="Previous slide">←</button>

        {/* Dots are TABS over the slides, so use the tab pattern: a
            real button each, with aria-current marking the active one. */}
        <div role="group" aria-label="Choose slide">
          {slides.map((s, i) => (
            <button
              key={s.id}
              onClick={() => goTo(i)}
              aria-current={i === active ? 'true' : undefined}
              aria-label={`Go to slide ${i + 1}`}
              className={i === active ? 'dot active' : 'dot'}
            />
          ))}
        </div>

        <button onClick={() => goTo(active + 1)}
                disabled={active === slides.length - 1}
                aria-label="Next slide">→</button>

        {autoPlay && (
          // WCAG 2.2.2: any content that moves automatically for more
          // than five seconds must have a pause control. This button
          // is not optional.
          <button onClick={() => setPaused((p) => !p)}
                  aria-label={paused ? 'Start automatic slideshow' : 'Pause automatic slideshow'}>
            {paused ? '▶' : '⏸'}
          </button>
        )}
      </div>

      {/* Announce changes, but only when the user caused them —
          announcing an autoplay change every five seconds is hostile. */}
      <div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" className="sr-only">
        {paused || !autoPlay ? `Slide ${active + 1} of ${slides.length}` : ''}
      </div>
    </section>
  );
}

Infinite looping

Users expect "next" on the last slide to wrap. Three approaches: 1 · DON'T — disable the buttons at the ends ✓ simplest, and the position is always honest ✓ the scrollbar and scroll position mean something → correct for a gallery of 4–8 images 2 · CLONE — render [last, 1, 2, 3, last, first] and jump the scroll position silently when a clone scrolls into view ✓ works with scroll-snap and native momentum ✗ duplicate DOM nodes that a screen reader will read twice unless hidden, and duplicate images to download ✗ the silent jump can be visible on a slow frame 3 · VIRTUAL — reposition slides around the current index ✓ no duplicates, unbounded length ✗ incompatible with native scroll-snap; you are back to implementing momentum yourself Recommendation: option 1 unless there is a product reason, then option 2, and reach for Embla or Swiper before option 3 — they have solved the jump-on-clone timing properly.

The swipe gesture, if you build it yourself

javascript · only needed when you have abandoned scroll-snap
function useSwipe({ onNext, onPrev, threshold = 50 }) {
  const start = useRef(null);

  return {
    onPointerDown: (e) => {
      start.current = { x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY, t: Date.now() };
    },
    onPointerUp: (e) => {
      const s = start.current;
      if (!s) return;
      start.current = null;

      const dx = e.clientX - s.x;
      const dy = e.clientY - s.y;
      const dt = Date.now() - s.t;

      // DIRECTION LOCK: if the movement is more vertical than
      // horizontal, it was a page scroll, not a swipe. Without this
      // check the carousel steals every attempt to scroll past it,
      // which is the most infuriating carousel bug there is.
      if (Math.abs(dy) > Math.abs(dx)) return;

      // VELOCITY as well as distance: a short, fast flick should
      // advance even though it did not travel far.
      const fast = Math.abs(dx) / dt > 0.5;
      if (Math.abs(dx) < threshold && !fast) return;

      dx < 0 ? onNext() : onPrev();
    },
    onPointerCancel: () => { start.current = null; },
    // touch-action: pan-y permits vertical page scrolling while the
    // component handles horizontal gestures.
    style: { touchAction: 'pan-y' },
  };
}

Before you build one

Carousels perform badly, and that is worth saying out loud

Usability research has consistently found that engagement drops sharply after the first slide, and that auto-advancing carousels are frequently missed entirely because users have learned to ignore anything that moves near the top of a page. They also carry real cost: multiple large images competing for bandwidth with your LCP element, layout shift if slide heights differ, and a genuine accessibility burden. If the content matters, consider a grid, a single strong hero, or a horizontally scrollable strip that does not pretend to be a slideshow. If a carousel is required — and for product galleries it genuinely is, because users expect to page through photographs of the thing they are buying — build it with scroll-snap, keep autoplay off by default, and load only the first image eagerly.

Libraries

NeedReach for
A product gallery, a few imagesThe scroll-snap version above
Loops, variable widths, momentum tuningEmbla — small, headless, accessible
Everything including the kitchen sinkSwiper — large, but complete
Full-bleed hero with text overlaysReconsider — a single hero usually converts better
Interview follow-up

“Build an image carousel.” The strongest opening is that the scrolling itself should be CSS scroll-snap, not a transform — you inherit touch momentum, trackpad support, keyboard scrolling and correct screen-reader reading order, and the JavaScript is reduced to the controls and the active index. Track the active slide with IntersectionObserver rather than scroll arithmetic, and navigate with scrollIntoView on the target child rather than computing scrollLeft, so variable widths and RTL work. Then the accessibility points that are usually missed: aria-roledescription="carousel", a pause control for anything that auto-advances (it is a WCAG requirement, not a nicety), respecting prefers-reduced-motion, pausing on hover and focus and when the tab is hidden, and not setting aria-hidden on off-screen slides, which would break Find-in-page.

I01

The React interview: understanding-level questions

Interviewers are not checking whether you memorised the hooks list. They are checking whether you have a model — whether, when something behaves unexpectedly, you can reason from how React works rather than guessing. This chapter is about how to answer; the bank at the end of the book has the questions.

What is actually being assessed

Every React question is one of five things in disguise: 1 · Do you understand rendering? state → re-render → reconcile → commit. Almost every "why does this happen" question resolves here. 2 · Do you understand closures and identity? stale state, stale props, dependency arrays, why a function in a dep array causes an infinite loop. 3 · Do you know what the framework is for? effects synchronise with external systems; they are not a place to compute values or respond to clicks. 4 · Can you reason about performance? what causes a re-render, whether a re-render is expensive, and what memo actually does. 5 · Do you have judgement? when NOT to use a tool. The candidate who says "I'd reach for context here, but only because X" outranks the one who lists every state library. A strong answer has three parts: the mechanism what React actually does the consequence therefore this behaviour the practice so in real code I do this

The answer shape, demonstrated

The ten questions that carry the most weight

“Walk me through what happens when you call setState.”
React marks the component as needing an update and schedules work. On the next render pass it calls your function again, builds a new element tree, diffs it against the current fiber tree by position and key, produces a list of effects, and applies them to the DOM in one synchronous commit — then runs layout effects, paints, and runs passive effects. Name the render/commit split: render is pure and interruptible, commit is synchronous and must not be. (W04)
“What is the virtual DOM, and is it faster?”
It is a tree of plain objects describing the UI. The honest answer is that it is not inherently faster than well-written imperative DOM code — a hand-tuned update will beat it. What it buys is that you write declaratively and React works out the minimal mutation, so your code stays a function of state rather than a pile of transitions. Saying “it's faster” without that caveat is the single most common way to sound like you learned React from a 2016 article. (W01)
“How does reconciliation decide what to update?”
Two heuristics, because a true tree diff is O(n³) and React needs O(n): different type at the same position means destroy and rebuild — state is lost, not moved — and keys identify children across renders. Then the consequence that matters in practice: index keys break when the list reorders, because React matches key 0 to key 0 and reuses state that belongs to a different item. (W02)
“What problem do keys solve?”
Identity. Without them React matches list children by position, so inserting at the front makes every item look changed. Keys must be stable across renders, unique among siblings, and derived from the data — never the index for a reorderable list, and never Math.random(), which regenerates every render and destroys all state. (R03)
“When does a component re-render?”
Its own state changed, its parent re-rendered, a context it consumes changed, or a store it subscribes to changed. Notice what is not on that list: a prop being deeply equal but referentially different is covered by “its parent re-rendered”, and mutating an object does not trigger anything because React compares with Object.is. Add that a re-render is not automatically a problem — React diffs and usually touches nothing. (R02)
“What does useEffect do, and when do you use it?”
It synchronises a component with something outside React — a subscription, a DOM API, a network connection, a timer. Then be decisive about when not to: not to transform data for rendering (compute it during render), not to respond to a user event (do it in the handler), not to reset state on a prop change (use a key). Mention the cleanup function and that Strict Mode double-invokes effects in development precisely to surface missing cleanup. (R07, R09)
“Explain the dependency array.”
It is React's way of asking “have any of the values this effect closes over changed since last time?” Every reactive value used inside must be listed, compared with Object.is. The failure mode is objects and functions, which are new on every render and therefore always “changed” — the fix is to move them inside the effect, hoist them outside the component, wrap them in useCallback/useMemo, or restructure so the effect is not needed. Omitting a dependency to “fix” a loop hides a real bug. (R07)
“useMemo vs useCallback vs memo.”
useMemo caches a value, useCallback caches a function, memo skips a re-render when props are shallow-equal. The interviewer is usually waiting for the judgement half: they are not free, they only pay off when the work is genuinely expensive or when a stable reference is needed to make a memo downstream work, and the React Compiler is making most manual memoisation unnecessary. (R14)
“Why can't you call hooks conditionally?”
Because hooks are stored as a linked list on the fiber, in call order, with no names. React does not know you called useState for name; it knows the first useState of this render maps to the first entry. Skip one and every subsequent hook reads the wrong slot — a state value lands in a ref, a dependency array is compared against the wrong thing. This question separates people who read the rule from people who know why it exists. (W05)
“What changed in React 18 and 19?”
18 introduced concurrent rendering: automatic batching everywhere, transitions, useDeferredValue, streaming SSR with selective hydration. 19 is about the server and about forms: Actions and useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, use(), Server Components and Server Functions, ref as a regular prop, and the React Compiler removing most manual memoisation. Frame it as a direction — React moving work to the server and to the compiler — rather than reciting a changelog. (Part IV)

Handling the questions you cannot answer

Reason out loud; do not bluff

“I haven't used that, but I'd expect it to work like X because Y — is that right?” is a strong answer. It shows the model is real enough to extrapolate from, and interviewers overwhelmingly prefer it to a confident wrong answer, which tells them nothing except that your confidence is uncalibrated. The one thing to avoid is silence: narrate the reasoning, name what you would check, and say what you would look up.

The follow-ups that catch people

They askThey are checking
“Is setState asynchronous?”Whether you say “it's a snapshot, and updates are batched” rather than “yes, it returns a promise”
“So can I await it?”That you know it returns nothing; the new value exists only in the next render
“Why not just mutate state?”Object.is comparison — a mutated object is the same reference, so nothing re-renders
“Why did you wrap that in useCallback?”Whether you can justify it, or cargo-culted it. “No reason here” is a fine answer.
“What if the effect's cleanup is missing?”Leaks, duplicate subscriptions, races — and that Strict Mode exists to expose exactly this
“Does context cause performance problems?”That every consumer re-renders on a value change, and that a non-memoised object value changes every render
“When would you NOT use React?”Judgement. A mostly-static site, a tiny widget, a team that does not need it.

Questions worth asking them

“Are you on the App Router, and how did that migration go?”
Tells you how much legacy there is and how the team handles large changes.
“How do you manage server state — a data library, or Server Components?”
Reveals the architecture and how current the codebase is.
“What's your testing setup for components?”
A team with no component tests is telling you something about the review culture.
“Has the React Compiler come up?”
Shows you follow the ecosystem, and their answer shows whether they do.
The one sentence to have ready

Almost every interview opens with some form of “what is React and why use it?” Have a two-sentence answer that is yours: React is a library for describing UI as a function of state, so that instead of writing every transition between every pair of states by hand — which grows quadratically — you describe what each state looks like and React works out the DOM changes. The cost is a runtime, a build step and a learning curve, which is why a mostly-static page is often better off without it. Saying the cost out loud, unprompted, reads as experience.

I02

Coding rounds: the exercises that actually come up

React coding rounds are remarkably repetitive. There are maybe a dozen exercises in circulation, and they test the same handful of things: can you manage state without mutating it, do you clean up, do you handle loading and error states, and do you notice accessibility. Here they are, with the versions that score well.

The rubric, stated plainly

Interviewers usually score five axes, whether or not they say so: correctness does it work, including the edge cases state design is state minimal, derived where possible, never mutated effects used only for synchronisation, always cleaned up, no unnecessary ones quality naming, decomposition, accessibility, loading and error states communication do you narrate, ask, and check assumptions What loses points fastest: mutating state, an effect with a missing or wrong dependency array, no cleanup on a subscription, index keys on a reorderable list, and forgetting the error case. What gains points fastest: saying "let me handle the error case too", adding a label to an input without being asked, and asking one clarifying question before writing anything.

1 · Debounced search with cancellation

javascript · the single most common exercise
function useDebounced(value, delay = 300) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);      // ← the cleanup IS the debounce
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}

export function Search() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle', results: [] });
  const debounced = useDebounced(query);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!debounced) { setState({ status: 'idle', results: [] }); return; }

    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState(s => ({ ...s, status: 'loading' }));

    search(debounced, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(results => setState({ status: 'success', results }))
      .catch(err => {
        // An aborted request is not an error to show the user.
        if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setState({ status: 'error', error: err });
      });

    return () => controller.abort();   // ← cancels the stale request
  }, [debounced]);

  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor="q">Search</label>
      <input id="q" value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)}
             aria-busy={state.status === 'loading'} />

      {state.status === 'loading' && <Spinner />}
      {state.status === 'error'   && <p role="alert">Search failed.</p>}
      {state.status === 'success' && state.results.length === 0 &&
        <p>No results for “{debounced}”.</p>}

      <ul aria-live="polite">
        {state.results.map(r => <li key={r.id}>{r.title}</li>)}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}
// The three things being scored: the cleanup that makes debouncing
// work, the abort that prevents the race, and the EMPTY state that
// most candidates forget.

2 · A todo list without mutation

javascript
function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return [...state, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), text: action.text, done: false }];
    case 'toggle':
      return state.map(t => t.id === action.id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t);
      //                                         ^ new object, not t.done = !t.done
    case 'remove':
      return state.filter(t => t.id !== action.id);
    case 'clearDone':
      return state.filter(t => !t.done);
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown action: ${action.type}`);
  }
}

export function Todos() {
  const [todos, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, []);
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('all');

  // DERIVED, not state. A `visible` state variable that an effect keeps
  // in sync is the classic mistake this exercise is designed to catch.
  const visible = todos.filter(t =>
    filter === 'all' ? true : filter === 'done' ? t.done : !t.done);
  const remaining = todos.filter(t => !t.done).length;

  function onSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const text = new FormData(e.currentTarget).get('text').trim();
    if (!text) return;
    dispatch({ type: 'add', text });
    e.currentTarget.reset();
  }

  return (
    <>
      <form onSubmit={onSubmit}>
        <label htmlFor="new">New todo</label>
        <input id="new" name="text" />
        <button>Add</button>
      </form>

      <ul>
        {visible.map(t => (
          <li key={t.id}>              {/* stable id, not the index */}
            <label>
              <input type="checkbox" checked={t.done}
                     onChange={() => dispatch({ type: 'toggle', id: t.id })} />
              {t.text}
            </label>
            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'remove', id: t.id })}
                    aria-label={`Delete ${t.text}`}>×</button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <p>{remaining} remaining</p>
    </>
  );
}

3 · An accessible modal

javascript · portal, escape, focus, scroll lock
export function Modal({ open, onClose, title, children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  const previouslyFocused = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!open) return;

    previouslyFocused.current = document.activeElement;
    ref.current?.focus();

    function onKey(e) { if (e.key === 'Escape') onClose(); }
    document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);

    const prevOverflow = document.body.style.overflow;
    document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden';

    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
      document.body.style.overflow = prevOverflow;
      // Returning focus is the detail that signals you have built one
      // of these for real.
      previouslyFocused.current?.focus();
    };
  }, [open, onClose]);

  if (!open) return null;

  return createPortal(
    <div className="overlay" onClick={onClose}>
      <div
        ref={ref} tabIndex={-1}
        role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="modal-title"
        className="modal"
        onClick={e => e.stopPropagation()}   // don't close on inner clicks
      >
        <h2 id="modal-title">{title}</h2>
        {children}
        <button onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
      </div>
    </div>,
    document.body,
  );
}
// Mention what you have NOT done: a full focus trap (tab cycling) —
// and that in production you would use the native <dialog> element or
// a library such as Radix, which handles it correctly.

4 · Fetch with loading, error and retry

javascript · the state machine, not three booleans
function useFetch(url) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle' });
  const [attempt, setAttempt] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState({ status: 'loading' });

    fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(res => {
        // fetch does NOT reject on 404 or 500. Forgetting this check
        // is one of the most common bugs in this exercise.
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return res.json();
      })
      .then(data => { if (!cancelled) setState({ status: 'success', data }); })
      .catch(err => {
        if (!cancelled && err.name !== 'AbortError')
          setState({ status: 'error', error: err });
      });

    return () => { cancelled = true; controller.abort(); };
  }, [url, attempt]);      // bumping `attempt` re-runs the effect

  return { ...state, retry: () => setAttempt(a => a + 1) };
}
// Three booleans (isLoading, isError, data) allow impossible states —
// loading AND error at once. One `status` field cannot. Say this out
// loud; it is the design point of the exercise.
//
// And add: "in production I'd use TanStack Query or a Server
// Component, because caching, deduplication and revalidation are
// where hand-rolled fetching actually falls over."

5 · The bug hunt

javascript · "this component has three bugs — find them"
function Counter({ step }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + step), 1000);
  });                                            // ← 1, 2, 3

  function addItem(item) {
    items.push(item);                            // ← 4
    setItems(items);
  }

  return (
    <>
      <p>{count}</p>
      {items.map((it, i) => <Row key={i} item={it} />)}   {/* ← 5 */}
    </>
  );
}

// 1 · NO DEPENDENCY ARRAY — the effect runs after every render, so a
//     new interval is created every second and they accumulate.
// 2 · NO CLEANUP — nothing clears the interval, including on unmount.
// 3 · STALE CLOSURE — `count` is captured from the render that created
//     the interval, so it computes 0+step forever.
// 4 · MUTATION — items.push mutates the array; setItems receives the
//     SAME reference, Object.is says nothing changed, no re-render.
// 5 · INDEX KEYS — fine for an append-only list, broken the moment
//     anything is inserted, removed or reordered.

// Fixed:
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setCount(c => c + step), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, [step]);

function addItem(item) { setItems(prev => [...prev, item]); }

{items.map(it => <Row key={it.id} item={it} />)}

Others that recur

ExerciseWhat it is testing
Infinite scrollIntersectionObserver in an effect, cleanup, and not re-observing every render
Autocomplete with keyboard navRefs, aria-activedescendant, controlled index state
Multi-step wizardState shape — one step plus one form object, not a state per field
Drag-to-reorderKeys, immutable array reordering, why index keys break here specifically
A custom useLocalStorageLazy initialiser, JSON errors, SSR safety (window is undefined)
Tabs or an accordionComposition, ARIA roles, controlled vs uncontrolled API design
A virtualised listWhether you reach for a library and can explain why hand-rolling is unwise
Render 10,000 rowsThat “memoise it” is the wrong answer and “virtualise it” is the right one
Narrate, and finish the sentence “in production I'd…”

Interviewers score communication as heavily as code. Say what you are about to do before you do it, ask one clarifying question at the start (“should this be controlled, or should it own its state?”), and when you take a shortcut, name it: “I'm hand-rolling this fetch for the exercise; in production I'd use TanStack Query for caching and deduplication.” That single habit turns a working answer into a senior one, because it shows you know the boundary between the exercise and the real system.

Before you say you are finished

Run a four-item checklist out loud. Loading and error states — does the UI show something sensible for both? Cleanup — does every subscription, timer, listener and request get cancelled? Keys — stable ids, not indices, on anything that can reorder? Labels — does every input have one, and does every icon-only button have an aria-label? Candidates who do this catch their own bugs before the interviewer does, which reads very differently from having the bug pointed out.

I03

The Next.js interview

Next.js interviews are harder than React interviews for a specific reason: the framework changed shape twice in three years, so the interviewer and the candidate are often describing different products. Establishing which version and which router you are talking about is not pedantry — it is the first point you score.

Establish the version first

Ask, early and once

“Are you on the App Router or Pages Router, and roughly which version?” It takes four seconds and it changes almost every subsequent answer: whether data fetching is getServerSideProps or async components, whether fetch caches by default (it did in 14, it does not in 15), whether params is a promise, whether Server Components exist at all. Candidates who ask this read as people who have actually maintained a Next.js app through an upgrade. Candidates who confidently explain getStaticProps to an App Router team read as people who learned from a tutorial in 2022.

The questions that carry the most weight

“React vs Next.js — what's the difference?”
Reframe it, because the question as posed is a category error. React is a UI library; Next.js is a framework that includes React and adds the things React deliberately leaves out — routing, server rendering, bundling, data fetching conventions, an image optimiser, a deployment target. So it is not “which one”, it is “React alone plus assembled tooling, or React inside an opinionated framework”. Then give the actual decision criteria: SEO and first-paint matter → Next.js; an authenticated dashboard with no SEO value → plain React and Vite is simpler and has less to learn. (X01)
“What are Server Components, and what can't they do?”
Components that run only on the server, whose output is serialised into the RSC payload — they never ship JavaScript to the browser. They can await directly, reach the database, and read secrets. They cannot use state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs, or any hook that implies interactivity, and every prop passed from a server to a client component must be serialisable. Then the architectural point: the goal is to push 'use client' as far down the tree as possible, because the boundary is a subtree — everything below it is client. (N04, X03)
“Explain Next.js caching.”
Four independent layers, one sentence each: request memoization (React, dedupes identical fetches within one render), the Data Cache (persists across requests, opt-in since 15), the Full Route Cache (rendered static routes), and the client Router Cache (visited payloads, so Back is instant). Then the two things that show real use: the defaults inverted in version 15, so most articles describe the opposite behaviour, and “I revalidated and it didn't update” is usually the client Router Cache, which a server-side revalidateTag does not clear until the next navigation. (X04)
“SSG vs SSR vs ISR — when do you use each?”
Static when the content is the same for everyone and changes on deploy. ISR when it is the same for everyone but changes independently of deploys — and specify on-demand revalidation via webhook rather than a timer, because a timer regenerates constantly and is still stale right after a real edit. Dynamic when the output depends on the request: cookies, headers, search params. Then add that the choice is becoming per-region rather than per-page with partial prerendering, where a cached shell streams instantly and only the request-dependent holes render per request. (X05)
“How do Server Actions work, and how do you secure them?”
The bundler splits the function out, gives it an id, and replaces the client-side reference with a stub that POSTs to it. Therefore — and lead with this — it is a public HTTP endpoint. Anyone who can read your bundle can extract the id and POST arbitrary data. So every action authenticates, validates with a schema, authorises the specific resource, and rate-limits if expensive; and “the button is hidden”, “it's only imported by the admin page” and “the id was bound” are none of those. Finish with the module trap: 'use server' applies to every export in the file. (N05, X07)
“Where does authentication go?”
In layers, with middleware as the outermost and weakest: a cheap cookie and signature check to redirect obvious anonymous traffic, because middleware runs on every request and cannot reach the database. The authoritative session check lives in the page, layout or action via a cache()-wrapped helper; authorisation is per-resource at the data layer, returning 404 rather than 403. Cite CVE-2025-29927 — a header-spoofing bug that let attackers skip middleware entirely — as the reason this layering is not theoretical. (X09)
“What does 'use client' actually do?”
It marks a boundary, not a file. The module and everything it imports go into the client bundle, and every component rendered beneath it is a client component — which is why a 'use client' at the top of a page defeats the point of RSC entirely. It does not mean “this does not render on the server”: client components still server-render for the initial HTML, then hydrate. That second half is the part most candidates get wrong. (N04, X03)
“Why would you not use Next.js?”
A genuinely good answer here is disproportionately valuable. An internal dashboard behind a login gets nothing from SSR or SEO and pays the full complexity cost of two runtimes and a caching model. A mostly-static site is better served by Astro. A team with no Node hosting story faces real operational work — shared ISR cache, image optimiser, a runtime — that a static SPA on a CDN does not have. And the lock-in is real: some features land on Vercel first and are awkward elsewhere. (X01, X12)

The mixed-up pairs

ConfusedThe distinction
next/router vs next/navigationPages Router vs App Router. Importing the wrong one throws at runtime with an unhelpful message.
redirect() vs router.push()Server (throws, must be outside try/catch) vs client (a transition).
revalidatePath vs router.refresh()Invalidates the server cache for everyone vs refetches this user's current route.
cache() vs unstable_cache()Per-request deduplication vs a persistent cross-request cache.
Route Handler vs Server FunctionStable URL for external callers vs RPC for your own UI.
loading.tsx vs <Suspense>Whole-segment, automatic vs placed exactly where you want it.
layout.tsx vs template.tsxPersists across navigation vs remounts every time.
Static export vs static renderingoutput: 'export' drops SSR, ISR, handlers and middleware entirely.

System-design rounds

"Design the front end for an e-commerce site in Next.js." Answer in the four decisions they are listening for: 1 · RENDERING, per route / static, ISR 1h /products static + generateStaticParams, tagged /products/[slug] static; stock in a Suspense boundary (or PPR) /search dynamic — it reads searchParams /cart, /account dynamic, uncached, never shared /checkout dynamic; no caching anywhere near it 2 · DATA & INVALIDATION fetch tagged `product:{id}` and `products` CMS/PIM webhook → revalidateTag on publish cart in a cookie or a per-user record; never in a shared cache 3 · THE CLIENT BOUNDARY server: product data, descriptions, reviews, navigation client: add-to-cart button, quantity picker, search input, the cart drawer measure First Load JS per route and fail CI on a regression 4 · OPERATIONS shared ISR cache if self-hosting more than one instance LCP: hero image with priority + sizes INP: virtualise long lists, defer the search filter Sentry via instrumentation.ts; Web Vitals from the field Then say what you would measure, and what would make you change your mind. That sentence is worth more than any individual choice.

The trap questions

“Is Next.js faster than React?”
Not a meaningful comparison — Next.js is React. It can produce faster first paints, because HTML arrives rendered rather than after a bundle downloads and hydrates, and because RSC keeps data-layer code out of the bundle. Runtime interaction speed is identical; it is the same React.
“Should everything be a Server Component?”
Everything that can be, which is the default — but the boundary is placed where interactivity begins, and pushing it too high (a 'use client' on the page) or too low (a client leaf that needs three server round trips for data it could have received as a prop) are both mistakes. It is a placement decision, not a maximisation.
“Does the App Router replace Redux?”
It replaces most uses of it. Server state — the thing global stores were usually caching — moves to the server, and URL state belongs in the URL. What is left is genuine shared client state: a theme, a cart drawer's open/closed, an editor's undo stack. That is small enough for context or Zustand, and rarely needs Redux.
“How do you handle authentication with Server Components?”
Sessions are cookies; Server Components can read cookies but cannot set them, so sign-in must happen in a Server Function, Route Handler or middleware. Wrap the session lookup in cache() so twenty components cost one query, and check it in every protected page rather than relying on a layout — a layout does not re-render on navigation and is not a gate.
Do not claim App Router experience you do not have

The follow-ups are specific and unbluffable: “how did you handle the caching change in 15?”, “where did you put your auth check?”, “what broke when you migrated?”. An honest “I've built with the Pages Router professionally and the App Router on side projects — here's what I found different” is a good answer and costs you almost nothing. An invented migration story collapses on the second question, and the interviewer will remember the collapse rather than anything else you said.

The framing that lands

When asked why a team should adopt Next.js, do not list features. Say what it removes: you stop assembling a router, an SSR pipeline, a bundler config, a data-fetching convention and an image pipeline, and you stop maintaining the seams between them. Then say what it costs — two runtimes to reason about, a caching model with real depth, slower builds, and genuine lock-in to a hosting story that is easiest on one vendor. Naming the cost unprompted is what makes the recommendation credible.

I04

Common mistakes and the review checklist

Everything in this chapter has been shipped to production by someone competent. These are not beginner errors — they are the things that look correct, pass review, and then produce a bug report three weeks later that nobody can reproduce.

State

MistakeSymptomFix
Mutating state directlyNothing re-rendersAlways produce a new object or array (R03)
Reading state right after setting it“It's one behind”State is a snapshot; use the value you computed, or the updater form (R01)
Three booleans for one statusImpossible states — loading and errorOne status field, or a reducer (R12)
Props copied into stateStale after the prop changesUse the prop; if it must reset, use a key (R09)
State lifted higher than neededWhole page re-renders on every keystrokePush it down to the component that uses it
Deeply nested state objectsSpread pyramids, accidental mutationFlatten, normalise by id, or use Immer

Effects

javascript · the four that cause real production bugs
// 1 · MISSING CLEANUP — the leak that grows with navigation.
useEffect(() => {
  const sub = socket.subscribe(onMessage);
  return () => sub.unsubscribe();       // ← without this, every mount
}, []);                                  //   adds another listener

// 2 · THE RACE — an older response overwrites a newer one.
useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;
  fetchUser(id).then(u => { if (!cancelled) setUser(u); });
  return () => { cancelled = true; };
}, [id]);
// Without the flag: click A, click B, A's slow response lands last,
// and the page shows B's URL with A's data. Intermittent, unreproducible
// locally, and reported as "sometimes it shows the wrong user".

// 3 · THE OBJECT DEPENDENCY — an infinite loop.
const options = { limit: 10 };                    // new every render
useEffect(() => { load(options); }, [options]);   // therefore runs
                                                  // every render
// Fix: move it inside, hoist it outside the component, or depend on
// the primitive: }, [options.limit]);

// 4 · AN EFFECT FOR AN EVENT — runs on mount and on unrelated renders.
useEffect(() => { if (submitted) showToast(); }, [submitted]);
// It belongs in the handler:
function onSubmit() { save(); showToast(); }

// And the meta-rule: if the effect has no cleanup and does not talk to
// anything outside React, it probably should not exist (R09).

Rendering and keys

javascript
// INDEX KEYS on a reorderable list. React matches key 0 to key 0, so
// after a sort or a delete the DOM node — and its state — belongs to a
// different item. Symptom: a checkbox ticks the wrong row.
{items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />)}       // ✗
{items.map(item   => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)}    // ✓

// A COMPONENT DEFINED INSIDE ANOTHER COMPONENT. It is a new function
// type on every render, so reconciliation unmounts and remounts the
// whole subtree — all state lost, all effects re-run, every render.
function Parent() {
  function Child() { … }        // ✗ move it out of the component
  return <Child />;
}

// && WITH A NUMBER. 0 is falsy but renderable, so this prints "0".
{items.length && <List />}              // ✗ renders 0
{items.length > 0 && <List />}          // ✓

// CONDITIONAL HOOKS. The hook list is positional (W05).
if (user) { const [x, setX] = useState(); }    // ✗ crashes on the
                                               //   render where the
                                               //   condition flips

Next.js

MistakeWhy it bites
'use client' at the top of a pageThe entire subtree ships to the browser; RSC gains nothing (X03)
A Server Component fetching from your own Route HandlerAn extra network hop and serialisation to call a local function (X04)
A secret in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variableInlined into the client bundle at build time — shipped to every visitor (X12)
Auth only in middlewareNot a security boundary; CVE-2025-29927 bypassed it entirely (X09)
A non-action export in a 'use server' fileEvery export becomes a public endpoint (X07)
redirect() inside try/catchIt throws by design; the catch swallows it and the redirect never happens
One uncached fetch in a shared layoutEvery route beneath it becomes dynamic (X05)
Module-scope mutable state on the serverShared across all users of that instance — a real data-leak vector
useSearchParams with no Suspense boundaryBuild failure, or the whole route silently opts out of prerendering (X08)
Returning a “not found” component instead of notFound()A 200 status for a missing page — an SEO bug (X08)
No priority on the LCP imageThe hero is lazy-loaded by default; LCP suffers by hundreds of ms (X10)

Performance

javascript
// MEMOISING EVERYTHING. Each useMemo/useCallback has a cost: the
// closure, the dependency array, the comparison. Applied to a cheap
// computation it is a net loss, and it hides where the real problem is.
// Profile first; and note the React Compiler is making most of this
// unnecessary (R14).

// A CONTEXT VALUE THAT CHANGES EVERY RENDER — every consumer
// re-renders, every time, regardless of what they use.
<Ctx.Provider value={{ user, signOut }}>              // ✗ new object
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, signOut }), [user, signOut]);  // ✓

// ONE CONTEXT FOR EVERYTHING. Split by change frequency: a theme that
// changes twice a year does not belong with a cursor position.

// MEMO ON A COMPONENT WITH CHILDREN. `children` is a new element
// object every render, so the memo never hits.
const Card = memo(function Card({ children }) { … });   // ✗ useless

// TRYING TO MEMOISE A 10,000-ROW LIST. No amount of memo fixes
// 10,000 DOM nodes — virtualise (X11).

// IMPORTING THE WORLD.
import { debounce } from 'lodash';       // ✗ pulls the library
import debounce from 'lodash/debounce';  // ✓ 2 kB

Accessibility

MistakeFix
<div onClick> as a buttonUse <button> — you get focus, Enter/Space, and the right role for free
An input with no label<label htmlFor>, or aria-label when there is genuinely no visible text
Icon-only buttonsaria-label describing the action, not the icon
A modal that does not trap or restore focusFocus it on open, restore on close, or use <dialog>/Radix
Errors shown only in colourrole="alert", aria-invalid, and text
Async content with no announcementaria-live="polite" on the region that updates
Removing focus outlinesStyle :focus-visible instead of deleting it
Skipped heading levelsOne h1, then descend in order

The review checklist

STATE □ nothing mutated — new objects and arrays throughout □ nothing stored that can be derived □ no impossible states (one status, not three booleans) □ state lives at the lowest level that needs it EFFECTS □ every effect has a reason to exist (R09) □ every subscription, timer and listener is cleaned up □ every fetch is cancellable or guarded against races □ the dependency array is complete, and the lint rule is on RENDERING □ keys are stable ids, not indices, on reorderable lists □ no component defined inside another component □ no `count && <jsx>` with a number on the left □ long lists are virtualised SERVER / CLIENT (Next.js) □ 'use client' is as low in the tree as possible □ no secret in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable □ every action: authenticate, validate, authorise, rate limit □ no module-scope mutable state on the server □ the right cache tag is revalidated after every mutation UX □ loading, empty and error states all exist □ forms disable on submit and show field-level errors □ every route has loading.tsx and error.tsx □ destructive actions confirm, or are undoable A11Y □ real buttons and links, labelled inputs □ keyboard reachable, visible focus □ errors announced, not only coloured PERFORMANCE □ First Load JS per route checked against the last build □ LCP image has priority and sizes □ no sequential awaits that could be Promise.all
Automate the mechanical half

Most of the first three sections are enforceable. Turn on eslint-plugin-react-hooks (exhaustive-deps as an error, not a warning) and eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y; add @next/eslint-plugin-next for the framework-specific rules; run tsc --noEmit in CI; and record First Load JS per route so a regression fails the build. That leaves human review for the things a linter genuinely cannot see — whether the state shape is right, whether the effect should exist at all, and whether the client boundary is in a sensible place.

Interview follow-up

“What do you look for when reviewing React code?” Answer with the layers rather than a list of nitpicks: first, state shape — is anything stored that could be derived, and is anything being mutated; second, effects — does each one have a reason to exist, and is everything cleaned up; third, the client boundary, because in a Next.js app that is where bundle size and security both live; then the states everyone forgets (loading, empty, error) and accessibility. Close by saying which of those you have automated, since a reviewer arguing about dependency arrays by hand is a reviewer whose lint config is not set up.

I05

Where to go next

You now have the model: UI as a function of state, rendering as a two-phase process, hooks as positional slots on a fiber, and a server that can render components. What remains is the ecosystem around that model, the things this book deliberately did not cover, and a way to keep up as it moves.

What you know now

Part I why React exists, and the JavaScript it assumes — closures, immutability, async, promises, errors, debounce and rate limiting Part II the whole practical surface: state, effects, refs, context, reducers, custom hooks, memoisation, Suspense, error boundaries, state management Part III what happens underneath — elements, reconciliation, fiber, the render/commit split, hooks as a linked list, lanes, hydration Part IV React 19 — Actions, use(), Server Components, Server Functions, the compiler Part V Next.js — the App Router, caching, rendering strategies, route handlers, middleware, performance, deployment Part VI TypeScript — why it, the type system, generics, narrowing, the utility types, React and Next.js typing, tsconfig, and the TS interview Part VII twelve things built end to end — the three hooks, infinite scroll, tables, wizards, drag-and-drop, trees, dialogs, OTP, tabs, carousels Part VIII the interview, the mistakes, the checklist That is enough to build and ship a production application, and enough to debug one when it misbehaves — which is the harder half.

The libraries worth knowing

NeedReach forNote
Server state in a client appTanStack QueryCaching, deduplication, revalidation, retries. Still the right answer for any client-fetching app — and in RSC apps, for the parts that genuinely fetch on the client.
FormsReact Hook Form + ZodUncontrolled inputs, so typing does not re-render the tree; Zod gives one schema for client and server.
Client stateZustand or JotaiFar less ceremony than Redux. Use only for genuine shared client state — not server data, not URL state.
Accessible primitivesRadix, React AriaUnstyled, correct behaviour. Do not hand-roll a combobox or a modal.
StylingTailwind, or CSS ModulesRuntime CSS-in-JS conflicts with RSC; both of these do not.
TestingVitest + Testing Library, PlaywrightTest behaviour through the DOM, not implementation details.
Routing without a frameworkTanStack Router, React RouterType-safe routing if you are on Vite rather than Next.js.
AnimationMotion (formerly Framer Motion)Layout animations and gestures without fighting React's render cycle.
Tables and virtualisationTanStack Table, TanStack VirtualHeadless. The only real answer for large datasets.
Add dependencies deliberately

Every library is a bundle cost, an upgrade cost and a hiring cost — someone must learn it. The ones above earn their place because the problem they solve is genuinely hard to get right (caching semantics, focus management, virtualisation) rather than merely tedious. A date formatter, a class-name joiner, a deep-equality check: write the twelve lines. And check whether the platform has it already — Intl, URLSearchParams, structuredClone, AbortController, <dialog> and IntersectionObserver have quietly replaced a lot of dependencies.

What this book did not cover

Testing, in depth
Testing Library's philosophy — query by role and label, never by class or test id where a real query exists — plus mocking network with MSW, and the fact that Server Components are best tested end-to-end because there is no client-side render to assert against.
TypeScript with React, in depth
Generic components, discriminated unions for props, ComponentProps<typeof X>, polymorphic as props, and typing custom hooks. Worth a book of its own; start with the React TypeScript Cheatsheet.
React Native
Same React, different renderer — the reconciler you learned in Part III is identical; only the host components and the commit target change. The New Architecture (Fabric, TurboModules, JSI) is worth understanding before starting.
Animation and gesture systems
The View Transitions API and React's <ViewTransition> are landing; spring physics, shared-element transitions and interruptible gestures are a genuine specialism.
Internationalisation
Message extraction, plural rules, RTL layout, locale-aware formatting, and routing by locale in Next.js.
Micro-frontends and Module Federation
Mostly an organisational solution to an organisational problem. Understand the trade-off before adopting it.

Where React is going

Three directions, all visible in the last three releases: 1 · MORE WORK ON THE SERVER Server Components and Server Functions move data access, heavy dependencies and mutation logic out of the bundle. The client bundle shrinks toward "only what is interactive". 2 · LESS MANUAL OPTIMISATION The React Compiler memoises automatically, which removes most useMemo/useCallback from application code. The skill shifts from applying memoisation to understanding when the compiler cannot help — which requires exactly the model in Part III. 3 · MORE OF THE PLATFORM, LESS OF THE LIBRARY <Activity> for pre-rendering hidden UI, View Transitions, native form integration, document metadata hoisting. React is increasingly a thin coordinator over web platform features rather than a replacement for them. What does NOT change: state → render → reconcile → commit, the snapshot semantics of a render, and the rules of hooks. Every version since 16.8 has preserved those, and everything new is built on top of them. That is why Parts I–III are the durable part of this book and Parts IV–V are the part to re-check.

How to keep up without drowning

Primary sources only, for facts
react.dev and the Next.js docs, plus the release notes and the RFC repository. The ecosystem's blog posts age badly and version-specific advice — especially about caching — is frequently wrong for the version you are running.
Read the changelog on upgrade, not continuously
You do not need to track every canary. When you upgrade, read the release notes for every version you skipped; that is a focused hour rather than a permanent background task.
Build the thing you are unsure about
Reading about Server Components produces an opinion. Building a small app with them produces a model. Half a day of building beats a week of articles.
Read React's source when something surprises you
ReactFiberHooks.js, ReactFiberBeginWork.js and ReactChildFiber.js are readable if you know what you are looking for — and after Part III you do.
Watch the boundary between versions
The single biggest source of confusion in this ecosystem is advice written for a different major version. Whenever something does not behave as documented, check which version the documentation was for before assuming you are wrong.

A last word on judgement

The best React code is not the cleverest. It is the code where someone else can open a component and immediately see what state it holds, what it renders, and what it talks to. Most of the skill in this book is knowing what NOT to reach for: not an effect, not a memo, not a context, not a state variable for something you can derive, not a library for twelve lines. React gives you one very good idea — UI as a function of state — and almost every problem people have with it comes from introducing a second source of truth alongside it. Keep one source of truth. Derive everything else.
Interview follow-up

“How do you stay current with React?” The answer that lands is not a list of newsletters. Say that you read the primary sources — react.dev, the release notes, the RFCs — and that you read the full changelog when you upgrade rather than tracking canaries continuously, because version-mismatched advice is the largest source of bad information in this ecosystem. Then give a concrete example: something that changed recently, what you had to unlearn, and how you found out. A specific instance of having been wrong and corrected it is worth more than any list of sources.

Q

563 questions with written answers, across React fundamentals, hooks, the runtime, React 19, patterns, state management, the JavaScript underneath — promises, errors, debounce and rate limiting — Next.js, TypeScript, and the twelve build-it chapters. Everything is searchable and every answer is deep-linkable.

How to use it

These are written as understanding questions rather than trivia: most of them ask why something behaves the way it does, because that is what a real interview is probing. Search for the area you are weakest on, open ten, and answer each aloud before expanding it — the gap between recognising an answer and being able to say it is the entire difference on the day.
